_comment: Per-work orientation descriptions shown in Browse Corpus and the Reader. Keyed by language, then by base work id (the .tess filename without language directory, extension, or .part suffix). Two or three plain sentences describing the TEXT itself: its contents, structure, and interest, with author and date kept brief. Every text import should add its entry here.

la.justin.epitome: An abridgement of the lost forty-four book universal history of Pompeius Trogus, made by Justin, probably in the second or third century AD. It narrates the empires of the Near East, Greece, and Macedon down to the rise of Rome, with special fullness on Alexander and his successors, and it is the main surviving narrative for much of Hellenistic history.
la.hyginus.fabulae: A handbook of roughly three hundred short mythological summaries compiled under the name of Hyginus, perhaps in the second century AD. Genealogies of gods and heroes, one-paragraph retellings of the great myth cycles, and catalogue chapters preserve the plots of many Greek myths and lost tragedies found nowhere else.
la.hyginus.astronomica: A handbook of the constellations attributed to the same Hyginus as the Fabulae. For each figure in the sky it tells the myth of how it was placed there, then describes its stars, drawing on the Greek catasterism tradition.
la.isidore.etymologiae: A twenty-book encyclopedia that approaches every subject through the origins of its words, covering grammar, rhetoric, law, medicine, the church, animals, geography, ships, buildings, food, and games. Compiled by Isidore, bishop of Seville (died 636), it preserves fragments of many lost ancient authors and became the most consulted reference work of the Middle Ages.
la.petrarch.africa: A Latin epic in nine books on Scipio Africanus and Rome's defeat of Hannibal in the Second Punic War, modeled on Virgil and drawing its history from Livy. Its set pieces include Scipio's dream, the love and death of Sophonisba, and Hannibal and Scipio meeting before Zama. Petrarch began it in 1338 and left it unfinished.
la.pomponius_mela.de_chorographia: The earliest surviving geography in Latin, written around AD 43. In three brisk books it tours the coasts of the known world, from the Strait of Gibraltar around the Mediterranean and back along the outer Ocean, mixing places and peoples with marvels.
la.varro.de_lingua_latina: A treatise on the Latin language by Varro (116 to 27 BC), of which books five through ten survive of twenty-five: three on where words come from and three on how they change form. It explains hundreds of Latin words for places, times, things, and actions, and it is a major source for archaic Latin and for Roman religious and legal antiquities.
la.varro.res_rusticae: A dialogue on farming in three books: field crops and the layout of the estate, cattle and sheep, and the profitable luxury trades of villa life such as aviaries, apiaries, and fishponds. Varro wrote it in 37 BC at the age of eighty, and with Cato's treatise it is our chief Roman work on agriculture.
la.velleius_paterculus.historiae_romanae: A compendium of Roman history in two books, running from the origins to AD 30 and moving quickly toward the writer's own times. It offers capsule sketches of Latin literary history found nowhere else and an admiring eyewitness portrait of Tiberius, under whom Velleius served as an officer.
la.frontinus.strategemata: A casebook of military stratagems arranged by type, on concealing plans, ambushes, sieges, discipline, and more, each chapter giving short historical examples of how commanders handled a recurring problem of war. Compiled by Frontinus, himself a senator and general, in the late first century AD.
la.frontinus.de_aquis: A treatise on the nine aqueducts of Rome: the history of each, its length and capacity, the laws governing the water supply, and the frauds uncovered when Frontinus became curator of the aqueducts in AD 97. A unique inside view of the administration of a great Roman public work.
la.sidonius.carmina: Twenty-four poems in the elaborate late antique manner: verse panegyrics of the emperors Avitus, Majorian, and Anthemius, and occasional pieces for friends on villas, baths, weddings, and books. Written by Sidonius Apollinaris in fifth-century Gaul before he became bishop of Clermont.
la.sidonius.epistulae: Nine books of literary letters modeled on Pliny, describing villas, dinner parties, libraries, church elections, and the Visigothic court while Roman rule in Gaul dissolved. They are the fullest picture we have of aristocratic life in the last generation of the western empire.
la.fronto.epistulae: The correspondence of the orator Fronto with Marcus Aurelius, his pupil and later emperor, together with letters to Lucius Verus, Antoninus Pius, and friends. The letters trade affection, criticism of each other's prose, and news of illness and family, and they were recovered from a palimpsest in 1815.
la.nemesianus.eclogae: Four pastoral poems in the line of Virgil and Calpurnius Siculus: shepherds mourn the dead poet Meliboeus, compete in song, and sing of love and of Pan and Bacchus. Written by Nemesianus of Carthage in the later third century AD.
la.nemesianus.cynegetica: A didactic poem on hunting: the breeding, rearing, and ailments of hounds, the choice of horses, and the huntsman's nets and gear, breaking off after 325 lines. Written by Nemesianus about AD 283.
la.nemesianus_pseudo.de_aucupio: Two short verse fragments on bird catching, one on taking partridge with an owl as decoy. Transmitted under the name of Nemesianus, though the attribution is doubted.
la.symmachus.epistulae: The collected letters of Symmachus, the leading pagan senator of late fourth-century Rome, published in ten books on the model of Pliny. Most are short notes of recommendation, courtesy, and senatorial business, and together they map the friendship networks of the late Roman aristocracy. Symmachus is best remembered for his plea to restore the Altar of Victory to the senate house.
la.abelard.historia_calamitatum: A long autobiographical letter, written about 1132, in which Abelard recounts his misfortunes: his rise as the most famous teacher of philosophy in Paris, the affair with Heloise and his castration, the condemnation of his book at Soissons, and his persecutions as monk and abbot. It frames the correspondence with Heloise that follows.
la.abelard.epistolae: The letters exchanged between Abelard and Heloise after the Historia calamitatum: her two letters of passionate reproach, his replies of consolation and counsel, and the letters of direction for the religious life of her convent of the Paraclete. Among the most famous correspondence of the Middle Ages.
la.gregorius_magnus.dialogi: Four books of dialogues on the miracles of the holy men of sixth-century Italy, told to the deacon Peter. The second book is a complete life of St. Benedict and the chief source for his biography, and the fourth treats the fate of the soul after death. Written by Pope Gregory the Great around 593.
la.gregorius_magnus.regula_pastoralis: A handbook on the office of bishop in four parts: who should undertake pastoral rule, the life the ruler ought to lead, how to adapt teaching to thirty-six contrasting pairs of characters, and the ruler's return to self-examination. Written by Gregory the Great soon after he became pope in 590, it shaped the medieval ideal of church leadership.
la.lactantius_placidus.in_statii_thebaida_c: An ancient line-by-line commentary on Statius's Thebaid, quoting the poem phrase by phrase and explaining its mythology, geography, and diction. Compiled perhaps in the fifth or sixth century AD under the name of Lactantius Placidus, it preserves a great deal of mythographic learning that would otherwise be lost.
la.aquinas.summa_theologiae_1: The First Part of Thomas Aquinas's Summa Theologiae, written around 1265 to 1268: 119 questions on God, creation, the angels, and human nature, each divided into articles that argue objections, an answer, and replies. The famous five ways of proving God's existence stand near the opening, and the whole is woven from quotations of Scripture, Aristotle, Augustine, and Dionysius.
la.aquinas.hymni: The five eucharistic hymns composed for the feast of Corpus Christi in 1264 and attributed to Thomas Aquinas: Pange lingua, Lauda Sion, Sacris solemniis, Verbum supernum, and Adoro te devote. Tantum ergo, O salutaris hostia, and Panis angelicus are stanzas of these hymns, still sung today, and the openings deliberately echo the older hymns of Venantius Fortunatus.
la.erasmus.moriae_encomium: A mock oration in which Folly praises herself as indispensable to every human pursuit, moving from playful teasing of lovers and scholars to hard satire of monks, princes, and theologians. Erasmus wrote it in 1509 at Thomas More's house, punning on his friend's name, and the Latin is dense with allusions to Lucian, Horace, and the classical proverbs of his own Adagia. The text carries the standard 68 sections plus the prefatory letter to More.
la.erasmus.colloquia: Eighteen of the most famous of Erasmus's Colloquia familiaria, the short Latin dialogues published between 1518 and 1533: a shipwreck, a pilgrimage sent up as tourism, an abbot bested by a learned woman, Charon ferrying the war dead, an alchemist's con, and more. Written to teach conversational Latin, they became some of the sharpest social satire of the sixteenth century, banned and bestselling at once.
la.alan_de_insulis.anticlaudianus: Alan of Lille's philosophical epic, written around 1182 to 1183 in nine books with a prologue and epilogue. Nature convenes the Virtues to fashion a new perfect man, Prudence journeys through the heavens to fetch him a soul from God, and the finished man is armed for a climactic battle against Vice. Its title mocks Claudian's invective poem against Rufinus by proposing an opposite, and it strongly shaped later medieval allegory, including Chaucer and the Roman de la Rose.
la.alan_de_insulis.de_planctu_naturae: Alan of Lille's De Planctu Naturae, a dialogue in alternating prose and verse written around 1160 to 1170. Nature appears to the narrator lamenting that humanity alone among creatures breaks her laws, above all through unnatural vice, and the poem closes with Genius pronouncing excommunication on the offenders. A major source for later personification allegory, again including the Roman de la Rose.
la.bernard_silvestris.cosmographia: Bernard Silvestris's Cosmographia, also called De mundi universitate, a philosophical poem in alternating prose and verse written around 1147 and dedicated to Thierry of Chartres. In two books, Megacosmus and Microcosmus, Nature and divine Providence shape the universe out of primal matter and then fashion humanity as its image, drawing on Plato's Timaeus by way of Chalcidius. A founding text of twelfth century cosmological allegory and the Chartrian school.
la.cassiodorus.institutiones: Cassiodorus's Institutiones divinarum et saecularium litterarum, a two book guide to study written around 560 for the monks of his foundation at Vivarium. Book one surveys the books of Scripture and the church fathers with practical advice on copying and correcting manuscripts, and book two summarizes the seven liberal arts, from grammar through music. Cassiodorus, a former Roman praetorian prefect turned monastic founder who died around 580, helped set the curriculum that carried classical learning into the Middle Ages.
la.cassiodorus.variae: Cassiodorus's Variae, twelve books of official letters and government orders that he drafted, in his own name and in the names of Ostrogothic kings, across decades as a Roman administrator in Italy. They range from tax disputes and building repairs to appointments and diplomatic correspondence, composed in an elaborate rhetorical style, and together form the fullest surviving record of Roman civil administration under Ostrogothic rule. Cassiodorus assembled the collection around 537 as a showcase of his own official prose.
la.venantius_fortunatus.carmina: Venantius Fortunatus's Carmina, eleven books of occasional Latin poetry written after he settled in Merovingian Gaul around 566. The collection holds panegyrics to Frankish kings and bishops, personal poems to his patron Radegund and her convent at Poitiers, epitaphs, and hymns, including Vexilla regis and Pange lingua gloriosi, sung in church liturgy ever since. Fortunatus, who lived from about 530 to shortly after 600, is often called the last poet of late antiquity and the first of the Middle Ages.
la.venantius_fortunatus.vita_martini: Venantius Fortunatus's Vita Sancti Martini, a four book hexameter epic on the life and miracles of Martin of Tours, closely based on the prose Life and Dialogues of Sulpicius Severus. Fortunatus casts a saint's biography in the meter and diction of Virgilian epic and dedicates the poem to Gregory of Tours. It shows classical epic form carried forward to celebrate a Christian holy man.
la.walter_de_chatillon.alexandreis: Walter of Chatillon's Alexandreis, a ten book Latin epic on the life of Alexander the Great completed around 1180, closely following the ancient historian Quintus Curtius Rufus. Written in polished classicizing hexameters full of allusions to Virgil, Lucan, and Statius, it became a standard schoolroom text and one of the most admired Latin poems of the Middle Ages. Walter, who died around 1201 or 1202, taught at Chatillon-sur-Marne and Reims.
la.nigel_wireker.speculum_stultorum: Nigel Wireker's Speculum Stultorum, a twelfth-century Latin beast-fable satire in elegiac verse. Its hero is Burnellus, a donkey dissatisfied with the length of his tail, whose quest to grow a longer one becomes a vehicle for mocking the ambitions and hypocrisies of monks, clerics, and scholars of Wireker's day, and drifts into extended satire of university life and the corruption of the church courts. Wireker, a monk of Christ Church, Canterbury, died around 1198 to 1200.
la.johannes_hanville.architrenius: Johannes de Hauvilla's Architrenius, a Latin allegorical poem in hexameter verse written around 1184. It follows its grieving hero, whose name means arch-weeper, through personified vices and follies of the age, including the court of Venus, the poverty of student life in Paris, and the corruptions of ambition and greed, before a final meeting with the goddess Nature, who delivers a long philosophical discourse and gives him a wife named Moderation. Curtius cites the poem as an early source for the world-upside-down and locus amoenus topoi that recur across medieval and Renaissance literature.
la.carmina_burana.carmina_burana: A selection from the Carmina Burana, the large thirteenth-century manuscript collection of Latin poems by wandering scholars and clergy, copied at the Bavarian abbey of Benediktbeuern around 1230. This import covers the collection's serious and moral-satirical poems, including the Fortune-wheel lyrics, satires on clerical corruption, and the Archpoet's tavern confession, drawn from J. A. Schmeller's 1847 edition, the first to print the manuscript in full. The manuscript's love, drinking, and gambling songs are not included in this pass.
la.tiberianus.carmina: Four short poems and a few fragments attributed to Tiberianus, a fourth-century Roman senator who served as praetorian prefect of Gaul under Constantine. The best known is a twenty-line trochaic description of a locus amoenus, a shaded stream valley full of birdsong and flowers, cited by Curtius as an early landscape set piece that later poets kept imitating.
la.pentadius.carmina: Six short poems by Pentadius, a minor Latin poet of the third or fourth century known only from Riese's Anthologia Latina. The best known, De adventu veris, describes the arrival of spring through repeated end-of-line echoes, and it became a model for later medieval spring poems in the locus amoenus tradition.
la.prudentius.cathemerinon: The Liber Cathemerinon, twelve hymns by the Christian Latin poet Prudentius (c. 348 to after 405) for set hours of the day and the church calendar, including morning, evening, before meals, and hymns for the dead and for Christmas and Epiphany. Hymn 3, sung before sleep, describes Paradise as a garden watered by four rivers, a passage Curtius cites as a landmark instance of the locus amoenus topos carried into Christian poetry.
la.matthew_of_vendome.ars_versificatoria: A late twelfth-century Latin handbook on composing verse by Matthew of Vendome, mixing prose instruction with worked verse examples on describing people, places, and things, and on constructing arguments and transitions. Its long example description of an ideal landscape, with birdsong, a murmuring brook, and a warm breeze, became a widely copied model for the locus amoenus in medieval Latin poetry.
la.geoffrey_of_vinsauf.poetria_nova: Geoffrey of Vinsauf's Poetria Nova, a verse treatise on rhetoric and poetic composition written around 1208 to 1213 and dedicated to Pope Innocent III. Organized around the stages of invention, arrangement, and style, it was one of the most widely used medieval arts of poetry and quotes or imitates a wide range of classical and medieval verse to illustrate its rules.
la.geoffrey_of_vinsauf.documentum: Geoffrey of Vinsauf's Documentum de modo et arte dictandi et versificandi, a prose companion to his Poetria Nova covering the same ground on letter writing and verse composition in more schoolroom-manual form. It works through ways to begin a text, develop its body, and close it, with abundant classical quotation used as models.
la.eberhard_the_german.laborintus: The Laborintus, a Latin verse treatise on poetic and rhetorical training by Eberhardus Alemannus, known as Evrard the German, written in the early thirteenth century and framed as a complaint about the state of contemporary education. It is not to be confused with the Graecismus, a grammar textbook by a different author, Evrard of Bethune.
la.petrus_riga.de_ornatu_mundi: A short Latin poem in ninety elegiac couplets on the adornment of the created world, attributed to Peter Riga, the twelfth-century canon of Reims better known for his long verse Bible paraphrase the Aurora. Printed in Patrologia Latina under Hildebert of Lavardin's name, a long-standing misattribution, it surveys the beauty of the heavens, birds, flowers, and gems as signs of divine order.
la.caesar_pseudo.de_bello_africo: An account of Caesar's African campaign of 47 to 46 BC, from the landing at Hadrumetum to the victory at Thapsus and the death of Cato at Utica, written by an officer who served in it. It continues Caesar's own Civil War commentaries in another hand, plainer in style and close to the events, and is the fullest narrative of a single campaign in the Caesarian corpus after the Gallic War.
la.caesar_pseudo.de_bello_alexandrino: The war at Alexandria in 48 to 47 BC, with Caesar besieged in the palace quarter beside Cleopatra, followed by the campaigns in Illyricum, Spain and Pontus that ended at Zela. Written soon after the events by an author in Caesar's circle, perhaps Hirtius, to bridge Caesar's Civil War and the African war.
la.caesar_pseudo.de_bello_hispaniensi: The last campaign of the civil war, against Pompey's sons in Spain in 45 BC, ending at Munda. A short and rough narrative by a participant with no literary training, valued for the soldier's view of the fighting and for what its Latin shows of everyday usage.
la.vegetius.epitoma_rei_militaris: A handbook of Roman military practice in four books, written about AD 390 for an emperor, on the selection and training of recruits, the organisation of the legion, tactics in the field, and siegecraft and naval war. Compiled from earlier writers rather than from experience, it became the standard military text of the Middle Ages and the Renaissance.
la.grattius.cynegetica: A didactic poem on hunting in hexameters from the age of Augustus, treating the nets, spears, dogs and horses of the chase, with digressions on the origins of hunting and the diseases of dogs. About 540 lines survive. Ovid names Grattius among his contemporaries.
la.germanicus.aratea: A Latin rendering of Aratus' Phaenomena in hexameters by Germanicus, nephew and adopted son of Tiberius, made early in the first century AD. It describes the constellations and their myths, adapts Aratus to Roman astronomy and to Augustan poetry, and survives with fragments of a second part on weather signs.
la.solinus.collectanea_rerum_memorabilium: A compendium of geography and natural marvels from about the third century AD, moving region by region through the known world with its peoples, animals, stones and curiosities. Drawn largely from Pliny and Pomponius Mela, it was widely read through the Middle Ages and is the source of much later lore.
la.censorinus.de_die_natali: A birthday gift in the form of a learned treatise, addressed to a patron in AD 238. The first part treats human generation, the guardian spirit and the stages of life, the second the reckoning of time, calendars, eras and the date of the present year. It preserves much from lost writers on chronology and music.
la.obsequens.liber_de_prodigiis: A year by year list of prodigies from 190 to 11 BC, with lightning strikes, monstrous births, rains of stones, plagues and portents, each entry naming the consuls of the year and the expiation performed. Excerpted in the fourth century from Livy's history, it is the fullest surviving record of the Roman prodigy lists.
la.adamnan.de_locis_santis: De Locis Sanctis is an early medieval Latin prose treatise in which Adamnan sets down the topography of Jerusalem and the surrounding holy places as reported by the bishop Arculf, who dictated what he had seen. Beginning with a chapter list, the work describes the city walls and gates, the round church of the Holy Sepulchre and the tomb at its centre, Calvary, Constantine's basilica and the sites of the True Cross, the Mount of Olives, Bethany, and the road toward Caesarea, supplying measured dimensions and schematic plans of the principal churches. Among contemporary sights it notes a rectangular house of prayer built by the Saracens upon the former temple site. Readers hunting intertexts will find here a major channel through which biblical memory and eyewitness pilgrimage observation entered later medieval writing on the Holy Land.
la.aethelwulf.carmen_de_abbatibus: Carmen de Abbatibus is a medieval Latin poem of 842 lines attributed to Aethelwulf and assigned to the Carolingian era. As its title indicates, it offers a verse account of abbots, opening with a dedicatory prayer for a bishop preeminent among the English, praising monks who ascend the path of light, and passing into royal narrative that includes the fall of Ecgfrid to the Picts and the seizure of the kingdom by Alfrid. Its blend of episcopal dedication, royal history, and hagiographic colour makes it a useful witness for readers tracing biblical, classical, and formulaic echoes in medieval Latin verse.
la.agius_of_corvey.epicedium_hathumodae: The Epicedium Hathumodae is a Carolingian Latin funerary lament in verse, attributed to Agius of Corvey, mourning Hathumoda, an abbess who died in the flower of her youth. Addressed to the grieving sisters of her community, the poem opens by recounting how the poet consoled them in person soon after her death and now casts that speech into verse at their request, adding further material so that they might reread his words of comfort. Across some 718 lines it praises the abbess's virtues and insists that grief, though natural, must be kept within the bounds of reason. Readers hunting parallels will find it a useful witness to the classical consolatio and epicedium traditions as refracted through Carolingian monastic verse.
la.agius_of_corvey.versus_computistici: Attributed to Agius of Corvey, the Versus Computistici is a Carolingian Latin didactic poem of 206 lines devoted to computus, the reckoning of the calendar. Its prologue praises number as the divinely granted fount of the arts and addresses a dedicatee named Rimbert, whose name is punningly glossed as 'renowned in number'; the verses then set out, for the benefit of learners rather than experts, the elements of time-reckoning — months, weeks, days and hours, epacts, concurrents, and the courses of sun, moon, and stars. The combination of computistical doctrine with a prefatory play on names and conventional gestures of command and obedience makes the poem a rewarding hunting ground for readers tracing textual parallels.
la.agnellus_ravennatis.liber_pontificalis: A Latin ecclesiastical history of the Carolingian era, the Liber Pontificalis of Agnellus of Ravenna narrates the succession of Ravenna's bishops from apostolic times down to the author's own day. A priest of the Ravennate church who bears the names Agnellus and Andreas, he opens the work with a rhymed hexameter prologue lamenting the long neglect of local episcopal record-keeping and invoking the reigns of the emperors Louis and Lothar. Beyond its importance as a source for early medieval Ravenna, the compilation blends scriptural, classical, and hagiographic diction, and its catalogue of episcopal lives invites comparison with the Roman Liber Pontificalis and other late-antique succession narratives, making it a productive quarry for verbal and structural parallels.
la.aimoin_of_saint_germain.carmen_de_transl: Carmen de Translatione Vincentii is a medieval Latin poem of sixty-five lines attributed to Aimoin of Saint Germain and assigned to the Carolingian era. It narrates how Audaldus, a priest-monk of Castellum who bears the honour of Aaron, journeys to Valentia in Spain, where his host Zacharias, won over by prayers and gifts of silver, discloses the resting place of Vincent the deacon and martyr; the relics are dug up by night amid miraculous signs and conveyed back to the fair cell of father Benedict at Castellum. The opening chronological computation, the nocturnal excavation, and the monks' joyful reception of the saint conform to the conventions of the relic-translation genre. The poem offers readers of intertexts Carolingian hagiographic diction, biblical allusion, and formulas shared with other accounts of the discovery and transfer of relics.
la.alcuin.carmina: A Carolingian corpus of Latin verse attributed to Alcuin, printed in E. Dümmler's 1881 edition and running to some 6,800 lines spread over eighty-seven files. The opening piece begins as a hymnic invocation of Christ before turning into a laudatory historical poem on York (Euborica urbs), tracing the city from its Roman foundation and its situation on the Ouse towards its Christian and ecclesiastical past. The collection at large assembles the devotional, encomiastic, and occasional verse characteristic of Alcuin's milieu at the Carolingian court. For readers of intertexts, these poems are a hub of borrowing and reworking, steeped in scriptural phrasing and classical epic diction inherited from late-antique Christian poets and Virgilian formulae.
la.amalarius.versus_marini: An eighty-line Carolingian Latin poem attributed to Amalarius, the Versus Marini stages a witty address in which a speaker questions why his abba is turning back to the narrow seas, then recounts a monk's storm-tossed voyage toward Constantinople and Attica. Its narrative mixes dialogue, mock-heroic storm description, and monastic anecdote, naming figures such as Agius, Maximus, Gregory, and Wippo, and closing with watchmen posted to keep a monk from slipping out through the darkened city. Readers of intertexts will find Virgilian sea-storm diction joined to Gospel echoes of disciples trembling on the waves and of a lord who stills the waters, making the poem a compact witness to classical and biblical imitation in early medieval verse.
la.ambrose.exameron: The Exameron is a Late Antique Latin theological treatise in prose by Ambrose, edited by Karl Schenkl in the Corpus scriptorum ecclesiasticorum Latinorum (1896), which expounds the Genesis account of the six days of creation. Setting Christian teaching against pagan cosmologies — Plato's eternal matter and ideal forms, Aristotle's principles, the atomist concourse, and disputes over the world's eternity — the work defends creation from nothing by a freely willing God and, in its opening sections, treats the meaning of 'in the beginning', the joint operation of Word and Spirit, the incorporeality of the creator, and the origin of evil. Its dense weaving of scriptural citation with explicit engagement of Greek philosophical authorities makes it a central witness to the transmission of hexaemeral tradition and classical cosmology into Latin Christian literature, and a rich quarry for readers tracing textual parallels.
la.ambrose.explanatio_psalmorum_xii: Ambrose's Explanatio Psalmorum XII is a Late Antique work of Latin prose theology, an exposition of twelve Psalms transmitted in Michael Petschenig's 1919 Vienna edition and running to some 1,479 lines. A prologue on delight (delectatio) as the incentive to virtue that God proposed and the devil counterfeited, and on the Psalms of David as medicine for the soul, gives way to running exegesis that begins with Psalm 1 (Beatus vir) and proceeds through moral and allegorical reading of the verses. Its dense weave of scriptural citation and patristic Latin idiom offers abundant verbal parallels for readers tracing biblical diction through later Latin prose.
la.ambrosiaster.pseudo_augustini_quaestione: A Late Antique collection of 127 questions on the Old and New Testament, written in Latin prose and transmitted under Augustine's name while being attributed to the anonymous exegete conventionally known as Ambrosiaster. The opening question alone treats the divine nature, evil as a transgression of the good rather than a substance, free will, the apostasy of Lucifer, the creation of matter, and the purpose of the Mosaic law, and the collection proceeds through further doctrinal and exegetical questions on Cain and Abel, the decalogue, and priestly benediction. Scripture is quoted and paraphrased throughout, with Paul, John, Isaiah, and Genesis supplying much of the fabric of the argument. Because the work circulated for centuries as the pseudo-Augustinian Quaestiones, its phrasing could pass under Augustine's authority, so readers tracing verbal parallels need to distinguish genuine Augustinian echoes from the diction of Ambrosiaster.
la.ammianus.rerum_gestarum: The Res Gestae of Ammianus Marcellinus is a Latin prose history of the Late Antique era, preserved in the corpus as eighteen books of continuous narrative. The opening book recounts the savage administration of Gallus Caesar in the eastern provinces, the depredations of the Isaurians and Saracens, and a frustrated Persian incursion, mixing military narrative with ethnographic and moralizing digression. Its dense, allusive prose and detailed coverage of campaigns, court intrigue, and frontier peoples make it a rich source of verbal and thematic parallels for readers tracing continuities with earlier Roman historiography.
la.angilbert_carmina: A corpus of medieval Latin verse, 262 lines in all, by the Carolingian poet Angilbert, for which the source record supplies no meter. The opening poem is a welcoming address to Pippin, whose return from the Hesperian shores will fill his father Charles with joy, and it stages the longing of the brother Charles, the consoling report of Chlodowih, and a dream apparition of the absent brother promising speedy arrival, culminating in the poet's self-identification as 'Somni sed fructus Angilbertus ego.' The dense classical surface — Phoebus rising from the eastern stars, the waxing moon's horns, the rhetoric of delay and longing — makes the carmina fertile ground for tracing Virgilian and Ovidian echoes, court panegyric formulas, and the dream-vision motif in Carolingian court poetry.
la.angilbert_versus: A short Latin poem of 55 lines, Carolingian in date and associated with the abbot Angilbert, which presents itself as a versified summary of Augustine of Hippo's De doctrina christiana. The opening announces that the pious teachings of Aurelius Augustine on doctrine shine forth here and describes four books treating in turn Christ's precepts, signs, signs and words, and what the preceding books teach, including the three styles of speech (summisse, moderate, granditer), while closing with prayer and praise of God who has ordered all things numero, mensura ac pondere. A concluding passage names the humble abbot Angilbert as the commissioner of the libellus, offered to the pious king Louis (Hlodoicus), praised for seeking the secrets of holy wisdom day and night. Readers of intertexts will find a compact Carolingian refashioning of Augustinian and scriptural language, valuable for tracing the verse reception of the De doctrina christiana.
la.angilbertus_miles.versus_de_fontaneto: The Versus de Fontaneto is a Carolingian Latin poem of 45 lines, attributed to a certain Angilbert, who names himself in the closing lines as a combatant in the fratricidal battle of Fontenoy ('Fontaneto') between Lothar and the forces of his brothers Charles and Louis. The speaker presents himself as the sole survivor of the first battle line and moves from vivid battle narrative through the mourning of the stricken countryside to an extended curse upon the day of slaughter. Its blend of biblical and classical allusion—Judas, Cerberus, the dawn formula—with a rare eye-witness, lay perspective on Carolingian civil war makes it a useful point of comparison for battle laments and for the Carolingian adaptation of Roman verse idiom.
la.anonymi.planctus_de_obitu_Karoli: The Planctus de Obitu Karoli is an anonymous medieval Latin lament of uncertain date on the death of Charlemagne, composed in short verses punctuated throughout by the refrain 'Heu mihi misero!' Its sixty lines describe grief sweeping from the lands of the rising sun to the western shore, afflicting Franks, Romans, infants, elders, bishops, matrons, and widows alike, and they close with a prayer that Christ grant Charles rest in his kingdom alongside laments for Rome, Italy, and Francia. As an example of the planctus on a ruler's death, the poem offers readers of intertexts a compact assembly of mourning formulae—the cosmos-wide reach of sorrow, the orphaned and widow-stricken world, the civic woe of Rome—and a witness to the emperor's posthumous image as father of the faithful and protector of pilgrims.
la.anonymous.breviarius_de_hierosolyma: The Breviarius de Hierosolyma is a brief anonymous Latin prose itinerary of uncertain date that leads the reader through the holy places of Jerusalem, from the basilica of Constantine, Golgotha, and the church of the Holy Sepulchre to holy Sion, the house of Pilate, and the Mount of Olives. Each station is tied to a biblical event and to the relics preserved on the spot, including the True Cross, the Lance, the crown of thorns, and the chalice of the Last Supper. As a compact catalogue of Jerusalem's sacred topography, it serves as a useful parallel for readers tracing pilgrimage itineraries, relic traditions, and the scriptural geography of the city.
la.anonymous_pilgrim_of_piacenza.itinerariu: The Itinerarium is a first-person prose itinerary of a pilgrimage to the Holy Land, attributed to an anonymous pilgrim from Piacenza and of uncertain date, though the narrative alludes to the emperor Justinian and to the empress Eudoxia's building works at Jerusalem. The account leads from Constantinople through Cyprus, the Phoenician coast, Galilee, Samaria, and Judaea to Jerusalem, Bethlehem, and Sinai, cataloguing churches, relics, tombs of saints, miraculous springs, and local customs, including Samaritan, Jewish, and Saracen practices. Readers of intertexts will find a dense matrix of place names, biblical allusions, apocryphal traditions, and formulaic descriptions of holy sites shared with other late-antique travel writing.
la.anonymus.carmen_ad_ludovicum_pium: The Carmen ad Ludovicum Pium is an anonymous Latin poem of 118 lines, of uncertain date, addressed by its title to a king named Louis styled 'the Pious', whom the opening lines greet as guardian of the fatherland and liken to Solomon. The speaker, who describes his verses as dactylic, urges on the ruler a full program of Christian conduct: steadfast faith, love of God and of brothers, hope of eternal life, regular reading of Scripture, mercy and remission of debts, patience, humility and cheerfulness, contrition with tears, true confession and amendment of sin, fear of the Lord, frequent fasting, almsgiving that frees the soul from punishment, and chastity. Standing in the tradition of admonitory verse to rulers, the poem's dense biblical diction — its comparison of the king to Solomon, its alms that ransom from death, its warning that death hastens — offers rich ground for readers tracing parallels with mirror-for-princes verse, penitential exhortation, and scriptural allusion in medieval Latin poetry.
la.anonymus.carmen_de_compoti_ratione: An anonymous medieval Latin didactic poem of uncertain date, the Carmen de Compoti Ratione comprises 147 lines of verse setting out the rudiments of the computus: the lengths of the months, the placement of nones and ides, and the procedure for finding on which day of the week each month's kalends fall in ordinary and bissextile years. Its central section explains the 'concurrent' numbers that govern the weekly cycle across the seven-year sequence, and the closing lines introduce a method of reckoning on the joints of the fingers. For readers tracing intertexts, the poem offers a compact specimen of the formulaic calendrical verse tradition, whose month catalogues and mnemonic rules circulate widely in medieval computistical and schoolroom poetry.
la.anonymus.carmen_de_conversione_saxonum: The Carmen de Conversione Saxonum is a short anonymous Latin poem of uncertain date, running to 75 lines, which commemorates the conversion of the Saxons under Charles, naming the ninth year of his reign. It opens with a providential survey of the world's ages, recounting creation, the fall, and Christ's redemptive victory over death and the underworld, before turning to the Saxons' former idolatry and bloody sacrifices and their reduction to Christianity by Carolingian arms. Its dense weave of biblical allusion and Christian Latin epic diction, together with its chronological and computistical framing, makes it rewarding material for readers tracing verbal and thematic parallels across patristic and early medieval verse.
la.anonymus.carmen_de_nynia_episcopo: A medieval Latin verse life of Bishop Ninian (Nynia), anonymous and of uncertain date, running to 504 lines. It opens with Christ's incarnation and the spread of grace through the world, then celebrates Ninian, named thus in his native tongue, his stupendous miracles, the crowds he won for Christ, and his voyage over the sea and across the Alps to be strengthened by the supreme pontiff. Its direct quotation of the Psalms and its high diction, which blends scriptural phrasing with classical poetic vocabulary, make it rewarding ground for readers tracing verbal and thematic echoes in hagiographic verse.
la.anonymus.carmen_de_pippino: The Carmen de Pippino is an anonymous medieval Latin poem of 46 lines, of uncertain date, celebrating the victory of a King Pippin over the Avars. Opening with an address to Christ as creator of all peoples, it laments Avar desecration of churches, monasteries, and sacred vessels, then recounts how God sends Saint Peter to accompany Pippin, a catholic king who encamps beside the Danube with the Frankish host. The terrified Avar ruler, the Cacanus, comes with his primates to adore the king and surrenders his realm, lands, and children into subjection, after which the poet gives thanks that God has confirmed a Christian kingdom over that of Hunnia and granted victory over the pagan peoples. Combining epic battle narrative, panegyric, and a closing prayer for the king's life, the poem offers readers of intertexts a compact instance of biblical and liturgical diction deployed in the celebration of Christian conquest.
la.anonymus.carmen_de_temporum_ratione: A medieval Latin poem of uncertain date, transmitted anonymously, on the reckoning of time (computus). Across its 902 lines it treats the threefold division of time under divine authority, human institution, and natural custom, covering the Sabbath commandment, Olympiads, the length of the month, the circuits of the zodiac, and the fractional nomenclature — unciae, sextantes, semisses and their kin — by which hours and moments were subdivided. For readers of intertexts its interest lies in the versification of material more often transmitted in prose computistical handbooks, which makes the poem a useful witness for shared phrasing and doctrine across the medieval calendrical tradition.
la.anonymus.carmen_de_timone_comite: The Carmen de Timone Comite is an anonymous medieval Latin poem of uncertain date, surviving in 150 lines, which praises Count Timo, dispatched as the envoy of a king addressed in the second person to administer justice in the Norican lands. After a reference to a toilsome journey to Rome, the poet invokes his Thalia and sketches Timo as a restorer of neglected law, a scourge of thieves, robbers, and strife, and a lighten­er of the burdens of the innocent. The encomium is sustained by a chain of biblical exempla: David's severity towards the wicked and mildness to the good, Job's endurance and just kingship, the gentleness of Moses and Joshua, and Joseph's harshness towards his treacherous brothers. The poem thus offers a compact specimen of the medieval mirror-for-rulers mode and rewards readers tracing biblical commonplaces and the classical muse-invocation in Latin panegyric.
la.anonymus.carmina_cenomanensia: An anonymous medieval Latin poem of about 410 lines, the Carmina Cenomanensia takes its title from Le Mans (Cenomanum) and is of uncertain date. Its opening verses invoke Christ and the Virgin Mary before extolling Bishop Aldric and recounting his pious placement there of the relics of the martyrs Gervasius and Prothasius and of Stephen, crowned with his martyr's palm. The poem moves on into prayer and commendation on behalf of Aldric and his flock, in the manner of a dedicatory devotional piece. Its conventional diction of episcopal praise, relic cult, and liturgical intercession makes it a useful comparand for readers hunting verbal parallels and hagiographic topoi across medieval Latin verse.
la.anonymus.corneli_translationes: The Corneli Translationes is an anonymous medieval Latin poem of uncertain date, celebrating the transfer of the relics of Saint Cornelius from Rome to France under a pious king named Charles. Its 163 lines narrate the saint's triumphant reception: a procession of clergy, bishops, soldiers and a plebs numbering twenty thousand, bearing crosses, candles and incense, while the king and bishops carry the sacred weight to the palace sanctuary amid hymns, trumpets, organs and tears of joy. The poem sets Rome's former enjoyment of the saint against the new felicity of Francia, which, sheltered by so great a patron, need fear no ruin. Readers hunting parallels will find dense clusters of translatio topoi — triumphal diction, processional spectacle, and hymnic and biblical echoes — readily comparable with other accounts of relic translation.
la.anonymus.hymnus_nynie_episcopi: The Hymnus Nynie Episcopi is an anonymous medieval Latin hymn of uncertain date in honour of Nynia, a bishop whose tomb and miracles it celebrates. Its fifty-four lines are arranged as an abecedarian series of couplets in which each second line repeats the closing words of the first, moving from praise of God the creator and of Christ born of a virgin mother to the saint's wonders, above all his cleansing of leprosy at his burial place beneath the church. The echoing verse form and the stock motifs of hagiographic praise — miraculous healing, the saint's resting place, the soul borne to heaven — make the hymn a useful point of comparison for readers tracing parallels in liturgical poetry and verse encomia of saints.
la.anonymus.karolus_magnus_et_leo_papa: Karolus Magnus et Leo Papa is an anonymous medieval Latin epic of 536 lines, of uncertain date, celebrating Charlemagne and his dealings with Pope Leo. The opening verses deploy the seafaring imagery of an epic prologue before moving into panegyric: Charlemagne, 'victor pius' and mightier than all kings in justice, is set against King David and the sun-god Phoebus, outshining the biblical king as the constant sun outshines the waning moon, while his rule joins piety, clemency, and divinely sanctioned discipline. Readers hunting textual parallels will find in the poem a Carolingian fusion of classical epic diction with biblical typology and the Latin panegyric tradition.
la.anonymus.laudes_mediolanensis_civitatis: Laudes Mediolanensis Civitatis is an anonymous medieval Latin poem of uncertain date, comprising 72 lines in praise of Milan. It celebrates the city's lofty situation, its twelve-foot walls, nine iron-bound gates, water supply, and splendid churches, then enumerates the saints buried there—Ambrose, Protasius, Gervase, Nazarius, Celsus, Benedict, and others—hailing Milan as queen of cities and metropolis toward which the bishops of Ausonia converge. As a specimen of the medieval urban encomium, it offers readers of intertexts parallels for topoi of city praise, relic catalogues, and the literary promotion of a see city through its sacred dead.
la.anonymus.laudes_veronensis_civitatis: The Laudes Veronensis Civitatis is an anonymous medieval Latin encomium of Verona, ninety-nine lines long and belonging to the genre of civic praise descended from classical laudes urbis. The poem extols the city's quadrangular walls, its forty-eight towers, its labyrinth, its stone-paved forum, and its temples of the pagan gods, then turns to the incarnation and resurrection of Christ, the conversion of the gentiles, and the preaching of Bishop Euprepus at Verona. Invoking Isidore as an authority for the city's position in the Veneto, the author weaves into the description scriptural diction, from the kenotic language of Philippians to the Davidic verse 'caeli enarrant gloriam altissimi.' For readers tracing intertexts, the poem marks the meeting of the secular tradition of urban encomium with the biblical and patristic phrasing through which a medieval author Christianizes a cityscape.
la.anonymus.tituli_metrici_saeculi_viii: A collection of 414 lines of medieval Latin verse inscriptions (tituli), anonymous, and assigned to the eighth century by its title. The opening piece is a first-person epitaph of Peter, bishop of Pavia ('Ticinensis gloria plebis'), recounting his upbringing in the church, his exile from his native soil, and his restoration in the reign of Charlemagne, followed by prayers asking passing readers to intercede and verses praising his episcopal virtues. The collection preserves the formulas of medieval epigraphic poetry — commemoration, lament, and commendation of the dead — composed in diction indebted to scriptural and late-antique inscriptional tradition. Readers pursuing intertexts will find here a repository of stock phrases on death, exile, judgment, and intercessory prayer that recur across Carolingian and later medieval Latin verse.
la.anonymus.versus_ad_ebonem_remensem: A medieval Latin poem of forty-six lines, of uncertain date and anonymous authorship, addressed to Ebbo, bishop of Reims, whom it praises through a dense string of honorific epithets. Its central section recounts the making of a Gospel book at Ebbo's command: the humble abbot and master Peter executed the commission, adorned the volume with gold within and ivory without, and dedicated it to the apostolic lord, while the poem enumerates the four Evangelists, Matthew, Mark, Luke and John, whose writings the book contains. Christ figures throughout as the radiant physician whose gospel remedies heal the sick, and the closing lines ask that supplicants who seek his aid be granted the crown of everlasting peace. Readers of intertexts may find it a rich specimen of verse book-dedication, with the Evangelists likened to the quadriga of Christ and the medicine-of-Christ motif inviting parallels with inscriptional and exegetical traditions.
la.anonymus.versus_de_eversione_monasterii_: An anonymous medieval Latin poem of 78 lines, of uncertain date, bearing the title Versus de Eversione Monasterii Glonnensis and lamenting the burning of the monastery of Glonn and its basilica of Saint Florentius by a cruel, brutish Britannic people. The verses open with an Orphic invocation to the Thracian lyre and then recount the foundation of the church by the mighty King Charles, who endowed it with fertile lands and a vessel of the Lord's Supper famed for restoring the sick, and its continued favour under his son Louis. On Louis's death the kingdom is partitioned four ways, discord spreads among the warring sons, and a once-poor husbandman named Nemenoius, enriched by a buried treasure, rises through deceit to take up arms against Charles. The poem offers readers of intertexts a classicizing proem alongside hagiographic and dynastic narrative, including an early account of a wonder-working eucharistic vessel.
la.apuleius.de_deo_socratis: De Deo Socratis is a Latin prose philosophical oration by Apuleius, a work of the later imperial period, expounding Platonic theology and demonology: it divides being into gods, daemons, and humans, presents daemons as aerial intermediaries who convey prayers and portents, catalogues their kinds (including Lemures, Lares, Larvae, and Manes), argues that the divine sign of Socrates was a guardian daemon rather than an audible voice, and closes with an exhortation to the study of wisdom. The argument advances through dense quotation and allusion, weaving in Ennius on the gods, Lucretius on the moon and thunder, Vergilian episodes from the Aeneid, Homeric scenes from the Iliad and the Odyssey, and verses of Terence and Accius. Readers hunting intertexts will find here a rich repertory of poetic citations embedded in philosophical argument, delivered in Apuleian prose at its most ornate and declamatory.
la.apuleius.metamorphoses: The Metamorphoses, better known as The Golden Ass, is an eleven-book Latin prose novel by Apuleius, composed in the later imperial period and announced in its prologue as a 'fabula Graecanica' in the Milesian manner. Its narrator Lucius, travelling to Thessaly out of curiosity about magic, is drawn first into hearsay tales of witches such as Meroe and then, through the maid Photis and the sorceress Pamphile, into an actual metamorphosis into an ass; his picaresque adventures among bandits, priests and households frame the celebrated inset tale of Cupid and Psyche and close with his restoration to human form through the goddess Isis. Satirical, ribald and densely allusive, the novel reworks Greek romance, fable and earlier Latin poetry, and its episodes and imagery have long served later writers and readers as a rich quarry for mythological and narrative parallels.
la.audradus_modicus.carmina: Carmina, a collection of Latin verse attributed to Audradus Modicus and belonging to the Carolingian period, comprises some 1,591 lines. The opening poem takes the form of an address to Hincmar, in which the speaker, exhorted by his friend, journeys to a miraculous fountain and there receives a revelation from its divine guardian, an episode blending classical diction with Christian symbolism. Readers of intertexts will find the inherited vocabulary of Latin poetry, from laurel and ivy to the living waters of the fontis vitae, reworked within a Carolingian devotional frame, making the collection a useful witness to the afterlife of classical and biblical motifs in medieval verse.
la.audradus_modicus.de_sancta_trinitate: De Sancta Trinitate is a Latin verse treatise of 172 lines on the doctrine of the Trinity, attributed to the Carolingian author Audradus Modicus. It opens with a prayer for mercy upon 'his Audradus' and surveys a twelve-book cycle dedicated in the trine name to feasts and saints, naming its author a chorepiscopus of Sens drawn by vow from the church of St Martin of Tours, and noting that a psalm and then a prose piece follow the verse. The doctrinal core sets out, in compact antithetical lines, the full and coeternal divinity of the Son — 'ex toto totum, de summo lumine summum' — insisting that one substance remains of Father and Son, in diction close to credal formulae. For readers hunting parallels, the poem offers a characteristic Carolingian combination of self-referential preface, liturgical dedication scheme, and Trinitarian verse theology steeped in credal phrasing.
la.augustine.confessiones: Augustine's Confessions is a Late Antique Latin prose work of theology, cast as a sustained prayer of praise, confession, and self-examination addressed directly to God. It interweaves autobiography with scriptural meditation and philosophical reflection, opening with an account of infancy, schooling, and adolescent waywardness and moving toward an account of the author's conversion and interior life. Its dense fabric of biblical allusion, drawn especially from the Psalms and Pauline letters, together with memorable formulations such as the restless heart that finds no rest until it rests in God, made it among the most quoted and imitated works of Latin literature. Readers hunting textual parallels will find it a central hub through which scriptural language and patristic idiom pass into later medieval and vernacular writing.
la.augustine.contra_adimantum: The Contra Adimantum is a late-antique Latin prose treatise of theology by Augustine, composed as a point-by-point reply to Adimantus, a disciple of Mani who had assembled passages from Genesis, Exodus, Leviticus, and Deuteronomy that he held to contradict the New Testament. Each chapter takes one such alleged contradiction—on creation, the sabbath, marriage and divorce, the image of God, divine retribution, dietary law, circumcision, and the worship of strange gods—and argues for the concord of the two Testaments, reading Old Testament observances as signs and figures of New Testament realities. The work preserves, in quotation and paraphrase, the shape of Adimantus's Manichaean list of capitula alongside Augustine's defensive exegesis, making it a compact witness to how Latin Christian readers reconciled troublesome Old Testament citations with Gospel and apostolic texts.
la.augustine.contra_duas_epistulas_pelegian: Contra duas epistulas Pelagianorum is a Latin prose treatise in epistolary form composed by Augustine of Hippo in the Late Antique period, addressed to Pope Boniface and framed as a report on the course of the Pelagian controversy. It answers, point by point, two hostile letters—one sent to Rome by Julian of Eclanum and another to Thessalonica by eighteen bishops sharing his error—defending the necessity of gratuitous grace, the transmission of original sin through concupiscence, the completeness of baptismal remission, and the proper reading of Romans 7. Along the way it surveys the divine institution of marriage, the condition of infants before baptism, and the salvation of Old Testament saints through the mediatorship of Christ. Readers hunting intertexts will find it densely woven with Pauline citation and with echoes of Augustine's own earlier anti-Pelagian works, and it preserves extensive verbatim quotation of the Pelagian letters it refutes.
la.augustine.contra_epistulam_fundamenti: A Latin anti-Manichaean polemic in epistolary form by Augustine, written in the late antique period against the creed set out in Mani's 'Letter of the Foundation', which it cites and refutes passage by passage. Addressed to Manichaean readers, the work urges calm joint inquiry, argues that faith in the gospel rests on the authority of the Catholic Church, and dismantles Mani's cosmogony of the realm of light, the five natures of the land of darkness, and the wedge of darkness that wounds the divine substance, defending creation from nothing and evil as a privation of good. Readers of intertexts will find here substantial embedded quotation of the Fundamental Letter itself and dense scriptural citation, from the Paraclete promise and Pentecost narrative of Acts to Johannine light imagery, in one of Augustine's most characteristic treatments of his former sect.
la.augustine.contra_epistulam_parmeniani: A brief Latin prose treatise in epistolary form by Augustine, of Late Antique date, answering the letter which the former Donatist bishop Parmenian had written to Tychonius, the Donatist exegete who had come to see that the church of God is diffused through the whole world. Augustine refutes Parmenian's scriptural objections one by one, defending the catholicity and unity of the church against the African schismatics and rehearsing the history of the controversy: the case of Caecilian, the councils and imperial judgments, rebaptism, the violence of the circumcellions, and the later schism of the Maximianists. The work is a dense weave of biblical citation and allusion, from the promises to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob to the parable of the wheat and the tares and passages from the Psalms, prophets, and apostle, and it preserves Parmenian's charges in Augustine's own reporting, making it a useful witness for readers tracing the scriptural and polemical intertexts of the Donatist controversy.
la.augustine.contra_felicem: Contra Felicem is a Latin prose record of a public disputation between Augustine, bishop of the Catholic church of Hippo Regius, and a Manichaean named Felix, held on 7 December in the sixth consulship of Honorius. In the exchange Augustine challenges the claims that Mani was an apostle of Christ and the promised Paraclete, arguing from the gospels and Acts that the Holy Spirit had already come upon the apostles at Pentecost, and pressing against Felix Paul's warnings about those who forbid marriage and certain foods. The disputation preserves substantial quotations from Mani's so-called Fundamental Epistle alongside dense citation of scripture, making it a valuable witness for readers tracing Manichaean doctrine and Augustine's biblical argumentation in anti-Manichaean polemic.
la.augustine.contra_litteras_petiliani: A late-antique Latin prose treatise of polemical theology by Augustine, directed against the letters of Petilian, a Donatist bishop. The work first answers portions of Petilian's letter that had come to hand and then, once the whole letter was recovered, replies to it point by point, setting out his words under his name and the response under Augustine's own. Its chief burden is the Donatist claim that baptism administered by unworthy or traditor ministers is invalid: Augustine contends that Christ alone is the true origin, root, and head of the baptized, and repeatedly presses the Donatist reception of the Maximianist schismatics as a self-contradiction. For readers of intertexts the treatise offers a dense weave of scriptural quotation and allusion drawn from the Pauline epistles, the Psalms, and the Gospels, alongside verbatim fragments of Donatist polemic preserved as a foil.
la.augustine.contra_partem_donati_post_gest: Contra Partem Donati post Gesta is a late-antique Latin prose polemic by Augustine, written after the official proceedings (gesta) of a public episcopal conference with Donatist bishops at Carthage and addressed to the Donatist laity to convince them that their leaders have been defeated. The treatise turns repeatedly on the formula 'nec causa causae nec persona personae praeiudicat', arguing that the old condemnation of Caecilian of Carthage cannot invalidate the worldwide catholic church, while rehearsing the Donatist bishops' admissions and contradictions in the acts, their charges of a bribed judge, and their claims about Donatus, Miltiades, and the council of Cirta. Against the Donatist demand for a visibly pure church, Augustine marshals scriptural testimony — the wheat and the tares, the dragnet and the threshing floor, the prophecy of Haggai, and Cyprian on the zizania within the church — to show that good and bad remain mingled until the last judgment. Readers hunting parallels will find a dense weave of biblical quotation and allusion, Cyprianic citation, and appeals to conciliar acta, imperial rescripts, and martyrs' gesta characteristic of the anti-Donatist controversy.
la.augustine.de_beata_vita: Augustine's De beata uita, a Latin prose dialogue of Late Antique date, is dedicated to Theodorus and recounts three days of philosophical conversation, beginning at a modest banquet held on the author's birthday, with his mother, his brother Navigius, his son Adeodatus, and other companions. After an extended nautical allegory of souls sailing towards the port of philosophy, the discussion proceeds dialectically through questions of desire, misery, and need to the conclusion that the happy life lies in possessing God, who is identified as wisdom, truth, and the supreme measure. The work quotes Cicero's Hortensius, contests the position of the Academic sceptics, invokes Plotinus, and closes with Trinitarian language drawn from Scripture, making it a dense meeting point of classical philosophy and Christian doctrine for readers tracing verbal and thematic parallels.
la.augustine.de_bono_coniugali: The De Bono Coniugali ('On the Good of Marriage') is a Latin prose treatise by Augustine, written in the Late Antique period, that defends marriage as a genuine good resting on three goods: offspring, marital fidelity, and the sacramental bond that makes the union indissoluble. Writing against those who denigrated wedlock, Augustine ranks continentia and virginity above marriage while insisting that conjugal chastity is no sin, defends the polygamous unions of the Old Testament patriarchs as fitting their own dispensation, and rebuts Manichaean objections to procreation. Sustained quotation and exegesis of Genesis and the Pauline epistles, together with its graded hierarchy of goods from wedlock through widowhood to virginity, make it a central witness to patristic marriage doctrine and an important intertext for tracing later Christian debate on concupiscence, divorce, and celibacy.
la.augustine.de_civitate_dei: De ciuitate Dei (The City of God), a Latin theological prose work by Augustine of the Late Antique era, written in response to the recent sack of Rome and addressed to Marcellinus, undertakes to defend the city of God, which lives by faith as a pilgrim among the impious, against pagans who prefer their own gods to its founder and blame the city's fall on neglect of the traditional cults. The opening book treats the calamities attending the barbarian capture of the city — massacre, famine, captivity, rape, and unburied corpses — arguing from Roman exempla such as Regulus, Lucretia, and Cato of Utica that suicide is never lawful and that the chastity of the will survives bodily violation without consent. Dense with quotation and critique of Virgil, Horace, and Sallust, and continually reworking scenes from the sack of Troy and Roman history, the work stands as a major meeting point between pagan literary tradition and Christian polemic.
la.augustine.de_continentia: A brief Latin prose treatise by Augustine of Late Antiquity, De Continentia argues that continence is a gift of God rather than a human achievement, a virtue that must guard not only the appetites of the body but the 'mouth of the heart' from which evil thoughts and consent proceed. Addressed in pointed part against the Manichaeans, it defends the goodness of the flesh against their dualism, expounds Pauline passages on the spirit warring against the flesh, and distinguishes true continence from pagan, heretical, and demonic forms of self-restraint. Densely woven with scriptural citation and allusion, from Wisdom and the Psalms to Romans, Galatians, Colossians, and Ephesians, the work offers readers of intertexts a compact witness to Augustine's biblical exegesis and his moral theology of grace. The text follows Joseph Zycha's 1900 Vienna edition.
la.augustine.de_doctrina_christiana: A late-antique Latin theological treatise by Augustine, De Doctrina Christiana sets out rules for interpreting and expounding the Christian Scriptures, dividing its instruction between the discovery of meaning and its communication. After a prologue defending the very project of teaching such precepts, it establishes the famous distinction between things (res) and signs (signa) and between enjoyment and use (frui and uti), before treating the Trinity, the Incarnation as the medicine of wounded humanity, and the order of love that governs the interpreter's journey. Its dense quotation and allegorical reading of biblical passages, together with its discussions of obscure expressions and the legitimate use of pagan learning, make it a central witness for tracing Scriptural allusions and classical intertexts in later Christian prose.
la.augustine.de_fide_et_symbolo: De Fide et Symbolo, preserved in Joseph Zycha's 1900 Vienna edition of Augustine's works, is a Latin prose exposition of the Creed (symbolum) by the late-antique Christian writer Augustine. Setting out the articles of faith clause by clause, it argues that the brief creedal formula must be guarded against heretical distortion, treating creation from nothing, the eternal generation of the Word, the incarnation and virgin birth, the Trinity as one God, the church, the forgiveness of sins, and the resurrection of the body, with dense citation of Scripture and polemic against heretics and pagan philosophers. An appended notice from the Retractationes records Augustine's own later correction of the work's discussion of the risen body. For readers of intertexts it offers an early landmark of creedal exegesis, rich in biblical allusion and in Trinitarian and anti-heretical formulae that echo through later patristic writing.
la.augustine.de_genesi_ad_litteram: Augustine's De Genesi ad Litteram, a late-antique Latin prose work of theology, expounds the opening chapters of Genesis according to the letter while holding that the same verses may also bear figurative senses. The argument works through the problems of the six days of creation in detail: how the eternal Word can utter the temporal 'fiat lux', whether the first light is spiritual or corporeal, when formless matter was made, and how the Trinity is intimated in the works of creation. A prominent passage warns against Christians expounding Scripture on natural questions in ways that experts will ridicule, lest disbelief spread to the central articles of faith. For readers hunting parallels, the treatise stands among the most influential patristic treatments of creation, time, divine speech, and the methods and limits of literal exegesis.
la.augustine.de_gratia_christi: A late antique Latin prose treatise by Augustine on the grace of Christ, occasioned by a consultation from Albina, Pinianus, and Melania, who had asked him for a written judgment on Pelagius and his teachings. The work quotes Pelagius at length from his books De libero arbitrio, his letter to Innocent, his verse epistle of some three hundred lines to Paulinus, and his treatise to the virgin Demetrias, scrutinising his distinction between possibility, will, and act (posse, velle, agere) and his tendency to place grace in law and doctrine alone; against this Augustine argues from Paul and the Gospels that grace assists not only natural capacity but will and deed alike, citing such proof-texts as Philippians 2:13, 2 Corinthians 12:9, and John 15:5. Discussion of infant baptism and original sin also enters the argument, alongside the recurring claim that charity itself is a divine gift rather than a human merit. Readers hunting intertexts will find it valuable both as a repository of verbatim Pelagian material and as a dense lattice of scriptural allusion within late-antique polemic.
la.augustine.de_nuptiis_et_concupiscentia: De Nuptiis et Concupiscentia ('On Marriage and Concupiscence') is a two-book Latin theological treatise by Augustine, addressed with a covering letter to Valerius, a comes of the late antique period. Written against unnamed new heretics who denied original sin in infants and accused their opponents of condemning marriage, it argues that carnal concupiscence, a consequence of the first sin, must be distinguished from the three goods of marriage: offspring (proles), fidelity (fides), and sacrament (sacramentum). The argument draws on the Genesis narrative, the marriages of the patriarchs and of Mary and Joseph, and a long exegesis of Romans 5 and 7 on the law of sin in the members, with pervasive Pauline quotation. Readers hunting intertexts will find here densely cited, formulaic treatments of concupiscence, original sin, and infant baptism that recur throughout late antique theological writing.
la.augustine.de_peccato_originali: A compact Late Antique Latin prose treatise by Augustine, directed against the teachings of Pelagius and Caelestius on original sin and the baptism of infants. Drawing on the Carthaginian proceedings against Caelestius, the letters and confession of faith of Pelagius, and correspondence involving the popes Zosimus and Innocent, the work argues that Adam's sin is transmitted to all humanity through carnal generation and that infants are baptized for the remission of that sin. It also treats marriage and concupiscence, circumcision as a figure of baptism, and the salvation of the pre-Christian righteous through faith in the future mediator Christ. For readers of intertexts it offers a dense accumulation of quoted documents, patristic and especially Pauline citations, making it a valuable node for tracing the formulae of the anti-Pelagian controversy.
la.augustine.de_peccatorum_meritis_et_remis: De peccatorum meritis et remissione et de baptismo parvulorum ('On the Merits and Remission of Sins, and on the Baptism of Infants') is a Late Antique Latin theological treatise by Augustine, cast as a reply to questions put to him by his correspondent Marcellinus. The argument holds that death is the penalty of Adam's disobedience, that original sin reaches all his descendants by propagation rather than imitation, and that infants are baptised for the remission of that inherited guilt, against opponents who attribute sin to imitation alone. Scriptural evidence is assembled throughout, most prominently Paul's contrast of Adam and Christ in Romans and 1 Corinthians, with further discussion of John 6, Psalm 51 and Ecclesiasticus. The treatise is a principal witness to the Latin doctrine of original sin and repays intertextual reading for its dense weave of biblical quotation and exegesis.
la.augustine.de_perfectione_iustitiae_homin: A short Latin theological treatise by Augustine, addressed to his fellow bishops Eutropius and Paul, written in Late Antique prose and traditionally titled On the Perfection of Human Righteousness (De perfectione iustitiae hominis). It takes up a series of definitions attributed to Caelestius on whether a human being can live without sin in this life, quoting each proposition in turn and answering it with the counterclaim that sin can be avoided only when wounded nature is healed by the grace of God through Jesus Christ, while the full perfection of justice is reserved for the life to come. The argument is densely interwoven with scripture—Paul on flesh and spirit and the law, the Psalms, Job, Deuteronomy, the Gospels, and the Lord's Prayer—so the work offers a compact witness to Augustine's refutational method, his formulaic responses, and his habits of biblical citation for readers tracing verbal parallels.
la.augustine.de_trinitate: Augustine's De Trinitate, a Late Antique Latin treatise in theological prose which its author says he began in youth and published as an old man, defends the doctrine that Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are one God of one and the same substance. The prefatory letter to Aurelius transmitted with the work reports the premature circulation and uneven copying of the early books, while the treatise itself assembles scriptural testimonies against subordinationist readings of passages such as 'The Father is greater than I' and proceeds to seek the image of the Trinity in the structure of the human mind. Its dense biblical citation and its vocabulary of unity, equality, and inseparable operation made it one of the most influential sources of Western doctrinal writing, and readers hunting parallels will find its phrasing echoed throughout later medieval theology.
la.augustine.epistula_ad_catholicos_de_sect: A late-antique Latin epistolary treatise by Augustine, bishop of Hippo, addressed to the Catholic brethren in his pastoral care and written against the Donatist sect, answering at length a letter of Petilian, Donatist bishop of Constantine. The work argues that the true church is the single Catholic body diffused through all nations rather than the restricted communion of the Donatists, assembling an extended chain of testimonies from Genesis, Isaiah, the Psalms, the Gospels, and Acts, and treating schism, traditio, persecution, and the mingling of good and evil within the church until the end of the age. For readers of intertexts it offers a dense lattice of biblical quotation and typological interpretation characteristic of Augustinian polemic, much of whose phrasing and scriptural argumentation recurs throughout the anti-Donatist controversy.
la.augustine.liber_qui_appellatur_speculum: The Speculum ('The Book Called the Mirror') is a late-antique Latin work of theology in prose, attributed to Augustine and printed from Franz Weihrich's edition in the Corpus scriptorum ecclesiasticorum Latinorum (vol. 12, Vienna, 1887). Its preface sets out the design: to gather from the canonical scriptures all commands, prohibitions, and permissions that still bear on Christian conduct in the time of the New Testament, arranging them 'as in a mirror' so that the already believing reader may gauge both his progress in good living and what he still lacks, with apparently contradictory passages reserved for later question-and-answer treatment. The body accordingly strings together extensive verbatim quotations, beginning with the Decalogue and the legal and moral precepts of Exodus, Leviticus, Numbers, and Deuteronomy, then continuing through Joshua, the Psalms, Proverbs, Ecclesiastes, the Song of Songs, Job, the minor and major prophets, Tobit, Wisdom, and Ecclesiasticus before turning to the evangelic writings, while distinguishing old-people ceremonial observances from precepts now binding. For readers hunting intertexts, the work is a dense repository of biblical citation as assembled by a patristic compiler and an early large-scale example of the scriptural moral anthology.
la.augustine.locutiones_in_heptateuchum: The Locutiones in Heptateuchum is a short Late Antique Latin prose treatise by Augustine, a philological and theological commentary of some 737 lines on the first seven books of the Bible. It proceeds phrase by phrase through Genesis and the following books, explaining Latin renderings that look awkward or ambiguous as products of Hebrew and Greek idiom, citing the Greek versions and variant Latin readings, and noting habitual scriptural formulas such as 'et factum est'. For readers of intertexts, the work is valuable because it records the wording of the Latin Bible Augustine knew, his awareness of translation problems behind familiar verses, and the interpretive habits that inform his own scriptural allusions elsewhere.
la.augustine.psalmus_contra_partem_donati: The Psalmus contra Partem Donati is a Late Antique Latin psalm composed by Augustine as a popular polemic against the Donatist party, expounding the parable of the dragnet (Matthew 13) to argue that the mingling of just and sinners within the church must be left to God's separation at the end of the age. Built around the recurring refrain 'Omnes qui gaudetis de pace, modo uerum iudicate', it denounces the Donatists for breaking the net of unity, setting altar against altar, traducing their opponents as traditores who betrayed the sacred books, and hiding malice as wolves beneath sheep's clothing. Its dense scriptural allusion, repeated refrain, and compact rehearsal of the standard arguments of the anti-Donatist controversy make it a productive source of parallels for readers tracing biblical paraphrase and polemical diction in Late Antique Latin.
la.augustine.quaestiones_in_heptateuchum: Augustine's Quaestiones in Heptateuchum is a late-antique Latin prose work of biblical theology, comprising 676 lines of questions and short solutions on difficulties arising in the first seven books of the Old Testament, printed in Joseph Zycha's 1895 Vienna edition. The prologue explains that the questions were gathered while reading the canonical scriptures and comparing codices of the Septuagint, and the surviving material works through problems largely in Genesis: the chronology of the patriarchs, the giants born of the 'sons of God', the dimensions and building of Noah's ark, the tower of Babel, and the deeds and sayings of Abraham. Augustine dissolves apparent contradictions by means such as recapitulation, weighs textual variants against the Hebrew and the versions of Aquila and Symmachus, and draws on earlier interpreters like Origen. Readers of intertexts may value the work for its quotations of classical authors such as Aulus Gellius and Horace and for the phrases and exegetical solutions that recur in Augustine's other writings.
la.augustine.retractationum: The Retractationes, a Late Antique prose work of theology by Augustine, surveys the author's own writings, listing his books in order and supplying for each a summary, corrections of passages later regretted, and clarifications of contested points. Opening with a catalogue that runs from the early dialogues De Academicis and De beata uita through anti-Manichaean treatises, Pauline expositions, De doctrina Christiana and the Confessiones, it serves as Augustine's authorised guide to his own corpus, written late in life. For readers tracing intertexts, it offers a contemporary index of Augustinian self-reception, revealing which formulations the author wished emended and how he intended individual works to be understood.
la.ausonius.cupido_cruciatus: A short lyric poem of 103 lines by Ausonius, a poet of the late antique period, the Cupido Cruciatus depicts the torments of mythological lovers—among them Semele, Caenis, Procris, Sappho, Pasiphae, Ariadne, Phaedra, Laodamia, Thisbe, Canace, and Dido—who wander the fields of the dead bearing the tokens and wounds of their deaths. The setting reworks the Elysian fields of Virgil's sixth Aeneid, as the opening line signals by invoking 'the muse of Maro', and the catalogue of unhappy lovers draws heavily on Ovidian material, above all the Heroides. The poem culminates in the lovers seizing Cupid and subjecting him to the crucifixion that gives the work its title. For readers of intertexts, the piece offers a dense late-antique compilation of earlier Latin phrasing and mythological exempla, well suited to tracing Virgilian and Ovidian echoes.
