la.ausonius.de_bissula: De Bissula is a short late-antique cycle in Latin by Decimus Magnus Ausonius, opening with a playful prose preface to his correspondent Paulus, who has pressed for the publication of verses composed in private, and continuing with brief lyric pieces on Bissula, a Suebian girl captured in war across the Rhine, who as a captive governs the household of the very master who took her. The poems dwell on her unadorned beauty set against cosmetics and artifice, her Rhine-born yet Latian character, and close with an injunction to a painter to emulate the Attic bees. A reader of intertexts will note the Horatian diction of the preface, with its profane intruder barred from sacred mysteries, and the elegiac commonplaces surrounding the puella, both readily traceable touchstones for imitation and allusion.
la.ausonius.de_herediolo: De herediolo ('On the Little Estate') is a short Latin poem of thirty-three lines by the late-antique poet Ausonius, prefaced by a prose note explaining that it was playfully composed in a 'Lucilian style' after the author, already a consul, returned to his native land and entered the small villa his father had left him. The verses address the herediolum itself, catalogue its modest assets — land, vineyard, meadows, woodland, well, spring, and a navigable stream — and reflect on inheritance, filial duty, and the setting of limits upon desire. Readers of intertexts will note the poem's parade of moral exempla from Croesus, Diogenes, Aristippus, and Midas, its quotation of the Delphic γνῶθι σεαυτόν, and its engagement with Roman traditions of rural contentment and alternating residence in town and country.
la.ausonius.eclogarum_liber: Eclogarum Liber is a book of short Latin poems in lyric meters by the Late Antique poet Ausonius, running to 445 lines of miscellaneous verse. It opens with a programmatic piece that rewrites Catullus's famous opening question 'Cui dono lepidum novum libellum?' and dedicates the poet's self-deprecating 'unpolished' verses to Pacatus, who is ranked above all other poets except Maro. Elsewhere the collection surveys the miseries that attend every age of life, marshalling mythological exempla such as Iuturna and Prometheus. Readers hunting textual parallels will find in it a compact showcase of Late Antique engagement with Catullus and Virgil and of classical lines repurposed for new dedicatory and rhetorical ends.
la.ausonius.ephemeris_id_est_totius_diei_ne: A late-antique lyric poem by Ausonius, the Ephemeris id est totius diei negotium ('the business of a whole day') traces the round of a single day, opening with a teasing wake-up address to the sluggard slave Parmeno before moving through ablutions, morning prayer, and the day's remaining occupations. Its 234 lines alternate Sapphic stanzas with limping iambics, metres the poem itself names, and the speaker's Christian prayer to God and the son of the highest God is grafted onto the classical lyric frame. Readers hunting parallels will find a compact late-antique reworking of Horatian and Catullan lyric forms and of the day-in-sequence tradition that later poets took up.
la.ausonius.epicedion_in_patrem: The Epicedion in Patrem is a brief late antique funerary poem by Ausonius, running to sixty-five lines, in which the poet's deceased father is made to speak his own epitaph: a retrospective self-portrait covering his practice of medicine, his life between Vasates and Burdigala (Bordeaux), his moderate means and habits, his detachment from faction and litigation, and a marriage of nine lustra that produced four children. A prose preface explains the Greek title as a funerary term taken from Greek usage and asks the reader for affection rather than praise, insisting that nothing is claimed that contemporaries of the father's age would not confirm. Readers of intertexts may value the poem for its adaptation of laudatio funebris and self-epitaph conventions, for its place in Ausonius's cycle of family poems, and for its dramatisation of filial piety through a first-person voice of the dead.
la.ausonius.epigrammata_ausonii_de_diversis: A Latin collection of 613 lines of short epigrams on varied subjects by the Late Antique poet Ausonius, opening with a playful address to the little book itself about the miseries of publication, the waste of oil and sleep, and a mock quarrel with one Proculus. The ensuing poems offer anecdotes and pointed moralising—on King Agathocles of Sicily rising from a potter's household, on an adulterous wife whose mingled poisons become an unintended antidote, on the physician Eunomus—exemplifying the epigrammatist's taste for wit, exemplum, and surprise endings. Several pieces rework themes, anecdotes, and turns of phrase familiar from Greek and earlier Latin epigram, which makes the collection a fertile hunting ground for readers tracing parallels and adaptations across the ancient poetic tradition.
la.ausonius.epistularum: A collection of prose epistles by the Late Antique author Ausonius, the Epistularum runs to some 1,623 lines and assembles short letters of friendship, thanks, and literary encouragement. The correspondence couples everyday courtesies—praise of a correspondent's writings, urging further composition, reflections on whether a published poem can be kept private—with polished Ciceronian diction, as in the opening letter's 'Tulliano melle' and its sententia that 'oratio publicata res libera est'. Readers hunting intertexts will find a late witness to the vocabulary and rhythm of classical epistolography, along with exempla drawn from the Roman stage (Roscius, Ambivius) and aphorisms readily reused across Latin prose.
la.ausonius.epitaphia_heroum_qui_bello_troi: A Latin poem of 185 lines by the late-antique poet Ausonius, presenting imagined epitaphs for the heroes of the Trojan War. Its prose preface to the reader explains that the author came upon the ancient sepulchral tituli of these heroes in the keeping of a philologist and rendered them into Latin, and the ensuing verses speak in the voices of Agamemnon, Menelaus, Ajax, Achilles, Odysseus, Diomedes, Antilochus, and Nestor, among others. Readers hunting intertexts will find dense reworkings of Homeric material, from Menelaus's allotted Elysium and Achilles' tomb on the Sigean shore to the epitaph that instructs the visitor to perlege Odyssean, read the Odyssey to know Ulysses, making the collection a compact late-antique exercise in ventriloquizing epic tradition.
la.ausonius.griphus_ternarii_numeri: The Griphus ternarii numeri, a riddling poem of some ninety lyric lines attributed to Ausonius in the late antique corpus, is an extended encomium of the number three, cast as a catalogue of triads drawn from mythology, ritual, and natural lore. Its verses enumerate such triplets as Nestor's nine-times-nine generations, the triform Hecate, the three Charites and Fates, and the Sphinx's riddle of two feet, four feet, and three, moving from sacred law to learned paradox. For readers of intertexts, the poem offers a dense web of allusions to Greek and Roman myth and a rare specimen of the numerical griphus as a literary form, making it a productive source for tracing triadic formulas and catalogue techniques in later verse.
la.ausonius.ludus_septem_sapientum: A short dramatic piece of 231 lines in lyric measures by the late-antique poet Ausonius, the Ludus Septem Sapientum stages the Seven Sages of Greece appearing palliati before a Roman audience. The prologue solicits the judgement of Drepanius Pacatus, casting him as an Aristarchus or Zenodotus over the verses, while a dialogue on the stone theatres built by Pompey, Balbus, and Caesar explains why Greeks, for whom the theatre stood in place of a senate-house, may act where a togate Roman should blush. Each sage then delivers one of his traditional apophthegms, and a closing song ascribed to Critias rounds off the performance. The dense engagement with Roman comedy, Horatian prologue conventions, and the proverb lore of the Sages makes the work rewarding ground for tracing verbal and thematic parallels.
la.ausonius.mosella: The Mosella is a Late Antique Latin poem of 484 hexameter lines by Ausonius, printed in Hugh G. Evelyn-White's 1919 Loeb edition. Although cataloged under epic, it is chiefly a panegyric of the Moselle river: the opening describes the traveler's road journey from the Nava past Dumnissus to Neumagen, with its memories of the deified Constantine's camp, before the poet hails the river as sovereign of all waters and goes on to praise its vine-clad slopes, its villas, its boatmen and fishermen, and its celebrated catalogue of fish. The poem belongs to the tradition of Latin river praise in hexameters and weaves travel narrative, ecphrasis, and learned enumeration into a densely allusive fabric. Readers hunting intertexts will find its verbal texture thick with echoes of Vergil, Ovid, and earlier Augustan and Silver Latin models, making it a key witness to the afterlife of classical diction and form in late antiquity.
la.ausonius.oratio_consulis_ausonii_versibu: Attributed to Ausonius and styled the prayer of Consul Ausonius in its title, the work is a late-antique Christian petition cast in forty-two rhopalic lines, each built from words of steadily increasing length. The poem addresses Christ as giver of eternal hope, asks pardon and steadfast faith for suppliants, and recalls the baptismal washing of the Jordan, the redeeming Cross, and the witness of Stephen, Paul, and the penitent thief before closing with a plea to be joined to the company of the glorified. A reader hunting intertexts may value its dense liturgical and biblical diction worked into an unusually rigid verbal pattern, a characteristic instance of late-antique formal experiment in devotional verse.
la.ausonius.ordo_urbium_nobilium: The Ordo Urbium Nobilium, a late antique Latin poem of 168 lines in lyric metre by Ausonius, ranks the leading cities of the Roman world in descending order of prestige, with Rome at the head and paired rivals — Constantinople and Carthage, Antioch and Alexandria — followed by Trier and Milan among the western centres. Each city is sketched in a handful of lines that weave together foundation legends, historical memory and topographical detail, from Elissa's Carthage and Byzantium's Lygos to Alexander's founding of Alexandria and the Moselle's commerce at Trier. Its combative pairing of eastern and western cities, and its partisan celebration of Trier, make the poem a compact example of late antique urban encomium, dense with allusion and a useful comparandum for later catalogues and praise-poems of famous cities.
la.ausonius.parentalia: The Parentalia is a short cycle of commemorative poems, 437 lines long, by the late-antique poet Ausonius, written in elegiac couplets in honour of deceased members of his family, beginning with his father and mother. A prose preface connects the title with the ancient festival of offerings to departed kin which it ascribes to Numa, and presents the verses as an annual offering, or nenia, to the shades of the household. Each poem names its subject and distils a life into a few lines of epitaph-like praise, so that the collection reads as a verse family register. Readers hunting parallels will find fertile material in its funerary vocabulary and formulas, its echoes of classical elegy, and its affinities with other commemorative pieces in the Ausonian corpus.
la.ausonius.praefatiunculae: The Praefatiunculae are a brief collection of prefaces, sixty-seven lines in lyric verse, by Ausonius, a Latin poet of the late antique period. The opening poem is largely autobiographical, tracing the poet's origins from a physician father at Burdigala and kin among the Vasates, the Haedui, and the Tarbelli, through his career as grammarian and rhetor, his appointment to teach the imperial family, and his ascent to the quaestorship, the prefecture of Gaul, Libya, and Latium, and the consulship; it closes by recruiting the reader as patron of his poems. Readers of intertexts will find here a compact exercise in poetic self-fashioning, dense with learned reference to figures such as Aemilius, Scaurus, the Berytian Probus, Alcides, the Aeacides, and Chiron, and a useful parallel for the Latin tradition of the autobiographical preface.
la.ausonius.technopaegnion: The Technopaegnion of the Late Antique poet Ausonius, dedicated in prose prefaces to the proconsul Pacatus, is a compact suite of some 193 lines of versicles, each engineered to begin and end with a monosyllable, the closing monosyllable of one verse serving as the opening word of the next in a linked chain. Written in lyric meters and prefaced by a wry apologia for its own difficulty and trifling subject matter, the collection moves through gnomic reflections on Fors, Spes, Mors, and Sol, mythological notices such as the birth of Mars and the ferocious customs of the Thracians, and moralising sententiae on law, piety, and human frailty. The self-imposed formal constraint produces compressed, aphoristic phrasing dense with personifications, proverbs, and mythological material, making the work a productive site for hunting verbal parallels and stock formulations within late antique verse.
la.avitus_of_vienne.de_consolatoria_laude_c: De consolatoria laude castitatis is a Late Antique Christian poem ascribed to Avitus of Vienne, preserved in Migne's Patrologia Latina (vol. 59, Paris, 1847) as a single poem of 1,331 lines without book division. The opening address names the sender as Alcimus, brother of the addressee, a virgin consecrated to Christ in infancy, and pointedly renounces Pegasus, the Pierian Muses, and Phoebus in favour of a 'verax musica plectrum' that sounds Christ. The poem praises chastity through biblical exempla such as Abel's acceptable offering, contrasting the virgin's vow with jewels, gold-woven raiment, twice-dyed Tyrian purple, and the silks of the Seres. Readers hunting parallels will find it a locus for the Latin Christian literature of consecrated virginity and for the strategy of rejecting classical poetic apparatus from within a classicising Latin idiom.
la.avitus_of_vienne.de_spiritalis_historiae: The De spiritalis historiae gestis of Avitus of Vienne is a Late Antique Latin epic in hexameter verse, running to some 2,550 lines and divided into five books. Opening with a prologue on the origin of human toil, sin, and mortality and on Christ's redemptive payment, the poem proceeds into a grand account of the creation of the world, its lights, and its living kinds. Its fusion of classical epic diction with the Genesis narrative makes the work a rich source of parallels for readers tracing how Virgilian language and style were turned to biblical story in late Latin poetry. The edition followed is Migne's 1847 Patrologia Latina text, presented in classical Latin orthography.
la.bede.historiam_ecclesiasticam_gentis_ang: Bede's Historia ecclesiastica gentis Anglorum is a Latin prose history of the conversion of the English to Christianity, presented here in Charles Plummer's 1896 Oxford edition and prefaced by Bede's dedicatory letter to King Ceolwulf. The five-book work opens with the geography of Britain and Ireland, narrates Roman Britain and the coming of the Saxons, and traces the growth of the English church from the Gregorian mission of Augustine of Canterbury through the affairs of Northumbrian kings and bishops, with embedded documents, papal letters, saints' lives, and miracle tales. Its account of Bede's sources and its incorporation of letters of Gregory the Great, Germanus of Auxerre, and other figures made it a central hub for readers tracing classical and patristic intertexts, from Gildas and Pliny to Prosper of Aquitaine, and a model for later medieval historiography.
la.bernowinus.carmina: A short collection of 388 lines of medieval Latin verse attributed to Bernowinus, an otherwise unidentified poet of the Carolingian period, printed by E. Dümmler in 1881. The poems move through the chief events of Christ's life — Gabriel's salutation of Mary, Joseph's presence, the nativity, passion, resurrection, and ascension — in short declarative couplets introduced by 'Hic', in the manner of tituli labelling scenes at a sacred site. The closing lines name Bernowinus as the maker of the work, refer to a saint's body resting within the building and to miracles worked there, and invite visitors to pray. For readers of intertexts, the sequence offers parallels with Carolingian ecclesiastical inscription verse and devotional treatments of the life of Christ.
la.bertharius_of_monte_cassino.carmen_de_sa: A medieval Latin verse life of Saint Benedict in 199 lines, attributed to Bertharius of Monte Cassino and belonging to the Carolingian period. Opening with an invocation of Benedict as father, way, guide, and teacher, the poem recounts celebrated episodes from his life, among them the enemy who shattered the boy's sieve with a stone, the Easter meal sent by the monk Romanus, the poisoned glass broken at the sign of the cross, a noxious bird, and the rod-wielding punishment of a brother who fled the sacred praises. The work sets the Benedictine hagiographic tradition in verse, making it a useful witness for intertextual study of miracle motifs, invocatory openings, and hagiographic diction in Carolingian Latin poetry.
la.boethius.commentaria_in_porphyrium_a_se_: A Latin prose commentary, in dialogue form, on Porphyry's Isagoge, transmitted with the second commentary on the same work and edited from the CSEL edition of Boethius's commentaries on Porphyry. The opening frame sets a winter-night conversation in which a master explains to Fabius the purpose, utility, and order of Porphyry's introduction to Aristotle's Categories, and the discussion then proceeds through the five predicables — genus, species, difference, property, and accident — including the famous passage on whether genera and species truly subsist or exist only in the mind. A foundational document for the Latin reception of Porphyry and the vocabulary of logic that shaped medieval philosophy, it is a rich source of parallels for traditions of Aristotelian, Neoplatonic, and early scholastic thought; its exact date within Boethius's career is not settled by the source record.
la.boethius.liber_de_persona_et_duabus_natu: A brief Latin prose treatise by the late antique philosopher Boethius, addressed as a letter to John the deacon and occasioned, as its opening narrates, by a dispute at a council over whether Christ subsists 'from two natures' or 'in two natures.' Against the opposed errors of Eutyches and Nestorius, the work argues for a middle position and supplies systematic definitions of natura in its several senses and of persona, glossed as an individual substance of a rational nature. Because these distinctions among nature, person, and hypostasis passed into later scholastic theology, readers of intertexts will find here a principal channel through which Aristotelian and Greek patristic vocabulary entered the Latin West.
la.boethius.utrum_pater: A short late-antique Latin prose treatise on the Trinity, headed as the work of Manlius Severinus Boethius, ex-consul and patrician, and addressed to John the Deacon. In sixteen lines it asks whether the names Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are predicated of the divinity substantially (substantialiter) or in some other way, and argues that names such as God, truth, goodness, justice, omnipotence, and immutability are said substantially of the one simple, undivided substance, while Father, Son, Spirit, and Trinity itself are said ad aliquid, arising from the plurality of persons rather than from the substance. Its compact demonstrations of substantial unity and relative predication supply formulae that recur throughout later medieval Latin Trinitarian writing, making it a useful point of comparison for treatments of divine naming and the grammar of the Trinity.
la.caesar.de_bello_gallico: De Bello Gallico is a prose work of historiography from the Roman Republic, written in Latin by Caesar, which recounts his campaigns in Gaul across eight books. The opening book famously surveys the geography and peoples of Gaul before narrating the Helvetian migration and Caesar's resistance to it, establishing the pattern of ethnographic and geographical digression combined with campaign narrative that runs through the whole work. Readers hunting intertexts prize its terse military style, its formulaic battle, siege, and embassy scenes, and its ethnographic descriptions, which later Latin historians, poets, and school authors echo and reuse extensively.
la.calpurnius_siculus.eclogae: The Eclogae of Calpurnius Siculus form a collection of Latin pastoral poems in hexameters, written in the Early Imperial period, of 759 lines in all. Following the Virgilian model, the poems stage conversations and singing contests among herdsmen, and the opening eclogue introduces verses carved on a beech tree in which the god Faunus prophesies a coming golden age, giving the pastoral world a distinctly political and panegyrical coloring. For readers tracing intertexts, the collection is valuable as a self-conscious and densely allusive reworking of Virgil's Eclogues and the Theocritean tradition, showing how Imperial Latin poetry deliberately reanimates its Augustan and Hellenistic models.
la.candidus_of_fulda.epitaphia_aegili: Attributed to Candidus of Fulda, a short Carolingian Latin composition of nineteen lines preserving two epitaphs for Eigil, abbot of Fulda. The first, a twelve-line titulus, summons the passing reader to read the inscription and recounts the abbot's deeds — his happy governance of the monastery, his translation of a martyr's relics with the bishop, the dedication of two churches — closing with a signature by his successor Hrabanus, who calls himself unworthy. The second gives Eigil a speaking voice from the tomb: he rests in the small sepulchre he built while alive and awaits the Lord who will loose the bonds of death and raise him. Readers hunting intertexts will find here the classic address to the passerby, the speaking-deceased inscription, and stock formulas of Carolingian memorial verse that reach back to late antique epitaph and epigram.
la.candidus_of_fulda.vita_aegili: A Carolingian Latin verse life of Aegil, abbot of Fulda, whose opening lines name Candidus of Fulda as the singer and dedicate the poem to his brother Modestus, composed at the aged abbot's own command. Across 834 lines the poem recounts Aegil's noble birth, his boyhood journey to the forest abbey of Fulda with its veneration of the martyr Boniface, and his rule over the community, enriched by the narrator's personal recollections of the man. A preface addresses readers with the image of the ant and its heap of grain, urging respectful handling of the work. For readers of intertexts, the vita offers self-conscious Carolingian hagiographic poetics and points of contact with the monastic literary tradition of Fulda.
la.cato_the_elder.de_agricultura: De Agricultura is a Latin prose treatise on estate management by Cato the Elder, composed during the Roman Republic. Opening with a defense of farming against trade and moneylending, it sets out practical precepts for buying and inspecting a farm, ranking soils and their best uses, supervising the vilicus and the slave familia, and cultivating vines, olives, and other crops, with attention to equipment, accounts, and the seasonal round of labor. Written in terse early Latin prose, the work preserves formulaic instructions and moral themes that later Roman agricultural and didactic writers drew upon, making it a key point of departure for tracing agrarian intertexts.
la.catullus.carmina: The Carmina of Catullus, a Republican collection of lyric poetry in mixed metres, comprises some 113 poems totalling about 2,300 lines in Merrill's edition. The book opens with a dedication to Cornelius and the famous passer poems for the beloved puella, and ranges from personal lyrics of love, friendship, and invective to learned mythological narratives such as the epyllion on the marriage of Peleus and Thetis and the Attis. Its compressed diction, Hellenistic models, and dense allusiveness made it a touchstone for later Latin poets, and it remains a prime hunting ground for readers tracing echoes, phraseology, and mythological material across classical and later literature.
la.celsus.de_medicina: De Medicina is a Latin prose treatise on the art of medicine by Celsus, an author of the early Imperial period, transmitted in eight books. Its opening book surveys the history of medicine from Aesculapius and Hippocrates onward and sets out the rival sects of rationalist, empiricist, and methodist doctors, before proceeding to regimen for the healthy, the signs and prognostication of disease, and general remedies such as bloodletting, cupping, purging, friction, gestation, and diet. Its dense citation of Greek physicians and its bilingual technical vocabulary make it a central witness to the Latin reception of Hellenistic medicine and a rich source of medical intertexts.
la.cicero.de_divinatione: De Divinatione is a Latin philosophical dialogue by Cicero of the Roman Republic, written in prose as a companion to his De Natura Deorum and framed as a conversation between Cicero and his brother Quintus at the Tusculan villa. The work surveys divination in two books: the first sets out the Stoic defence of prophecy in its many forms, including augury, haruspicy, astrology, oracles, dreams, and ecstatic vaticination, drawing on Roman history and Greek philosophy alike; the second replies with Academic scepticism in the manner of Carneades, weighing whether any art of foretelling the future can be rationally justified. Beyond its doctrinal argument, the dialogue preserves a wealth of exempla, from the auguries of Romulus and Attus Navius to quoted verse from Cicero's own De Consulatu Suo, and offers an unusually full Roman account of how religious signs, omens, and philosophical argument intersect. For readers tracing intertexts, it is a central repository of allusions to Ennius, Pacuvius, Stoic writers such as Chrysippus and Posidonius, and Cicero's own earlier philosophical works.
la.cicero.de_domo_sua: An oration of the Roman Republic, the De Domo Sua is Cicero's address to the college of pontiffs seeking restitution of his house on the Palatine, which P. Clodius as tribune had confiscated and consecrated to Libertas during Cicero's absence from the city. Cicero argues before the priests that the consecration is void because Clodius's adoption into a plebeian family and his tribunician legislation were themselves invalid, and he supports the religious case with sustained invective against Clodius and with reflections on the grain crisis, extraordinary commands, and the roles of Caesar, Pompey, Cato, and Bibulus. Combining sacral law with political invective, the speech offers dense material on auspicia, adoption, and consecratio, and its allusive attacks on contemporary figures make it a rich source of parallels for Republican oratory, religious institutions, and the politics of exile and restoration.
la.cicero.de_haruspicum_responso: The De Haruspicum Responso is a senatorial oration in Latin prose by Cicero, belonging to the oratory of the Roman Republic, in which the speaker answers the Etruscan haruspices' report of prodigies that P. Clodius had turned against him as a pretext for challenging the religious standing of Cicero's Palatine house. The speech defends that house as freed from consecration by the verdict of the pontifical college and the decrees of the senate, and attacks Clodius for the slave violence at the Megalesian games, the violation of the rites of the Bona Dea, the destruction and sale of sanctuaries such as Pessinus, and the murder of envoys. A reader of intertexts will find dense mythological and literary allusion — Greek tragic figures such as Philoctetes and Athamas, exempla of Scipio and Claudia, and invective against Clodius as a second Catiline — alongside the Republic's characteristic vocabulary of prodigies, expiation, augury, and pontifical law.
la.cicero.de_imperio_cn_pompei: A Republican-era prose oration by Cicero, De Imperio Cn. Pompei is a speech addressed to the Roman people in support of conferring supreme command in the Mithridatic war on Gnaeus Pompeius. The speaker, presenting himself as addressing the popular assembly from the rostra for the first time, argues the case under three heads — the kind of the war, its magnitude, and the choice of commander — reviewing Lucullus's campaigns, the danger to Asia's revenues and to Roman credit, and Pompey's scientia rei militaris, virtus, auctoritas, and felicitas, including his rapid clearing of the seas of pirates. Dense with historical exempla from Sulla and Murena to the destruction of Corinth and the story of Medea, and memorable for formulations such as vectigalia nervos esse rei publicae, the speech is a central witness to Republican rhetoric on empire, taxation, and extraordinary command, and offers rich material for readers tracing textual parallels.
la.cicero.de_natura_deorum: Cicero's De Natura Deorum, a philosophical dialogue in three books composed during the Roman Republic, stages a debate on the nature of the gods between the Epicurean Velleius, the Stoic Balbus, and the Academic Cotta, prefaced by an address to Brutus on Academic scepticism. The work surveys Greek and Roman theological speculation, criticising Presocratic thinkers, Plato, Aristotle, and the Stoic school while weighing divine providence, creation, and the gods' care for human affairs. Its dense engagement with Plato's Timaeus, Hesiod's Theogony, and a quotation from Caecilius Statius' Synepheba, together with its learned exposition of competing philosophical schools, makes it a rich source of parallels for readers tracing classical intertexts.
la.cicero.de_oratore: Cicero's De Oratore is a three-book rhetorical treatise in Latin prose, composed during the Roman Republic and dedicated to the author's brother Quintus. It stages a dialogue at Crassus's Tusculan villa among leading statesmen-orators of the previous generation—L. Crassus, Q. Mucius Scaevola, and M. Antonius—who debate whether eloquence rests on broad philosophical learning, on natural talent and practice, or on the union of all three, and survey the perfect orator's full equipment, including law, history, psychology of emotion, style, wit, gesture, and memory. Readers hunting intertexts will find dense engagement with Plato (especially the Phaedrus), Aristotle, Isocrates, and Greek rhetorical schools, alongside Cicero's programmatic claim that Roman exempla and orators rival Greek doctrine, making the work a central node for later imitations, quotations, and treatises on eloquence.
la.cicero.de_republica: Cicero's De re publica, a Latin prose philosophical dialogue on the best constitution of a state, composed during the Roman Republic and here edited from C. F. W. Mueller's Teubner edition of 1889, survives only in fragments, of which the present record preserves some 257 lines. Its dramatic frame gathers Scipio Aemilianus, Laelius, Furius Philus, Manilius, Tubero, and their circle during the Latin holidays, and its preface argues that the wise man owes service to the state rather than retreat into learned otium. The surviving discussion defines the res publica as res populi, a people joined by consent of law and community of advantage, in conscious rivalry with Plato's Republic, while quoting Ennius and Pacuvius and invoking Archimedes' sphere, eclipses, and Roman exempla from Camillus and Cato to the aftermath of Tiberius Gracchus. Readers of intertexts will find here a dense meeting of Greek philosophy and Roman political idiom, with named citations of Greek and Roman poets woven into Cicero's defense of active civic life.
la.cicero.de_senectute: Cicero's De Senectute (also transmitted as the Cato Maior) is a Latin prose philosophical dialogue on old age, composed during the Roman Republic and prefaced with a dedication to Cicero's friend Atticus. In the dialogue the aged Cato the Elder, questioned by Scipio Aemilianus and Laelius, answers the four standard complaints against old age — that it withdraws men from activity, weakens the body, cuts them off from pleasure, and brings death near — marshalling exempla from Fabricius and Appius Claudius Caecus to Masinissa, Sophocles, and Nestor. For readers hunting parallels the work is densely embedded in earlier literature: Cato's argument quotes and closely alludes to Ennius, Naevius, Caecilius, the Synephebes of Statius, Homer, and Greek writers such as Xenophon and Plato, while its own formulations on aging passed into the common stock of later Latin and vernacular treatments of old age.
la.cicero.divinatio_in_q_caecilium: A short Latin forensic oration by Cicero of the Republican era, delivered at the divinatio, the preliminary hearing in which a court chose among rival claimants the prosecutor for the extortion trial of C. Verres. Cicero contends that the Sicilians themselves petitioned him to take up their case against Verres's depredations, and that his rival Quintus Caecilius, formerly quaestor in Sicily and closely tied to the defendant, is disqualified both by partiality and by lack of forensic ability. Readers of intertexts will find here the first statement of the charges, personae, and themes—provincial plunder, the lex de pecuniis repetundis, the health of the courts—that recur in Cicero's later speeches against Verres.
la.cicero.in_catilinam: Cicero's In Catilinam, prose oratory of the late Roman Republic, comprises the speeches delivered by Cicero as consul against the conspiracy of L. Sergius Catilina, opening with the celebrated senatorial invective that begins 'quo usque tandem abutere, Catilina, patientia nostra?'. The orations denounce Catiline's attempted coup, justify the consul's refusal to execute him, drive him from Rome, and then report his flight as the start of open war against an openly declared enemy. Readers hunting intertexts will find here some of the most persistently quoted passages of Latin prose, including 'O tempora, o mores!', the exhortation of the personified patria, 'abiit, excessit, evasit, erupit', and 'O fortunatam rem publicam', phrases and set pieces echoed by later Latin authors and by writers of the Renaissance and beyond.
la.cicero.in_vatinium: Cicero's In Vatinium, preserved in Albert Clark's Oxford text of 1909, is a brief speech of the Roman Republic consisting almost entirely of a caustic interrogation of Publius Vatinius, who appeared as a witness in the trial of Sestius. Question by question the orator exposes the witness's perjury, disreputable youth, corrupt quaestorship, tribunate marked by contempt for the auspices and the leges Aelia et Fufia, entanglement in the Vettius affair, and dependence on the patronage of Caesar and Clodius, setting Vatinius's sordid career against Cicero's own exile and recall. Readers hunting textual parallels will find in it a dense matrix of Republican invective formulae, legal and religious vocabulary, and echoes of the political crises that also animate the Pro Sestio and the Pro Milone.
la.cicero.letters_to_atticus: Cicero's Letters to Atticus (Epistulae ad Atticum), here in the Oxford edition of L. C. Purser (1906), form a collection of Latin prose correspondence in sixteen books addressed to Cicero's intimate friend Atticus during the Roman Republic. The letters move between confidential political reporting—election campaigns, rivalry with contemporaries such as Catiline, Caesar, and Pompey—and domestic and personal matters: family news, financial affairs, grief, reconciliation, and the collecting of books and sculptures for Cicero's villas, with frequent Greek phrases reflecting the cultivated idiom shared by the correspondents. Their unguarded, near-contemporary register makes them a rewarding quarry for readers tracing echoes of Republican political life, epistolary style, and Cicero's engagement with Greek language and thought.
la.cicero.pro_a_caecina: Pro Caecina (Pro A. Caecina) is a forensic oration by Cicero, composed during the Republic, defending Aulus Caecina against Sextus Aebutius in a recuperatorial trial arising from an interdict de vi hominibus armatis, after Aebutius stationed armed men to bar Caecina from an estate in the territory of Tarquinii that Caecina claimed through his inheritance from Caesennia. The speech couples a vivid narrative of the armed confrontation and a mordant gallery of opponents and witnesses, above all the senator Fidiculanius Falcula, with a sustained argument over whether a man repelled by force at a boundary counts as 'ejected' within the meaning of the praetor's interdict. Readers hunting parallels value its dense legal diction, its engagement with juristic formulae and the interpretation of an interdict's wording, and allusive touches such as the comparison of the witness Sex. Clodius Phormio with Terence's Phormio.
la.cicero.pro_a_cluentio: A Latin forensic oration by Cicero of the Republican era, the Pro Cluentio defends Aulus Cluentius Habitus of Larinum against the charge that he bribed the judges of the iudicium Iunianum to procure the condemnation of Statius Albius Oppianicus for poisoning. Cicero's strategy inverts the accusation: Oppianicus, depicted at length as a serial poisoner of wives, brothers, and stepchildren and as a violent beneficiary of the Sullan proscriptions, is shown to have been justly condemned, while suspicion is redirected onto Sassia, Cluentius' own mother, in some of the fiercest invective in Roman oratory. Readers hunting parallels will find here the exordium's sustained antithesis of invidia and criminal proof, topoi of judicial corruption and popular rumor, extended narratives of veneficium and household crime, and abundant detail on legal procedure and municipal life at Larinum and Rome.
la.cicero.pro_archia: Pro Archia is a prose oration by Marcus Tullius Cicero of the Roman Republic, delivered in defence of the Greek poet A. Licinius Archias against a challenge to his Roman citizenship. The speech marshals testimony for Archias's enrolment at Heraclea before turning to a celebrated digression on the value of literature, invoking Ennius, Homer, Alexander, and Roman commanders who honoured poets. Readers hunting intertexts prize it as a locus classicus for Latin claims that poetry immortalises achievement, and for its dense web of allusion to Greek and Roman literary precedent.
la.cicero.pro_balbo: A forensic oration by Cicero of the Roman Republic, delivered in defense of Lucius Cornelius Balbus of Gades, who stood accused of having obtained Roman citizenship unlawfully through a grant by Pompey. The preserved portion opens as the closing peroration, following speeches on Balbus's behalf by M. Crassus and by Pompey himself, and defends the citizenship against the charge that it violated the treaty between Rome and Gades. Cicero argues from the lex Gellia Cornelia, which authorized Pompey to grant citizenship with his council's consent, and refutes at length the prosecution's reading of the Gaditan treaty, treating along the way the history of enfranchisement from Romulus onward, dual citizenship, the legal force of foedera and of sacrosanct leges, and the interpretation of the formula maiestatem comiter conservanto. Its dense legal and antiquarian argument, its exempla from the Scipiones to the war in Spain, and its sustained encomium of Pompey make it fertile ground for parallels in oratory, legal reasoning, and Republican political vocabulary.
la.cicero.pro_c_rabirio_perduellionis_reo: A forensic oration by Cicero, delivered during his consulship in the late Roman Republic, in defence of Gaius Rabirius, who stood accused by the tribune Titus Labienus of perduellio (high treason) for his part in the death of the tribune Lucius Appuleius Saturninus decades earlier. Cicero recasts the trial as an attack on the authority of the senate and the senatus consultum ultimum, dwelling on the archaic ritual of the perduellionis iudicium and denouncing the revival of crucifixion as a penalty for Roman citizens, with pointed appeals to the precedents of Gaius Gracchus and the Porcian laws. For readers of intertexts the speech offers rich material on republican liberty rhetoric, the politics of popularis tribunes, and Cicero's self-fashioning as a consular defender of concordia ordinum, much of it later echoed in his other political speeches.
la.cicero.pro_fonteio: A Latin forensic oration of the Roman Republic, Cicero's Pro Fonteio defends Marcus Fonteius against charges of misappropriating public money during his quaestorship and of improper exactions and misconduct during his command in Gallia Narbonensis. Transmitted incomplete and beginning abruptly in mid-argument, the surviving defence scrutinises the public accounts, contrasts Roman colonists, negotiatores, and the loyal Massilians with Gallic accusers whose credibility it relentlessly attacks, and answers specific accusations over a wine toll, the construction of the Via Domitia, and the war with the Vocontii. The speech is also a locus for ethnographic invective on Gallic irreligion, human sacrifice, and the menace of a new Gallic war, and so rewards comparison with Roman ethnographic commonplaces from Caesar's commentaries onward and with Cicero's treatment of provincial testimony in his other speeches. The text is printed here from Clark's Oxford edition of 1909.
la.cicero.pro_ligario: Cicero's Pro Ligario is a defense speech in Republican Latin prose oratory, addressed to Julius Caesar as victor in the civil war and pleading for the acquittal of Quintus Ligarius, whom Quintus Tubero accused of bearing arms against Caesar in Africa. The argument concedes the charge outright and relocates the case from guilt to pardon, contrasting the clemency and mercy appropriate to a victor with the accuser's own service under Pompey, whom the speech treats as dead. For readers of intertexts it offers loci on clementia in civil discord, suppliant tears and fraternal pietas, and exile worse than death, along with memorable sententiae such as the claim that humans come nearest to the gods when they give salvation to others. The work is printed here in Albert Clark's Oxford edition of 1918.
la.cicero.pro_milone: A forensic oration in Latin prose by Cicero, composed for the defence of Titus Annius Milo, who stood trial during the Roman Republic for the killing of Publius Clodius on the Appian Way. Cicero argues that Milo struck back at an ambush laid by Clodius, appealing to an unwritten natural law of self-defence, to the maxim that laws fall silent amid arms, and to a chain of Roman exempla from Horatius and Servilius Ahala through the Gracchi and Marius, alongside close argument over senatorial decrees and Pompey's special commission. Readers hunting parallels will find in the speech a dense repertory of legal and philosophical commonplaces—necessity, natural right, and justifiable political violence—that later authors quote and rework, above all the celebrated sentence on laws silent among arms.
la.cicero.pro_plancio: Cicero's Pro Plancio is a forensic oration of the Roman Republic, defending Gnaeus Plancius against a charge of electoral corruption brought under the lex Licinia de sodaliciis by Marcus Laterensis. The speech intertwines the legal defense with public gratitude, recalling how Plancius protected Cicero during his exile and arguing that the Roman people's judgment in the comitia cannot itself be treated as a crime. Alongside sustained reflection on ambitus, comitial procedure, and the rival dignitas of defendant and prosecutor, the oration offers rich material on municipal Italy, the equites, and Cicero's own political fortunes, making it a fertile hunting ground for intertexts of late Republican oratory.
la.cicero.pro_publio_quinctio: Pro Publio Quinctio is a forensic oration in Latin prose from the Roman Republic, in which Cicero speaks for the defense of Publius Quinctius in a civil action against Sextus Naevius, addressing the judge Gaius Aquilius and contending with the opposing advocate Quintus Hortensius. The speech opens with an exordium on the unequal contest between the plaintiff's influence and eloquence and the defendant's isolation, then proceeds to a narrative of a Gallic business partnership with the late C. Quinctius, the heir's alleged debts, the seizure and possession of Quinctius' goods under a praetor's edict, and a disputed sponsio over whether that possession was lawful. Readers of intertexts will find here a dense repertory of Republican legal vocabulary and procedure (vadimonia, bonorum possessio, iudicatum solvi, de probro priore loco dicere) together with classic exordium topoi of patron, client, and adversarial gratia that later oratory repeatedly echoes.
la.claudian.carmina_minora: The Carmina Minora assembles the shorter poems of Claudian, a Latin poet of Late Antiquity writing in hexameter and largely in the panegyric mode. The opening lines celebrate the general Stilicho, playing on his marriage ties to the imperial house ('Stilicho socer est, pater est Stilicho'), while other passages build mythological set pieces that set contemporary subjects against Geryon's triple-bodied cattle, the bulls of Clitumnus, and the monsters of Crete. Spanning some 1,867 lines as a single collection, the work offers readers of intertexts a compact quarry of mythological exempla, Castalian and Apollonian diction, and encomiastic invention through which late antique court poetry reworked classical tradition.
la.claudian.de_bello_gothico: A Latin panegyric in 665 hexameter lines by the late antique poet Claudian, De Bello Gothico celebrates the campaigns of Stilicho against the Goths. Its prologue announces the poet's return to song after an absence of years and weighs the hazards of praising Stilicho before a public audience, while the narrative opens with an extended comparison between the general and Tiphys, who steered the Argo through the clashing Symplegades. Dense with epic and mythological allusion in the service of contemporary politics, the poem offers fertile ground for tracing how late antique panegyric reworks heroic and voyage imagery from earlier Latin and Greek tradition.
la.claudian.de_consulatu_stilichonis: A panegyric in three books of Latin hexameter by the late antique poet Claudian, running to 1254 lines and celebrating the consulship of Stilicho. The opening weighs which of its subject's merits can be crowded into a single song — the defeat of Gildo, the wedding songs of the imperial house, Africa restored to Roman obedience, justice joined with martial glory — and undertakes to follow Stilicho's career from his youth onward. The poem carries the machinery of classical epic and encomium into a late antique court setting, its diction and motifs densely indebted to earlier Latin verse. For readers tracing intertexts, it offers a rich field of verbal echoes and traditional praise-formulae reshaped to flatter a contemporary general.
la.claudian.de_raptu_proserpinae: Claudian's De Raptu Proserpinae is a Late Antique Latin epic in hexameters, transmitted in three books totalling 1172 lines, devoted to the abduction of Proserpina by Dis. The proem opens with the figure of the first mariner venturing onto the deep as an emblem of audacity before summoning the powers of the underworld — Hecate in her triple form, Iacchus crowned with ivy, the Eleusinian retinue, and the smoking floods of Avernus — to reveal by what flame of love Dis was won and in what rapture Proserpina seized her dowry of Chaos. Composed in a richly allusive epic manner, the poem refashions the mythological material of earlier Latin verse, and its dense web of verbal, mythological and cosmological echoes makes it a fertile hunting ground for readers tracing parallels across classical and late-antique poetry.
la.claudian.epithalamium_de_nuptiis_honorii: An epithalamium in hexameters by the late antique poet Claudian, celebrating the marriage of the emperor Honorius to Maria. The poem opens with the mythological wedding feast of Peleus and Thetis, where Apollo's song foretells the deeds of Achilles, before turning to Honorius's lovesick longing for his bride, whose adornment is measured against that of Livia and other imperial women. Its dense weave of epic and elegiac allusion, especially around the Peleus and Thetis tradition and the figure of Achilles among the women of Scyros, makes it rewarding ground for readers tracing classical intertexts in late antique court panegyric.
la.claudian.in_consulatum_olybrii_et_probin: A Late Antique Latin panegyric in hexameters by Claudian, running to 279 lines, composed in honour of the joint consulship of Olybrius and Probinus. The poem opens with a cosmological address to the sun and the turning of the consular year, then praises a noble lineage in which the fasces descend unbroken from ancestor to heir, before celebrating the deeds and virtues of the two consuls in turn. For readers hunting textual parallels it offers a compact specimen of Late Antique encomium, dense with epic diction, celestial similes, and echoes of Augustan and imperial Latin verse.
la.claudian.in_eutropium: In Eutropium is a two-book Latin poem in hexameters by the Late Antique poet Claudian, totalling 1191 lines and catalogued as panegyric though in substance a sustained invective against the eunuch consul Eutropius. The first book opens with a catalogue of prodigies attending the consulship — wolf-born offspring, talking cattle, twin suns and clashing moons — and an appeal to the Sibylline verses and Etruscan haruspicy, before a speech of Fortune laments the consul's servile origins, his degraded past, and his corruption of public life. For readers of intertexts, the poem offers dense Virgilian and Ovidian texture and a showpiece Late Antique deployment of the Roman traditions of prodigy, Sibylline consultation, and divine personification.
la.claudian.in_rufinum: In Rufinum is a two-book Latin invective in hexameters by the Late Antique poet Claudian, directed against the courtier Rufinus and cast as a panegyric in reverse. The poem opens with an elaborate allegory of Apollo's slaying of Python, moves into a debate over divine providence provoked by the prosperity of the wicked, and proceeds toward an account of Rufinus's fall. Its sustained imitation of Virgilian, Ovidian, and Lucanian diction, together with its systematic inversion of encomiastic topoi, makes it a rich source of parallels for readers of late Latin epic and the reception of classical models.
la.claudian.panegyricus_de_quarto_consulatu: A late antique Latin panegyric in hexameter verse by Claudian, celebrating the fourth consulship of the emperor Honorius in a single continuous poem of 656 lines. The opening casts the consular year as a fusion of war and civic ritual — returning fasces, a soldiery grown togate, Bellona herself laying aside helmet and shield — before a genealogical encomium traces the imperial line and its conquests from the frozen north, where the Orcades ran with Saxon blood and ice-bound Hibernia mourned her dead, to the deserts of Libya, the Mauretanian strongholds, and the burning reaches of Ethiopia. Readers of intertexts will find the poem dense with epic diction, mythological exempla, and recycled Augustan and Silver Latin material, and it stands as a principal witness to the rhetoric and political imagery of late Roman court panegyric.
la.claudian.panegyricus_de_sexto_consulatu_: A late antique Latin panegyric in hexameters by Claudian, running to 686 lines, celebrating the sixth consulship of the emperor Honorius. The poem opens with a nocturnal dream vision in which the poet's devotion to the Muses bears his song before the very throne of Jupiter, recounting the defeat of Enceladus and Typhoeus and the rewards of the Phlegraean campaign, until Honorius himself appears as 'orbis apex aequatus Olympo' and the dream proves true. The praise then unfolds through the temple owed to Fortune, the auguries of the auspicious year, and a fusion of civic and martial imagery — consular robes, the Campus Martius, the joining of Quirinus to the soldiery — that presents the emperor's majesty as native, cosmic, and divinely sanctioned. Its dream proem, mythological exempla, and dense epic diction make the work a productive source of parallels for classical epic language and panegyrical convention.
la.claudian.panegyricus_de_tertio_consulatu: A Latin panegyric in 229 hexameter lines by Claudian, a Late Antique court poet, celebrating the third consulship of the emperor Honorius. The poem opens with the allegory of the mother eagle exposing her eaglets to the sun as a test of worth, an emblem of innate imperial virtue, before turning to the poet's summons from Rome and praise of an emperor nurtured in palace and camps, whose birth shook Germany, the Caucasus, and Meroe with prodigies; the emperor's brother, ruling in the East, is also acknowledged. Readers hunting parallels will find dense engagement with classical epic diction and the stock topoi of imperial encomium, and the poem's phrasing and themes recur across Claudian's consulship panegyrics, making it valuable for tracing allusive and formulaic reuse.
la.claudius_mamertinus.panegyricus: The Panegyricus of Claudius Mamertinus, preserved in the collection of the XII Panegyrici Latini, is a Latin thanksgiving oration of the later imperial period in which a newly appointed consul renders formal gratitude to the emperor Julian. The speaker excuses his earlier silence, rehearses the honours Julian had conferred upon him, and praises the emperor's recovery of Gaul, his destruction of the Alamanni, his sudden descent into Illyricum, and his beneficent voyage down the Danube, while pointedly contrasting Julian's virtues with the failings of the late Constantius. Its dense mythological exempla, including allusions to the Golden Fleece and Triptolemus, its recycled panegyric topoi, and its ornate later-imperial prose make it a rewarding source of verbal and thematic parallels for readers tracing the tradition of Latin panegyric and other accounts of Julian's reign.
la.columella.de_re_rustica: De Re Rustica is a Latin prose treatise on agriculture by Columella, a writer of the Early Imperial period, opening with a preface addressed to P. Silvinus. The preface laments the neglect of farming by the Roman elite, blames the enslavement and ignorance of estate labor rather than any decline in the soil, and argues that agriculture, as an art nearest to wisdom, deserves the same systematic instruction as rhetoric or philosophy. Columella then sketches the vast range of knowledge the ideal farmer requires, from varieties of soil, climate, and the movements of the stars to viticulture, fruit trees, livestock, and poultry, while weighing the claims of Greek and Roman predecessors such as Hesiod, Xenophon, Varro, Tremelius, the Sasernae, and Stolo. The book is densely allusive, invoking Cicero's Orator, the poets Accius and Vergil, and the exempla of Cincinnatus, Fabricius, and Curius Dentatus, and so offers readers of intertexts a rich web of references to the earlier agricultural and literary tradition.
la.commodian.carmen_apologeticum: An apologetic and theological work in Latin, the Carmen Apologeticum is attributed to Commodian, a Christian writer of the Later Imperial era, and runs to 1,057 lines. It opens with an autobiographical account of conversion, in which the speaker recounts youthful wandering in pagan error, including Marsic incantations, until study of the law in a codex reveals to him the one supreme God of heaven. From that personal testimony the work proceeds to exhortation, urging high and low alike to read Scripture continually on the grounds that life is brief and ignorance befits only beasts, while rebuking the wealthy who trust in Caesar and live like fatted swine. Readers hunting intertexts will find dense biblical diction, a programmatic appeal to the law as the source of wisdom, and the anti-pagan argument characteristic of Later Imperial apologetic.
la.commodian.instructiones: The Instructiones of Commodian, a theological work of the later Imperial period in Latin, runs to 1,257 lines across two books. Its opening preface announces the aim of showing the errant the way to eternal life and recounts the author's own turn from pagan observance after reading the law. The instruction that follows urges abandonment of vain idols, rehearsing the giving of the law through Moses, the fall of the angels and the birth of the giants, and polemic against deities such as Saturn. Readers hunting biblical paraphrase, apologetic commonplaces, and anti-pagan topoi in later Imperial Latin Christian literature will find dense material for parallel-hunting.
la.corippus.johannis: Corippus's Johannis is a Late Antique Latin epic in hexameters, comprising eight books and 4,669 lines, named for the commander John and recounting the wars waged in Africa under the emperor Justinian, whom the proem celebrates in the language of triumph and restored peace. Its opening lines enumerate the themes of wild peoples, slaughter, treachery, famine, denied water and captivity, and portray Libya wasted by barbarian fury until Pax, Victoria, Pietas, Iustitia and Concordia return to a world rejoicing under Roman rule. The programmatic summons to the Camenae to 'resound the Aeneads again' announces a deliberately Vergilian project, and the poem's dense reworking of classical epic diction makes it a rewarding source for readers tracing intertexts from Vergil into Late Antique verse.
la.cyprian.ad_donatum: Ad Donatum is a brief Latin prose treatise of late-antique date in which the Christian writer Cyprian addresses his friend Donatus, opening with a congenial garden scene before turning to graver matters. The work recounts the author's own conversion and baptism, then surveys the corruption of the surrounding world — the gladiatorial arena, the theatre, the lawcourts, the pursuit of wealth and office — against which it sets the security and purity of the new life in God. Its polished, rhythmical prose is deeply indebted to classical moralising traditions, and its first-person account of a decisive religious change makes it an early landmark in the Latin literature of conversion, a natural point of comparison for later autobiographical writing and for the Christian reworking of pagan literary forms.
la.cyprian.de_lapsis: De Lapsis is a late-antique Latin prose treatise by Cyprian, addressed to a Christian community rejoicing at peace restored after a recent persecution. It praises the confessors who stood firm, then mourns and rebukes the many who sacrificed to idols or obtained certificates of compliance, condemning the lax clergy who admitted them to communion at once and insisting instead on long, tearful penance, while denying that martyrs can forgive sins on their own authority. Woven through with quotation and allusion to scripture, from Daniel, Ezekiel, and Joel to the Gospels and Paul, the work is a key witness to early controversies over penitential discipline and martyr prerogatives, and a rich quarry of biblical diction for readers tracing textual parallels.
la.cyprian.de_mortalitate: De mortalitate is a late-antique Latin prose treatise, transmitted under the name of Cyprian, written to console Christians confronting a lethal pestilence. It argues that the present mortality is not a common ruin but a testing and a deliverance, since death for the believer is a passage to immortality, the reward of intended martyrdom, and the true homeland of paradise. Its argument rests on dense citation and paraphrase of scripture—Simeon's Nunc dimittis, Job, Tobias, Abraham, Paul, and John among others—woven together with similes drawn from shipwreck, agriculture, and military discipline. For readers of intertexts, the work offers a rich witness to the scriptural texture of early Christian consolation and a source for images of death, exile, and pilgrimage that echo throughout later Latin literature.
la.cyprian.epistulae: The Epistulae of Cyprian, a late antique collection of Latin ecclesiastical prose letters printed in Wilhelm August Ritter von Hartel's 1871 Vienna edition of the Opera Omnia, gathers episcopal correspondence on questions of church order and pastoral discipline. The letters preserved here pronounce conciliar rulings against clergy who accept testamentary guardianships, debate whether an actor may hold communion, rebuke an insubordinate deacon, treat virgins cohabiting with men, and exhort confessors imprisoned for the faith, with instructions on prayer, fasting, almsgiving, and the commemoration of martyrs. Its dense weaving of scriptural citation and allusion, along with its recurring formulas of address and farewell, offers readers of intertexts a central witness to how biblical language circulates in late antique epistolary prose.
la.cyprian_pseudo.ad_senatorem_ex_christian: A short Latin invective of uncertain date, assigned to the later imperial era and transmitted under the name of Cyprian, addressed to a senator who has renounced Christianity for the servitude of idols. Across its eighty-five lines the speaker voices astonishment at the addressee's relapse, ridicules the effeminate Galli of the Great Mother who change their dress, sex, and shed their own blood, mocks a former consul now serving as a minister of Isis, and urges him to exchange darkness for light and return to the faith. The work offers a concentrated example of later Roman anti-pagan polemic, its vocabulary of error, apostasy, idolatry, and cult mockery supplying rich points of contact for readers tracing apologetic and satirical motifs through late antique Latin literature.
la.cyprian_pseudo.de_pascha: De Pascha is a short Latin poem of 69 lines, transmitted under the name of Cyprian and assigned to the later imperial period, that presents an allegorical vision of Easter centred on Golgotha. In the opening hexameters a tree cut from barren wood and planted on the site of the Crucifixion bears salutary fruit, grows to heaven in forty days, puts forth twelve branches spread through the whole world for the sustenance of all peoples, and after fifty days distils the nectar of the divine Spirit, while nations of every age, sex, and rank gather at a fountain beneath its shade to wash away the stains of their former life. Readers hunting textual parallels will find here a compact example of later imperial Christian allegory, reworking Passover typology through the imagery of the cross as life-giving tree, baptismal washing, and Pentecostal outpouring in a diction close to that of biblical epic.
la.cyprianus_cordubensis.cypriani_et_samson: A short collection of eighty-four lines of Latin verse transmitted under the names of Cyprian of Córdoba and Samson, its date given only broadly as later imperial to medieval. It opens with a dedicatory inscription in verse in which Count Adulf records how, at his own expense, he renewed a book-case (teca) holding books of the Old and New Testament at the church of the martyr Acisclus in Córdoba, asks his son Fredenandus to keep and reread the volumes, and closes with lines on a fan inscribed in golden letters with the name Guifredus. Imagery of the soul nourished on scripture rather than food, of paradise springs, and of Christ cleansing sin weaves dense biblical allusion through the poem, whose Cordoban vocabulary and spelling make it a rewarding comparison for Iberian dedicatory verse and inscriptional poetry.
la.cyprianus_gallus.heptateuchos: A late antique Latin biblical epic of uncertain date, attributed to the poet known as Cyprianus Gallus, the Heptateuchos renders the Heptateuch—the first seven books of the Old Testament, from Genesis through Judges—into hexameter verse across seven books totaling some 5,550 lines. Its opening book paraphrases the Genesis account of the six days of creation, the fashioning of Adam and Eve, and the naming of humanity in classicizing epic diction. Readers hunting parallels will find the poem valuable both for the way Virgilian language and formulae are retooled for scriptural narrative and for comparison between its cosmogony and Ovidian accounts of chaos and creation.
la.descartes.meditations: René Descartes' Meditations, a Latin prose treatise of philosophy from the modern era, preserved in the Adam and Tannery edition of the Oeuvres de Descartes (Paris, 1904), undertakes a methodical demolition of received belief in search of something firm and enduring in the sciences. From doubt cast upon the senses, the dream argument, and the hypothesis of a supremely powerful and cunning deceiver, the argument arrives at the celebrated certainty 'Ego sum, ego existo' and the definition of the self as a res cogitans. Subsequent reflections on the melting piece of wax and on the division of ideas into innate, adventitious, and factitious ground the rule that whatever is perceived clearly and distinctly is true. As the classic formulation of the cogito, the malicious demon, and rationalist epistemology, the work stands behind centuries of later philosophical and literary allusion and is a prime resource for readers tracing skeptical and foundationalist intertexts.
la.dhuoda.rhythmy_ex_manuali_dhuodanae: The Rhythmy ex Manuali Dhuodanae gathers the Latin verses transmitted with Dhuoda's Carolingian Manual, a didactic work of uncertain date addressed by a mother to her son William. Across 289 lines the pieces open with a hymn-like invocation of God as maker of light and eternal king, confess the speaker's frailty and exile, and commend young Willelmus to divine protection, grace, and peace of body and mind. Verse by a named Carolingian woman is rare, and the hymnic formulas, biblical diction, and language of parental solicitude here give readers of intertexts abundant points of comparison.
la.dicuil.versus: A short Carolingian Latin poem of nineteen lines ascribed to Dicuil, who names himself within the verses and addresses the son begotten of Charles together with Louis, Charles's successor, placing the piece in the circle of the Carolingian court. The poet presents his work as playful 'argumenta' composed in praise and riddling fashion, taking the calendar as its theme from the month of April onward, and closes with a humble offering likened to the widow's two mites of the Gospels. Its internal computation of years points to a composition in 814, at the transition from Charlemagne's reign to that of Louis the Pious. The poem offers useful parallels for intertextual study of Carolingian occasional verse, calendrical riddling, and scriptural allusion in courtly panegyric.
la.dracontius.de_laudibus_dei: De Laudibus Dei is a Christian didactic epic in Latin hexameters by the late antique poet Dracontius, transmitted in three books totalling 2,327 lines. The opening announces its program: to make known the anger and mercy of the thundering God, cataloguing the regions of the sky, the elements, weather, and calamities, together with the contrasting lots of rich and poor, blessed and miserable, all descending from the seat of God. The poem moves from creation and providence toward prophecy and the coming of Christ, though the passage describing the advent is damaged in the transmitted lines. For readers of intertexts, the work fuses inherited epic diction—epithets of Jupiter such as Tonans now applied to the Christian God—with biblical narrative and moral doctrine, making it a productive locus for parallels between classical epic formulas and the Latin Christian tradition.
la.dracontius.romulea: The Romulea of Dracontius, a Late Antique poet, is a compact collection of short mythological poems in lyric measures, preserved in some 2,350 lines and edited by Vollmer in 1905. Its preface invokes a revered teacher credited with restoring letters to the African city and joining Romulean youths with barbarian pupils in his lecture room, before the collection turns to mythological narrative, opening with the tale of Hylas borne off by the nymphs to the grief of Hercules. The poems gather familiar figures — Orpheus, Venus, Hercules and their peers — retold in polished miniature, and offer rich hunting ground for readers tracing reworkings of classical myth and allusion to earlier Latin narrative poetry.
la.engelmodus.carmina: A collection of 400 lines of Latin verse attributed to Engelmodus, a poet of the Carolingian period, transmitted without division into books. The opening poem is an elegiac verse epistle in which a personified letter (cartula) is dispatched to a beloved friend, charged with kisses, greetings, and affectionate praise of one Agi, extolled for Ciceronian eloquence and Platonic acuteness. Its Ovidian treatment of the speaking letter and its self-conscious invocation of classical auctores make the collection a characteristic instance of Carolingian friendship poetry, of particular interest for readers tracing the medieval afterlife of Ovidian epistolary and elegiac motifs.
la.ennius.annales: The Annales of Ennius, an epic in dactylic hexameters of the Roman Republic, survives only in fragments, some 680 lines collected in E. H. Warmington's Remains of Old Latin, Volume One (Harvard University Press, 1935). The preserved passages range from the poet's celebrated dream of Homer and the transmigration of his soul, through the voyage of Aeneas to Hesperia and the reign of Saturn among the Latin peoples, to episodes of Alban and early Roman legend such as Ilia's prophetic dream. Although incomplete, the poem established the hexameter as the standard vehicle of Latin epic, and its lines were among the most frequently quoted in antiquity. For readers tracing intertexts, the Annales supplies both direct reworkings of Homer and a stock of phrasing and motifs repeatedly borrowed by later Latin poets.
la.ennodius.carmina: Ennodius' Carmina is a Latin collection of poetry by the late antique author Ennodius, preserved in Wilhelm von Hartel's Opera Omnia (Vindobonae: Gerold, 1882); the source record fixes neither the date of composition nor the metres employed. The roughly 1,024 lines open with a narrative poem recounting a punishing journey across the Alps, in which the speaker, exposed to summer heat and wintry cold within a single day, invokes the Muses and casts his route through Daedalus, the Pierides, and hazardous rivers such as the Duria, Sessis, Stura, and Orgus. This mixture of mythological exempla, rhetorical set pieces, and contemporary geography makes the collection a rewarding quarry for readers tracing classical allusion and poetic diction in late antique verse.
la.ermenricus_elwagensis.epistola_ad_grimal: A Carolingian Latin verse epistle, attributed by its title to Ermenricus Elwagensis and addressed to a Grimald. Running to some 230 lines, the poem opens with an invocation of the Trinity and a meditation on the incomprehensibility of God, proceeds through prayer for divine aid in singing of Gallus, and closes with reflections on a Godhead free of measure, degree, and time, together with counsel to its reader. Its hymnic opening, professions of authorial inadequacy, and direct address to the reader place it among Carolingian verse prefaces, and it rewards readers of intertexts for the light it sheds on the passage of classical and Christian invocatory conventions into medieval Latin poetry.
la.ermoldus_nigellus.carmen_in_honorem_Ludo: An epic of 2,653 Latin hexameters by the Carolingian poet Ermoldus Nigellus, written in honor of the emperor Louis the Pious and framed, on its own testimony, as a plea from exile for that ruler's favor. Its opening prayer to Christ pointedly renounces the Nymphs, the Pierides, Phoebus, and Apollo as sources of poetic power, invoking instead Davidic prophecy and Christian grace for the task of singing Caesar's deeds. The poem thus adapts the classicizing heroic epic to the panegyric of a Christian emperor, a hallmark of Carolingian court verse. Readers of intertexts will find here a deliberate inversion of the pagan epic invocation alongside a dense weaving of biblical, liturgical, and classical diction into praise poetry.
la.ermoldus_nigellus.carmen_in_laudem_pippi: Ermoldus Nigellus's Carmen in Laudem Pippini Regis is a Carolingian panegyric epic of 423 Latin hexameters in praise of a King Pippin. The poem opens with an invocation to Thalia and an account of a favoured river landscape with its golden fields and a royal palace completed at the command of a Louis, before moving to scenes of court ceremonial: officials hastening to their duties, a king radiant as Phoebus, and a queen proceeding with her maidens to the church. Its classicising diction and epic apparatus make it a useful point of comparison for readers tracing Muse invocations, solar similes, and panegyric formulas across Latin verse from late antiquity into the Carolingian period.
la.ermoldus_nigellus.carminum_appendix: A brief appendix of 52 hexameter lines, classed with epic verse, attached to the Carmina of the Carolingian poet Ermoldus Nigellus. The opening sequence addresses a pipe and a boy performer charged with singing for King Pippin, pairing catalogue lines on exotic tribute and wares — Indian ivory, Sabean incense, Jordan balsam, Attic agates, Arabian gold — with recurring refrains urging the child to gather heavenly gifts and learn what Sophia teaches. A closing section turns commemorative and autobiographical, recording how Louis was crowned by Pope Stephen with Bishop Ebbo present, foundations of a place renewed, and the poet's own rearing on the Rhine, Loire and Seine. Readers of intertexts will note the explicit signposting of Virgil's Muse and Cato's sayings alongside the psalms, and the refrain-based structure, which makes the piece a compact showcase of Carolingian classical and biblical synthesis.
la.eucherius_of_lyon.formulae_spiritalis_in: The Formulae spiritalis intellegentiae is a Late Antique Latin treatise on theology in which Eucherius of Lyon, addressing his son Veranus, explains how the figurative language of Scripture is to be understood spiritually. After a preface laying out the historical, tropological, and anagogical senses of the Bible, the work proceeds through ten classes of terms—the members of the Lord, heavenly and earthly creatures, animals, numbers, Jerusalem, and others—defining each expression's allegorical meaning and supporting it with a proof text drawn chiefly from the Psalms, the prophets, and the apostolic writings. Its compact catalogue of equivalences, from the eyes of the Lord as divine inspection to fire as the Holy Spirit and clouds as the prophets, serves readers of intertexts as a reference for the stock allegorical readings circulating in later Latin exegesis.
la.eucherius_of_lyon.instructiones: The Instructiones of Eucherius of Lyon, a Late Antique work of theological prose in two books, expounds difficult words and passages of Scripture in the form of questions put by Salonius and answered by the author. Its preface, addressed to a correspondent who entered the desert as a boy under Honoratus and was formed by the teaching of Hilary, Salvian, and Vincent, disclaims originality, offering what rests on the judgement of illustrious doctors rather than on the author's own ingenuity. The body of the work glosses Hebrew and Greek terms frequent in the sacred books, such as alleluia, diapsalma, amen, and ephod, resolves cruxes falling chiefly in Genesis, among them the Spirit borne over the waters, the tree of knowledge, the ages of the patriarchs, and the allotment of the earth to the sons of Noah, and handles doctrinal questions such as the scriptural proof of the Trinity. For readers hunting intertexts, the work serves as a compact repository of the allegorical and etymological readings of Late Antique exegesis, attached to scriptural loci that recur as commonplaces in later writers.
la.eutropius.breviarium: Eutropius's Breviarium is a Latin prose epitome of Roman history, composed in the late imperial period and dedicated to the emperor Valens by the author, who signs himself magister memoriae. Promising a brief narrative arranged in chronological order from the founding of the city down to the writer's own day, it moves rapidly through the kings, the Republic, and the Empire, concentrating on wars, constitutional changes, and the outstanding deeds of commanders and emperors. Since it condenses the long tradition of Roman historiography into compact and memorable episodes, from the Fabii and Cincinnatus to Camillus and the contests with Pyrrhus, its phrasing and exempla repay attention from readers tracing verbal and thematic parallels in later Latin literature.
la.fardulfus.carmina: The Carmina transmitted under the name Fardulfus form a brief corpus of Carolingian Latin verse, 43 lines in all, edited by E. Dümmler in 1881. The surviving poem is a dedication in which Fardulf recounts his exile, his fidelity to Charlemagne, and the royal favour that raised him to the abbacy of Saint-Denis, celebrating the church he built, its ciborium, the relics of the saints resting there, and the king who commanded its construction. Readers of intertexts may value it for the Carolingian idiom of dedication and panegyric, its blend of classical and biblical diction, and its witness to the cult and royal patronage of the abbey of Saint-Denis.
la.faustus_of_riez.de_gratia_libri_duo: The De gratia libri duo of Faustus of Riez is a Late Antique Latin prose treatise on grace, written at the request of Leontius, styled papa, who had convened a council of Gallic bishops to condemn the 'error of predestination' and then sought Faustus's judgment on the doctrines to be affirmed. The two books attack Pelagian teaching on original sin, infant baptism, and the sufficiency of unaided human effort, but they denounce with equal force the opposing extreme, a doctrine of one-sided predestination that would render prayer and human striving vain, arguing throughout that divine grace and human free will must labor together. The case is made through a dense catena of prophetic, evangelic, and especially Pauline testimony on justification, election, and merit, with a nod to Augustine's rule that not everything left unsaid is denied, and the preface notes additions made after the synods of Arles and Lyons. Readers of intertexts will find here a central witness to the late antique controversy over grace, labor, and liberum arbitrium, preserving the scriptural proof-texts and patristic formulas on which both sides of that debate drew.
la.faustus_of_riez.sermones: A collection of Latin prose sermons by the Late Antique author Faustus of Riez, comprising the sermons printed under his name with those transmitted under the name of Eusebius set aside. The homilies gathered here treat the feasts of the Christmas cycle, including the Nativity, Saint Stephen the first martyr, the Holy Innocents, and Epiphany, moving from moral exhortation on worthy reception of the Eucharist, love of enemies, almsgiving, and the dangers of hatred, anger, and drunkenness to typological exposition of the Magi, the baptism in the Jordan, and the wedding feast at Cana. Scriptural quotation and allusion run throughout, and recurring motifs such as hatred as murder and penitence as medicine give the collection a strongly cohesive ethical stamp. For readers hunting intertexts, the sermons offer festive homiletic material and exegetical topoi of the kind that circulated widely in later Latin preaching.
