la.florus.epitome_bellorum_omnium_annorum: A Latin prose epitome of Roman history stretching from the foundations under Romulus to the early empire, attributed to Florus and composed in the early imperial period. The work compresses some seven centuries of warfare into a brief panorama, framing Roman history as the life-cycle of a single people — infancy under the kings, youth in the conquest of Italy, manhood under Augustus, and old age under the Caesars, briefly revived under Trajan — before proceeding king by king and war by war through celebrated episodes such as Romulus and Remus, the rape of the Sabines, and the duel of the Horatii and Curiatii. Its polished, epigrammatic retelling of material otherwise transmitted in fuller historians, above all Livy, makes it a productive hunting ground for textual parallels and for tracing how early imperial style reshapes inherited narrative.
la.gerwardus.versus: A six-line Latin poem of Carolingian date by the poet Gerward, cast as the offering of a suppliant client to a prince whose praise and everlasting memory it seeks to advance. The opening self-deprecatingly calls the piece 'versiculos', while the closing couplet directs the reader to Einhard as the writer of the gesta of great Charles, so the verses evidently served as a dedicatory preface to a copy of Einhard's account of Charlemagne's life and deeds. For readers of intertexts the poem matters as a contemporary witness to the circulation and presentation of Einhard's famous biography, and as a compact specimen of the formulas of princely praise in Carolingian occasional verse.
la.giovanni_aurelio_augurelli.chrysopoeia: Chrysopoeia ('gold-making') is a Latin didactic poem in four books, totalling 2,056 lines, by the Renaissance author Giovanni Aurelio Augurelli, on the alchemical art of producing gold. The proem claims that no poet before him had treated the gold-bearing art in verse, addresses a patron imagined as sent from heaven to relieve a weary world and to usher in a golden age of peace, and defends the poem's use of pagan deity-names such as Sol, Luna and Vulcan as conventional cover for alchemical materials and processes. For readers of intertexts, the poem offers a striking example of the classical didactic tradition — invocation of the Muses, patronal dedication, mythological allegory — refashioned for Renaissance alchemy, and it stands as a locus for tracing how ancient metallurgical and mythological vocabulary passed into early modern technical verse.
la.godescalcus_saxus.carminum_appendix: Carminum Appendix is a short collection of medieval Latin devotional verse (91 lines) attributed to Godescalcus Saxus and assigned to the Carolingian era. The opening poem is a penitential prayer that addresses Christ as the light of the speaker's darkness and pleads for deliverance from sin and a heart that loves God, before passing into hymnic praise of Christ as the eternal Word through whom the heavens, stars, seas, and earth were made. For readers hunting textual parallels, the work's compact scope and its pairing of penitential supplication with a creation hymn make it a convenient touchpoint for comparison with Carolingian devotional and hymnic verse.
la.hegesippus_pseudo.de_excidio_hierosolymi: A late antique Latin prose history of uncertain date attributed to Hegesippus (hence Pseudo-Hegesippus), the De Excidio Hierosolymitano recounts Jewish history from the Maccabean revolt down to the Roman capture of Jerusalem and the burning of the temple under Titus. Its prologue presents the work as a continuation of sacred history in historiographical style and openly reworks Josephus, whom the author faults for partiality toward the Jews and for failing to grasp the divine cause of their calamities. Readers hunting intertexts will find here a dense Christian Latin recasting of Josephus interwoven with biblical diction and the idiom of classical historiography, making the work a key witness to the Latin transmission of the Jerusalem narrative.
la.hibernicus_exul.carmina: The Carmina attributed to Hibernicus Exul ('the Irish exile'), a poet of the Carolingian period, are preserved in E. Dümmler's 1881 edition and total 594 lines of Latin verse. The collection opens with a prayer asking God to strengthen, prolong, and crown the life of Caesar Karolus — Charlemagne — whose peace, victories, and future heavenly reward it celebrates, and then turns to a covering note and an epistolary poem addressed to Gundrada, a girl praised for beauty and virtue, which unfolds into a vision of the world's magnates honouring their king with silver, gold, gems, purple, and horses. The verse's stated artlessness ('versibus incomptis' offered 'summo mentis amore'), its biblical and liturgical cadences, and its formulas of Christian rulership panegyric make the corpus a rewarding witness for readers tracing shared diction and topoi among the Latin poets who wrote for and about Charlemagne.
la.hilary_of_poitiers.fragmenta_historica: A Late Antique Latin prose collection of fragmentary historical documents transmitted under the name of Hilary of Poitiers and edited by Alfred Leonhard Feder in the Vienna edition of Hilary's works (1916). Its pieces are chiefly episcopal letters and conciliar material arising from the doctrinal conflicts surrounding the councils of Nicaea and Ariminum: correspondence of Gallican bishops with their Eastern colleagues, the profession of faith of Bishop Germinius, condemnations of Ursacius, Valens and Auxentius, polemic against Marcellus of Salacia and his associates, and reports of accusations against Athanasius of Alexandria. Readers hunting intertexts will find contemporary formulations of the homoousion, the disputed 'silence concerning usia' and related creedal language, much of it embedded in the same ecclesiastical letters and synodical acts on which later conciliar and polemical writers drew.
la.hilary_of_poitiers.tractatus_mysteriorum: A brief Latin prose treatise of Late Antique date, attributed to Hilary of Poitiers and edited by Alfred Leonhard Feder in his 1916 Vienna edition of Hilary's Opera, expounds the earliest narratives of Genesis as prefigurations of Christ and the church. Its programmatic claim, stated in the opening lines, is that every work and word of Scripture announces the Lord's advent, passion, and resurrection, so that the sleep of Adam, the sacrifice of Abel, the marriages of Lamech, and kindred patriarchal episodes foreshadow the incarnation and the gathering of the church from Jew and Gentile. The argument unfolds through close typological exegesis sustained by dense quotation and allusion to Genesis, the Pauline epistles, Ezekiel, and the Gospels. Readers of intertexts will find an early and systematic instance of Christian figural interpretation, useful for tracing how Old Testament types were read onto Christ and ecclesiology in later exegetical tradition.
la.hilary_of_poitiers_pseudo.de_evangelico: De Evangelico, a Latin theological work of 114 lines preserved under the name of Hilary of Poitiers and assigned to the later imperial period, offers an allegorical and narrative treatment of Christ's coming. Opening with Christ figured as flower and unfailing fountain, it goes on to depict the virgin birth, the light flooding a rejoicing earth while the serpent trembles, the Magi following the star and offering gold, myrrh, and frankincense, and a closing litany of titles addressed to Christ as lion and lamb, word born of the Father, and judge of the living and the dead. Readers hunting intertexts will find it useful for the way gospel material is recast in diction reminiscent of classical Latin verse—heaven begrudging earth its glory, earth laughing with sacred offspring—and for verbal formulas shared with other early Christian paraphrase of scripture.
la.hilary_of_poitiers_pseudo.hymni: A short Latin collection of Christian hymns transmitted under the name of Hilary of Poitiers, though the ascription is conventional and the authorship uncertain. The work, placed in the Later Imperial period and classed as theology, opens with a morning hymn hailing Christ as the true light of the world, outshining the lesser luminary that merely announces the coming day, and continues with penitential pieces in which the sinner, weighed down by the burden of sin, implores the Redeemer for pardon. Despite the prose classification in the source record, the hymns display the rhythmic, stanza-like character of early Latin Christian song, with dense biblical diction throughout. Readers hunting intertexts will find early formulations of the Christ-as-light topos and liturgical phrasing that resonate across patristic writing and later hymnody.
la.hilary_saint_archbishop_of_arles.epistul: A brief Latin epistle of late antiquity addressed to Eucherius and transmitted under the name of Hilary, archbishop of Arles; the corpus preserves it as a single short piece. In ornate Christian prose the writer explains that he has sent on copies of his correspondent's flourishing works despite anxiety for their safety, has read them through at once with wonder, and begs to be counted among the pupils trained by their instruction, since the weakness of old age presses upon him. He closes by greeting Eucherius as 'most blessed pope.' For readers of intertexts the letter is valuable as evidence for the circulation and reception of late antique theological writings and for its blend of classical epistolary courtesy with biblical idiom.
la.hilary_saint_bishop_of_poitiers.collecta: A Latin compilation of documents from the Arian controversy, attributed to Hilary, Bishop of Poitiers, and edited by Alfred Feder in the Corpus Scriptorum Ecclesiasticorum Latinorum (1916). Its 559 lines gather credal confessions and epistolary exchanges, opening with a confession and collective letter of the Gallican bishops to their Eastern counterparts on the silence imposed on the term ousia at Rimini and the defense of the homousion. Further items include a letter of Eusebius to Gregory of Spain, the creed of Bishop Germinius, and a synodical letter tied to the council of Serdica that denounces Marcellus of Galatia and recounts accusations against Athanasius of Alexandria. The collection repays readers hunting intertexts with its dense store of formulaic credal Latin, biblical citation, and the polemical epistolary conventions shared among bishops of Hilary's circle.
la.hildebert_of_lavardin.carmen_in_libros_r: Carmen in Libros Regum is a medieval Latin verse paraphrase in four books, totalling 1,350 lines, attributed to Hildebert of Lavardin. It recasts the biblical Books of Samuel and Kings in continuous verse, opening with Elkana, the rivalry of Hannah and Phenenna, and the birth and calling of Samuel at Shiloh, before proceeding through the loss of the ark to the Philistines and the fortunes of the Israelite monarchy. For readers of intertexts the poem is a substantial specimen of biblical epic, showing how scriptural narrative was refashioned in classical Latin diction, and it affords abundant verbal and thematic material traceable in later literary treatments of the same stories.
la.hildebert_of_lavardin.carmina_minora: The Carmina Minora is a medieval Latin collection of some 1,100 lines of short poems attributed to Hildebert of Lavardin, each piece introduced by a heading naming its addressee or subject — bishops, an abbot, the queen of the English, a merchant, and unnamed friends. Its pieces are epigrammatic moral and devotional verse on themes such as virtue above rank, death's levelling of master and servant, the origin of evil, the workings of prosperity and adversity, and the uses of secrecy, alongside lighter satirical portraits of contemporary figures. Composed of uncertain date within the medieval period and transmitted without division into separate books, the collection compresses biblical and classical moral commonplaces into quotable distichs. Readers tracing verbal echoes and shared sententiae between medieval Latin verse and its antique models will find in it a dense source of parallel phrasing.
la.hildebert_of_lavardin.carminum_supplemen: "Carminum Supplementum" preserves 151 lines of medieval Latin verse attributed to Hildebert of Lavardin, transmitted as a supplement to his collected poems. The opening piece reads sun, water, crystal and fire as figures of the Word born of a virgin, and a following sequence assigns to each hour of the day its own meditation and prayer, from the first light of dawn through the hours of Christ's passion. For readers of intertexts the work offers a compact specimen of medieval allegorical exegesis, in which light, gemstones and the canonical hours are interpreted Christologically, and it invites comparison with the Latin tradition of day-cycle poetry. The poems are of uncertain date within the medieval period and stand as a miscellaneous collection rather than a unified composition.
la.hildebert_of_lavardin.de_machabaeis: De Machabaeis is a medieval Latin verse narrative of 479 lines attributed to Hildebert of Lavardin. The poem opens with the fall of the Persian kingdom to Alexander of Macedon and his partition of its lands among his successors, Ptolemy, Lysimachus, Seleucus, Cassander and Antigonus, before tracing the rise of the Seleucid line to Antiochus, depicted as the sword of heaven's wrath and a plague upon the Jewish people. From this political prelude the work passes to the Maccabean history announced by its title, recasting biblical material in the manner of classical epic. Readers of intertexts will find it a useful witness to the fusion of classical historiographical diction with biblical narrative in medieval Latin poetry.
la.hildebert_of_lavardin.de_mysterio_missae: A medieval Latin poem of 788 lines, De Mysterio Missae is attributed to Hildebert of Lavardin, whose speaker names himself in the opening lines as Hildebert of Le Mans (Cenomanus). The work begins with a riddling apology in which the poet pleads indulgence for his faults, styles himself Davus and dares the reader to be Oedipus, the successive lines being linked by the repetition of their closing words. The body of the poem expounds the mystery of the Mass: Christ the true host offered once for the many, the priest's ministry at the altar of temple and cross, and the fulfilment of the old law's figures in the true sacrifice. For readers of intertexts, its dense weave of scriptural and liturgical phrasing and its typological treatment of sacrificial imagery make it a rewarding witness to medieval Latin diction on the Eucharist.
la.hildebert_of_lavardin.de_ordine_mundi: De Ordine Mundi is a medieval Latin poem of uncertain date, attributed to Hildebert of Lavardin, surviving in 560 lines of verse. It opens with an urgent prayer calling on Christ to come in judgement and end a corrupt age, and then surveys sacred history as the origin of the world's disorder, beginning with Adam's fall beneath the tree, the transmission of sin to his posterity, and Cain's murder of Abel. In retelling Genesis material with classical allusion and epic-flavoured diction, the poem offers readers of intertexts a medieval reworking of biblical narrative whose phrasing and themes invite comparison with earlier Latin poetry.
la.hildebert_of_lavardin.de_querimonia_et_c: A medieval Latin poem of 154 lines, of uncertain date and attributed to Hildebert of Lavardin, the De Querimonia et Conflictu Carnis et Spiritus stages the contest between flesh and spirit as a lament answered by consolation. The opening complaint gives voice to a soul figured as a frail and crumbling house, held in servile condition, and as a woman wed to Christ whose early devotion to her heavenly bridegroom is betrayed through the wiles of an adulterer who flatters her with delights, riches, and name. Yearning for release from a bitter covenant, she asks for a dwelling where she may live free, and a comforting voice replies that her desire will be granted. The poem's allegory of the soul as the spouse of Christ led astray, together with its imagery of house, prison, bridal chamber, and adulterer, makes it a useful witness for readers tracing the body-and-soul debate and the personified complaint tradition in medieval moral verse.
la.hildebert_of_lavardin.in_primum_caput_ec: In Primum Caput Ecclesiastes is a medieval Latin poem of 171 lines by Hildebert of Lavardin, a versified commentary on the opening chapter of Ecclesiastes. The poem takes successive clauses of the Vulgate—'Vanitas vanitatum, dixit Ecclesiastes', 'generatio praeterit, et generatio advenit', 'oritur sol et occidit'—as lemmata and expounds each in verse. Its themes run from the vanity of all created things and the restless mutability of nature through the passing of generation after generation and death's scattering of amassed wealth to the final fire in which the four elements perish so that a purified earth may endure. Readers of intertexts will find it a compact witness to the medieval currency of the Vanitas vanitatum formula and of the Preacher's images of the sun's circuit and fleeting generations, stock material on which later writers repeatedly drew.
la.hincmar.carmina: The Carmina of Hincmar is a Carolingian collection of medieval Latin verse, 378 lines in all, largely dedicatory and epigraphic in character. The opening poems honor an altar to the Mother of God adorned by the bishop Hincmar, preserve an epitaph he composed for the bishop Tilpinus, and present Hincmar as the shepherd sent to the people of Reims, before turning to doctrinal verses on the Virgin's conception of Christ and the one person and double substance of the incarnate Word. For readers hunting parallels, the collection offers characteristic Carolingian formulas for Marian devotion, episcopal commemoration, and Christological definition, couched in diction indebted to classical verse and the language of the liturgy.
la.horace.ars_poetica: Horace's Ars Poetica is a hexameter poem of 476 lines from the Augustan age, a didactic and satirical verse treatment of literary craft in which the poet offers counsel on writing to the Pisones. Its argument ranges over artistic unity and decorum, the choice and handling of subject matter, diction and meter, the training and office of the poet, and the conventions of Roman drama, rejecting the 'purple patch' and urging matter matched to the writer's strength. Because its maxims and turns of phrase were quoted, translated, and reworked by later writers across antiquity and the vernacular traditions, it stands among the most consequential Latin sources of poetic theory and a dense node for readers tracing classical commonplaces into subsequent literature.
la.horace.carmen_saeculare: A Latin lyric hymn of the Augustan era by Horace, the Carmen Saeculare comprises seventy-six lines framed as the ritual song that chosen youths and maidens sing to Apollo and Diana at Sibylline command ('Virgines lectas puerosque castos... dicere carmen'). The prayer asks for fruitful marriage and offspring, abundant crops and herds, and a Rome without equal, invoking the centennial cycle of games ('undenos deciens per annos... ludos') from which the carmen takes its name. Its diction and hymnic formulas recur throughout Horace's Odes and Epodes, the collection with which Shorey's edition prints it, so the poem serves as a touchstone for tracing ritual language and prayer formulae across Augustan poetry and later imitation.
la.horace.epistles: Horace's Epistles, an Augustan sequence of moral verse letters in hexameters closely allied to the satiric tradition, comprises two books totalling 1,513 lines and is presented here in H. Rushton Fairclough's 1929 edition. The first book opens with a programmatic letter to Maecenas renouncing the poet's earlier ludus and professing allegiance to no single philosophical master, and the epistles proceed to treat friendship, wealth, contentment, and the art of living in a style rich in memorable sententiae. The second book turns largely to literary questions, and the collection as a whole became one of the most quarried reservoirs of moral and critical commonplaces in Latin, making it a natural point of comparison for later epistolary, satiric, and didactic verse.
la.horace.epodes: A book of short Augustan lyric poems in Latin by Horace, running to 641 lines and printed here in Vollmer's Teubner edition of 1912. The opening poem addresses Maecenas, vowing to share the perils of Caesar's campaigns as a companion in arms, while the second begins with the celebrated praise of rural retirement, 'Beatus ille qui procul negotiis.' The collection moves between friendship, politics, invective, love, and pastoral idealisation in compact stanzas. Its memorable phrasing and motifs recur throughout later Latin and vernacular poetry, making the Epodes a productive source for readers tracing textual parallels.
la.horace.odes: The Carmina of Horace, a lyric poet of the Augustan age, are collected here in four books comprising some 3,136 lines of Latin lyric verse in varied metres. The first book opens with the address to Maecenas and a programmatic survey of human ambitions—athletic victory, office, wealth, farming, trade, war—against which the poet stakes his own claim to a place among the lyric vati. The collection ranges over divine festivals, love, wine, friendship, and the fortunes of Rome, as when the second ode takes up Jupiter's wrath and its thunderbolts against the city. Readers hunting intertexts will find in it a principal wellspring of lyric themes, diction, and formal models for later Latin and European verse.
la.horace.satires: Horace's Satires (Sermones), two books of hexameter verse from the Augustan period and addressed in part to Maecenas, examine human discontent, avarice, ambition, and the ideal of the simple life in a colloquial blend of comic dialogue and moral reflection. The opening of Book 1, on envy of other men's callings and on the licence to 'laugh while telling the truth', serves as a programmatic statement of the genre's mixture of jest and seriousness. The Latin text is drawn from C. Smart's edition of the Works of Horace published in Philadelphia in 1836. Its rich engagement with Greek philosophy, Roman comedy, and contemporary legal and commercial life makes the work a frequent source of parallels for later satirists and moral poets.
la.hrabanus.carmen_evangeliorum: A brief Latin poem attributed to the Carolingian author Hrabanus (Hrabanus Maurus), of uncertain exact date, on the four Evangelists and their symbolism. Its thirty-seven lines enumerate Matthew, Mark, Luke, and John, the regions of their preaching (Judaea, Egypt, Achaia, Asia), and the tetramorphic figures of man, ox, lion, and eagle, before offering a tropological reading of these mystical forms and closing on the concord of the four Gospels. Readers of intertexts will find here a compact Carolingian witness to the evangelist iconography and allegorical exegesis inherited from patristic tradition.
la.hrabanus.carmina: A Carolingian Latin verse collection of 3,237 lines transmitted under the name of Hrabanus. The opening poem, a dedicatory prayer to a saintly bishop, recounts how a Frankish boy was sent by his abbot, rector of the Fulda fold, from the forest of Bochonia to learn at the saint's church the art of metre and sacred scripture, and how, once thirty years had passed ('sex lustra'), he offered a book in praise of Christ, instilled with typological numbers and tropological figures to display the gifts of God and the glory of Christ's passion foretold by prophets and by the letter of the law. Its self-conscious account of figured and typological verse-making, together with dense biblical diction throughout the collection, makes it rewarding terrain for readers tracing Carolingian engagement with earlier poetic and scriptural models.
la.hrabanus.carminum_appendix: Carminum Appendix is a collection of Carolingian Latin verse attributed to Hrabanus, transmitted as an appendix to his poems and running to 725 lines of medieval religious poetry. Its opening poem, arranged in four-line stanzas of elevated hymnic diction, extols caritas as the supreme heavenly gift: the light of the world, the origin of celestial and earthly creatures, the principle by which Adam bore the image of the Creator, and the inspiration of the prophets and patriarchs. Charity is further credited with Christ's descent, passion, and victory over death, Paul's apostleship, the outpouring of the Spirit at Pentecost, and the mission of the preachers who brought salvation to the world. Its dense scriptural vocabulary and hymnic phrasing make it fruitful ground for readers tracing verbal and thematic parallels in medieval Latin verse.
la.hrabanus.laudes_crucis: A Latin poem in praise of the cross by the Carolingian writer Hrabanus, Laudes Crucis runs to some 1,110 lines of medieval devotional verse. Its proem invokes the Muse and, in a humility topos, presents the speaker as a poor and needy servant whose slight offering is justified by the biblical examples of the widow's mite and the gifts brought to the temple under the old law. The poem then exalts the cross as the sacred trophy of the crucified king, full of divinity and apt for every good. Readers tracing intertexts may find it valuable as an instance of Carolingian cross-veneration poetry that fuses classical invocation conventions with scriptural exempla and allegorical reflection on the Passion.
la.iulius_firmicus_maternus.liber_de_errore: The De errore profanarum religionum of Iulius Firmicus Maternus is a Christian polemic, addressed to the emperors, that attacks the mysteries of Isis and Osiris, the Phrygian cult of Attis, Mithraism, Liber, and Ceres and Proserpina as rites that consecrate the crimes and deaths of mortals rather than honor any god. Written in prose during the later imperial era, it retells each pagan myth in detail—the dismemberment of Osiris, the annual mourning of Attis, the effeminacy of the Great Mother's priests, the suppression of the Bacchanalia under the consul Postumius, and the rape of Proserpina near Henna—arguing that such stories cannot mask the wickedness they commemorate. The work quotes Greek verse, including a Homeric passage on Dionysus's flight into the sea, and its dense compilation of mythological narrative, ritual description, and anti-pagan argument makes it a valuable witness for readers tracing how classical myth and cult were transmitted, allegorized, and contested in later Roman and Christian writing.
la.jerome.epistulae: The Epistulae of Jerome, a Late Antique corpus of Latin prose letters totalling some 17,300 lines, opens with an address to his correspondent Innocentius recounting the judicial torture of a woman at Vercellae on a false charge of adultery and the miracle by which the executioner's blade refuses to strike her. The correspondence ranges across spiritual direction, consolation, scriptural exegesis, and ecclesiastical polemic, binding together correspondents scattered across the Latin Christian world of late antiquity. For readers tracing intertexts, the letters offer a dense weave of biblical citation and allusion to classical prose and verse, and they stand as a principal conduit of that composite style into later epistolary and hagiographic writing.
la.jerome.in_hieremiam_prophetam: Jerome's In Hieremiam Prophetam is a Late Antique Latin prose commentary on the Book of Jeremiah in six books, addressed in its preface to a correspondent named Eusebius and presented as the last of Jerome's commentaries on the prophets after the twelve prophets, Isaiah, Daniel, and Ezekiel. Working from Hebrew sources, Jerome restores matter missing from the Septuagint, repairs the disorder of the prophet's words, declines to expound Baruch and the Epistle of Jeremiah, and constantly compares the Hebrew with the Septuagint, Aquila, Symmachus, and Theodotion, often etymologizing Hebrew terms. The exposition alternates literal and historical explanation with allegorical and Christological readings, quoting scripture extensively and reporting the opinions of earlier interpreters, named and anonymous, while defending Jerome's method against detractors. Readers of intertexts will find a dense lattice of biblical allusion, versional comparison, and Late Antique exegetical formulae touching the prophets, the apostles, and the church.
la.jerome.vulgate: The Vulgate is Jerome's Latin version of the Bible, a work of late antique scriptural prose that became the authoritative biblical text of the western Latin tradition. The collection runs to some 39,000 lines distributed across 79 book files, opening with the Genesis account of creation ('in principio creavit Deus caelum et terram') and proceeding through the books of the Old and New Testaments. Because its phrasing supplied the standard diction of scripture for writers throughout the Middle Ages and beyond, the Vulgate stands behind an immense quantity of quotation, allusion, and verbal echo in Latin and vernacular literature, making it a primary point of reference for readers tracing scriptural intertexts.
la.johannes_hymonides.versiculi_de_cena_cyp: A Carolingian Latin poem of 383 lines attributed to Johannes Hymonides, the Versiculi de Cena Cypriani offers a versified treatment of the Cena Cypriani, the allegorical banquet tale that its prologue associates with Cyprian of Carthage. The poem frames itself as a learned jest ('satira') for the pope's Easter festivities and for the banquet of the emperor Charles, and then unfolds a wedding feast at Cana hosted by King Iohel, at which Adam, Eve, Cain, Abel, Noah, the apostles, and a long train of biblical figures take their seats, each marked out by an action drawn from scripture. Its dense chain of scriptural reminiscences and its recasting of a prose banqueting catalogue into verse make it a rewarding witness for readers tracing the medieval Cena Cypriani tradition and the play of biblical intertext at the Carolingian court.
la.john_scotus_eriugena.carmina: A collection of medieval Latin verse attributed to John Scotus Eriugena, of Carolingian date, comprising some 845 lines. The opening poem is programmatic, setting the pagan epic tradition—Homer's songs of Hellas and Troy and Virgil's Romulean progeny—against Christian hymnody on Christ's Passion, the wood of the cross, the two thieves, and the darkness and earthquake at the Crucifixion. Classical allusion and biblical paraphrase are interwoven throughout, and the explicit staging of Homer and Virgil as foils makes the collection valuable for tracing how Carolingian Latin poets refashioned inherited classical models for Christian themes.
la.juvenal.satires: The Satires of Juvenal, sixteen poems in dactylic hexameter composed in early imperial Rome, lash the manners and morals of the capital with unmatched ferocity, from noisy reciters and hypocritical philosophers to legacy-hunters, grasping clients, and the vanity of all human prayers. The opening poem announces the program — deep indignation itself makes verse — and the collection ranges through the miseries of city living, the vices of women, the humiliations of dependence on the rich, the emptiness of worldly ambitions, and even religious savagery in Egypt. For readers of intertexts the poems are doubly valuable: they rework Homer, Virgil, and Horace with pointed distortion, and they coined proverbial phrases — mens sana in corpore sano, panem et circenses — that echo through later Latin, medieval, and modern writing.
la.juvencus.historia_evangelica: The Historia Evangelica of Juvencus, a Latin poem of the later imperial period, casts the narrative of the Gospels into four books of hexameter verse in the manner of classical epic. Opening with the annunciation of John the Baptist to the priest Zacharias, the poem retells the gospel story in elevated epic diction across 3,182 lines. It offers readers of intertexts a central example of biblical epic, in which the conventions of Latin hexameter poetry are turned to scriptural material, and a rich source of verbal and stylistic parallels between classical and Christian traditions.
la.lactantius.carmen_de_passione_domini: The Carmen de Passione Domini is a short Late Antique Latin poem of eighty lines attributed to Lactantius. Christ himself is the speaker, addressing a passer-by at the doors of a temple and recounting the Incarnation, his birth in a Judaeaean manger, the flight from Herod into Egypt, a ministry of teaching and miracles pursued in poverty, and finally the betrayal, trial before Pilate, and crucifixion. By recasting the Gospel Passion narrative in the diction and posture of classical epic, the poem offers intertext-seeking readers a compact case study in how Christian Latin verse absorbs and repurposes earlier poetic language.
la.lactantius.de_ave_phoenice: A Late Antique Latin poem on the phoenix, attributed to Lactantius and edited from Samuel Brandt's 1897 Vienna edition of the Opera omnia. Its 170 lines portray an idyllic eastern paradise, a grove sacred to the Sun that escaped the flames of Phaethon and the flood of Deucalion and knows neither disease, old age, nor death, where the solitary phoenix dwells as the servant of Phoebus and renews its life through its own death. The poem's fusion of classical mythological allusion with a theological vision of rebirth made it a key vehicle for resurrection and paradise imagery, and its dense engagement with earlier phoenix and Golden Age traditions rewards readers hunting verbal and thematic parallels in late antique verse.
la.lactantius.epitome_divinarum_institution: The Epitome Divinarum Institutionum is a Late Antique Latin prose epitome attributed to Lactantius, written at the request of Pentadius, whom the author addresses as brother, and condensing the seven books of his Divinae Institutiones into under five hundred lines. Its arguments move from divine providence against the Epicureans to the unity, omnipotence, and ineffability of God, adducing as witnesses pagan poets, philosophers, and the Sibyls—Orpheus, Virgil, Ovid, Plato, Hermes Trismegistus, Seneca, Cicero—before exposing deified mortals such as Hercules and Aesculapius as men of all too human lives. For readers of intertexts the work is valuable both as a repertory of classical quotations and testimonia redeployed in Christian apologetic and as a compact witness to the argumentative architecture of the longer Institutiones.
la.lios_monocus.libellus_sacerdotalis: A Latin didactic poem of 565 lines from the Carolingian period, the Libellus Sacerdotalis is attributed to an author given as Lios Monocus. The work opens with a prayer to Christ for eloquence before turning to exhortations addressed to priests, urging them to cultivate fitting conduct and to resist the devil, who is depicted tempting a young man with seductive arguments that divine mercy will excuse persistent sin. Its stark contrast of infernal darkness with the bliss of the saints in paradise, together with its staging of demonic rhetoric and advice to clergy, makes it relevant to readers tracing temptation scenes and admonitory clerical verse in the medieval Latin tradition.
la.livy.ab_urbe_condita: Livy's Ab Urbe Condita is a monumental Latin prose history composed in the Augustan era, narrating Roman affairs from the city's foundation onward. The opening preserves the celebrated preface on the moral and exemplary value of history, then proceeds through the legends of Aeneas' arrival in Latium, the founding of Lavinium and Alba Longa, and the royal succession down to Numitor and Amulius. The corpus holds the work in four book files totalling more than twenty thousand lines. Readers hunting intertexts will find in it a prose counterpart to Augustan poetic treatments of early Rome such as Virgil's Aeneid, and its preface, diction, and exemplary narratives are recurrent points of comparison for later historians and rhetoricians.
la.lucan.bellum_civile: The Bellum Civile (or Pharsalia) of Lucan is an Early Imperial Latin epic in dactylic hexameters, transmitted in ten books, that recounts the war between Caesar and Pompey as 'worse than civil' strife in which Rome turns its victorious right hand against its own vitals. Opening with a paradoxical encomium in which the crimes of the civil wars appear as the price of Nero's forthcoming apotheosis, the poem abandons divine machinery for rhetorical and philosophical intensity, dwelling on battle, tyranny, and the dismemberment of the Roman world. Its pointed inversions of Virgilian epic, its Ovidian erudition, and its memorable sententiae make it a central witness to the allusive texture of Silver Latin and a rich source for readers tracking epic's self-conscious rewriting of its predecessors.
la.lucretius.de_rerum_natura: Lucretius' De rerum natura is a didactic epic in six books of Latin hexameters, written during the Roman Republic, that expounds Epicurean natural philosophy in verse. Opening with a celebrated invocation to Venus and addressed to a Memmius, the poem explains the atomic constitution of the world, the workings of mind and soul, the origins of religion and civilization, and celestial and meteorological phenomena, before closing with the plague of Athens. Its fusion of philosophical argument with elevated and formulaic diction made it a fundamental model and quarry for later Latin poets, notably Vergil, and it remains a rich source of parallels for readers tracing didactic and philosophical intertexts.
la.lupus_servatus.versus: A brief Latin poem of twenty-seven lines attributed to Lupus Servatus, a Carolingian author, and addressed to an Evrardus. The verses form a dedication for a law book that Evrardus had caused to be written, cataloguing the peoples depicted in its pictures — the Salian Franks, Ripuarians, Lombards, Alamanni, and Bavarians — together with their laws, and acclaiming the figures of Carolingian rulers from Charles and Pippin to the emperor Louis and Lothar. The closing lines carry an authorial signature ('infimus ecce Lupus'), a promise of worthier song should life be spared, and a trinitarian blessing on the dedicatee. For readers hunting intertexts, the poem offers a compact instance of Carolingian verse attached to the transmission of the early medieval law codes, its diction echoing the language of legal compilation and book presentation.
la.macrobius.fragment: A brief Latin prose fragment, twelve lines in all, transmitted under the name of Macrobius, a Late Antique author. Its lines sketch a satirical scene of dissolute Roman public life: men gamble, drench themselves in perfume, and drain every amphora on the way to the comitium, where a drowsy judge demands documents he can scarcely read, before the deliberation collapses into a banquet catalogue of mulsum mixed with Greek wine, a fat thrush, a fine fish, and a wolf caught between two bridges. The comic diction and stock episodes — the drunken juror, the parade of dishes — echo the manner of earlier Latin satire and comedy, giving readers of intertexts a compact locus for verbal parallels within Roman satiric writing.
la.macrobius.in_somnium_Scipionis_commentar: Macrobius's Commentarii in Somnium Scipionis, a Late Antique prose work of philosophy, is a commentary on the dream narrative that concludes Cicero's De re publica, addressed to the author's son Eustathius. Opening with a defence of philosophical fiction that pairs Cicero's dream with Plato's myth of Er, the work goes on to classify the five kinds of dreams and their divinatory worth, and to expound the immortality and fate of the soul, the harmony of the spheres, and the order of the cosmos. Its dense texture of quotation from and allusion to Cicero, Plato, Virgil, and earlier Greek thinkers, together with its role as a conduit of Platonist doctrine into later Latin reading, makes it a natural hunting ground for readers in search of textual parallels.
la.macrobius.saturnalia: The Saturnalia, a late-antique Latin prose work in seven books by Macrobius (Ambrosius Theodosius Macrobius), casts its erudition as a series of banquets held during the Saturnalian festival at the house of Vettius Praetextatus, where Symmachus, Albinus, Servius, Eusebius the rhetorician, and other Roman notables discuss antiquities, religion, grammar, literature, and philosophy. The prefatory letter to the author's son Eustachius presents the work as a digest of wide Greek and Latin reading, in which material from earlier authors, often in their very words, is reordered into an organic whole, as bees gather and transform the nectar of many flowers. Its dense texture of quotation and adaptation makes the dialogue a prime hunting ground for textual parallels and for the transmission of classical learning in late antiquity.
la.magnus_felix_ennodius.benedictio_cerei_i: A Latin blessing of the Paschal candle for the Easter Vigil, the Benedictio Cerei I is a single continuous prose prayer attributed to Magnus Felix Ennodius, a late-antique author. It opens with the liturgical formula of dignum et iustum, gives thanks for creation and for speech itself, and elaborates the symbolism of the candle—wax from virgin bees, wick from water, light from heaven—before developing the Exodus typology of the column leading the faithful through the sea and closing with petitions for protection against storms and for the fruits of the renewed spring earth. Its dense biblical allusion, creation praise, and the imagery of the virgin bees and the spotless Lamb make it a productive source of parallels for Easter candle blessings, liturgical prose prayer, and the survival of classical themes in late-antique and medieval Christian writing.

The Benedictio Cerei II of Magnus Felix Ennodius is a Latin prose blessing of the paschal candle, a Late Antique liturgical composition that opens with the formula 'Dignum et iustum est' and unfolds as a solemn preface. The work moves from the concord of water and flame in the paschal night, through a meditation on creation, the fall, and regeneration by baptism, to the consecration of the candle itself, praising the wax produced by chaste bees and the fire that recalled the burning bush unconsumed. Its dense scriptural typology and rhythmical prose make it a rewarding comparand for the Exsultet tradition and for baptismal and creation imagery in Late Antique and early medieval religious prose.
la.magnus_felix_ennodius.carmina_1_praefati: A pair of Latin prose prefaces by Magnus Felix Ennodius, a late antique author, serving as introductions to the first book of his Carmina. The first justifies the act of composition by contrasting the joy of homecoming with the anxieties of exile, invoking prophetic song and the verse of 'Mantuanus' (Virgil) as precedents, while the second thanks an unnamed patron whose encouragement is credited with unlocking the author's eloquence. Rhetorically elaborate, the prefaces combine classical modesty topoi, scriptural echoes, and explicit Virgilian allusion, making them valuable for readers tracing how late antique prose frames, defends, and legitimises poetic production.
la.magnus_felix_ennodius.petitorium_quo_abs: A Latin prose petition (petitorium) by Magnus Felix Ennodius, a writer of the late antique period, in which the speaker formally manumits his slave Gerontius and requests his admission to the ecclesiastical college of Rome. The piece opens with a meditation on divine justice, the rewards of the faithful, and the consolation grace affords to those bound by earthly cares, then praises Gerontius' faith, chastity, and freeborn character before restoring his liberty and asking that he be released from every obligation in the church's records, with his property secured without diminution. Readers of intertexts may find value in the way the document fuses late Roman legal formulae of manumission with Christian vocabulary of grace, judgment, and reward, framing freedom as both a judicial act and a return of the soul to its divine origin.
la.magnus_felix_ennodius.vita_epiphanii: The Vita Epiphanii of Magnus Felix Ennodius is a late-antique Latin prose saint's life of Epiphanius, bishop of Ticinum (Pavia), opening with a prologue on the perils of encomium before tracing the bishop's rise from lector under his predecessor Crispinus to the episcopal throne. The narrative follows Epiphanius through legations to Ricimer and the emperor Anthemius, an embassy to Euric at Toulouse, negotiations with Odoacer and Theoderic, and a celebrated journey to the Burgundian ruler Gundobad that won the release of thousands of Italian captives, interspersed with miracles, exorcisms, and church rebuilding. The narrator presents himself as an eyewitness and participant in several episodes, lending the hagiography the character of contemporary reportage on the closing decades of the Western empire. Its formal speeches, scriptural allusion, and classical exempla such as David and Alexander make it a productive source for readers tracing parallels in late antique panegyric and hagiographic diction.
la.manilius.astronomica: A didactic epic in five books of Latin hexameters, totaling 4,255 lines, by Marcus Manilius, a poet of the Augustan age. The Astronomica expounds the structure of the heavens and the doctrine that stars and zodiacal signs shape human fortunes, moving from cosmology and the constellations to the technical rules of horoscopic astrology; the proem addresses the emperor Caesar as patron and credits Mercury with the first discovery of celestial knowledge. Its sustained engagement with the Latin didactic tradition and its dense vocabulary of stars, signs, and fate make it a rich source of parallels for poets handling astronomical and astrological material.
la.marbodus_redonensis.certamina_septem_fra: A medieval Latin poem of 157 lines attributed to Marbod of Rennes (Marbodus Redonensis), retelling the martyrdom of the seven Maccabean brothers and their mother under Antiochus. Each brother in turn refuses the royal command to eat forbidden food, answering the tyrant with defiant speeches before mutilation and death, while the mother praises their contests and receives the promise of a crown. The poem compresses the biblical Maccabean narrative into a sequence of set-piece disputations and torments, marked by formulas of steadfastness, trial by fire, and the soul's radiance like gold in the flame. Readers tracing intertexts will find here a compact medieval verse treatment of the martyr legend whose phrasing of defiance, sacrifice, and heavenly reward recurs in later martyrological and dramatic writing on the Maccabees.
la.martial.epigrams: The Epigrams of M. Valerius Martial, a Latin poet of the early Imperial period, comprise short satiric verse gathered in fourteen books and some 9,375 lines. The poems move from pointed invective, obscene humour, and mock encomia to scenes of Roman daily life—clients, dinner invitations, legacy-hunters, the theatre—and self-conscious commentary on the poet's fame and the travels of his books, as in the opening self-introduction ('Toto notus in orbe Martialis') and the plea to Caesar that 'lasciua est nobis pagina, uita proba'. Densely allusive toward earlier Latin poetry and itself a model for later epigrammatists, the collection offers readers of intertexts an exceptionally rich field for tracing verbal echoes and generic play.
la.martialis.de_spectaculis: De Spectaculis is a short cycle of satiric epigrams in hexameters by Martial, a Latin poet of the early imperial period, running to some 220 lines. The poems celebrate the Flavian Amphitheatre at Rome and the spectacles staged there, ranking the building above the pyramids, Babylon, and the Mausoleum, recording spectators drawn from every people of the empire, the exile of informers, and mythological shows such as the tale of Pasiphaë, while repeatedly contrasting the new structure with the works and lake of Nero. Readers hunting intertexts find in the collection a dense knot of allusion, as the canonical catalogue of ancient marvels and the language of imperial panegyric are reworked in compressed and often quoted form, making the opening sequence a familiar source and target of verbal parallels in later verse.
la.micon_of_saint_riquier.opus_prosodiacum: A nine-line Latin poem of the Carolingian period transmitted under the name of Micon of Saint-Riquier, titled Opus Prosodiacum, a designation that points to a prosodiacal verse form although the metre is unspecified in the record. The piece is an occasional epigram composed around a gift of soap, praying that washing with living water dissolve the heaps of sin and that a box emptied of virtues be refilled with them. Its playful fusion of physical cleansing and moral purification, in the tradition of the verse donum, offers useful parallels for readers of Carolingian occasional poetry and of classical epigram's gift-poem motifs. The final line breaks off incomplete in the source record.
la.micon_of_saint_riquier.prologus_in_tract: A fifty-two-line Latin verse prologue of the Carolingian period, attributed to Micon of Saint-Riquier, introducing a treatise on the quantity of first syllables. The poet explains that, since no established art has shown how the first syllable may be identified, he will set out metrical headings in brief form and then treat lengthened initial syllables in six parts, while leaving aside the interjection, the part of speech the Greeks do not number, because it rarely occupies a metrical foot. He likewise announces discussion of the inseparable preposition 'pro', distinguished from the seventh part of the Roman tongue that Honoratus had briefly described, together with defective impersonal verbs and the force of the gerund. Readers hunting intertexts will find here a compact witness to how Carolingian school verse reworks late antique grammatical doctrine on prosody and the parts of speech.
la.minucius_felix.octavius: The Octavius of Minucius Felix is a Latin apologetic dialogue of uncertain but late antique date, cast as the narrator Marcus's fond recollection of a debate held on the shore at Ostia. The pagan Caecilius opens by defending traditional cult, scepticism, and Roman religious custom against Christianity, whereupon the Christian Octavius answers with a case for monotheism, divine providence, and the resurrection, refuting popular superstition and the slanders levelled at believers; Marcus moderates and records Caecilius's final concession. Composed in polished Ciceronian prose and relatively compact in scale, the dialogue repurposes classical authors and Roman exempla—from Cicero and Seneca to Socrates, Camillus, and the Decii—in the service of Christian argument. For readers of intertexts it offers a rich case study in how Latin apologetic absorbs and redirects the language and authorities of the pagan literary tradition.
la.moduin.carminum_appendix: A short Carolingian Latin poem of thirty lines, ascribed to Moduin, preserved as an appendix to a collection of carmina. The aging speaker urges a young brother to abandon Virgil, whose pagan epic matter and praise of Venus are dismissed as chaff, and to embrace Arator instead, whose verse on the apostles' virtues is extolled as grain teaching what endures. Antithetical couplets set the fates of Virgilian and apostolic heroes against one another, from Cerberus and hell to Michael and the heavenly kingdom, and Aeneas's wars to Paul's conquest of the world. The poem offers a compact witness to Christian revaluation of classical epic and to Carolingian engagement with both poets, making it useful for readers charting the reception of Virgil and Arator in medieval Latin verse.
la.moduin.eclogae: Eclogae attributed to Moduin, a poet of the Carolingian age, is a work of medieval Latin pastoral verse running to some 245 lines without internal book division. The opening poem addresses a wise Charles in terms of courtly panegyric, promising songs that will never perish, and stages shepherd speakers, including an aged vates protected beneath a shady tree who is called by the feigned name of a soldier and honored with a victor's laurel. Across the poems the speakers move between praise of the ruler, complaints of storm and shipwreck, longing for a homeland, and the desire to reach the seats of David, blending bucolic diction and figures such as Palemon with biblical and courtly resonance. Readers hunting intertexts will find dense engagement with the Virgilian eclogue tradition as refashioned for a Carolingian setting, offering parallels for medieval pastoral allegory and the transposition of ancient topoi into praise of a living ruler.
la.nithardus.historiae: A Carolingian Latin prose history transmitted under the name of Nithardus, the Historiae recounts the quarrels that followed the death of Charlemagne, the reign and humiliations of Louis the Pious, and the wars among his sons Lothar, Louis the German, Pippin, and Charles over the divided empire. The narrative runs from the rebellions against Louis and the successive partitions of the kingdom through the fighting by the Fontanetum brook, and it closes around the alliance sealed when the two brothers swore mutual oaths at Strasbourg in both the Romance and the Germanic tongue, with the author presenting himself as a participant in the events and writing at the command of an unnamed lord. Readers of intertexts value the work both as an eyewitness narrative of the Carolingian civil wars and as the witness that preserves those vernacular Strasbourg oaths, a landmark for the earliest surviving French and Germanic formulae embedded in a Latin frame.
la.optatian.epistula: A short Latin prose work of the Later Imperial period, the Epistula of Optatian is a panegyric letter addressed to the emperor Constantine, whom it hails as lord, greatest and invincible, eminent in piety no less than in valor. Running to only two lines in the corpus, it gives thanks for the emperor's gracious reception of a poem the author says he had bound in the tighter fetters of the Muses, and it asks pardon for the audacity of the dedication. Its self-presentation proceeds through classical allusion: the poet contrasts his slight talent with Virgil, the noble Mantuan priest of the Roman Muses, glories in the precedent of Maecenas, and invokes Helicon, the Castalian spring, Apollo's lyre, and Parnassus. Readers of intertexts will find it a compact witness to the Virgil-Maecenas paradigm of poetic patronage recast for an emperor praised as a devotee of the Muses.
la.optatus_saint_bishop_of_mileve.s_optati_: A Latin prose polemic in seven books, attributed in the corpus to Optatus, bishop of Mileve, and composed in late antiquity, directed against the Donatist bishop Parmenianus. The opening book defends the unity and catholicity of the African church, tracing the origins of the schism in the traditio of the scriptures during persecution, the contested ordinations of Caecilian and Majorinus, Constantine's judicial interventions, and the practice of rebaptism, and expounding the dowries of the true church, including the episcopal chair of Peter at Rome. Readers of intertexts will find it dense with biblical citation — Isaiah, Ezekiel, the Psalms, the Song of Songs, the Gospels and the Pauline letters — woven together with quoted imperial letters, conciliar proceedings and trial records, making it a rich source of both scriptural and documentary parallels for later ecclesiastical writing.
la.ovid.ars_amatoria: The Ars Amatoria is a didactic elegy in three books of elegiac couplets (2333 lines) by Ovid, written in the Augustan period, which teaches the art of love in three stages — finding a partner, winning her, and keeping the affair alive — with the last book turning to instruct women. Its proem casts the poet as the 'Tiphys and Automedon of Love' and as a rival preceptor to Chiron, parodically claiming the authority of didactic poetry and the elegiac topos of the soldier-lover, and the whole work proceeds by witty mock-technical precept. Densely stocked with mythological exempla and playful reworkings of Greek legend, it served later Latin and vernacular writers as a principal model for erotic instruction and as a repertory of Ovidian allusion.
la.ovid.ex_ponto: Ex Ponto is a collection of four books of verse epistles that Ovid sent from exile at Tomis on the Black Sea in the Augustan age, addressed to friends, to members of the imperial house, and to the emperor himself in a continuing plea for recall. The letters blend courtly appeal and protestations of loyalty with vivid pictures of exile life among the Getae, mythological exempla, and reflections on the poet's dimmed fame, continuing the project of his earlier exile elegies. Readers of intertexts will find in its some 3,200 lines a dense network of allusions to Augustan ideology and to Ovid's own earlier works, as well as an influential self-portrait of the banished poet that later European writing repeatedly reworked.
la.ovid.fasti: The Fasti of Ovid, an Augustan poem in elegiac couplets preserved in six books and some 4,978 lines, presents the Roman calendar month by month, giving the religious festivals, anniversaries, and risings and settings of constellations that punctuate the year, together with the myths and aetiological explanations attached to each date. The opening lines address the poem to Germanicus, set aside martial epic in favour of 'Caesar's altars', and invoke the prince's approval as a necessary licence for song. For readers hunting textual parallels, the work offers a dense repository of Roman ritual lore, learned etymology, and mythological narrative in elegiac form, constantly inviting comparison with Ovid's other poetry and with the annalistic and calendrical traditions it reworks.
la.ovid.heroides: The Heroides, an Augustan collection of verse epistles in elegiac couplets by Ovid, presents fictional letters from heroines of myth — beginning with Penelope writing to the still-absent Ulysses — to their absent or faithless lovers and husbands. Each letter compresses an entire epic or tragic storyline into the voice of female complaint, rewriting Homer and the tragic tradition from the perspective of the women left behind. For readers of intertexts the collection is central both as an intricate reworking of earlier Greek and Roman literature and as a model repeatedly imitated, answered, and reworked by later Latin, medieval, and Renaissance writers.
la.ovid.ibis: Ovid's Ibis, an Augustan Latin elegy of 642 lines in elegiac couplets, is a curse poem aimed at an unnamed enemy whom the prologue blames for hounding the poet in his banishment to the cold shores of the Pontus. The speaker announces that after a career of unblemished verse his Muse must now take up unaccustomed weapons, withholding the foe's name for the present while promising a reckoning. The poem then marshals a long catalogue of mythological catastrophes, mutilations, and monstrous punishments as curses, working in the invective tradition associated with Callimachus' Hellenistic poem of the same title. Readers of intertexts will find in it an unusually dense web of mythological exempla and pointed reworkings of Greek and Latin models, framed by the exilic persona of the poet's later elegy.
la.ovid.medicamina_faciei_femineae: Ovid's Medicamina faciei femineae, a didactic elegy in elegiac couplets of the Augustan period, survives as a brief poem of 101 lines addressed to Roman women on the care and adornment of the face. It opens with a defence of cultus, or cultivated beauty, illustrated by examples drawn from agriculture, dyeing, and luxury wares, before proceeding to the cosmetic recipes promised in its instruction to the puellae. The poem belongs with the Ars amatoria and Remedia amoris in Ovid's erotic-didactic project, and its playful handling of moralising commonplaces about dress, grooming, and ancient simplicity gives readers of intertexts ample material for tracing echoes across Latin poetry.
la.ovid.metamorphoses: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, an Augustan epic in Latin hexameters divided into fifteen books, offers a continuous mythological history of the world in which transformation serves as the unifying thread. Opening with the creation of the cosmos from chaos, it moves through the ages of gods, heroes, and lovers, retelling in linked narrative hundreds of Greek and Roman legends, from Daphne and Narcissus to the Trojan cycle and beyond. For readers tracing intertexts, the poem stands as the most compendious poetic repository of classical myth in Latin, and its phrasing and episodes echo through later Latin poetry, medieval narrative, and early modern literature.
la.ovid.remedia_amoris: Ovid's Remedia Amoris, an Augustan elegy of 814 lines in elegiac couplets, presents itself as the therapeutic counterpart to the Ars amatoria: having taught how love is acquired, the poet now offers remedies to lovers whom unhappy passion drives to desperation. The opening dialogue has Cupid read the book's title and protest, while the speaker defends his earlier instruction and promises aid to those suffering under the rule of cruel girls, even invoking lovers driven to the brink of suicide. For readers of intertexts, its running engagement with Ovid's own amatory poetry and its dense texture of mythological exempla make it a central site for tracing allusion within Roman elegy.
la.ovid.tristia: The Tristia is a five-book collection of Augustan elegies by Ovid in elegiac couplets, in which a first-person speaker laments his banishment from Rome and petitions the emperor for the mitigation of his punishment. The opening prologue dispatches the book itself to the city in the poet's stead, unkempt as befits an exile's lot, and the roughly 3,582 lines that follow address the emperor, friends, and the poet's wife, alternating appeals for recall with defenses of his life and art and reflections on fortune and poetic permanence. Readers of intertexts will find here a retrospective reworking of Ovid's earlier amatory, didactic, and epic poetry, making the work a central site for the study of self-allusion, of the Roman book-prologue tradition, and of Latin exile literature more broadly.
la.paschasius_radbertus.carmina: A brief Carolingian Latin verse collection of 235 lines ascribed to Paschasius Radbertus and transmitted without book division. The opening and longest piece is an elaborate funerary lament (planctus) for a departed 'father', urging every rank — men, boys, girls, clerics, and rustics speaking Roman and Latin alike — to weep, strew flowers, raise a tomb, and add song to it, while alternating voices deliver divine poems and prayers for the old man's pardon and reception into paradise. Its diction fuses biblical and liturgical language with the rhetoric of classical lament and epitaph, and a versicle introduced by 'cecinit quam maximus ille' embeds quotation of earlier verse within the mourning. For readers of intertexts the poem offers evidence for Carolingian reworking of the planctus and consolatio traditions and for the citation of prior poetry inside an elegiac frame.
la.paul_the_apostle_saint.epigramma: A brief Latin item attributed in the source record to Paul the Apostle under the title Epigramma, its six lines being the edition's prefatory prose rather than verse: a note on transmission followed by an argumentum. The note reports that the piece survives in Parisinus 7558 appended to Claudius Marius Victor's Alethia under the inscription 'S. Paulini epigramma', that Gagneius first printed it as Victor's work, and that Wernsdorf judged it a sermon rather than an epistle, so that its authorship remains disputed; the accompanying summary relates how Salmon, a priest revisiting the city of his upbringing after long absence, discusses with the aged monk Thesbo the vices of its men and, more severely still, of its women despite the blow of barbarian ravages. Dated in the record to the Early Imperial era and classed as theology, the item serves readers of intertexts chiefly as evidence for the attribution history of a Christian moral dialogue and for themes of civic corruption in Christian Latin poetry.
la.paulinus_of_aquileia.carmina: A collection of Latin verse attributed to Paulinus of Aquileia, a poet of the Carolingian period, running to about 1,721 lines across seventeen book files. The opening poem is a long versified confession of trinitarian faith, affirming one God in three persons and one divine substance before narrating Christ's baptism in the Jordan and the Transfiguration in richly elaborated diction. The collection as a whole gathers doctrinal and devotional poems of the kind produced in Carolingian ecclesiastical circles. Its scriptural paraphrase and its inheritance of the vocabulary and formulas of earlier Christian Latin verse make it a rewarding site for readers tracing intertexts.
la.paulinus_of_aquileia.versus_de_destructi: A 92-line Carolingian Latin poem ascribed to Paulinus of Aquileia, the Versus de Destructione Aquilegiae is a lament for the destruction of Aquileia, once the wealthy and illustrious metropolitan city of Venetia, resplendent with clergy and churches dedicated to Christ. The poem casts the catastrophe as divine punishment: the city's pride, swollen amid its delights, provoked the wrath of the eternal judge, who raised up a cruel people from the east under Attila, depicted as a savage, godless lion, whose vast host besieged, burned, and razed the city, sparing neither age nor sex and driving the survivors into captivity. Readers hunting parallels will find here a Carolingian instance of the planctus over a fallen city, with the augural omen of birds nesting in the towers and the recurrent medieval motif of civic superbia drawing down vengeance in the enduring tradition of Attila's sack of Aquileia.
la.paulinus_of_nola.carmina: The Carmina of Paulinus of Nola, a Late Antique Christian poet writing in Latin, are transmitted in Wilhelm von Hartel's 1894 Vienna edition and comprise roughly 9,340 lines of occasional and devotional verse. The opening pieces exhibit the collection's characteristic texture: prose letters of dedication introducing gift-poems about fig-peckers and shellfish, catalogues of ancient kings and geography with an appeal to Sallust, and direct prayer to God as omnipotent creator. Verse epistles of friendship and gift exchange stand alongside hymnic and devotional poetry. Paulinus deploys a deep classical literary culture in a Christian key, and the constant juxtaposition of mythological, historical, and biblical matter makes the collection unusually rewarding ground for readers tracing the afterlife of classical allusion in Late Antique verse.
la.paulinus_of_nola.epistulae: The Epistulae of Paulinus of Nola (Pontius Meropius Paulinus) preserve the prose correspondence of a Late Antique aristocrat who renounced wealth and worldly standing for ascetic and clerical service, with ties to Barcelona, Bordeaux, and Nola. The letters counsel friends and fellow churchmen on renunciation, spiritual friendship, ordination, and endurance of slander, and they include exchanges with Augustine of Hippo and other figures of the African church. Written in an ornate style saturated with scriptural quotation, frequently unmarked, the collection rewards readers hunting intertexts for biblical and classical echoes alike.
la.paulinus_of_pella.eucharisticus: The Eucharisticus (or Eucharisticon) of Paulinus of Pella is a Late Antique Latin Christian poem of thanksgiving in which an aged aristocrat recounts his whole life as a sequence of divine gifts, prefaced by a prose introduction explaining his purpose. The verse narrative recalls his birth near Thessalonica, his childhood and education at Bordeaux, a worldly youth of wealth and leisure, the loss of family and property during the Gothic and Alanic devastations of Gaul, and a poor old age spent at Massilia (Marseilles), all offered to Christ in gratitude. Readers of intertexts will find it valuable both as an early experiment in Christianized autobiography and for its self-conscious engagement with the classical authors—Homer and Virgil among them—whom the poet names as formative reading.
la.paulus_albarus.carmina: A medieval Latin collection of verse (541 lines, with no division into books) attributed to Paulus Albarus and assigned to the Carolingian era, its meter unspecified. The opening poem summons the nightingale (philomela) to surpass every human music — meter, organ, the Muses, and the lyre — and to raise its song in praise of Christ, while later passages bring in the cock (gallus) as a fellow and rival singer and frame the verses as 'responsa poetica' answering the birds. The collection thus recasts the classic nightingale topos in a Christian key, setting bird-song against lyric and hymnic praise. Readers of intertexts will find here a compact witness to the medieval transmission of the philomela and cock motifs, with diction inviting comparison across classical, biblical, and Carolingian song traditions.
la.paulus_diaconus.carmina: The Carmina of Paulus Diaconus, the Lombard scholar and historian of the Carolingian period, are transmitted with his Historia Langobardorum in G. Waitz's edition of 1878 and run to some 1,714 lines of verse. The collection opens with a versified computation of world history from creation through the patriarchs, the Mosaic law, and the Babylonian captivity down to the poet's own day, set amid the reigns of Desiderius and Adelchis and of Arichis of Benevento with his queen Adelperga. Further pieces address Arichis and his household and rise into triumphal, hymnic praise of a Benedict. Its blend of biblical chronology, dynastic panegyric, and devotional address offers readers of intertexts a dense stock of formulas and phrasings shared with late antique and early medieval Latin verse.
la.persius.saturae: The Saturae of Persius, a satirist of the Early Imperial period, consist of six hexameter poems totalling 656 lines. The opening satire stages a dialogue over whether anyone will read such austere verse, and the collection proceeds in a compressed, contorted idiom aimed at literary vanity, fashionable recitation, and moral complacency. Writing within the satiric tradition of Lucilius and Horace, Persius recasts the diction of earlier Latin poetry into an idiosyncratic, heavily allusive style. Its programmatic first poem and dense verbal texture throughout make the work a rewarding hunting ground for readers tracing parallels in Roman satire and its afterlife.
la.petronius.satyricon: The Satyricon, a Latin satire of the Early Imperial period attributed to Petronius, is represented here by 315 lines of verse in mixed metres. The opening sequence sets a programmatic poem on poetic discipline and the assimilation of Greek and Roman models from Homer and Demosthenes to Cicero beside satiric epigrams on the rule of money in the lawcourts, the tyranny of desire, a scornful summons to effeminate dancers, and a bleak reflection on human mortality. With its generic variety and densely allusive engagement with canonical literature, the work serves as a central point of reference for studies of satire, parody, and intertextuality in early imperial Latin poetry.
la.petrus_riga.aurora: The Aurora is a medieval Latin versification of the Bible with continuous moral and allegorical exposition, transmitted under the name of Petrus Riga and presented here in P. E. Beichner's 1965 edition. Running to 16,762 lines in twenty-three books, it opens with prefatory verses in which an unnamed canon praises the book as manna from heaven, as Ezekiel's scroll written within and without, and as Moses' face unveiled at the light of Christ. The preface announces the poem's governing method, that the letter of scripture narrates the old law in figure while a mystical sense lies within its plain surface, pairing literal history with spiritual meaning throughout. A reader of intertexts will find a dense rehearsal of biblical diction and typology, verse after verse recasting the books of scripture into Latin poetry and cataloguing the allegorical readings on which later medieval writers drew.
la.phaedrus.fabulae_aesopiae: Phaedrus, a fabulist of the early imperial period, recasts Aesopic material in Latin verse, announcing in the prologue that he has polished Aesop's matter into senarii and that the book's double gift is laughter and prudent counsel for life. Its nearly two thousand lines consist of short animal fables, such as the wolf and the lamb, each rounded off with an explicit moral, alongside anecdotes in which fables intervene in political situations, notably Aesop speaking to Athenians groaning under Pisistratus. Satiric in temper, the collection repeatedly defends fiction as the veil behind which truths unwelcome to the powerful may be told. For readers of intertexts, it offers the principal Latin verse repository of fable plots, proverbial animal types, and sententious morals that echo through ancient and later literature.
la.philastrius.diversarum_hereseon_liber: A late antique Latin heresiology in prose, the Diversarum Hereseon Liber is attributed to Philastrius and is read here in Friedrich Marx's 1898 Corpus Scriptorum Ecclesiasticorum Latinorum edition. Announcing its aim to enumerate the heresies that have arisen from the beginning of the world, first among the Jews and then after the coming of Christ in the flesh, it opens with an allegory of the devil as the partridge of Jeremiah before cataloguing sect after sect: Ophites, Cainites, Sethians, Dositheans, Sadducees, Pharisees, Samaritans, Nazoreans, Essenes, sun-worshippers, and further groups, each furnished with doctrine, etymology, and scriptural proof-text. In its six hundred and sixty-six lines a reader tracing intertexts finds a compact Latin repertory of sect names, teachings, and biblical quotation that parallels the heresiological traditions of Greek and Latin Christian writers.
la.plautus.amphitruo: A Latin comedy of the Republican period by Plautus, printed here in F. Leo's 1895 edition and running to 1175 lines. The play opens with a prologue delivered by Mercury, who announces his father Jupiter's request for silence and favourable judgement and introduces the plot in which Jupiter impersonates Amphitryon to gain access to Amphitryon's wife Alcmena, with Mercury attending on the deception. Its mythological subject and divine disguises set it apart from Plautus' other comedies of ordinary Roman life, and its sustained double plot of mortal and immortal impersonation has made it a recurring point of comparison for later comic treatments of mistaken identity and divine intervention.
la.plautus.bacchides: The Bacchides is a Roman comedy by Titus Maccius Plautus, a playwright of the Republican period writing in the palliata tradition that recast Greek New Comedy for the Latin stage; it survives here in F. Leo's 1895 Teubner edition, in 1,253 lines of dramatic verse. The plot turns on two courtesan sisters who bear the same name, Bacchis, the young lovers Pistoclerus and Mnesilochus, a soldier's gold that passes through scheming hands, and the resourceful slave Chrysalus, whose deceptions of the old men supply the play's comic engine. Its blend of duplicity, self-conscious theatricality, and burlesque of tragic diction made it a rich quarry for later comic writers. Among the loci of interest to readers of intertexts is the lovers' comparison of themselves to Ulysses, one errant twenty years abroad, the other wandering 'within the city walls,' an inversion with a long afterlife in European literature.
la.plautus.cistellaria: The Cistellaria is a Latin comedy of the Roman Republican period by Titus Maccius Plautus, composed in dramatic metres within the palliata tradition of Roman plays adapted from Greek models. The work survives only in part, and the 680 lines preserved in Leo's 1895 edition centre on the world of the courtesans: the opening scene follows Selenium and her companions as they weigh friendship, freedwoman status, and the raising of daughters against the hazards of their trade, while the plot as a whole turns on recognition and a young woman's recovered parentage, as the title 'The Casket' suggests. For readers hunting intertexts, the play offers parallels with Greek New Comedy and with other Plautine and Roman comic treatments of recognition tokens, stock lovers, and courtesan diction.
la.plautus.curculio: Curculio is a Latin comedy attributed to Plautus, belonging to the fabula palliata tradition of the Republican stage and preserved here in F. Leo's edition of 1895, running to some 727 lines of dramatic verse. Its plot turns on the lover Phaedromus, the parasite Curculio who acts as his go-between, the pimp Cappadox, and a braggart soldier, set at Epidaurus and resolved by a ring and a recognition scene. The opening, in which the lover slips out by night toward the temple of Aesculapius, contains the celebrated passage declaring that no one may be barred from the public road and that one should love what one loves 'with witnesses present.' Readers hunting intertexts will find the play a rich source of Plautine wordplay, reworked Greek comic material, and stock figures that reverberate through later Roman and early modern comedy.
la.plautus.epidicus: Epidicus is a Latin comedy of the Republican period transmitted among the plays of Titus Maccius Plautus, presented here in F. Leo's 1895 Berlin edition. In 741 lines of dramatic verse it takes its name from the quick-witted slave Epidicus, whose opening banter with Thesprio sets the comic register and whose schemes on behalf of the young Stratippocles supply the play's intrigue. The dialogue is studded with proverbial repartee and playful epic allusion, from armour forged by Mulciber to Thetis and the daughters of Nereus, offering abundant material for readers tracing verbal and thematic parallels. As the classic showcase of the Plautine clever slave and of Republican comic diction, it stands as a recurrent source and analogue within Roman comedy and the wider Latin tradition.
la.plautus.menaechmi: Plautus' Menaechmi, a comedy of the Roman Republic in dramatic verse, runs to 1,155 lines and is printed here in F. Leo's 1895 edition of Plautus' plays. A prologue speaker outlines the plot and jokes that the play 'sicilicissat' rather than 'atticissat': twin brothers of Syracuse were separated in childhood when one was carried off to Epidamnus, and the surviving twin was renamed after the lost brother. The comedy unfolds when one twin arrives in the other's city, generating escalating errors of identity involving a wife, a courtesan, a parasite, and the twins' grandfather before the brothers are reunited. As the canonical Roman comedy of twin-based confusion, it matters to readers of intertexts as the principal ancient model for later mistaken-identity plots, most famously Shakespeare's Comedy of Errors.
la.plautus.miles_gloriosus: Miles Gloriosus is a Latin comic drama of the Roman Republic by Plautus, edited by F. Leo (Berlin, 1895) and running to 1431 lines of dramatic verse. Its opening scene sets the tone with a braggart soldier inspecting his gleaming armour while his parasite Artotrogus flatters him with absurd tales of battlefield prowess. The play goes on to centre on the deception of this boastful officer and the spiriting away of the mistress he keeps, in the manner of Greek New Comedy refashioned for the Roman stage. For readers of intertexts, it is a principal source of the miles gloriosus stock figure, whose swaggering descendants recur throughout later European comedy.
