la.plautus.stichus: Stichus is a drama in Latin verse by the Republican-era playwright Plautus, printed here from F. Leo's edition (Berlin, 1895) and running to 772 lines. The opening scene presents two sisters whose husbands have been away for three years; they measure their own faithfulness against the example of Penelope and debate how to respond to a father who would take them from the absent men. As Plautine dramatic verse, the play supplies comparanda for Penelope allusions, scenes of sisterly conference, proverbial turns of colloquial Latin, and the recurring comic situation of the steadfast wife awaiting a long-absent husband.
la.plautus.truculentus: Truculentus is a Latin comedy by Plautus of the Republican period, presented here in F. Leo's 1895 Berlin edition of Plauti Comoediae and running to 966 lines of dramatic verse. Its prologue playfully begs the audience for a patch of ground on which to set the stage at Athens and introduces Phronesium, a courtesan who strips her admirers of everything they own, duping a soldier with a feigned child while the rustic Truculentus of the title is tamed amid her schemes. The long speech on the countless ways lovers are impoverished and undone — blandishments, tantrums, supplications, annuities, and gifts — stands among the most quotable sententiae of Roman comedy. Readers tracing intertexts will find fertile material in its self-aware prologue, its portrait of the mercenary courtesan, and its catalogue of love's expenses.
la.pliny_the_younger.letters: Pliny the Younger's Letters, an Early Imperial prose epistolary collection in ten books, presents correspondence with a wide circle of addressees, including the historian Tacitus, arranged by association rather than in chronological order, as the opening letter to Septicius Clarus explains. The letters move from villa life, travel, and the claims of otium to courtroom advocacy, literary recitation, and the aftermath of Domitian's reign, building pointed character portraits of figures such as Regulus. Readers of intertexts will find a dense web of allusion throughout: the author professes rivalry with Cicero, imitates Demosthenes and Calvus, quotes Virgil, and seasons his prose with Greek terms. As a self-conscious heir to Ciceronian epistolography, the collection is a central witness to Early Imperial literary culture and a rich quarry of verbal echoes.
la.poeta_saxo.annales_de_gestis_karoli_magn: The Annales de Gestis Karoli Magni, attributed to a poet known as Poeta Saxo, is a Carolingian Latin epic in hexameters, preserved in five books totaling 2694 lines. It recounts the deeds of Charlemagne, opening with his sole rule after his brother Carlomann's death and turning early to the wars against the neighboring and still pagan Saxons, whose conquest the poet frames as divinely sanctioned. As a substantial verse treatment of recent Frankish history, it offers readers of intertexts a Carolingian fusion of classical epic diction with biblical and Christian material, and a point of contact for formulas shared with annalistic prose and panegyric tradition.
la.polignac.antilucretius: Polignac's Antilucretius is a Modern Latin philosophical work of nearly twelve thousand lines, conceived as a sustained rejoinder to Lucretius and the Epicurean school. Its opening invocation, addressed to a dedicatee named Quintus, declares war on the sect that abandons the world to fortune and denies providence and the life to come, calling instead upon the eternal Wisdom, Reason, and Light of God to guide the argument. Readers hunting intertexts will find the work in constant dialogue with De rerum natura, adopting Lucretian diction and opening formulas while reversing their doctrine in defense of a divinely ordered cosmos.
la.pontius_diaconus.acta_proconsularia: The Acta Proconsularia, a brief Latin prose work attributed to Pontius the Deacon and transmitted among the writings of Cyprian, recounts the trial and martyrdom of Cyprian, bishop of Carthage, in the persecution under the emperors Valerian and Gallienus. It stages his interrogation by the proconsul Paternus and banishment to Curubis, then his second hearing and condemnation before Galerius Maximus, closing with an account of his beheading and burial. Its laconic courtroom dialogue ('Christianus sum et episcopus') and ritualized death scene supplied a pattern for later Latin passiones, making the work a natural point of comparison for readers tracing confessional formulae and martyr narrative conventions in late antique literature.
la.priscian.perihegesis: The Periegesis is a Late Antique Latin didactic poem attributed to Priscian, running to 2,174 lines and printed in the 1953 edition of P. van der Woestijn. Opening with an invocation to the creator who governs the universe, the work surveys the inhabited world: the encircling Ocean with its many names, the tripartite division of the earth into Libya, Europe, and Asia, and the rivers, straits, coasts, cities, and peoples that define them, from Gades and the mouths of the Nile to the Tanais, the Hellespont, and the Caspian and Euxine waters. Its compact verse rendering of geographical teaching in Latin makes it a rich source for intertextual study, sharing formulas and subject matter with didactic epic, ethnographic description, and the late antique school tradition.
la.propertius.elegies: The Elegies of Propertius, an Augustan collection of love poetry composed in elegiac couplets, comprises four books totalling 3,982 lines. The opening poem announces the poet's capture by Cynthia and his conscription into a life of unrelenting passion, and the collection elaborates such elegiac staples as the lover's madness and servitude to Amor, mythological exempla like Milanion's labors for Atalanta, appeals to magic, and admonitions from friends. For readers hunting intertexts, the work offers the diction, situations, and mythological machinery of Roman love elegy in dense concentration, making it a rich source of verbal and thematic parallels within Augustan poetry.
la.prudentius.apotheosis: A Late Antique Latin Christian poem by Prudentius, the Apotheosis runs to 1,152 lines in H. J. Thomson's Loeb edition. It opens with a compact confession of the triune God—Son begotten as Wisdom from the Father's heart, Spirit subsisting eternally—before turning to an anxious inquiry after right faith and a sustained attack on heretical doctrines, whose crooked paths and sophistic syllogisms lure the unwary into the robbers' pit. Readers hunting textual parallels will find here a dense weave of scriptural language, trinitarian formulae, and anti-heretical polemic characteristic of Late Antique Christian verse.
la.prudentius.contra_symmachum: Contra Symmachum is a two-book Christian polemical poem in Latin by the late antique poet Prudentius, transmitted in some 1,943 lines. Directed against the defence of the old Roman cults associated with the senator Symmachus, it sets scriptural authority and a providential reading of Roman history against the claims of paganism. The prefatory narrative of Paul, who after shipwreck gathers kindling, is bitten by a chilled viper, and shakes the creature off unharmed, announces the governing theme of Christian truth disarming pagan menace. For readers of intertexts the poem offers a dense repertory of classical allusion and exempla, as Prudentius turns the inherited language of Roman literature to apologetic ends.
la.prudentius.dittochaeon: Prudentius's Dittochaeon is a late antique cycle of Latin quatrains, each condensing a biblical episode into four densely allusive lines, from the fall of Eve and the offerings of Cain and Abel through the patriarchs and the wonders of Moses. Across some 196 lines the sequence runs through Old Testament history and on into the New, its epigrammatic compression serving as a chain of compact verse glosses in the manner of captions for biblical pictures. For hunters of intertexts, the work offers a rich field for comparison both with its scriptural sources and with Prudentius's own longer poetic treatments of the same narratives.
la.prudentius.epilogus: The Epilogus is a brief Latin poem of 34 lines with which Prudentius, a late-antique Christian poet, closes his collection of verse. The speaker contrasts two offerings made to God—the gifts of a pure conscience and money given for the relief of the poor—with his own sacrifice of swift iambics and whirling trochees, verses he can make despite lacking holiness and wealth. The poem then develops the Pauline image of the household vessel (Romans 9:21; 2 Timothy 2:20), asking Christ to find use even for a worn earthenware pot in the corner of his hall, and ends by affirming that the lowliest service to God is worthwhile, since whatever befall it is a joy to sound the name of Christ aloud, with a final echo of Philippians 1:18. Readers tracing intertexts will find here a compact statement of Christian poetic humility built on explicit biblical reminiscence.
la.prudentius.hamartigenia: The Hamartigenia, a didactic Christian poem of 1,029 lines by the Late Antique Latin poet Prudentius, polemicizes against Marcionite dualism by arguing that sin originates not in an evil principle of matter or a rival creator but in the perversion of the good human will. Its opening typology presents Cain's rejected sacrifice as a figure of Marcion, who offers the gifts of contaminated flesh and divides the eternal godhead, and the poem then traces how rightly intended offerings are corrupted into perverted sin. Combining sustained engagement with Genesis and Pauline teaching with classical diction and rhetoric in the service of Latin theology, the work offers readers of intertexts a dense field of biblical, classical, and early Christian allusion.
la.prudentius.peristephanon: The Peristephanon is a late antique Latin collection of fourteen hymns by Prudentius, totalining some 3,762 lines, celebrating Christian martyrs and their cults. The opening poem, on two Iberian martyrs, establishes the cycle's recurring motifs: martyrs' names inscribed in heaven, relics that draw pilgrims from across the world, blood shed for Christ as a healing and redemptive force, and martyrdom figured as military service in which soldiers exchange Caesar's standards and dragon banners for the sign of the cross. For readers of intertexts, the cycle is a key witness to the transfer of classical lyric and epic diction into Latin Christian poetry and a rich source of language, imagery, and narrative patterns for later medieval writing on the saints.
la.prudentius.psychomachia: The Psychomachia of Prudentius, a Late Antique Latin Christian poem of 988 lines, stages the struggle for the human soul as an armed combat between personified Virtues and Vices. It opens by presenting the patriarch Abraham as the first exemplar of faith, whose rescue of Lot from the captive kings prefigures the believer's warfare against profane gentibus before the soul may bear offspring pleasing to God. The poem then unfolds a sequence of duels—faith against the worship of old gods, chastity against lust, patience against wrath—in which biblical figures and allegorical warriors alternate. Readers of intertexts will find it a dense meeting point of Virgilian epic diction, biblical narrative, and personification allegory, and a foundational model for the later medieval allegorical tradition.
la.pseudo_cyprian.adversus_judaeos: Adversus Judaeos is a Latin prose work of theology of later imperial date, of uncertain authorship, transmitted under the name of Cyprian of Carthage and printed in Hartel's Vienna edition of the Cyprianic corpus. It argues that Israel, having scorned God's testimonies and put Christ to death, forfeited the old testament, and it retells salvation history from Adam through Noah, Abraham, and Moses to show the divine inheritance transferred to the Gentiles of every condition. Its dense scriptural quotation and paraphrase, together with its pronounced debts to Cyprianic themes and diction, make it a valuable witness for readers tracing biblical and patristic intertexts in the Latin anti-Judaic tradition.
la.pseudo_cyprian.de_duplici_martyrio: A Latin prose treatise transmitted under the name of Cyprian and printed among the pseudo-Cyprianic works of Hartel's 1871 Vienna edition of Cyprian's Opera Omnia; its author and date are uncertain, though it presents itself as written some two hundred and forty years after the coming of Christ. Framed as a second book addressed to a correspondent named Fortunatus, it distinguishes two kinds of martyrdom: the public shedding of blood under persecution, and a hidden, unbloody martyrdom of daily witness in which a pious life, the confession of sins, and endurance of temptation glorify God no less than death at a tyrant's hands. Along the way it discusses the threefold testimony of spirit, water, and blood, denounces clergy and laity guilty of avarice, drunkenness, and other covert idolatries, and weighs the claims of confessors, monks, and virgins to the martyr's crown. Readers hunting intertexts will find a dense web of biblical citation and a late-antique example of how martyrdom vocabulary could be extended from execution to the whole Christian life.
la.pseudo_cyprian.de_singularitate_clericor: A Latin prose treatise on clerical continence, transmitted under the name of Cyprian of Carthage (hence pseudo-Cyprianic) and preserved in Hartel's Vienna edition of 1871; its author and precise date are uncertain, though its concerns belong to the later imperial church. Framed as an exhortatory letter to beloved 'sons' and presented as prompted by a divine revelation, it argues that clerics must shun cohabitation with women, answering in turn the excuses drawn from Elijah and the widow, the apostles accompanied by women, and Christ's own dealings with the Samaritan woman, Martha, and the sinful woman at his feet. The case is sustained by an exceptionally dense tissue of scriptural citation, in which Proverbs and Sirach are pressed into service against self-styled 'eunuchs' of a false chastity and Pauline texts are wielded against their own misusers, alongside an apocryphal saying about Adam's penitence. Readers hunting intertexts will find rich material in its recombination of biblical loci, its savouring of forensic and medical imagery against female company, and the closing virtuoso string of antithetical definitions in praise of singular chastity.
la.quintilian_pseudo.major_declamations: The Major Declamations, transmitted under the name of Quintilian and composed in prose oratory of the Early Imperial period, gather lengthy declamations on fictitious legal cases of deliberate extravagance. Each speech is prefaced by a statement of its theme—here a blind son and a stepmother who accuse one another of murdering the father—followed by a sustained judicial oration built on paradox, sententiae, and minute psychological argument. For readers of intertexts, the collection offers a dense web of rhetorical commonplaces, imagery, and verbal echoes shared with Silver Latin oratory, epic, and tragedy, and ranks among the richest witnesses to the declamatory style that informed early imperial literary diction.
la.rufinus_of_aquileia.interpretatio_oratio: Rufinus of Aquileia's Latin version of nine orations of Gregory of Nazianzus, a late antique prose translation whose prologue is addressed to Apronianus, opens with a biographical encomium of Gregory before rendering his Apologeticus, the defense of his withdrawal from priestly office. The work makes a major corpus of Greek theology available in Latin, embracing Gregory's reflections on pastoral responsibility and the care of souls as a medicine, his critique of clerical ambition, and his anti-Arian and anti-Sabellian exposition of the Trinity. For readers tracing intertexts, the translation repays comparison with Gregory's Greek for the study of Rufinus's translational diction and for identifying the Latin phrasing by which Gregory's thought passed into Western theological discourse.
la.rusticus_presbyter.epistula_ad_eucherium: A brief Latin prose letter of Late Antique theological interest, attributed in the source record to a priest named Rusticus and addressed to Eucherius of Lyon, preserved as a single unit. The letter effusively praises Eucherius's doctrina, extolling his resolution of the questions and aenigmata of both Testaments as a veil removed from the eyes of the heart, and closes with a request for prayer. Of particular note for readers of intertexts is its quotation of Virgil ('Virgilium uatem melius sua carmina laudant'), set within an anecdote about epigrams under portraits in a library, showing how Christian epistolary praise could invoke the authority of the classical canon.
la.rutilius.de_reditu: De Reditu, a late-antique Latin poem of 878 lines in elegiac couplets by Rutilius, takes the form of a first-person travel narrative recounting a journey from Rome back to the poet's native Gaul. The opening verses extol Rome and the men of foreign birth whom her curia honours, then turn to the Gallic fields that summon the speaker home, lands disfigured by long wars and by recent ravage at the hands of the Goths, whether by sword or by fire. Mingling Roman panegyric, coastal itinerary, and lament for a ruined countryside, the poem offers readers of intertexts a late exemplar of the classical elegiac tradition, its allusive diction pressed into the service of contemporary history.
la.sallust.catilina: A Latin prose monograph of historiography from the Roman Republic, by Sallust and titled Catilina in the corpus, recounting the conspiracy of Lucius Sergius Catilina against the Roman state. It opens with a preface on the pursuit of glory and the primacy of excellence of mind, sketches Catiline's audacious and corrupted character, and digresses on the transformation of Roman morals from the city's Trojan origins onward, blaming luxury and avarice for the crisis. Its compressed, archaizing prose and pointed moralizing sententiae became a model for later historians, and its portrait of Catiline endured as the touchstone against which subsequent treatments of the conspirator were measured.
la.sallust.jugurtha: Sallust's Bellum Iugurthinum, a prose historiographical monograph of the Roman Republic, recounts Rome's war against Jugurtha, king of Numidia, opening with a moralizing preface on the sovereignty of the animus over the body and the author's withdrawal from public life into the writing of history. The narrative traces the Numidian succession from Masinissa through Micipsa to Jugurtha's rise, his military distinction under Scipio at Numantia, and his exploitation of a venal Roman nobility, framing the war as the first open challenge to noble superbia and as a prelude to civil discord. Its compressed, archaizing style, aphoristic moral reflections, and memorable portraits of ambition and corruption made it a touchstone for later Latin historiography and a rich quarry for verbal and thematic echoes in subsequent literature.
la.salvianus.ad_ecclesiam: Ad Ecclesiam is a late-antique Latin prose treatise on avarice and the right use of riches by Salvian, presbyter of Massilia (Marseilles), cast in the form of an epistle addressed to 'Timothy', a figure for the universal church. The author laments that a church grown vast in numbers has grown poor in devotion, rebukes believers who hoard wealth or devote it to heirs rather than works of mercy, dismisses the plea that obligations to children justify accumulation, and insists that all substance is God's loan, to be repaid through almsgiving. Scriptural authority carries nearly every turn of the argument, from the command to store up treasure in heaven and the camel through the needle's eye to James's denunciation of the rich and the Acts portrait of the primitive church holding all things in common. For readers of intertexts, the work offers a compact late-antique example of hortatory prose built from epistolary convention and a dense lattice of biblical quotation and allusion, with the church itself dramatized as addressee and charged with having the letter of scripture without its virtue.
la.scriptores_historiae_augustae.historia_a: The Historia Augusta is a late-antique Latin prose historiography presenting serial biographies of Roman emperors, transmitted under the collective authorship of the Scriptores Historiae Augustae, with individual lives assigned to named writers such as Aelius Spartianus and Iulius Capitolinus, and prefaces here addressed to Diocletian. The opening books treat Hadrian's life and reign in exhaustive detail, followed by the short life of the Caesar Aelius Verus and the accession of Antoninus Pius. In the Suetonian tradition, the biographies mix administrative, military, and legal record with gossip, omens, documents, and verse quotations, including the Virgilian lots consulted over Hadrian's future rule. Its dense echo of earlier Latin poetry and prose, together with its habit of citing and imitating authors such as Virgil, Ennius, and Marius Maximus, makes it a rewarding hunting ground for readers tracing intertexts.
la.secundinus.epistula_secundini_ad_augusti: The Epistula Secundini ad Augustinum is a brief Late Antique theological letter in prose, sent by Secundinus to Augustine and opening with an elaborate address to him as 'domino merito honorabili atque laudabili'. Writing after Augustine's break with the Manichaean community, Secundinus pleads with his addressee to abandon his anti-Manichaean polemic and return to the faith he once shared, explaining Manichaean teaching on the two natures, the cosmic combat of spirits for the soul, and the coming new age, while urging reconciliation through a face-to-face disputation. Along the way the letter attacks Augustine's use of the Old Testament, invokes Pauline texts on the armour of God and the principalities against which the apostle contended, and contrasts Augustine's eloquence with his supposed lack of Christian substance. As one of the few substantial specimens of Manichaean Latin prose to survive, and one that engages directly with Augustine's early writings and scriptural exegesis, it offers readers of intertexts a rare witness to the polemical exchange between Catholic and Manichaean authors.
la.sedulius.a_solis_ortus_cardine: A late antique Latin Christian poem by Sedulius, 'A solis ortus cardine' is an alphabetic hymn whose stanzas on the birth and infancy of Christ begin in sequence with the letters of the alphabet. Its 92 lines rehearse the gospel Nativity episodes one by one: the Word made flesh of the Virgin, the annunciation and the leaping of John in the womb, the manger and the angels' song to the shepherds, Herod's alarm, the adoration of the magi, and the slaughter of the Innocents. The poem belongs to the same corpus as the Paschale carmen with which the CSEL edition presents it, and stanzas such as 'Hostis Herodes impie' had a long independent life in the Latin liturgy, making the hymn a recurrent reservoir of phrases and motifs for later writers of gospel verse.
la.sedulius.carmen_paschale: The Carmen Paschale is a Latin Christian epic in hexameters by Sedulius, a poet of the Late Antique period whose precise dates and biography are uncertain. After a prefatory invitation to the paschal banquet that contrasts the author's humble Christian song with the grandiose fictions of pagan poets, the poem unfolds an account of the miracles and saving work of Christ in diction deeply indebted to classical epic. It runs to 1,754 lines and is divided here into six book files, following the edition of Huemer in CSEL 10 (1885). Readers of intertexts will find it a central instance of biblical epic, where Virgilian language and form are systematically redirected to scriptural narrative.
la.sedulius.carmina_ad_sedulium_spectantia: A small Late Antique collection of Latin poems connected with the Christian poet Sedulius rather than composed by him, transmitted with his works and printed among the Poetae Christiani Minores in the CSEL volume of 1888. It opens with a dedicatory poem by Turcius Rufus Asterius praising Sedulius's verse as free from fictive fault, followed by acrostic lines of the scholasticus Bellesabius that name Sedulius as the versifier of Christ's miracles and invite a guest to a humble banquet. The collection closes with a poem on the Incarnation, from the Annunciation and Nativity to an eschatological promise of peace and plenty, built largely out of Virgilian lines and phrasing. A reader of intertexts will find both testimony to Sedulius's early reception and a dense cento whose individual verses invite comparison with the Eclogues, Georgics, and Aeneid.
la.sedulius.epistola_ad_macedonium: Sedulius's prose dedicatory letter to the presbyter Macedonius prefaces his Paschale carmen, the late-antique Latin verse work gathering from the four gospels an account of Christ's miracles, passion, resurrection, and ascension. Writing as a former devotee of secular letters and self-described tiro in sacred learning, Sedulius explains why he clothed scriptural matter in meter—for readers whom the pleasures of verse reach where prose rhetoric does not—and commends the completed four books to Macedonius's protection against critics. The letter also names the priests and consecrated women of his circle (Ursinus, Laurentius, Gallianus, Felix, Syncletica, and Perpetua), invokes Jerome as a model for addressing devout noblewomen, and defends the union of Christian truth with classical poetic craft. For readers of intertexts it offers rich ground: dense scriptural allusion (the parable of the talents, the beatitudes, 'pascha nostrum immolatus est Christus'), sustained nautical and military metaphor, and proverbs such as the eagle that must sometimes descend from the clouds.
la.sedulius.hymnus_i: A Latin Christian hymn attributed to the Late Antique poet Sedulius, opening with the summons 'Cantemus, socii, Domino, cantemus honorem'. The poem runs through salvation history in paired lines, each matching an Old Testament episode—the fall of Adam, Cain's murder of Abel, the Flood, the Exodus, the manna and the water from the rock, Gideon's fleece, David and Goliath—with its fulfilment in Christ, before turning to the virginal birth, the Passion, and a closing doxology to the Trinity. Its compressed, formulaic mapping of biblical type onto Gospel antitype made it a natural quarry for later hymnographers and preachers, and it offers readers of intertexts a compact Late Antique model of typological exegesis in verse.
la.sedulius_scotus.carmen_pastorale: Carmen Pastorale is a Latin poem of 157 lines attributed to the Carolingian author Sedulius Scotus, preserved in B. Bischoff's edition of 1981. Cast as a string of gnomic exhortations addressed to a priest ('sacer'), it urges vigilant care of the flock against the wolf, dwells on the crushing honour and responsibility of the priestly office, and includes a substantial section 'de legendi studio' in which sacred reading is made the wellspring of all profit and moral discernment. Its dense web of biblical allusion and its concern with pastoral duties offer readers of intertexts a compact instance of the mirror-for-clergy mode in Carolingian verse, where shepherding imagery, priestly topoi, and scriptural commonplaces circulate in concentrated form.
la.seneca.agamemnon: Agamemnon is a Latin tragedy in dramatic meters on a Greek mythological subject, composed in the Early Imperial period by L. Annaeus Seneca and running to 1,060 lines. The ghost of Thyestes opens the play, rising from Tartarus to crave vengeance upon the house of Pelops, and the action then turns on Agamemnon's homecoming from Troy, his murder at the hands of Clytemnestra and Aegisthus, and the prophetic ecstasy of Cassandra, with the escape of young Orestes leaving the cycle of revenge open. Reworking the material of Aeschylus' Oresteia and the wider epic and tragic traditions of the house of Atreus, the drama offers dense verbal echoes and choral meditations on Fortuna, kingship, and blood-guilt, making it a key witness to Roman tragedy's engagement with Greek models and a fertile source of parallels for later drama.
la.seneca.apocolocyntosis: The Apocolocyntosis, attributed to Seneca and dating from the early imperial period, is a brief satirical treatment of the death of the emperor Claudius and his unsuccessful bid for divine honours, told in hexameter verse with a mock-epic apparatus of the Parcae, Apollo, and the gods of heaven. The opening scenes depict the Fates spinning a golden thread for the newborn Nero while Apollo prophesies a new age for Rome, setting up the satire's contrast between the young princeps and his predecessor. Its sustained parody of Homer, Vergil, and other canonical poets makes it a rich hunting ground for intertextual readers, as does its position as a rare surviving contemporary satire on imperial apotheosis.
la.seneca.de_consolatione_ad_helviam: The De Consolatione ad Helviam is an Early Imperial Latin prose consolation in which Seneca addresses his mother Helvia, writing as an exile who resolves to cure her grief by proving that his banishment is no true evil. The speaker first recounts the calamities fortune has already dealt her, then argues that the wise man stands secure against fortune and dismantles the conventional terrors of exile as a mere change of place, illustrated through exempla of peoples' migrations, foundation legends from Antenor to the Roman colonists, and the repeatedly resettled island of his own exile. Readers hunting parallels will find a compact repository of consolatory topoi—virtue as the only secure good, the devaluation of popular opinion, and the catalogue of wandering nations—that echo throughout the consolatio tradition and Senecan philosophical prose.
la.seneca.medea: Seneca's Medea, an Early Imperial Latin tragedy in dramatic meter, runs to 1068 lines in the Teubner edition of Peiper and Richter. The play opens with Medea's nocturnal invocation of Hecate, the underworld powers, and the gods by whom Jason swore, as she prays for the ruin of his new marriage, and it proceeds through her revenge to the killing of the children and her escape in the chariot of the Sun. As a Latin reworking of the Euripidean story saturated with Ovidian diction and Senecan rhetoric of furor and nefas, it offers rich ground for verbal and thematic parallels within the tragic, epic, and witchcraft traditions, and it became a principal conduit of the Medea legend to later European drama.
la.seneca.octavia: Octavia is a Latin drama of Early Imperial date transmitted with the tragedies of L. Annaeus Seneca, though its authorship is disputed and its precise date uncertain; it stands alone as the surviving example of the fabula praetexta, a Roman historical play in place of the customary mythological subject. In 1020 lines of dramatic verse it stages the ruin of Nero's marriage to Claudia Octavia, her repudiation in favor of Poppaea, and her exile and death, employing laments, formal debates, the ghost of Agrippina, a chorus of Roman citizens, and a character modeled on Seneca himself. Readers of intertexts will find the play turning the diction, ghosts, and lyric odes of Senecan tragedy onto recent imperial history while drawing richly on earlier Latin poetry, and its contested attribution makes it a special case in any study of Neronian literary networks.
la.seneca.oedipus: Seneca's Oedipus is an Early Imperial Latin tragedy in dramatic verse, retelling the Theban story of a king whose city wastes under plague while he seeks the murderer of Laius and finds himself to be both that killer and the husband of his own mother. Across its 1,092 lines the play moves from a plague-stricken Thebes through Tiresias's prophecy and the necromantic raising of Laius to the catastrophe of recognition, incest revealed, and self-blinding. For readers of intertexts it matters as a Roman reworking of the Oedipus myth familiar from Greek tragedy, marked by Senecan set pieces on Fortune, pestilence, and the perils of kingship, and as a principal channel by which the story passed into later European drama.
la.seneca.phoenissae: The Phoenissae is a Latin tragedy of Early Imperial date by Lucius Annaeus Seneca, preserved in roughly 672 lines of dramatic verse. Bearing the traditional title of dramas on the Theban legend, the play opens with the blind Oedipus, guided by his daughter Antigone toward Cithaeron, and belongs to the cycle of stories surrounding Oedipus' cursed house and the strife of his sons. Even its opening speech displays the compressed mythological texture typical of Senecan tragedy, piling up exempla of Actaeon, Pentheus, and Ino in rapid rhetorical succession. For readers of intertexts, the play stands as a major Latin reworking of Greek tragic material on Thebes and a rich source of verbal and thematic echoes for later European drama.
la.seneca.quaestiones_naturales: Seneca's Quaestiones Naturales is a Latin prose treatise on natural philosophy of the early Imperial period, addressed to Lucilius and arranged in seven books. It examines meteorological and celestial phenomena — atmospheric fires, halos, thunder, comets, and related prodigies — within a Stoic framework that presents the study of nature as a path to knowledge of God, whose mind pervades the universe. The preface contrasts the part of philosophy concerned with human affairs with the loftier inquiry into things divine, and the discussion repeatedly engages Greek predecessors such as Aristotle while weighing whether portents carry signs or causes. Its systematic explanations, technical Latin vocabulary for physical phenomena, and anecdotal material on omens and prodigies make it a productive source for readers tracing textual parallels in later scientific, philosophical, and literary writing.
la.seneca.thyestes: An early Imperial Latin tragedy by L. Annaeus Seneca in about 1,166 lines, Thyestes dramatises the culmination of the house of Pelops' curse: Atreus lures his exiled brother back to Argos, slays his sons, and serves them to him at a banquet, closing with Atreus' exultant revenge speech and the ghost of Tantalus framing the action. The play opens with Tantalus summoned from the underworld and unfolds through five acts with choral odes, including a well-known meditation on kingship and power after the second act. Because Seneca's treatment of the myth gathers nearly every earlier Greek and Roman version of the Atreus-Thyestes feud, it stands as a hub for intertextual study of the story and, in turn, exercised wide influence on later European revenge drama.
la.seneca.troades: Seneca's Troades is a Latin tragedy of the Early Imperial period, preserved in the Teubner edition of Peiper and Richter, dramatizing the aftermath of Troy's fall: Hecuba's grief, the ghost of Achilles demanding the sacrifice of Polyxena, Andromache's concealment of her son Astyanax, and the quarrels among the Greek victors over the children's fates. Its opening choral ode on the instability of royal fortune exemplifies the gnomic, epigrammatic style of Senecan drama, carried through some twelve hundred lines of dramatic verse. The play reworks situations familiar from Greek tragedy, above all Euripides, while giving them a compressed Latin rhetoric of lamentation and debate. Readers tracing intertexts will find here both the reuse of Euripidean material and distinctive Senecan phrasing whose choruses and sententiae echo widely in later Latin and vernacular writing.
la.seneca_the_elder.controversiae: The Controversiae of Seneca the Elder, a Latin prose work of the early imperial period, records the sententiae, divisiones, and colores of declaimers on a series of fictitious legal cases. An extended preface addressed to the author's three sons Novatus, Seneca, and Mela explains the project, dwelling on the author's celebrated memory and offering sketches of figures such as Cicero, whom he reports having heard in his youth, and his close friend Porcius Latro. Under each controversia the epigrams of named speakers — Gallio, Cestius Pius, Arellius Fuscus, Junius Otho, Pompeius Silo, and others — are gathered by theme, followed by the divisiones laying out the quaestiones of the case. Readers hunting textual parallels value the collection as a storehouse of rhetorical topoi, historical and mythological exempla such as Marius, Cineas, and Cato's definition of the orator, and quotable phrasing that circulated throughout imperial Latin literature, as well as a witness to declaimers whose works survive nowhere else.
la.seneca_the_elder.fragmenta: A short collection of fragments from the oratorical and rhetorical writings of the early Imperial rhetor Seneca the Elder, edited by Adolf Gottlieb Kiessling in the 1872 Teubner volume Oratorum et rhetorum sententiae divisiones colores. The excerpts survive as quotations in later authors, chiefly Quintilian and Donatus's Life of Virgil, and preserve a debate on tragic diction, specimens of bold declaimers' imagery from a controuersia in which a father kills his son and stepmother taken in adultery, an aphorism on oath-taking, and Julius Montanus's remark that he would steal verses from Virgil if he could also have his voice, mouth, and delivery. For readers of intertexts, the fragments are valuable because their phrases and anecdotes circulate within Quintilian and the Virgilian biographical tradition, so parallels may surface in those authors as well as in the declamatory corpus.
la.sigloardus_remensis.rhytmi: Rhytmi is a short work of 125 lines of Carolingian Latin verse attributed to Sigloardus Remensis, edited by P. v. Winterfeld in 1899. Its opening poem is a rhymed rhythmical lament for Bishop Fulco, praised as a wise, eloquent, and noble prelate who adorned the church and governed his people, before the poem recounts his treacherous murder by Guinemarus, who attacked him with sword, clubs, and armed soldiers, and closes with clergy and people bearing away the slain bishop's body amid curses on the murderer. Readers of intertexts will find here characteristic Carolingian formulas of episcopal encomium and invective, a vivid instance of the rhythmus as a vehicle for mourning a contemporary figure, and rich material for parallels in lament diction and the rhetoric of violent death.
la.smaragdus.carmen_in_psalterio: A brief Latin poem of twelve lines attributed to the Carolingian author Smaragdus, presented as a prologue to a treatment of the Psalter. Its speaker describes a copy of the Psalms enclosed in a golden and ivory case, outwardly plain yet bearing within the mystical words that David sang under the covering of the literal sense, and announces the aim of plucking choice gems from the book so that its pages may shine. The poem interests readers of intertexts for its programmatic contrast between the letter and the mystical meaning of the Psalms, its appeal to newer expositors who clarify the praise of the old prophets, and its reuse of stock prefatory imagery of the adorned codex familiar from other medieval verse prefaces.
la.smaragdus.carmina: A Carolingian Latin collection of roughly 500 lines attributed to Smaragdus, the Carmina open with a verse prologue that invites the reader into a libellus versifying scriptural matter: the deeds of the patriarchs and prophets, the Ten Commandments from Sinai, the Psalms, the three books of Solomon read as ethics, physics, and logic, and the preaching of the Gospels and apostles. The prologue's formula 'Scripturam retinet, grammatica redolet' announces poetry that retells the Bible while displaying the tools of the grammatical schoolroom, with classical terms such as Camena and the Cithaeronian plectrum alongside heavy biblical allusion. For readers of intertexts, the collection offers a compact witness to Carolingian biblical versification and to the fusion of scriptural allegory with inherited poetic diction in the medieval classroom tradition.
la.smaragdus.epitaphium: An eight-line Latin epitaph of the Carolingian period, attributed to Smaragdus and commemorating a Smaragdus who flourished as abbot of the place for which it was composed. Written while the emperor Louis the Pious held the reins of empire, it relates how the abbot, judging his original site ill suited to human uses, transferred his seat to a spot not far away, and how on his call to the heavenly kingdom his body was carried back to the old place for burial. The closing lines fix his death beneath the sun in Scorpio, when the stars lay open to the theologian. Readers tracing parallels will find here a compact Carolingian instance of classical funerary diction, Phoebus's course and the opening heavens, adapted to monastic commemoration.
la.smaragdus.versus_ad_filium_ludovici_pii: Versus ad Filium Ludovici Pii is a Carolingian Latin didactic poem of 175 lines, ascribed to Smaragdus and addressed to a son of the emperor Louis the Pious. It opens by urging the young prince to love and obey God, to heed the divine precepts, and to draw living water from the eternal fountain of Scripture, whose draughts quench deadly thirst and lead to the everlasting kingdom. The counsel then turns to the qualities befitting a Christian ruler — royal wisdom, prudence, simplicity of heart, patience, and vigilance against sloth — together with guidance on speech and conduct. Direct quotation of the Gospel ('Si quis me diligit') and pervasive biblical diction make the poem a useful witness to Carolingian advice-literature for princes and a rewarding source for readers tracing shared scriptural paraphrase and gnomic moral formulae across medieval Latin verse.
la.statius.achilleid: The Achilleid is an unfinished Latin epic in hexameters by the early imperial poet Statius, surviving in two books of just over 1,100 lines. Its opening programme promises to sing the whole life of Achilles rather than merely his Trojan deeds: Thetis, warned by prophecy, hides her son on Scyros among the daughters of Lycomedes, where his liaison with Deidamia and his education under Chiron give way to the mustering of the Greek fleet and his departure for Troy, at which point the poem breaks off. Readers of intertexts will find a deliberate counter-epic to the Iliad, rich in Ovidian play with disguise and gender, and the Scyros episode became a favourite topos for later Latin, medieval, and Renaissance retellings of Achilles' youth.
la.statius.silvae: The Silvae of Statius, a poet of the Early Imperial period, is a five-book collection of occasional poetry amounting to some 3,925 lines, edited by John Henry Mozley in 1928. The poems, composed predominantly in hexameters, mark occasions as varied as imperial panegyric, marriage and consolation, the dedication of artworks, and the praise of villas, refracting contemporary figures through mythological exempla. The opening poem measures an equestrian statue of the emperor against the wooden horse of Troy, invoking Aeneas, Hector, and the Cyclopean forges in its comparison. Rich in allusion to earlier Latin poetry, above all the epics of Virgil and Ovid, the collection offers readers of intertexts a dense repertory of mythological and panegyric topoi.
la.statius.thebaid: Statius's Thebaid is a Latin epic in twelve books of dactylic hexameters, composed in the early Imperial period, retelling the strife of Eteocles and Polynices and the war of the Seven against Thebes. Its proem confines the poem's compass to the doomed house of Oedipus, declining contemporary imperial triumphs, and looks back through Cadmus's founding of the city to the origins of the Theban curse. Across its 9,731 lines the poem reworks Virgilian epic diction, Ovidian narrative, and Greek tragic treatments of the Theban cycle in a densely allusive, self-consciously literary manner. Readers hunting intertexts will find it a principal conduit through which Augustan and earlier literary models pass into later Latin poetry.
la.sulpicius_severus.chronica: The Chronica of Sulpicius Severus is a late antique Latin prose work of theology and sacred history, composed, as its preface explains, at the urging of readers who wanted the contents of many volumes condensed into two short books spanning from the world's creation to the author's own day. The narrative retells the biblical story from creation, the fall, and the patriarchs onward through the cross of Christ and the acts of the apostles, and then continues with the fall of Jerusalem, the persecution of the Christian people, and the troubled and peaceful times of the churches. The author openly acknowledges that he drew on secular historians to distinguish and connect the epochs and supply what sacred books alone could not, making the work a deliberate fusion of scriptural narrative and classical historiographical practice. For readers tracing intertexts, its compressed, often idiosyncratic Latin rephrasing of nearly the whole biblical story offers a dense field of verbal and thematic parallels between scripture, apocryphal tradition, and classical writing.
la.sulpicius_severus.vita_martini: Sulpicius Severus' Vita Martini, a Latin prose work of Late Antique theology, narrates the life of Martin from his birth at Sabaria in Pannonia and upbringing in Italy through his reluctant military service, baptism, renunciation of arms, and episcopate. The prologue sets the project against pagan biography, contrasting the pursuit of perishable fame in accounts of figures like Hector and Socrates with the commemoration of a holy man whose example leads readers toward true wisdom and heavenly reward. The episodes recounted here, among them Martin dividing his cloak for a beggar at Amiens and beholding Christ clothed in it, his refusal to fight under Julian Caesar, and his association with Hilary of Poitiers, are densely woven with Gospel allusion and biblical diction. For readers of intertexts, the work is a prime site where classical life-writing conventions are consciously repurposed for Christian ends, and its blend of biographical form, scriptural echo, and moral exemplarity rewards parallel hunting across pagan, biblical, and early Christian traditions.
la.tacitus.agricola: Tacitus' Agricola, a short work of Early Imperial Latin prose that blends biography with ethnography and political reflection, commemorates Gnaeus Iulius Agricola, the author's father-in-law, from his early service in Britain under Suetonius Paulinus through his provincial governorship and northern campaigns to his death. The opening chapters oppose the freedom restored under Nerva and Trajan to the preceding years of enforced silence under Domitian, and the narrative later pauses for an account of Britain and its peoples and for set speeches, including the famous address of the Caledonian leader Calgacus. Its programmatic remarks on writing lives under tyranny, its compressed and allusive style, and its many memorable phrasings have made it a frequent source of verbal echoes for readers tracing intertexts in later Latin and European literature.
la.tacitus.annales: The Annales (ab excessu divi Augusti) of Cornelius Tacitus, a Latin prose historiography of the early imperial period, opens with a programmatic preface promising an account, 'sine ira et studio', of Augustus' last days and the reigns of Tiberius, Gaius, Claudius, and Nero. The narrative preserved here, printed in C. D. Fisher's Oxford edition of 1906 and divided across twelve book files, begins with the death of Augustus, the accession of Tiberius, and the great mutinies of the Pannonian and German legions. Its compressed, epigrammatic style and its canonical scenes—the funeral and deification of Augustus, the army seditions, the figures of Germanicus, Drusus, Livia, and Agrippina—were constantly imitated and echoed, and the work stands among the most fertile sources of allusion for later classical and vernacular writers, making it a prime hunting ground for intertextual parallels.
la.tacitus.de_origine_et_situ_germanorum_li: An ethnographic treatise in Latin prose on the Germanic peoples and their lands, written by Tacitus in the early imperial period and transmitted among his minor works (here in Furneaux's 1900 edition of the Opera Minora). Opening with the geography bounded by Rhine, Danube, and Ocean, it proceeds through origins and early migrations, tribal names, warfare and arms, government, religion and divination, and domestic and social customs. Its accounts of Tuisto and Mannus, the baritus war chant, prophetesses such as Veleda, and its dense catalogue of nations and customs supplied later poets, historians, and antiquarians with a rich stock of names, motifs, and ethnographic commonplaces, making the work a frequent source for intertextual study of writing about the north.
la.tacitus.dialogus_de_oratoribus: A Latin prose dialogue of the Early Imperial period, the Dialogus de Oratoribus is preserved among the minor works of Tacitus and edited here from Henry Furneaux's Opera Minora (1900). Framed as an answer to Fabius Iustus's question why the eloquence of earlier ages has withered, the work stages a debate in which Curiatius Maternus defends his poetic vocation while Marcus Aper and Iulius Secundus press the utility, pleasure, and glory of forensic oratory. Speakers invoke contemporary figures such as Eprius Marcellus, Vibius Crispus, and Saleius Bassus, and allude to tragic subjects like Cato, Medea, and Thyestes, making the dialogue a rich hunting ground for parallels with Ciceronian rhetoric and Augustan poetry. Its 226 lines constitute a compact but programmatic meditation on the relationship between literary genre, public life, and the practice of eloquence under the principate.
la.tacitus.historiae: The Historiae of Tacitus, a Latin prose historiography of the Early Imperial period, printed here from Charles Dennis Fisher's 1911 edition and arranged in five books, recounts the crisis of the Roman state after Nero's fall: the brief principate of Galba and his murder in the forum, the coup of Otho, the revolt of the Rhine legions, and the accession of Vespasian amid civil war. Its programmatic preface contrasts the free eloquence of the republican past with the compromised truth-telling of the principate, and the narrative combines battle scenes, formal speeches, prodigies and omens, and pointed characterization of emperors, armies, and provinces. For readers hunting textual parallels, the work rewards attention for its compressed, allusive, Sallust-inflected style and dense verbal texture, which later Latin prose and European writers repeatedly imitated, quoted, and reworked.
la.terence.adelphi: The Adelphi of Terence is a Roman comedy of the Republican period, written in dramatic verse and running to 1,013 lines in the Parry edition of 1857. Its opening prologue famously defends the poet against charges of plagiarism, explaining that the play draws on Diphilus' Synapothnescontes, which Plautus had already Latinized as the Commorientes, and that one passage has been rendered word for word in the Adelphos. The plot turns on two elderly brothers who bring up their sons by opposite methods, one permissive and one severe, and their quarrel over education frames the comedy's resolution. For readers of intertexts the play is a central node in the transmission of Greek New Comedy into Latin, and its self-conscious discussion of translation, adaptation, and literary theft invites close comparison with Plautus and with the Greek models it reworks.
la.terence.andria: Andria is a Latin comedy in dramatic meter by Terence, a playwright of the Roman Republic, comprising 982 lines. Adapted from Menander's Greek Andria and drawing additionally on his Perinthia, the play opens with a prologue in which the poet answers his detractors and defends the combining of Greek material, the practice the prologue itself calls contamination, appealing to Naevius, Plautus, and Ennius as precedents. The action then turns to the tangled love affair and marriage negotiations within a citizen's household, treated in the manner of Greek New Comedy. For readers of intertexts, the play is a central witness to the Roman reworking of Menandrean material, and its prologue offers one of the clearest ancient statements on adaptation and literary polemic.
la.terence.heautontimorumenos: Terence's Heautontimorumenos ('The Self-Tormentor') is a Latin comedy of the Roman Republican period, preserved in some 1,112 lines of dramatic verse. Its opening prologue, delivered by an actor at the poet's request, defends Terence's habit of combining material from several Greek plays in single Latin works and explains why an old man has been given parts conventionally assigned to the young. The play's Greek title and its open engagement with Greek models make it a key witness to the adaptation of Greek comedy on the Roman stage, and a natural point of comparison for readers tracing such transpositions between traditions.
la.tertullian.adversus_hermogenem: A late-antique Latin theological polemic by Tertullian, printed in Emil Kroymann's 1906 Vienna edition, directed against the teacher Hermogenes, whose doctrine held matter to be unbegotten, eternal, and coeternal with God, the stuff from which God fashioned the world. The treatise argues instead that God created all things from nothing, setting the rule of truth against Hermogenes' borrowings from the Stoa and testing his proofs from Genesis — 'in principio', the earth invisible and unformed, the darkness, abyss, spirit, and waters — while weighing the personified Sophia of Proverbs, the prologue of John, and prophetic promises of the world's final dissolution. Its blend of invective against an opponent still alive, close exegesis of the creation narrative, and philosophical argument over matter, motion, and eternity makes it a rich witness for tracing early Christian ex nihilo apologetic and its reworking of scriptural and philosophical intertexts.
la.tertullian.adversus_marcionem: Adversus Marcionem is a Late Antique Latin anti-heretical treatise in prose by Tertullian, directed against the Marcionite doctrine that the god proclaimed by Christ is other than and superior to the creator. The opening preface recounts the work's reissue after earlier, imperfectly circulated editions, and the ensuing argument contends that only one God, the creator, can be the summum magnum, that Marcion's previously unknown deity lacks the works and revelation by which a god might be known, and that the creator's goodness, justice, and gift of free will answer the problem of evil. The polemic is densely woven from scriptural quotation and allusion, from the prophets and the Psalms to Paul on law and gospel, together with classical and philosophical references running from the Symplegades and Prometheus to Thales and Epicurus, and it repeatedly engages Marcion's Antitheses, making the work a principal witness to Marcionite teaching and a rich node of biblical and classical intertexts. Its opening also glances at Tertullian's De praescriptione haereticorum and documents the textual transmission of his own corpus.
la.tertullian.de_anima: A Late Antique Latin prose treatise on the soul by the Christian writer Tertullian, preserved in Georg Wissowa's 1890 Vienna edition. Opening against Hermogenes, who derived the soul from matter rather than from the breath of God, the work argues for a soul that is corporeal, simple, immortal, and propagated from Adam at conception rather than pre-existent, moving through questions of substance, faculties, senses, intellect, and destiny after death. Along the way it stages extended debates with Plato, the Stoics, Epicurus, and Greek physicians such as Soranus and Herophilus, and refutes Platonic recollection and Pythagorean metempsychosis. Readers of intertexts will find a dense weave of scriptural citation and Greek philosophical vocabulary, allusion, and anecdote, from Socrates' daimonion to the vision of a prophesying sister in the author's own congregation.
la.tertullian.de_idololatria: A prose treatise on idolatry by Tertullian, De Idololatria belongs to late-antique Christian theology and argues that idolatry is the principal crime of humankind, a charge into which homicide, adultery, fraud, cupidity, and every other sin are folded. The discussion ranges across the hidden breadth of the vice: artisans and craftsmen who fashion images, astrologers and teachers of literature, merchants supplying temples, pagan festivals and gifts, lamps and laurels on doorways, public office and military service, and even oaths and everyday speech, each case weighed against biblical precept. Readers of intertexts will find abundant material in the treatise's dense weaving of scriptural quotation and allusion, drawing on Enoch, Isaiah, Daniel, and Gospel sayings on oath-taking, as well as in its detailed witness to the calendar, rituals, and vocabulary of Greco-Roman civic and domestic religion.
la.tertullian.de_pudicitia: De Pudicitia is a Latin prose treatise on chastity by the Christian author Tertullian of Late Antiquity, preserved in Georg Wissowa's 1890 Vienna edition of his opera. It polemicises against an episcopal edict granting forgiveness for adultery and fornication after penance, arguing that such capital sins committed post baptismem are remissible by God alone and not by bishops or martyrs, and it marshals dense scriptural argument in support: the parables of the lost sheep, the drachma and the prodigal son, Paul's handling of the incestuous man at Corinth, 1 John, the Apocalypse, and the Levitical leprosy laws read allegorically, while the Shepherd of Hermas is rejected as apocryphal and opponents are styled 'psychici'. For readers of intertexts the treatise is valuable both for its extensive quotation and allegorical exegesis of scripture and for its idiosyncratic Tertullianic vocabulary ('paracletum', 'psychici'), which echoes through later Latin Christian writing on penance and ecclesiastical authority.
la.tertullian.scorpiace: The Scorpiace, a Latin prose treatise against heretical opponents of martyrdom attributed to Tertullian, the Carthaginian Christian author of the late second and early third century, survives here in the CSEL edition of Reifferscheid and Wissowa. Working through an elaborate conceit that figures heresy as a scorpion whose venomous sting is countered by a healing theriac, the work argues from scriptural precept, Old Testament examples, and the witness of the apostles that persecution is divinely willed and that martyrdom is both necessary and salutary. Readers of intertexts will find dense citation and adaptation of biblical material, from Genesis and the Mosaic law to the Gospels, Pauline epistles, and Revelation, alongside engagement with Nicander on scorpions and classical agonistic spectacle.
la.theodulf_of_orleans.carmina: The Carmina of Theodulf of Orleans form a substantial corpus of Latin verse from the Carolingian period, running to 5,193 lines distributed across 72 book divisions. The collection opens with a lengthy didactic poem on tristitia, distinguishing a sorrow ruled by reason and divine law from the corrupting grief born of frenzy and despair, and buttressing its argument with the words of the Gospel and the apostle. Composed within the learned Latin culture of the Carolingian court and of uncertain precise date within that era, the poems repeatedly rework biblical, patristic, and classical material, making them a rich hunting ground for readers tracing textual parallels between late antique and medieval verse.
la.theodulf_of_orleans.epitaphia: A short Carolingian Latin epitaph poem of 47 lines attributed to Theodulf of Orléans, composed in verse and cast in the poet's own voice as a memorial over his grave. The speaker recounts his birth in Spain and upbringing in Gaul, his tenure as bishop and abbot at Orléans under Charlemagne, and his banishment after Louis, the hereditary successor, gave credence to the false words of informers. It closes with the exile buried far from his flock yet confident that he will rise from the dust at the command of the coming Judge. Readers of intertexts will find a Carolingian reworking of classical epitaph and exile conventions, from the delator motif to the first-person funerary inscription, making the poem a productive parallel for the autobiographical epitaph tradition.
la.unknown.corpus_scriptorum_ecclesiasticor: A Latin prose treatise on sin, nature, and grace, preserved in the CSEL edition of Augustine's Opera (Sectio VIII, Pars I, vol. 60, ed. Karl Urba and Joseph Zycha, 1913) and of uncertain date. It quotes and refutes at length a book sent to the author by his correspondents, which argued that a human being without sin is possible by natural ability and that Adam's sin passes to his descendants by imitation; in reply it defends the woundedness of human nature, original sin, the need of infants for baptism, and the necessity of divine grace, arguing from James on the tongue, the Psalms, Paul, and John. For readers of intertexts the work offers dense, repeatedly reinterpreted scriptural citation in a Latin form close to the Vulgate, along with extensive embedded excerpts from the opponent's treatise, making it a valuable witness to the vocabulary of the Pelagian controversy.
la.valerius_flaccus.argonautica: Valerius Flaccus' Argonautica is an early Imperial Latin epic in dactylic hexameters, transmitted in eight books and some 5,600 lines, which retells the voyage of Jason and the Argonauts toward Colchis and the Phasis. The poem opens with an invocation to Phoebus and a prayer to the sun that ties the poet's task to the reigning emperor, before turning to Pelias' fearful resolve to send the young Aesonid against the perils of the sea. As a Roman epic reworking of the Argonautic legend, it offers dense material for readers tracing parallels with Greek mythological epic and with earlier and contemporary Latin verse.
la.vergil.aeneid: Vergil's Aeneid, an epic in dactylic hexameter composed in the Augustan period, recounts in twelve books the flight of the Trojan exile Aeneas from his burning city, his wanderings and stay with Dido at Carthage, his descent to the underworld, and his war in Latium in fulfillment of the destiny that links his descendants to the founding of Rome. Its opening arma virumque signals a deliberate reworking of Homeric epic, pairing the theme of war with that of wandering in a narrative shaped to bear Roman and Augustan meaning. As the canonical Latin epic, it stands behind nearly all later European verse narrative, and its episodes, formulas, and phrases number among the most frequently echoed material in Western literature, making it an essential touchstone for readers tracing textual parallels.
la.vergil.eclogues: Ten Latin pastoral poems in dactylic hexameter, also known as the Bucolics, composed by Vergil in the Augustan age. The collection stages conversations and singing matches among herdsmen, turning scenes of dispossession, lost love, and rural song into pointed reflections on contemporary politics and on Greek models such as Theocritus. Among the most intensively imitated poems of antiquity, it stands at the head of the European pastoral tradition and is a near-obligatory source for readers tracing echoes and allusions in later literature.
la.vergil.georgics: The Georgics is a Latin didactic poem in hexameter by Vergil, an Augustan-era poet, addressed to Maecenas. Its four books, totalling 2183 lines, treat the growing of grain, the grafting of vines and the cultivation of trees, the care of cattle and flocks, and beekeeping, set within a proem that invokes the agricultural deities and looks toward Caesar. Dense with reworkings of earlier Greek and Roman verse and itself a master source of allusion for later didactic, pastoral, and georgic writing, it stands as a central node for readers tracing textual parallels across classical and European literature.
la.vergil_pseudo.aetna: The Aetna is a Latin hexameter poem of 646 lines on the fires of Mount Etna, transmitted under Vergil's name but of uncertain authorship and assigned by its source record to the Augustan era. Its proem invokes Apollo and sets the mountain's eruptions against the stock themes of epic — the golden age, the Argonauts, the fall of Troy — before undertaking a systematic account of the volcano's behaviour in physical rather than mythological terms, explicitly rejecting the notions that the crater houses Vulcan's forge or serves as the workshop of the Cyclopes. The poem's fusion of didactic explanation with epic diction, and its dense verbal engagement with earlier Latin poetry, make it fertile ground for readers tracing parallels with Lucretius and the Vergilian corpus.
la.vergil_pseudo.ciris: The Ciris is a pseudonymous Latin epic of Augustan date, transmitted under Vergil's name but generally regarded as the work of an unknown poet, comprising 541 hexameter lines. It retells the myth of Scylla, daughter of Nisus of Megara, whose betrayal of her father for love of Minos ends in her transformation into the sea-bird ciris, prefaced by a programmatic proem in which the poet rejects philosophical grandeur for a small and polished song. Its mannered diction, learned etymologies, and dense verbal echo of Vergil and the neoterics make it especially rewarding for readers tracing intertextual allusion. The text follows R. Ellis's Oxford edition of 1907.
la.vergil_pseudo.dirae: The Dirae is a Latin hexameter poem of 103 lines, transmitted under the name Pseudo-Vergil and of uncertain authorship, though assigned to the Augustan era. The speaker pronounces curses upon the lands and home that have been divided and taken from him, wishing barrenness on crops, trees, fountains, and vineyards, and calling down ruin on the soldier who has seized the estate, while addressing companions named Battare and Lycurge. Its theme of confiscated and redistributed land, together with its dense pastoral diction, invites comparison with Vergil's Eclogues and other Augustan treatments of dispossession, making it a productive site for readers tracing intertexts.
la.vergil_pseudo.moretum: The Moretum is a short Latin poem of uncertain authorship, transmitted under Virgil's name and generally placed in the Augustan era. In 122 lines it follows the smallholder Simylus through a winter morning as he rises before dawn, grinds his meagre store of grain at the hand-mill, rouses his African serving-woman Scybale to kindle the fire, and finally prepares the cheese-and-herb relish that gives the poem its title. Its vivid attention to kitchen implements, food preparation, and the speech and bodies of the rural poor offers rich pickings for readers tracing verbal echoes of the Eclogues and Georgics and parallels in the ancient literature of rustic life.
la.vergil_pseudo.priapea: A compact collection of 46 lines of Latin lyric verse attributed to Vergil but of uncertain authorship, generally assigned to the Augustan era. The poems are spoken in the voice of Priapus, the wooden guardian god of the garden, who enumerates the seasonal produce and offerings set before him, boasts of his care for a poor homestead and its animals, and threatens would-be thieves with the obscene punishment that gives the collection its notorious character. Composed in a variety of lyric meters, the collection reworks phrases and motifs from Augustan epic, elegy, and epigram, echoing Vergil, Horace, and the elegists, and so offers intertext-hunters an unusually dense web of verbal parallels.
la.victor_vitensis.historia_persecutionis_a: A late antique Latin prose history of the persecution of African Catholics at the hands of the Arian Vandals, written by Victor, bishop of Vita. Framed as composed in the sixtieth year since the Vandals under Genseric crossed from Spain into Africa, the work opens with a preface addressed to the bishop Diadochus and then recounts the devastation of the provinces, the burning and seizure of churches, the torture and exile of clergy such as Quoduultdeus of Carthage, the capture of Rome, the relief of captives by the bishop Deogratias, and the trials of confessors such as Martinianus, Saturianus and Maxima. Its prose is densely woven with scriptural quotation and allusion, and its blend of martyrology, anti-Arian polemic and lament for a ruined landscape makes it a fertile source of parallels for readers of late antique biblical intertextuality and the literary memory of the Vandal conquest.
la.victorinus_saint_bishop_of_poetovio.comm: A Latin prose commentary on the Book of Revelation by Victorinus, bishop of Poetovio, belonging to the later imperial era. The work expounds the Apocalypse section by section, interpreting the seven churches, the seals, the four living creatures, and the trumpets and plagues as figures of the two testaments, the life of the church, and the last things, with sustained attention to Antichrist, the return of Elijah, and the thousand-year reign. A prefatory epistle addressed to Anatolius stands at the head of the commentary, explaining its correction in revision and setting Victorinus alongside Papias and Nepos on the millennial kingdom. Readers tracing intertexts will find a dense lattice of scriptural citation and typology, from Genesis and the prophets to the Gospels and Paul, woven through the apocalyptic exposition.
la.vitruvius.de_architectura: Vitruvius' De Architectura, a Latin prose treatise in ten books of technical genre composed in the Augustan era, is dedicated to the emperor Caesar and promises a complete account of the architect's discipline, from the education required of the practitioner to building, gnomonics, and machines. The opening book defines architecture through ordinatio, dispositio, eurythmia, symmetria, decor, and distributio, insists on firmitas, utilitas, and venustas, and argues that the architect must master letters, drawing, geometry, history, philosophy, music, medicine, law, and astronomy, illustrating the argument with exempla such as the caryatids and the Persian portico. For readers of intertexts, the treatise is valuable as an encyclopedic conduit of Greek technical and historical learning into Latin, naming authorities from Pytheos and Ctesibius to Archimedes and Aristarchus, and supplying definitions, etymologies, and anecdotes that later authors repeatedly echo.
la.vulfinus_diensis.vita_marcelli_metrica: A Carolingian Latin verse life of Saint Marcellus, bishop of Die, attributed to Vulfinus of Die and preserved in Strecker's 1923 edition. Running to 398 lines, the poem opens with an encomium of Marcellus as a radiant prelate of the see of Die and celebrates his ascetic renunciation, his camel-hair garb in imitation of John the Baptist, his contempt for wealth in comparison with Croesus, and his devotion to the divine law. For readers of intertexts, the work offers a Carolingian specimen of the metrical vita, rich in biblical allusion and hagiographic topoi that invite comparison with earlier saints' lives and classical models.
la.walafrid_strabo.de_cultu_hortorum_carmen: De cultu hortorum ('On the cultivation of gardens'), a Latin poem of 444 lines attributed to the Carolingian author Walafrid Strabo, sets out in verse the planting and keeping of a kitchen garden. Its opening lines weigh horticulture among the quiet goods of life, survey the soils and situations that yield garden produce, and follow the gardener through the year's round, from winter's loosening grip to the spring clearing of a small plot choked with nettles. Written in a self-consciously classical idiom that invokes Priapus and adopts the georgic manner, the poem stands as a key witness to the survival of ancient didactic form and plant lore in Carolingian letters, and offers readers of intertexts a dense field of classical echoes reworked for a medieval setting.
la.walafrid_strabo.de_vita_et_fine_mammae: An 804-line Carolingian Latin verse life attributed to Walafrid Strabo, De Vita et Fine Mammae recounts the life and death of the saint Mamma. Its preface pointedly contrasts the pagan poets' invocations of Mars, Hercules, Pan, and the nymphs with its own opening prayer to the Christian God, framing the work as a deliberate transfer of classical epic conventions to hagiography. The narrative of the saint's merits is interwoven with appeals for his intercession, and the poem offers ample material for readers tracing biblical, liturgical, and classical echoes in medieval verse narrative.
la.walafrid_strabo.in_natalem_s_mammetis_hy: A Latin hymn of forty-eight lines for the feast of Saint Mammes, attributed to the Carolingian writer Walafrid Strabo. It praises the martyr's virtues and contempt for worldly wealth, recounts his endurance of adversity, his victory over princes and the dragon, and closes with a prayer for his intercession on behalf of suppliants. Readers of intertexts may find its dense hagiographic diction, including the coronation of witnesses and the conquest of the dragon, useful for tracing Carolingian devotional formulae and their parallels in liturgical poetry.
la.walafrid_strabo.visio_wettini: The Visio Wettini is a Latin epic in hexameters, some 1000 lines long, by the Carolingian poet Walafrid Strabo, recounting a vision of the afterlife granted to Wettin, a monk of the island monastery of Reichenau (Augia). After a proem in which the young poet offers his first fruits to Christ, the poem sketches Reichenau's foundation by Pirmin and the line of its early abbots before narrating the vision, in which the dreamer is conducted through scenes of punishment and reward among the dead and shown the lot of souls famous and obscure. As a Carolingian reworking of the otherworld vision, the poem blends Virgilian epic diction with Christian eschatology and stands near the head of the medieval visionary tradition, making it fertile ground for tracing classical, biblical, and later medieval parallels.
la.walahfrid_strabo.carmina: A Carolingian collection of Latin verse attributed to Walahfrid Strabo, comprising some 2,805 lines. The opening poem addresses a bishop as 'pontificum sublime caput' and exhorts him to build up the church's members through sound teaching and example, citing the Pauline injunction against giving scandal to Jew, gentile, or the church of God. The individual poems are of uncertain date within the Carolingian period, and no division into books is recorded. For readers hunting textual parallels, the collection repays attention to its fusion of direct scriptural quotation, episcopal admonition, and the Latinate school diction characteristic of Carolingian poetry.
la.walahfrid_strabo.carminum_appendix: A brief Carolingian Latin appendix of 142 lines of verse transmitted under the name of Walahfrid Strabo. Its opening piece is an epitaphic elegy mourning his death, recalling his crossing of the Loire and his burial at Auua, and addressing the passing traveller with the classic formula 'What you are, I once was; what I am now, you are soon to be.' The collection continues with verses in which the scribe Reginbert commits the completed book to safekeeping under a curse against unauthorised copying, followed by short complimentary couplets accompanying humble gifts. Readers tracing intertexts will find the epitaphic memento mori, the manuscript book-curse, and the conventions of poetic gift exchange present here in miniature.
la.walahfrid_strabo.versus_de_Blaithmaic: A Carolingian Latin hagiographic poem of 172 lines by Walahfrid Strabo, the Versus de Blaithmaic speaks in the voice of one Strabus, born of Alamannic soil, who dedicates the work to a beloved father named Felix and undertakes to write on the life and end of the blessed Blaithmaic. The opening frames the poem as a corrective to the fame that impious poets win for wicked deeds, asking why the deeds of the saints should not be sung more freely, and grounds the undertaking in a quotation from scripture. The narrative follows Blaithmaic, a saint of royal Irish stock whose Latin name 'pulcher natus' signals his fair birth, as he secretly forsakes princely expectation for monastic life and moves toward martyrdom. Readers hunting parallels will find classicalizing encomiastic diction, extended catalogues of virtues, and hagiographic topoi of renunciation and humility joined to biblical citation.
la.wandalbert.de_creatione_mundi: De Creatione Mundi is a Latin poem of 285 lines on the creation of the world, attributed to the Carolingian poet Wandalbert. Its opening invokes the one and triune God as the eternal fount of goodness through whose Word the fabric of the universe was made, and moves from the creation and fall of the angels to the fashioning of the high heaven and the earth sunk in weight amid the great void. As a Carolingian verse rendering of the Genesis narrative, it invites comparison with other Latin creation poems and biblical paraphrases, making it a useful point of contact for readers tracing shared diction and motifs across the tradition.
la.wandalbert.horarium: The Horarium is a short Latin poem of the Carolingian period, ascribed to Wandalbert, which sets out the lengths in feet of a gnomon's shadow at successive hours for each month of the year. The months are treated in pairs of similar daylight length — January with December, February with November, March with October, April with September, May with August — each pair receiving precise numerical rules for telling the time from the shadow. A closing precept directs the reader to observe this numerical method everywhere, marking the poem as practical instruction in shadow-based time-reckoning cast in verse. Its compact scheme of paired months and measured shadows makes it a useful point of comparison for computistical poetry, calendrical verse, and the didactic tradition of horological instruction in medieval Latin.
la.wandalbert.horologium: The Horologium is a short Carolingian Latin poem attributed to Wandalbert, a versified lesson in reckoning the seasonal hours. Across its forty lines it pairs each month of the year with hours of corresponding length, notes the sixth hour as the one that keeps its own measure, and explains how shadows grow short in lands scorched by the south wind and long among peoples beneath the northern pole, framing its rule for a zone stretching from the Danube through Lugdunum and the Rhone to the Britons by the Ocean. As compact didactic verse on time-reckoning in the Carolingian manner, it offers useful parallels for the language of sun, months, hours, and the turning year elsewhere in classical and medieval poetry.
la.wandalbertus.martyrologium: A Latin martyrology in verse of the Carolingian period, attributed to Wandalbertus, opening with a formal invocatio in which the poet begs the creator for aid in setting out in song the battles and deaths of the saints. As the prologue indicates, the work is arranged around the recurring days of the annual cycle, distributing verse commemorations of martyrs drawn from the innumerable company of saints within a liturgical frame across nearly 1,200 lines. Its interest for readers of intertexts lies in its dense biblical paraphrase — the opening reworks the Apocalypse image of the Church as a bride in white robes, washed in the blood of the Lamb and following it — and in its transmission of hagiographic diction and narrative formulae shared across the medieval martyrology tradition.
la.william_of_tyre.historia_rerum_in_partib: A Latin prose chronicle of twenty-three books attributed to William of Tyre, twelfth-century archbishop of Tyre and chancellor of the kingdom of Jerusalem, recounting the history of the Latin East from the First Crusade down to the reign of Baldwin IV.
