Opening with a lengthy prologue on the duties and dangers of the historian, the work surveys the condition of Christians under Muslim rule, the rise of the Turks, Peter the Hermit and the preaching of Urban II at Clermont, and the deeds of the crusading princes through the capture of Jerusalem and its aftermath, drawing on Greek and Arabic sources as well as oral testimony. The opening books circulated widely, and the chronicle's mixture of royal biography, character sketches, and episodic narrative made it a staple source for later retellings of crusading history; its rare vocabulary and idiosyncratic diction have also furnished frequent parallels for readers tracing the Latinity of medieval historiography.

grc.septuaginta.genesis: The opening book of the Greek Pentateuch, translated from Hebrew in Alexandria in the third century BC and the oldest portion of the Septuagint. It runs from the creation of the world and the flood through the patriarchs Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob to the story of Joseph and his brothers in Egypt. This Greek text is the version the New Testament writers quote when they invoke Adam, Abraham, or the promises made to the patriarchs.
grc.septuaginta.exodus: The second book of the Pentateuch, continuing the third-century BC Alexandrian translation of the Torah. It tells of the Israelites' bondage in Egypt, the plagues, the escape through the sea, and the giving of the law at Sinai, then turns to detailed instructions for building the tabernacle. Its Greek vocabulary for covenant, law, and sacrifice became the standard later drawn on by the New Testament and the early Christian writers.
grc.septuaginta.levitikon: The priestly law code at the center of the Pentateuch, covering sacrifice, ritual purity, the priesthood, and the annual festivals, including the Day of Atonement. It is organized as instructions delivered to Moses at Sinai rather than as narrative, and its vocabulary for sacrifice and purity later shaped Christian theological language. Traditionally ascribed to Moses, like the rest of the Pentateuch, and translated into Greek in the third century BC.
grc.septuaginta.arithmoi: The fourth book of the Pentateuch, named in Greek for the two censuses of the Israelite tribes that frame it. It narrates the forty years of wandering in the wilderness after Sinai, including the rebellion of Korah, the crisis at Kadesh, and the story of Balaam and his donkey, before ending with preparations to enter Canaan. Genealogical and legal material is interwoven with the narrative throughout.
grc.septuaginta.deuteronomion: The last book of the Pentateuch, presented as Moses's farewell speeches to Israel on the plains of Moab before his death. It restates the law given at Sinai, adds the Shema and other core declarations of Israelite faith, and closes with blessings, curses, and the account of Moses's death. Its Greek phrasing for exclusive devotion to God is quoted directly in the New Testament, including by Jesus in the temptation narrative.
grc.septuaginta.basileion_a: The first of the four Books of Kingdoms in the Septuagint, corresponding to 1 Samuel in the Hebrew Bible. It follows the judge and prophet Samuel, the rise and fall of King Saul, and the young David's anointing, his years as an outlaw, and his friendship with Saul's son Jonathan. The four Kingdoms books together form one continuous history running from Samuel through the fall of the two Israelite monarchies.
grc.septuaginta.basileion_b: The second Book of Kingdoms, corresponding to 2 Samuel, narrating David's reign after Saul's death: his consolidation of power, the bringing of the ark to Jerusalem, the dynastic promise delivered through the prophet Nathan, and the family disasters that follow his affair with Bathsheba and the death of Uriah, including Absalom's revolt. It continues directly from 1 Kingdoms, divided from it for length rather than content.
grc.septuaginta.basileion_g: The third Book of Kingdoms, corresponding to 1 Kings, opening with the succession struggle in David's final days and Solomon's accession. It covers Solomon's wisdom, wealth, and construction of the Jerusalem temple, the kingdom's split after his death into Israel and Judah, and the early kings of both, including the prophet Elijah's confrontations with King Ahab and Jezebel.
grc.septuaginta.basileion_d: The fourth and final Book of Kingdoms, corresponding to 2 Kings, continuing the parallel histories of Israel and Judah through the ministry of Elisha and other prophets. It narrates the Assyrian conquest of Israel in 722 BC, the reforms and failures of Judah's later kings, and ends with the Babylonian destruction of Jerusalem and the temple in 586 BC.
grc.anthologia_graeca: The Palatine Anthology, some four thousand Greek epigrams by several hundred poets spanning the Hellenistic period to the Byzantine era, gathered by Constantinus Cephalas around 900 AD and preserved in a tenth-century manuscript rediscovered at Heidelberg in 1606. Its sixteen books cover epitaphs, dedications, erotic and convivial verse, and epideictic epigrams, and include celebrated short poems like Meleager's welcome to spring (9.363) that were widely read and imitated.
grc.achilles_tatius.leucippe_et_clitophon: The Leucippe and Clitophon of Achilles Tatius, an ancient Greek prose romance of uncertain date, is presented here from Hercher's Teubner edition of the Erotici Scriptores Graeci (1858). After an extended ekphrasis of a painting of Europa at Sidon, the story unfolds as the first-person narration of Clitophon of Tyre, whose love for the Byzantine maiden Leucippe is driven through oracle, elopement, shipwreck, piracy, banditry, and a sequence of apparent deaths and recognitions as far as Egypt. The romance is celebrated for its descriptive brilliance, erotic rhetoric, dreams, and digressions, and its knowing play with the conventions of the ideal Greek novel makes it a fertile hunting ground for verbal and thematic parallels.
grc.acta_joannis.acta_joannis: The Acta Joannis is a Greek apocryphal act of the apostle John, of anonymous authorship and uncertain date, preserved and printed in Bonnet's edition of the Acta Apostolorum Apocrypha (1898). Its opening narrative places John before the emperor Domitian, who has begun a persecution of Christians: the apostle travels from Ephesus to Rome, drinks deadly poison unharmed, raises a condemned criminal from death, and is exiled to Patmos, whence he returns to Ephesus after Nerva's recall of the exiles. The subsequent episodes recount John's miracles in Ephesus, notably the resurrections of Cleopatra and Lycomedes, Lycomedes' painted portrait of the apostle and John's discourse on the true colors that paint the soul, a sermon and healings in the theatre, and the collapse of the altar and temple of Artemis. Readers of intertexts will find here a dense web of motifs shared with the canonical Acts, the other apocryphal acts of the apostles, and Greco-Roman traditions of miracle, martyrdom, and sacred portraiture.
grc.aelian.de_natura_animalium: The De Natura Animalium of Claudius Aelian, presented here in Greek from Rudolf Hercher's Teubner edition of 1864, is a collection in seventeen books of short chapters on the traits, intelligence, and remarkable behaviour of animals. Its prologue argues that creatures lacking reason nonetheless share in virtue, prudence, and affection, and the work assembles anecdotal proof in the form of devoted fish, grieving dolphins, industrious bees, vengeful morays, and other exempla that blend natural history with moralising and marvels. Aelian describes the compilation as a treasury gathered in his accustomed literary style and acknowledges earlier writers on the same themes as predecessors. For readers of intertexts, its set pieces and stock animal lore offer a dense control for tracing motifs and their recombination in later Greek and Latin writing.
grc.aelian.varia_historia: Aelian's Varia Historia is a Greek miscellany of short anecdotes and notices on animal behaviour, human customs, historical episodes, and memorable sayings, compiled from earlier writers. The collection, given here in Rudolf Hercher's Teubner edition of 1866, runs to nearly two thousand lines and opens with accounts of the cunning of octopuses, the weaving of spiders, and the resourcefulness of Egyptian frogs, dogs, and foxes, before proceeding to further stories of animals and men. Aelian names and paraphrases earlier authorities such as Aristotle and preserves versions of many anecdotes otherwise lost, making the work a rich quarry for readers tracing parallels in ancient natural lore and moralising narrative.
grc.aelius_aristides.orationes: A collection of Greek orations attributed to Aelius Aristides, printed from William Dindorf's recension in the two-volume Weidmann edition (Leipzig, 1829). The speeches open with a cycle of prose hymns to the Olympian gods—Zeus, Athena, Poseidon, Dionysus, Heracles, and Asclepius—framed as votive thank-offerings and dream-visions and recounting each deity's birth, dominion, titles, and benefactions to gods and mortals. Recasting the archaic hymnic tradition in elevated rhetorical prose, the hymns are saturated with Homeric and Pindaric diction, Platonic theological language, and mythological exempla, and repay close attention from readers hunting textual parallels.
grc.aeschines.against_ctesiphon: A forensic speech in Attic Greek by the Athenian orator Aeschines, prosecuting Ctesiphon by a graphē paranomōn for proposing a decree that Demosthenes be crowned with a golden wreath for his services to the city. The argument centres on the liability of every public official to audit and examination, and it presses each point by quoting Athenian laws, decrees, oaths and public records verbatim against the defence. As the direct counterpart to Demosthenes' reply On the Crown, the speech forms half of the most celebrated exchange in classical oratory, making it a prime node for tracing parallels in legal diction, civic ideology and personal invective between rival rhetoricians.
grc.aeschines.on_the_embassy: A Greek forensic oration attributed to Aeschines, the Athenian orator and adversary of Demosthenes, delivered in his own defence at his trial on Demosthenes' charge of bribery and misconduct arising from the embassies to Philip II of Macedon and the peace negotiated with him. The speech answers the prosecution point by point, retelling the origins of the peace, the conduct of the second embassy at Philip's court, and earlier Athenian relations with the Macedonian dynasty, while mounting sustained invective against Demosthenes and citing decrees, letters and witness testimony. As the direct rejoinder to Demosthenes' On the False Embassy, covering the same diplomacy from the opposite side, it offers a prime site for intertextual comparison, from mirrored narratives and document citations to Homeric and tragic colouring in its invective.
grc.aeschylus.agamemnon: The Agamemnon is a Greek tragedy by Aeschylus, running to 1,645 lines and opening with the watchman on the palace roof at Argos who sights the beacon fire announcing the fall of Troy. The play follows Agamemnon's homecoming and his murder at the hands of Clytemnestra, and it stands as the first part of a trilogy tracing the curse on the house of Atreus. Its choral odes, gnomic lyric passages, and celebrated episodes—the beacon speech, the carpet scene, Clytemnestra's exultation over the corpse—have made it one of the most heavily echoed works of ancient drama for readers hunting textual parallels.
grc.aeschylus.agamemnon_hypothesis: The Agamemnon Hypothesis is a brief ancient argument, or prose summary, transmitted with Aeschylus' tragedy Agamemnon, the first play of the Oresteia, and printed in Herbert Weir Smyth's Loeb edition of 1926. In a handful of lines it recounts the plot — the beacon watched for at Clytemnestra's command, Agamemnon's return with Cassandra, her prophecy of her own death and of Orestes' future matricide, the killing of the king, and the rival claims of Clytemnestra and Aegisthus — and then appends the didascalic notice and a list of the dramatis personae. The didascalia places the production in the archonship of Philocles, second year of the 80th Olympiad (458 BC), with Xenocles of Aphidnae as choregus and Aeschylus placed first with the Agamemnon, Choephoroi, Eumenides, and the satyr play Proteus. Readers tracing parallels value the hypothesis for its ancient critical observations, including its praise of Cassandra's silent death and its remark on Aeschylus' distinctive handling of Agamemnon's murder, and for the performance data against which echoes of the play are commonly measured.
grc.aeschylus.eumenides: The Eumenides, the concluding play of Aeschylus' Oresteia, dramatises Orestes' pursuit by the Erinyes after the murder of his mother, his trial before the Areopagus at Athens under Athena's presidency, and the transformation of the vengeful goddesses into the benevolent Eumenides. Opening with the Pythia's prayer and alarm at Delphi, the action moves from Apollo's sanctuary to Athens and closes with a choral performance instituting the cult of the Kindly Ones. Its treatment of justice, civic institutions, and ritual aetiology makes it a recurrent point of comparison for readers tracing legal, theological, and tragic intertexts.
grc.aeschylus.eumenides_hypothesis: A Greek hypothesis, or prose argument, transmitted with the Eumenides attributed to Aeschylus, of uncertain authorship and date. The hypothesis summarizes the drama's action: Orestes, pursued by the Erinyes and directed by Apollo, comes from Delphi to Athens and the sanctuary of Athena, is tried and acquitted through Athena's counsel, and returns to Argos, whereupon the appeased Erinyes are renamed Eumenides; it closes with the critical note that the story is found in neither of two unnamed poets. Such plot summaries are valuable to readers tracing the mythographic tradition of the Orestes legend, the motif of trial before an Athenian court, and the transformation of the Erinyes into benevolent goddesses across classical and later literature.
grc.aeschylus.persians: A Greek tragedy by Aeschylus, preserved here in Herbert Weir Smyth's 1926 edition, dramatizing the reaction of the Persian court to the defeat of Xerxes' invasion of Greece. The play opens with the chorus of Persian elders appointed by Xerxes to guard his wealthy palaces, who voice anxiety over the king's long absence and name the vast host of commanders he has led from Susa and Ecbatana; it then traces the report of the naval disaster at Salamis, the summoning of Darius' ghost, and the king's dishevelled return. As the only surviving Greek tragedy on a contemporary historical subject, it presents the Greek victory through the eyes of the vanquished, and its epic-style catalogue, funerary lament, and reworking of Homeric language make it a frequent reference point for intertextual comparison.
grc.aeschylus.persians_hypothesis: A brief Greek hypothesis, or prefatory notice, to Aeschylus' Persians, anonymous and of uncertain date, transmitted with the play. It reports the ancient claim preserved by Glaucus that the Persians was modeled on Phrynichus' Phoenissae, contrasts the openings and staging of the two dramas, and places the scene at the tomb of Darius with a chorus of elders in place of Phrynichus' eunuch messenger. It then summarizes the action of Xerxes' expedition against Greece, defeated by land at Plataea and by sea at Salamis, adds the didascalic note that Aeschylus won the tragic competition with Phineus, Persians, Glaucus Potnieus, and Prometheus, and closes by distinguishing Darius' ill-fated advance on Marathon from Xerxes' second invasion. Readers of intertexts will find it valuable chiefly for its ancient testimony to Aeschylus' debt to Phrynichus and for the didascalic information attached to the play.
grc.aeschylus.seven_against_thebes: Seven Against Thebes is a Greek tragedy by Aeschylus, preserved in Herbert Weir Smyth's Loeb edition of 1926 and running to 1,068 lines. It dramatizes the Argive assault on the city of Cadmus: King Eteocles rallies the Thebans, assigns champions to the seven gates in response to the scout's report of the enemy leaders, and the play ends with the mutual slaughter of Oedipus' sons and the chorus's anguished lament. The long catalogue of shields and their blazons, dense with simile and allusion to the wider Theban and Argive saga, makes the play a central witness to the myth and a key point of comparison for later treatments, from Euripides' Phoenissae to Statius' Thebaid.
grc.aeschylus.suppliant_women: The Suppliant Women (Hiketides) is a Greek tragedy of uncertain date by Aeschylus, preserved in some 1,072 lines in the edition of Herbert Weir Smyth. It opens as the Danaids, daughters of Danaus, land on the Argive coast after fleeing Egypt, invoking Zeus and recounting their descent from Io and their escape from a forced marriage with the sons of Aegyptus. The action centres on their ritual supplication of the king and people of Argos and on the city's deliberation over whether to grant them asylum. Its sustained supplication vocabulary, its handling of the Io myth, and its place in the Danaid legend make it a natural point of comparison for readers tracing asylum, marriage, and pursuit motifs in Greek poetry.
grc.andocides.on_the_mysteries: On the Mysteries is a forensic oration of uncertain date in which Andocides defends himself before an Athenian jury against charges of impiety arising from the profanation of the Mysteries and the mutilation of the Herms. The speech rehearses the series of denunciations brought by informers such as Andromachus, Teucrus, Agariste, and Diocleides, recites the names of the men accused in each, produces witnesses, and rebuts the claim that Andocides informed against his own father. Its dense fabric of personal names, legal formulas, and ritual vocabulary, together with its narrative of political crisis surrounding Alcibiades and the Sicilian expedition, makes it a rich source of parallels for readers of Attic oratory and Athenian civic history.
grc.anonymous.stadiasmus_magni_maris: The Stadiasmus Magni Maris is an anonymous Greek coastal sailing guide, of uncertain date, preserved in Karl Müller's Geographi graeci minores (Paris, 1855). Framed as a letter promising a learned correspondent the most accurate possible periplus of the great sea, its 358 lines record stade distances between successive ports, anchorages, headlands, islands, watering places, and cult sites, beginning at Alexandria and running through the Mediterranean coasts to the Pontus as far as Dioscurias, and onward to the Pillars of Heracles and Gades. Its dense toponymy, notices of harbours, temples, and oracles, and remarks on winds and sailing conditions make it a rich source of parallels for readers tracing place-name traditions, itineraries, and geographical formulae shared with other periploi, itineraries, and poetic accounts of the sea.
grc.apollodorus.library: The Library is a prose compendium of Greek mythology attributed to Apollodorus, printed in Frazer's Loeb edition of 1921, and of uncertain date and authorship. It opens with the rule of Uranus and proceeds genealogically through the castration of Uranus, the Titanomachy, the accession of Zeus, the Gigantomachy and Typhoeus, Prometheus and the flood of Deucalion, to the offspring of Zeus and the descendants of Hellen. Variant versions are flagged throughout with formulas such as 'as some say,' together with occasional appeals to Homer and other poets. Since it condenses the divine and heroic traditions presupposed by epic, lyric, and tragedy, it offers readers hunting intertexts a compact index of mythic material.
grc.apollonius_of_perga.conica: The Conica of Apollonius of Perga is a Greek geometrical treatise of uncertain date, edited by J. L. Heiberg in the second volume of his Teubner Apollonii Pergaei quae graece exstant (Leipzig, 1893). Composed in the proposition-and-proof manner of Euclidean mathematics, the portion preserved here establishes properties of tangents and secants drawn from external points to conic sections and circles, with particular attention to the hyperbola, its asymptotes, and its opposite branches, and repeatedly argues by reductio ad absurdum. For readers hunting intertexts, the excerpt offers dense examples of ancient technical mathematical diction — terms such as ἐφαπτομένη, ἀσύμπτωτος, and ἀντικείμεναι τομαί — and of ratio-based geometric argumentation later authors echo or reuse.
grc.apollonius_rhodius.argonautica: The Argonautica of Apollonius Rhodius is a Greek epic in four books, totalling 5,834 lines, opening with an invocation to Phoebus Apollo. It recounts Pelias' charge to Jason, the building of the Argo under Athena's guidance, and the muster of heroes beginning with Orpheus, then follows the voyage through the Cyanean Rocks toward Colchis in quest of the Golden Fleece, with Medea's passion for Jason at its centre. As the fullest surviving treatment of the Argonautic saga, it offers rich material for readers tracing epic diction, heroic catalogues, and the Jason–Medea story across later Greek and Latin literature.
grc.archimedes.arenarius: The Arenarius or Sand-Reckoner, a short prose treatise in Doric Greek by Archimedes, addressed to King Gelon and written against those who hold the number of grains of sand to be infinite. To carry the argument it devises a nomenclature of orders and periods of numbers reaching far beyond the traditional myriad, and then demonstrates by geometric proof that named numbers can exceed the grains of sand needed to fill a sphere the size of the cosmos, even as enlarged under the hypotheses of Aristarchus of Samos, whose account of an unmoving sun with the earth revolving about it is set out in some detail. Along the way it records assumptions about the earth's circumference, ratios among the diameters of sun, moon, and earth attributed to earlier astronomers including Eudoxus and Archimedes' own father Phidias, and an instrumental measurement of the sun's apparent diameter. For readers of intertexts its chief interest lies in the Aristarchus passage, among the clearest ancient testimonies to heliocentric speculation, and in its dense allusion to earlier mathematical and astronomical writing.
grc.archimedes.de_corporibus_fluitantibus: A Greek mathematical treatise in two books by Archimedes, De Corporibus Fluitantibus sets out the behaviour of solid bodies in fluids as a sequence of postulates, definitions, numbered propositions and proofs. The first book postulates a mechanical model of fluid pressure, shows that the surface of a fluid at rest is spherical with the same centre as the earth, and establishes the laws of buoyancy and flotation, including the result that a body immersed in fluid loses weight equal to the weight of the fluid it displaces. The second book determines when segments of a right-angled conoid, floating at any given ratio of weight to fluid, return to the upright or remain inclined, drawing on centres of gravity and conic geometry and referring to Archimedes' mechanical works. Preserved partly in Doric Greek and partly in a Latin rendering, the treatise exemplifies the deductive prose of ancient applied mathematics and supplies the technical vocabulary and formulae of hydrostatics, mechanics and conics for readers tracing parallels in Greek scientific writing.
grc.archimedes.de_lineis_spiralibus: De Lineis Spiralibus (On Spirals) is a Greek geometrical treatise by Archimedes, cast in the form of a letter and opening with a preface that reviews problems once sent to Conon, some since proved and some shown false, before announcing its own subject. The work defines the spiral traced by a point moving uniformly along a straight line that rotates uniformly about a fixed end, then demonstrates the areas swept out in successive turns, the ratio of the spiral's area to the containing circle, and the properties of tangents to the curve, prefacing these with lemmas on ratios, circles, and the squares of lines in arithmetic progression. Composed in the Doric dialect characteristic of Archimedes' mathematical prose, it supplies parallels for the conventions of Greek mathematical prefaces, definitions, and lemma-based argument, and documents the earliest systematic treatment of the curve later known as the Archimedean spiral.
grc.archimedes.de_planorum_aequilibriis: A treatise on statics by Archimedes, the De Planorum Aequilibriis (On the Equilibrium of Planes) derives, from seven postulates on weights suspended from a balance, the law of the lever and the properties of the centre of gravity of plane figures, with propositions on commensurable and incommensurable magnitudes, composite bodies, and the parallelogram. It is written in the Doric dialect characteristic of ancient Greek mathematical prose, with forms such as τᾶς for τῆς, μακέων for the beam of the balance, and σαμεῖον for σημεῖον, which distinguish it sharply from Attic literary Greek. For readers tracing intertexts it offers the canonical formulation of mechanical vocabulary — κέντρον τοῦ βάρεος (centre of gravity), ἰσορροπέω (to balance), ῥέπω (to incline) — on which later discussions of the lever and the balance in Greek technical and literary authors draw.
grc.archimedes.problema_bovinum: A short Greek epigram attributed to Archimedes, the Problema Bovinum challenges a 'stranger' to reckon the bulls and cows of Helios in four colours — white, dark, yellow and piebald — grazing in Sicily, and closes with added conditions on square and triangular totals that make the arithmetic famously demanding. The verse presents itself as a problem devised by Archimedes for the mathematicians working at Alexandria and sent in a letter to Eratosthenes of Cyrene, while a prose appendix recaps the solution in archaic numeral notation. Composed in Homericising hexameters, the poem reworks the cattle of the Sun familiar from the Odyssey as a computational exercise and stands as the outstanding instance of mathematics dressed in epic diction. Readers of intertexts will find here a nexus of learned epigram, verse epistle and number problem, bridging poetic form and Hellenistic geometrical enquiry.
grc.archimedes.quadratura_parabolae: A Greek geometrical treatise by Archimedes, edited in the second volume of Mugler's Budé Archimède (Paris, 1971) and running to some fifty-four lines, the Quadratura Parabolae takes the form of a letter to Dositheus that opens by mourning the death of the geometer Conon. It establishes that every segment bounded by a straight line and a section of a right-angled cone — the parabola of the title — is four-thirds of the triangle on the same base and of equal height, first by mechanical balancing arguments on a lever and then by purely geometrical demonstration, with preliminary lemmas drawn from conic elements. For readers of intertexts, the work preserves Archimedes' explicit engagement with the quadrature attempts of earlier geometers, appeals to results from his Mechanics, and the formulaic propositional and reductio style of Greek mathematical prose that later technical writers perpetuate.
grc.aretaeus.curatione_acutorum_morbum: The Curatione acutorum morborum (On the Cure of Acute Diseases) of Aretaeus the Cappadocian is a Greek medical treatise on the treatment of acute illness, composed in prose of markedly Ionic coloring. Aretaeus' own date is uncertain; the opening lines preserved here furnish a sustained clinical portrait of the epileptic fit, tracing its visual aura — flickerings likened to a rainbow in the sky — through the fall, the convulsions compared with those of slaughtered oxen, and the numb, dispirited aftermath. Such close observation and vivid simile earned Aretaeus a lasting place in the ancient medical tradition, and readers of intertexts will find in his wording and imagery a fertile quarry of parallels for later descriptions of disease, seizure, and the body in extremis.
grc.aristophanes.clouds: Clouds (Nephelae) is a Greek comedy by Aristophanes, preserved complete in 1,481 lines and edited by F. W. Hall and W. M. Geldart in the second volume of their Oxford Clarendon edition of 1907. The plot opens with the elderly Strepsiades lying awake over debts run up through his son Pheidippides' passion for horses, and follows his attempt to enrol in the thinking-house of Socrates to master specious argument and evade his creditors, an education that rebounds when the son turns his new skills against his own father. The comedy's caricature of Socrates, its satire of sophistic instruction, and its debate between Just and Unjust Argument made it a touchstone for ancient and later portrayals of philosophy, and its scenes, characters, and phrases supply plentiful parallels for readers tracing intertexts.
grc.aristophanes.ecclesiazusae: Aristophanes' Ecclesiazusae, a Greek comedy of uncertain date running to 1219 lines, is edited by F. W. Hall and W. M. Geldart in their Oxford Clarendon Press edition of 1907. The play opens before daybreak with a woman apostrophising a lamp while the women of Athens, disguised as men, prepare to infiltrate the assembly and vote themselves into power; the plot then follows their rule of the city and the communal regime of property, wives, and daily life that they establish. Readers hunting intertexts will find Aristophanic parody of assembly rhetoric and civic ritual alongside a comic enactment of community of property and wives that invites comparison with Platonic speculation on the same themes.
grc.aristophanes.frogs: Aristophanes' Frogs (Batrachoi) is an Attic comedy of uncertain date, running to 1545 lines in the Hall–Geldart Oxford edition of 1907. The opening dialogue between Dionysus and his slave Xanthias, with its banter about what will amuse the spectators, sets the tone for the god's journey to the underworld, where the title-giving frog chorus and a judging contest between tragic poets supply the play's central action. Its sustained parody of tragic diction and its explicit quotation of earlier poets make it a rich source of verbal echoes for readers tracing intertexts. The comedy also offers self-conscious commentary on comic technique and literary taste, itself a frequent object of allusion in later literature.
grc.aristophanes.knights: The Knights is a political comedy by Aristophanes, transmitted in 1,393 lines in the Hall–Geldart Oxford text of his plays. The action opens with two household slaves bewailing their master's overbearing favourite, the Paphlagonian, and turns on their discovery of a vulgar sausage-seller groomed to outdo him in effrontery and supplant him in the affections of the people, personified as the irascible old man Demos; the chorus of Athenian horsemen gives the play its title. For readers of intertexts, the comedy is rich in parody of oracular pronouncements and of tragic and dithyrambic diction, and its dense, quotable verbal texture makes it a frequent point of contact with comic, tragic, and oracular fragments.
grc.aristophanes.lysistrata: Aristophanes' Lysistrata is a Greek comedy in verse, running 1288 lines, printed here in the Oxford Clarendon edition of F. W. Hall and W. M. Geldart (1907). The plot gathers the women of Athens, Sparta, and Boeotia, led by Lysistrata and Calonice, who conspire to deny their husbands until the men negotiate peace and so end the war between Athens and the Peloponnesians. Its humor rests on domestic inversion, ribald banter, oaths, and the parody of tragic and diplomatic language, carried in a mixture of iambic, trochaic, and lyric meters. For readers tracing intertexts, the play offers dense seams of colloquial idiom, choral song, and recast tragic phrasing that recur throughout ancient Greek comedy and its later imitators.
grc.aristophanes.peace: Peace is a Greek Old Comedy by Aristophanes, surviving in 1332 lines and presented here in the Hall–Geldart Oxford text of 1907. Its protagonist Trygaeus flies to heaven on an enormous dung beetle to retrieve the goddess Peace and restore her to a war-weary Greece, and the play pairs scatological farce of unusual exuberance with Aristophanes' habitual satire on demagogues and profiteers of war. Readers hunting intertexts will find a dense web of parodic allusion to epic and tragic diction, grotesque comic idiom, and choral hymns in praise of Peace that later poets and rhetoricians repeatedly echo.
grc.aristophanes.wasps: A Greek comic drama by Aristophanes, printed here in the Oxford text of Hall and Geldart (1907) and running to 1530 lines. The play takes its title from its chorus of elderly jurors costumed as wasps and satirises Athenian legal culture through the figure of the incorrigibly litigious Philocleon, whom his son tries to cure of his addiction to jury service; contemporary politicians such as Cleon and Cleonymus come in for mockery from the opening scene onward. The exuberant parody of courtroom rhetoric, demagogic speech, and tragic language makes it a rich quarry for readers tracing echoes of Athenian institutions and literary commonplaces in later authors.
grc.aristotle.analytica_priora: The Analytica Priora, Aristotle's Greek treatise on the syllogism, printed here from Immanuel Bekker's Oxford edition of the Opera (1837), opens by defining its subject as demonstration and demonstrative science, and proceeds through the definitions of premise, term, and syllogism, the distinction between perfect and imperfect syllogisms, and the rules governing the conversion of categorical propositions. From these foundations it works out the valid and invalid moods of the three figures and extends the system to modal premises concerning what is necessary and what is possible. The work stands at the head of the subsequent logical tradition, and its technical vocabulary and stock examples—pleasure and the good, horse and swan, waking and sleeping—are echoed throughout later Greek and medieval philosophical writing, so that verbal and doctrinal parallels to its definitions and demonstrations recur across a wide range of texts.
grc.aristotle.de_caelo: De Caelo (On the Heavens) is Aristotle's Greek treatise on the physical cosmos, covering the simple bodies and their natural motions, the circular motion of the first body or aether, the finitude, uniqueness, and eternity of the universe, the spherical shape of the heavens and of the earth resting at the center, and the nature of heavy and light. It argues against an infinite body and against multiple worlds, defends the eternity of the single heaven, and treats in its course the composition and mutual transformation of the four elements. Readers hunting intertexts will find throughout an unusually rich engagement with earlier cosmologies — the Pythagoreans, Empedocles, Anaxagoras, Democritus, Leucippus, Thales, and Xenophanes, with verbatim quotation of Empedocles' verse — as well as with Plato's Timaeus, whose accounts of the generated heaven and of elemental figures are repeatedly cited and criticized.
grc.aristotle.de_generatione_animalium: A Greek prose treatise in five books by Aristotle on the generation of animals, preserved in Immanuel Bekker's Berlin edition of 1829. The work argues that the male supplies form and the principle of motion while the female supplies matter, and then examines semen and menstrual fluid as residues of the final nourishment, the successive formation of the embryo beginning from the heart, the structure and incubation of eggs, spontaneous generation in insects and shellfish, and the causes of sterility, including the barrenness of mules. In developing these accounts it cites and corrects earlier thinkers such as Empedocles, Democritus, and Anaxagoras, and it repeatedly cross-refers to the zoological writings on the parts and history of animals, making the treatise a central point of comparison for intertexts within the Aristotelian corpus and for Presocratic physiological doctrines echoed elsewhere in Greek literature.
grc.aristotle.de_interpretatione: De Interpretatione (Peri Hermeneias) is a short Greek treatise by the philosopher Aristotle on the logic of predication, printed here from Immanuel Bekker's Oxford edition of 1837. It defines name, verb, sentence, affirmation, and negation, and analyses contradictory and contrary opposition, before examining modal terms such as the possible and the necessary. Its famous discussion of future contingents — whether a present truth about tomorrow's sea battle makes the outcome necessary — poses the problem of determinism in deliberately paradoxical form. Readers hunting intertexts will find here a seedbed for later theories of signification, contradiction, and modal logic, since the treatise's definitions and distinctions were repeatedly cited and reworked in ancient, medieval, and early modern writing.
grc.aristotle.de_sophisticis_elenchis: Aristotle's De Sophisticis Elenchis, given here in Immanuel Bekker's 1837 Oxford edition of the Opera, is a systematic treatise on sophistical refutations: arguments that appear to be refutations or syllogisms but are in fact fallacies, the stock in trade of sophists who cultivate apparent rather than real wisdom. It distinguishes didactic, dialectical, peirastic, and eristic reasoning, then catalogues thirteen kinds of fallacy, six dependent on language (homonymy, amphiboly, composition, division, accent, and form of expression) and seven arising outside it, including accident, the consequent, begging the question, false cause, and the double question, before showing how each may be solved. Its illustrative examples repeatedly touch on Homer and on the arguments of thinkers such as Zeno and Melissus, and its analysis of dialectic and syllogistic method made it a fountainhead for the later vocabulary of logic, rhetoric, and disputation.
grc.aristotle.divisiones_aristoteleae: A compact Greek collection of dichotomous divisions (diaireseis) attributed to Aristotle but of uncertain authorship and date, preserved in Hermann Mutschmann's 1906 Teubner edition. Its brief chapters divide goods, friendship, constitutions, justice, the sciences, medicine, law, discourse, music, nobility, beauty, the soul, virtue, rule, rhetoric, benefaction, ends, causes, and power into their species, and nearly every division appears twice in closely parallel versions, one set introduced by an excerpt from Diogenes Laertius (III 80 sqq.) citing a division of goods made by Aristotle. The conventional attribution flagged in the title (quae vulgo dicuntur Aristoteleae) marks the work as a product of the school tradition of diaeresis rather than securely of Aristotle's own hand, and readers of intertexts will find it a useful witness to the divisional method and its formulas as they circulate between Plato, the Peripatetics, and later doxography.
grc.aristotle.epistulae: A short set of Greek letters attributed to Aristotle, transmitted in Rudolf Hercher's Epistolographi Graeci (Didot, 1873), of uncertain date and authorship. The six epistles offer elevated moral and political counsel on the mutability of fortune, the ethics of rule, benefaction, gratitude, and friendship; one cites Theophrastus on gratitude and another alludes to Plato. The collection closes with a letter about the 'acroamatic discourses', said to be both published and unpublished and intelligible only to those who heard them, a formulation that plays on the ancient distinction between Aristotle's exoteric and esoteric writings. Readers hunting textual parallels may find here a compact vein of topoi on kingship, fortune, and liberality circulating in the Greek epistolary tradition.
grc.aristotle.magna_moralia: A Greek prose treatise on ethics attributed to Aristotle and transmitted as the Magna Moralia—the edition's title 'quae feruntur' and the Susemihl Teubner of 1883 mark a traditional but uncertain attribution, and the work is of uncertain date. It opens by placing the study of character (ēthos) within politics, reviews earlier accounts of virtue by Pythagoras, Socrates, and Plato, and then moves through classifications of goods, ends, and capacities toward an account of eudaimonia as the complete good. Because its arguments and phrasing run closely parallel to the Nicomachean and Eudemian Ethics, readers tracing intertexts find it a key witness to shared formulae and doctrinal variants across the Aristotelian ethical tradition.
grc.aristotle.meteorologica: Aristotle's Meteorologica is a Greek treatise of uncertain date on sublunary natural phenomena, positioned in its opening chapter as the next inquiry after the first causes, the heavens and the elements. It first treats atmospheric and celestial appearances such as shooting stars, comets and the Milky Way, then clouds, rain, dew, frost, snow and hail, winds and their compass, rivers and the sea, earthquakes, thunder, lightning and firewinds, halos, rainbows and parhelia, closing with exhalations trapped within the earth that produce metals and the homoiomerous bodies. Throughout, Aristotle weighs the explanations of earlier thinkers such as Anaxagoras and Democritus against his own doctrine of the two exhalations, the moist and the dry. For readers of intertexts the work is a rich repository of technical vocabulary and doctrines on weather, optics and terrestrial change that later Greek, Latin and medieval authors repeatedly echo and contest.
grc.aristotle.nicomachean_ethics: Aristotle's Nicomachean Ethics, edited by J. Bywater (Oxford, Clarendon Press, 1894), is a Greek treatise on ethics that opens by declaring that every art, inquiry, action and choice aims at some good, and proceeds to identify happiness as the supreme end of human life. Its argument ranges over virtue of character and intellect, the doctrine of the mean, voluntary action, friendship and pleasure, closing with an endorsement of the contemplative life. Readers of intertexts will find sustained engagement with Plato, above all the critique of the Form of the Good in the opening discussion, alongside quotations from Hesiod and Homeric allusion and appeals to received sayings, making the work a rich source of ethical vocabulary and allusion in later Greek, Latin and European writing.
grc.aristotle.physica: A Greek philosophical treatise by Aristotle, the Physica (Physics) opens with the programmatic claim that the science of nature must begin from its first principles and causes, and proceeds through discussions of nature, the four causes, chance and spontaneity, motion, the infinite, place and the void. Along the way it examines the doctrines of Parmenides, Melissus, Heraclitus, Empedocles, Anaxagoras and Democritus, criticises Plato's appeal to the great and the small and the Timaeus, and quotes Hesiod's account of Chaos. For readers of intertexts the treatise ranks among the richest repositories of Presocratic fragments and doxographic report, and its vocabulary of dynamis, energeia and entelecheia furnished conceptual terms that pervade later Greek and Latin philosophical writing.
grc.aristotle.politics: The Politics of Aristotle, transmitted in Greek and printed in W. D. Ross's Clarendon edition (1957), is a philosophical treatise on the polis, opening from the claim that the city is a natural community ordered toward the good life and proceeding through household management, slavery, wealth-acquisition, and the appraisal of existing and proposed constitutions. Sustained attention is given to Plato's Republic and Laws and to the constitutional schemes of Phaleas of Chalcedon and Hippodamus of Miletus, together with analysis of Sparta and Crete. Readers of intertexts will find the work rich in explicit quotation of Homer, Hesiod, Euripides, Sophocles, and Solon, embedded within close argumentative engagement with earlier poetry and philosophy.
grc.aristotle.αριστοτέλους_φυσικά_προβλήματα: A Greek prose collection of question-and-answer medical problems attributed to Aristotle and of uncertain date, transmitted under the title Φυσικὰ Προβλήματα κατ᾿ εἶδος συναγωγή (Problems arranged by kind). Each entry asks 'why' some bodily or environmental phenomenon occurs — why extremes cause disease, why changes of season, winds, waters or ages bring on fevers, inflammations and other ailments — and follows it with one or more causal explanations grounded in ideas of heat, cold, moisture, excess and deficiency. Later items extend the same method to diet and drinking, purgative drugs, cautery, incision and the dressing of wounds. The recurring διὰ τί formula and its stock causal reasoning echo themes familiar from Hippocratic medicine, making the collection fertile ground for readers tracing shared phrases and explanations across Greek medical and natural-philosophical writing.
grc.aristotle.φυσιογνωμονικά: A short Greek treatise on physiognomy, attributed to Aristotle and of uncertain date, arguing that affections of soul and body arise together — drunkenness and illness visibly alter the mind — so that a given character must attend a given bodily form. After reviewing and criticising earlier methods, whether drawn from animal genera, from comparison of whole bodies, from ethnic types such as Egyptians, Thracians and Scythians, or from transient expressions alone, it catalogues the durable signs of particular dispositions — the courageous, cowardly, naturally well-endowed, insensitive, shameless, orderly, cheerful and despondent, closing with the kinaidos — as read from movements, shape, colour, hair, flesh, voice and the build of individual parts. Readers hunting parallels will find here the body–soul correspondence topos, stock animal exempla such as the lion, deer and hare, and sign-lists that later physiognomic writing echoes.
grc.arrian.cynegeticus: The Cynegeticus of Arrian of Nicomedia, preserved in Hercher and Eberhard's Teubner Scripta Minora (Leipzig, 1885) in some 146 lines, is a compact Greek treatise on hunting with dogs, framed as a supplement to the manual transmitted under Xenophon's name and addressed in its proem to Xenophon son of Gryllus. Its chapters set out what the author judges Xenophon to have omitted, above all the swift Celtic hounds called ouertragoi in Celtic, and then cover the conformation, temperament, feeding, breeding and training of dogs, hare coursing without nets in the Celtic manner, the Celts' observances toward Artemis, and a closing appeal to Homeric authority; a eulogy of the author's own devoted bitch Horme gives the work a personal colour. For readers of intertexts it matters chiefly because it corrects and cites Xenophon chapter by chapter, invokes Homer as witness, and presents Arrian as a namesake successor of Xenophon in hunting and generalship, making it a natural comparison point for the Greek technical prose tradition on hunting and for the reception of Xenophon and Homer in later Greek literature.
grc.bacchylides.dithyrambs: Fragmentary Greek choral lyrics (dithyrambs) of Bacchylides, printed from Bruno Snell's Teubner text of 1970; the poems survive in a damaged state, with heavy lacunae, conjectural supplements, and metrical signs marking the verse. The pieces draw on mythological material shared with epic and tragedy, and the substantial opening fragment, concerned with the Trojan war, brings Athena, Odysseus, Menelaus, and Priam into view and preserves a speech on Zeus's justice and the ruinous growth of Hybris. The collection repays readers hunting intertexts, since these dithyrambic treatments of heroic legend offer verbal and thematic parallels to the Homeric poems and to tragic versions of the same stories.
grc.bacchylides.epinicians: The Epinicians of the Greek lyric poet Bacchylides, edited by Bruno Snell in the Teubner series (1970), preserve roughly 993 lines of choral victory songs written for victors in the great panhellenic games, as the opening invocation of the Pierian Muses and the allusion to Isthmian competition show. Epinician poetry characteristically frames a victor's achievement with mythological narrative, and the opening passage's evocation of Pelops and the gates of his sacred island exemplifies the genre's mythic exempla. For readers hunting textual parallels, the odes are a rich source of mythic variants, formulaic diction, and gnomic reflection that run alongside Pindar, tragedy, and the epic tradition.
grc.basil_of_caesarea.epistulae: The Epistulae gathers the Greek correspondence of Basil of Caesarea as preserved in Roy J. Deferrari's four-volume edition (London and New York, 1926), ranging across letters of friendship, consolation, ascetic counsel, patronage, and ecclesiastical crisis. The opening letters to Gregory of Nazianzus weigh providence, grief, and withdrawal from the world, while later pieces defend the homoousion of the Son and the divinity of the Holy Spirit against the Anomoean followers of Eunomius and expound the distinction between ousia and hypostasis. Dense with Homeric, Platonic, and biblical quotation, the collection offers rich material for readers tracing the weave of classical allusion through Christian epistolary prose.
grc.bion_of_phlossa.epitaphius: The Epitaphius (Lament for Adonis), a Greek bucolic threnos of uncertain date attributed to Bion of Phlossa and edited by J. M. Edmonds in his 1919 Greek Bucolic Poets, stages the ritual cry 'Woe for Adonis' as Aphrodite mourns her lover slain by the boar. Across its ninety-eight lines the refrain passes between Erotes, mountains, springs, and rivers; the wounded Adonis dies on the hills, the dishevelled goddess searches the woods crying her Assyrian lord, and a closing catalogue tells how the flowers redden from his blood now that beauty itself lies dead. For readers of intertexts the poem is the locus classicus of the Adonis lament, whose antiphonal refrain, bleeding blooms, and theme of universal mourning echo throughout later Greek and Latin pastoral elegy.
grc.bion_of_phlossa.epithalamium: A Greek poem of thirty-two lines attributed to Bion of Phlossa and transmitted under the title Epithalamium, though it breaks off mid-sentence and must be a fragment of a larger work. Framed as an exchange between the herdsmen Lycidas and Myrson, it opens with a call for a Sicilian song like the serenade Polyphemus sang to Galatea, then recounts the story of Achilles hidden among the daughters of Lycomedes on Skyros, disguised as a girl and loved by Deidameia, against the backdrop of Paris the cowherd's abduction of Helen. The poem fuses bucolic framing and diction with epic material from the Achilles-on-Skyros tradition, making it a compact testing ground for parallels between pastoral song and heroic myth.
grc.callimachus.epigrams: Callimachus' Epigrams is a collection of short Greek poems, totalling some 294 lines, edited by G. R. Mair and printed with his Callimachus and Lycophron (London; New York, 1921). Composed largely in elegiac couplets, the pieces comprise epitaphs, dedicatory verses, erotic epigrams, and satirical sketches, among them the epitaph on Heraclitus and the dedication of a conch to Arsinoe. Their compressed phrasing and dense mythological and literary allusion made them a storehouse of expressions and motifs for later poets, and the collection repays searches for verbal echoes and thematic parallels in Greek and Latin literature.
grc.callimachus.hecala: Hecale, the Hellenistic epyllion of Callimachus, told of Theseus and the old woman Hecale who sheltered him during the hunt for the Marathon bull and was honoured after her death; it survives only as some seventy lines of fragments and testimonia gathered from lexicographers, scholiasts, and later writers. The collection opens with Crinagoras' epigram praising Callimachus' craftsmanship and with the scholiast's notice that the poem was composed in answer to critics who mocked the poet for never having written a long work, followed by scraps of narrative such as Theseus' homecoming with the bull, the crow's prophecy, and Hecale's humble rustic hospitality. Its miniature-epic form, learned aetiology, and Attic detail made it a model and a quarry for later poets, as the quoted lines of Petronius and Nonnus attest, so that readers tracing intertexts will find here the Alexandrian source of a whole tradition of small-scale epic.
grc.callimachus.hymns: A cycle of six hexameter hymns—to Zeus, Apollo, Artemis, Delos, the bath of Pallas Athena, and Demeter—transmitted under the name of the Greek poet Callimachus and printed in Wilamowitz-Moellendorff's 1897 Berlin edition. The poems adopt epic diction but foreground learned aetiology and self-conscious literary play: the opening hymn weighs Arcadian against Cretan accounts of Zeus' birth and lands on the quip that 'Cretans are always liars,' while the Delos hymn famously breaks off to speak in the poet's own voice. Together the six poems run to just over a thousand lines and are dense with obscure myth, cult explanations, and Homeric and Hesiodic echo. They are a prime hunting ground for readers of intertexts, both as a repository of mythological variants and as a model constantly quarried by later Greek and Latin poets.
grc.claudius_ptolemaeus.μαθηματικὴ_σύνταξις: The Mathēmatikē Syntaxis of Claudius Ptolemaeus is a Greek prose treatise setting out a complete mathematical astronomy of the sun, moon, fixed stars, and planets. Its opening book, addressed to one Syrus, defends the certainty of mathematics through Aristotle's division of theoretical philosophy into physics, mathematics, and theology, argues that the heavens move spherically and that the earth is spherical, central, and without translational motion, and supplies the chord tables and preliminary results on which the later demonstrations rest. The preface promises an orderly progression from solar and lunar theory through the sphere of the fixed stars to the five wandering stars, each established from observations of both the ancients and the author's contemporaries and confirmed by geometrical proof. For readers of intertexts, the work stands as the authoritative matrix of ancient geocentric astronomy, whose assumptions, terminology, and argumentative habits were repeatedly borrowed, contested, and reworked across the later scientific tradition.
grc.clement.exhortation: A Greek Christian paraenetic work attributed to Clement and of uncertain date, transmitted as a single continuous piece. Its opening precept — to practise quietness in words and quietness in deeds — sets the tone for a chain of second-person injunctions on restraint of speech, moderation in food and drink, gentleness in dealing with others, honour to elders, unceasing prayer, and the fixing of the mind upon Christ. The aphoristic hortatory manner invites comparison with classical traditions of ethical exhortation, and readers tracing intertexts will find here a point where pagan paraenetic forms and Christian piety converge.
grc.clement_of_alexandria.protrepticus: The Protrepticus of Clement of Alexandria, surviving in the Greek text edited by G.W. Butterworth (1919), is an early Christian apologetic work that urges Greeks to abandon pagan religion and philosophy for the Christian faith. Beginning with the comparison of the Thracian Orpheus' song with a new, true song of the Word, Clement surveys and exposes the myths, mysteries, oracles, cult statues, and philosophical views of Greek religion as frauds or demon-worship, while citing poets, philosophers, and the Sibyl as witnesses to the one true God. Readers tracking intertexts will find the work a dense repository of quotations from Homer, Hesiod, Euripides, Orpheus, Plato, and many other Greek authors, assembled for polemical purposes.
grc.demetrius.elocutione: A Greek treatise on prose composition, transmitted under the name of Demetrius and conventionally cited by its Latin title De elocutione, of uncertain date. It analyzes the building blocks of prose as against metrical poetry, treating the kôlon, the komma, and the period, their proper lengths, rhythms, and antithetical arrangement, and distinguishes four simple characters of style (plain, grand, elegant, forceful), illustrating each with quotations from Homer, Herodotus, Thucydides, Xenophon, Plato, Demosthenes, Isocrates, and other classical authors. Because it embeds so many excerpted passages, including characteristic specimens of Thucydides, Gorgias, and Demosthenes, the work is a rich repository of quoted language and ancient stylistic terminology, and a useful point of reference for readers tracing intertexts and formulae across Greek prose.
grc.demosthenes.against_aphobus_3: A short forensic speech in Attic Greek, transmitted in the Demosthenic corpus as the third oration Against Aphobus and of uncertain date, in which Demosthenes answers a suit for false witness brought by his former guardian Aphobus. The charge concerns testimony about Milyas, once a slave of Demosthenes' father, whose manumission Aphobus had acknowledged; the speaker rehearses the guardians' dissipation of the patrimony left in their charge, dwells on their refusal of the torture-challenge (basanos), and supports his case with laws, depositions, and challenges read aloud to the jurors. Closely linked to the two earlier speeches against Aphobus, the oration offers dense material on Athenian procedural vocabulary, including guardianship, paraklesis, and the public suit for false testimony, and on the rhetoric of evidence, inheritance, and family enmity within Attic oratory.
grc.demosthenes.against_boeotus_2: A forensic speech of uncertain date, transmitted among the private orations of Demosthenes and spoken in an Athenian court by a litigant named Mantitheus against his half-brother Boeotus, whom their father had named so while the adversaries claimed the name Mantitheus for themselves. The second of two speeches arising from the same quarrel, it pleads a suit over a dowry: the speaker recounts his mother's properly dowered marriage, the oath-bound deception by which Plangon forced recognition of her sons on the household, years of thwarted arbitration, and the opponent's counter-charges, including the alleged debt from Mantitheus' mercenary levy at Mytilene and the wounding case tried before the Areopagus. Interwoven with laws, depositions, and testimony, it supplies dense evidence for Athenian family law — engye and dowry, adoption into a phratria, anakrisis before arbitrators, and the scrutiny of an elected taxiarch — and offers parallels in legal vocabulary and household-conflict motifs for readers comparing Isaeus, Lysias, and the neighboring Demosthenic private speeches.
grc.demosthenes.against_midias: A forensic speech of the Athenian orator Demosthenes, prosecuting Midias by probole for hubris and other offenses committed against him while serving as choregos for his tribe at the Dionysia. The speaker recounts the blows he received during the festival, Midias' nocturnal sabotage of the chorus' golden crowns and gilded robe, the corruption of the chorus-trainer, and a wider catalog of Midias' acts of violence, reinforcing the case with quotations of the laws governing probolai and offenses at religious festivals and with witness testimony. In a compact 227 lines it offers dense festival and legal vocabulary — choregia, probole, hieromenia, hubris as an actionable offense — and programmatic arguments that an outrage against a public liturgist is an outrage against the city itself, making it a productive source of parallels for readers of Attic oratory and Greek festival practice.
grc.demosthenes.against_onetor_30: A short forensic speech in the Demosthenic corpus, written in Attic Greek for delivery before an Athenian jury in a private suit against Onetor, brother-in-law of Aphobus and son of Timocrates. The speaker, engaged in prolonged litigation to recover the estate of which Aphobus had been guardian, argues that Onetor never paid the dowry promised with his sister, that her reported abandonment and the assessment of a farm in lieu of it were a sham to shield Aphobus' property, and he supports the claim with witnesses, challenges, and the threat of torture evidence for slaves. Readers of intertexts will find it valuable for its legal vocabulary (apoleipsis, apotimēma, basanos), its rhetoric of character and shamelessness, and its place within the Demosthenic sequence of orations arising from the guardianship dispute.
grc.demosthenes.against_phormio: An Athenian forensic speech of uncertain date, transmitted among the orations of Demosthenes and edited by W. Rennie in the 1921 Oxford edition. Delivered by the prosecutor in a commercial suit, it answers Phormio's paragraphe, a preliminary plea that a twenty-mina maritime loan advanced for a voyage to the Bosporus had been repaid there to the shipmaster Lampis, and argues from the written contract, witness depositions, and the wreck of the overloaded ship that the pledged cargo was never loaded and the money never returned. The speech also parades the plaintiff's services to Athens in the grain trade, including imports during shortages at below-market prices. Its dense layer of quoted laws, contracts, witness citations, and maritime-commercial vocabulary makes it a productive source of parallels for readers tracing Attic legal and commercial diction.
grc.demosthenes.against_polycles: An Athenian courtroom speech of uncertain date, preserved in the corpus of Demosthenes, Against Polycles is spoken by a former trierarch who prosecutes Polycles for refusing to take over his trireme when his term had expired, leaving him to bear five months and six days of further expense. The speaker recounts manning and outfitting the ship at his own cost, convoy duty and hostilities in the Hellespont and off Thasos and Maroneia, and his repeated demands before witnesses that Polycles assume the command and reimburse his outlays, framing the case as one that tests the laws of trierarchic succession and concerns the city as a whole. Its dense vocabulary of liturgies, naval finance and Attic forensic procedure, along with its recurring courtroom formulae, makes the oration a fertile source of parallels for readers tracing intertexts in classical Greek oratory.
grc.demosthenes.against_stephanus_2: A forensic speech of the Demosthenic corpus, Against Stephanus 2 belongs to the series of inheritance disputes over the estate of the banker Pasion, in which the speaker, Apollodorus, prosecutes Stephanus for giving false witness on behalf of Phormion. The speech argues that Stephanus perjured himself in testifying that documents in a sealed chest were copies of Pasion's wills, drawing on the Athenian laws concerning wills, legitimate sons, adopted citizens, and heiresses, several of which are quoted in full. Composed in fourth-century Athenian courtroom prose, it interlocks closely with the first speech Against Stephanus and with the speeches Against Phormion and Against Aphobus, offering rich parallels for Attic arguments about testimony, perjury, and the citation of statute.
grc.demosthenes.against_timocrates: An Attic forensic oration attributed to Demosthenes, Against Timocrates is a prosecution speech attacking a law proposed by Timocrates that allowed citizens condemned to fines for offences against the state to escape imprisonment by furnishing sureties. The speaker rehearses the earlier proceedings against Androtion and Euctemon over sacred and public monies, quotes the statutes and decrees allegedly contravened, and argues that Timocrates rushed his measure through in violation of the established nomothesia procedures during a sacred truce. For readers hunting parallels, the speech offers a dense tissue of embedded laws, decrees, and procedural formulas, and it belongs closely with the Demosthenic speeches against Androtion and Aristocrates, making it a key witness to the rhetoric of legislative illegality and to Athenian legal vocabulary.
grc.demosthenes.exordia: A collection of brief exordia for speeches before the Athenian assembly, preserved in the Demosthenic corpus and of uncertain date and authorship, though conventionally printed among Demosthenes' orations. Each short piece, typically opening with an address to 'men of Athens', supplies a generic preface urging the assembly to hear all speakers with patience, warning against flattery, personal invective, and idle self-display in place of practical counsel, and reflecting on fortune, preparation, and the duty of proposing what benefits the city. For readers hunting intertexts, the collection serves as a repertory of the stock formulae and commonplaces of Greek deliberative oratory, many of them echoed, varied, or expanded elsewhere in the speeches of the Demosthenic corpus.
grc.demosthenes.for_phormio: A Greek forensic oration of the classical Athenian courts, transmitted among the speeches of Demosthenes and printed in Rennie's 1921 Oxford edition, and comparatively brief at sixty-two lines. The speaker defends Phormio, the freedman and former slave of the banker Pasion, against a twenty-talent damages suit brought by Pasion's son Apollodorus, arguing by way of paragraphē that the claim is inadmissible because the matters at issue had already been settled by arbitration and formal release. The speech rehearses the history of Pasion's bank and shield factory, the lease, the will, Phormio's marriage to Pasion's widow, and the division of the estate, punctuated by witness testimony and citations of law. Readers tracing intertexts will find it rich in Attic legal idiom and linked by shared persons and circumstances to the other private orations arising from the Pasion-Apollodorus affairs.
grc.demosthenes.olynthiac_2: The second of the three Olynthiac orations of Demosthenes, a deliberative speech in classical Attic prose addressed to the Athenian assembly during the conflict between Philip II of Macedon and Olynthus. The speaker argues that the goodwill of the gods has offered Athens a timely ally in the Olynthians, that Philip's power, built on perjury and the successive deception of the Olynthians, Thessalians, and others, is inherently unstable and must collapse at the first setback, and that the Athenians must end their procrastination by voting money, sending embassies, and taking the field themselves. Along the way it surveys weakness within Macedonia, contrasts Philip's ambition with the hardships of his soldiers and companions, and rebukes Athenian factionalism under the symmories. Readers hunting parallels may note its gnomic reflections on fortune and the foundations of power, its similes of the house, ship, and ailing body, and its episodes, such as the loss of Amphipolis and Potidaea, that recur across the other Olynthiacs and the Philippic corpus.
grc.demosthenes.on_organization: On Organization (Peri syntaxeōs) is a brief deliberative speech of the Demosthenic corpus, attributed to Demosthenes and of uncertain date, addressed to the Athenian assembly on the provision of assembly-pay and the mustering of the city's forces. The speaker argues that Athens should spend revenues not on distributions but on organizing citizens, cavalry, and allies for war under accountable generals, and he contrasts the public austerity of the ancestors under Themistocles and Miltiades with contemporary extravagance and the over-honoring of individual commanders. Its repeated motifs—the healing of the citizens' corrupted ears, the claim that safety lies in arms rather than in courts, and the decline from ancestral power—offer fertile ground for parallels within Demosthenes' other deliberative orations and for later political rhetoric.
grc.demosthenes.on_the_chersonese: On the Chersonese (Περὶ τῶν ἐν Χερρονήσῳ), an assembly oration preserved among the public speeches of Demosthenes and edited by S. H. Butcher for the Clarendon Demosthenis Orationes (Oxford, 1903), belongs to the period of Athenian confrontation with Philip of Macedon. The speaker warns that Philip, campaigning in Thrace and pressing towards the Hellespont, is already at war with Athens notwithstanding the peace, defends the general Diopeithes against his accusers, and urges the assembly to send money and troops rather than prosecute the men standing against Philip's advance. For readers of intertexts it offers a dense quarry of deliberative formulae — war and peace, eisangelia and wartime finance, the invective against Philip's partisans — closely echoed in the Olynthiacs, the Philippics, and On the Crown.
grc.demosthenes.on_the_crown: On the Crown is a forensic oration by Demosthenes, delivered at Athens in the trial arising from Aeschines' prosecution of Ctesiphon for proposing an honorary decree in Demosthenes' favour. The exordium prays for the gods' favour and an impartial hearing, and the speech then expands into a sweeping retrospective of the speaker's career, defending his policy towards Philip of Macedon, rehearsing the history of the Peace of Philocrates and the Phocian War, and attacking Aeschines' conduct as ambassador and informer. Among the most celebrated of all Greek speeches, with famous set pieces such as the tribute to the Athenians fallen in battle, it has been a constant source of quotation and imitation, and a reader hunting intertexts will find its phrases and scenes echoed throughout later classical and European literature.
grc.demosthenes.on_the_false_embassy: A Greek forensic oration by Demosthenes, preserved in S. H. Butcher's Oxford edition of 1903, spoken in prosecution of Aeschines at the audit following the second embassy to Philip of Macedon. Demosthenes accuses his fellow ambassador of accepting bribes, misreporting Philip's intentions, and betraying the city's interests over the peace and the fate of Phocis, rehearsing the course of the negotiations, the part played by Philocrates, and the letters, decrees, and testimony read in evidence. Since the speech restates material from Demosthenes' other public orations and stands as the counterpart to Aeschines' own account of the embassy, it offers a dense web of overlapping arguments, phrases, and rival narratives of the same events, making it especially fertile ground for readers tracing verbal and thematic parallels across the Demosthenic and Aeschinean corpora.
grc.demosthenes.philippic_1: Demosthenes' first Philippic is an Attic deliberative oration, of uncertain date, addressed to the Athenian assembly ('ὦ ἄνδρες Ἀθηναῖοι' punctuates the argument throughout), printed here from Butcher's 1903 Oxford edition. The speaker reproaches the Athenians for the negligence that has let Philip II of Macedon seize places once theirs, such as Amphipolis, Pydna, Potidaea, and Methone, and contrasts Philip's tireless energy with Athenian delay, announcing that Philip's power rests on their own inaction. The speech then sets out a concrete programme: a standing force of two thousand infantry and two hundred cavalry drawn by rotation from the citizens, fifty triremes with ten fast cruisers, and a fixed annual fund of about ninety talents, so that war may be waged by sustained preparation rather than belated rescue expeditions. Its aphoristic maxims on initiative and laziness, its reading of a Philip's letter to the Euboeans, and its memorable simile of Athenians fighting Philip as barbarians box made it a touchstone for later writers on rhetoric and a rich source of verbal parallels.
grc.demosthenes.philippic_3: Demosthenes' third Philippic is an Athenian assembly speech urging the citizens to treat the encroachments of Philip of Macedon in the Chersonese and across Greece as open war, notwithstanding the nominal peace, and to act for the defence of all Greeks rather than their own interests alone. The speaker surveys Philip's rise from small beginnings and his treatment of Olynthus, Methone, Phocis, Euboea, Thessaly, and the cities of Thrace, contrasts his thirteen years of aggression with the older hegemonies of Athens, Sparta, and Thebes, and attributes the Greeks' inability to resist to corruption and mutual distrust rather than to any lack of resources. A celebrated example of deliberative oratory, the speech is a recurrent source of formulations on the Greek–barbarian distinction, the dangers of flattering orators in the assembly, and the need for common action, and so repays attention from readers tracing such themes elsewhere.
grc.demosthenes.philippic_4: A deliberative speech of uncertain date, transmitted among the orations of Demosthenes and counted as the fourth Philippic, addressed to the Athenian assembly in the crisis with Philip of Macedon. The speaker surveys Philip's successive encroachments in Thrace, Euboea, Megara and Oreus, argues that Philip's true war is against the Athenian democracy itself, and urges steady military and financial preparation, including a reconsideration of the theoric fund and an embassy to the Persian king. Readers hunting parallels will find compact formulations of anti-Macedonian commonplaces here, above all the antithesis of Athenian sloth against Macedonian energy and the argument that free men are constrained by shame where slaves yield to blows, motifs that resonate across the Demosthenic corpus and the later rhetorical tradition.
grc.diogenianus_of_heraclea.παροιμίαι_δημώδε: A collection of popular Greek proverbs handed down under the name of Diogenianus of Heraclea, a Greek writer of uncertain date, as edited by Leutsch and Schneidewin in the first volume of their Paroemiographi Graeci (Göttingen, 1839). The work opens with a short essay on the definition and origin of the proverb, distinguishing it from allied forms such as the Aesopic fable and the Carian, Sybaritic, Cyprian, and Libyan ainos, and then proceeds through an alphabetical series of proverbs, each supplied with a gloss on its application and frequently with an explanatory story drawn from myth, history, or comedy. Because Greek poets and prose writers constantly deploy proverbial phrases, the compilation offers readers of intertexts a compact repertory of such expressions together with the ancient interpretations attached to them.
grc.dionysius_calliphontis.dionysii_callipho: A brief prose periegesis of Greece, the Anagraphe tes Hellados ascribed to Dionysius son of Calliphon, an otherwise obscure figure of uncertain date, printed by Karl Müller in the first volume of the Geographi Graeci Minores (Didot, Paris, 1855). Addressed to one Theophrastus, it announces a swift, versified rendering of what older authors recorded and conducts a coastal circuit from Ambracia through Acarnania, Aetolia, Locris, Phocis, and Boeotia toward the Peloponnese, cataloguing cities, harbours, rivers, mountains, islands, and sanctuaries with mythological notices such as Agamemnon's foundation at Aulis and the oracle at Delphi. Its dense toponymy and cult legends make it a useful hunting ground for parallels with Homeric geography, the periploi, and later geographic literature. The corpus record preserves the whole as a single unnumbered line, with lacunae and a marked discontinuity in the sequence where the progression resumes at Crete.
grc.dionysius_halicarnassensis.de_isocrate: A brief work of ancient rhetorical criticism in Greek by Dionysius of Halicarnassus, De Isocrate opens with a concise life of Isocrates, running from his birth in the eighty-sixth Olympiad and his studies under Gorgias, Prodicus, and Tisias to his death, close to a hundred years old, in the days after the battle of Chaeronea. The main body assesses Isocrates' style against that of Lysias, treating purity of diction, periodic and rhythmically wrought composition, the pursuit of elevated grandeur, and the faults of prolixity and overwrought figuration, with appeal to Theophrastus' triad of word choice, harmony, and figures. Extensive quotation from the Panegyricus, the address to Philip, the De pace, the Areopagiticus, the Archidamus, and the Trapeziticus illustrates both the moral force and the mannered excesses of the orator's manner. Readers hunting intertexts will find here a full ancient comparison of Lysias and Isocrates, with verbatim excerpts embedded in the critical argument.
grc.epictetus.discourses: The Discourses of Epictetus, preserved in Greek as compiled from the philosopher's spoken lectures by Arrian, open with a dedicatory letter in which Arrian explains to Lucius Gellius that he transcribed his teacher's words as memoranda rather than as polished compositions. The lectures expound Stoic doctrine in the form of informal dialogues, exhortations, and anecdotes, treating the distinction between what lies within one's power and what does not, the proper use of impressions, the freedom of the prohairesis, and indifference to externals, with recurring examples drawn from Socrates, Diogenes, and figures of the Roman world such as Nero and Vespasian. Readers hunting parallels will find the collection unusually dense with quotation and allusion, invoking Homer, the tragedians, Plato, and earlier Stoics including Zeno, Cleanthes, and Chrysippus, and it stands as a central witness to Stoic teaching and to the philosophical idiom of its age.
grc.epictetus.enchiridion: A compact Greek handbook of Stoic ethics in fifty-three short chapters, transmitted under the name of Epictetus and preserved with the Dissertationes that Arrian digested from his teaching. The opening chapter sets out the celebrated division of things into what is and is not within our power, and the succeeding chapters offer precepts on the use of impressions, desire and aversion, endurance of loss, grief, and insult, the duties arising from social roles, piety toward the gods, and the conduct expected of the aspiring philosopher. Socrates, Diogenes, Heraclitus, and Zeno are invoked as exemplars, and many of the maxims run parallel to passages of the longer Dissertationes, so the work serves as a dense repository of Stoic phrasing for readers tracing such formulations and their reuse in later moral literature.
grc.epicurus.epistula_ad_herodotum: Epicurus' Epistula ad Herodotum is a Greek epitome of Epicurean physics, addressed by Epicurus to a correspondent named Herodotus and transmitted by Diogenes Laertius, edited here from von der Mühll's Teubner text. The letter distils the whole doctrine of nature for readers unable to master the longer treatises, covering atoms and void, the infinity of the universe and of worlds, the criteria of truth, and perception, hearing, and smell through eidola or atomic films. A reader of intertexts values it as the canonical summary of Epicurus' natural philosophy, closely echoed in Lucretius' De rerum natura and in later doxographic reports of the school.
grc.epicurus.gnomologium_vaticanum_epicureum: The Gnomologium Vaticanum Epicureum is a Greek gnomologium, a collection of some eighty brief Epicurean maxims transmitted under the name of Epicurus and printed in von der Mühll's Teubner volume together with the letters and Ratae Sententiae preserved by Diogenes Laertius. Its sayings compress the ethical core of Epicureanism into aphoristic form: the blessedness of the gods, death as nothing to us, the management of pain and desire, the primacy of friendship and justice, and the self-sufficiency of the wise. The compilation itself is of uncertain date, but its sentences largely parallel or overlap the Principal Doctrines and other strands of the Epicurean tradition. Readers hunting intertexts will find here many of the school's most quotable formulations, whose themes and phrasing recur in later Greek and Latin writers.
