grc.euclid.elements: Euclid's Elements is the Greek mathematical treatise that opens with terse definitions of point, line, surface, angle, circle, and rectilineal figures, then lays out postulates and common notions before advancing to propositions with formal proofs, beginning with the construction of an equilateral triangle on a given straight line. The Greek text is taken from J. L. Heiberg's Teubner edition (Leipzig, 1883–1888). The preserved lines include the definitions, the five postulates, the common notions on equals, and the first propositions on constructing and transferring magnitudes. Because its formulae — from the point as that which has no part to the axioms about equals added to or subtracted from equals — became stock phrases echoed across Greek and later prose, the Elements is an essential reference point for hunting verbal and conceptual parallels in philosophical, rhetorical, and scientific writing.
grc.euripides.alcestis: Alcestis is a Greek tragedy by Euripides, of uncertain date, running to 1,179 lines and opening with a prologue in which Apollo recounts how, after killing the Cyclopes in revenge for Asclepius, he was forced by Zeus to serve the mortal Admetus as a herdsman, and how he then tricked the Fates into letting Admetus escape death if a substitute should die in his stead. Only Admetus' wife Alcestis proved willing, and the play follows her sacrifice on the appointed day, Admetus' grief and vow of continued fidelity, and the intervention of Heracles, who wrestles with Thanatos and brings back a veiled woman whom he persuades his host to receive. Its mingling of funerary solemnity with a happy ending, and its defining bargain of a life ransomed by another's death, made the story a touchstone for later treatments of devotion, hospitality, and return from the grave.
grc.euripides.andromache: Andromache is a Greek tragedy by Euripides, running to 1266 lines. Its action centres on Hector's widow, enslaved to Neoptolemus after the fall of Troy and mother of his child, whose life is threatened by the jealous Hermione and her father Menelaus until the aged Peleus comes to her aid; the plot then shifts to Delphi, where Orestes brings about Neoptolemus' death, and the play closes with an epiphany of Thetis. Euripides here reworks Homeric figures and material — Andromache, Menelaus, Peleus, Thetis, the house of Achilles — dwelling on the survivors of the war and the enmity between the houses of Troy and Peleus. For readers tracing intertexts, its dense engagement with the Iliad and the epic tradition of Troy's destruction, alongside its affinities with Euripides' other plays on Trojan themes, makes it a rich locus for mythic and verbal parallels.
grc.euripides.bacchae: A Greek tragedy in 1393 lines by Euripides, given here in Gilbert Murray's Oxford edition of the Euripidis Fabulae (1913). Dionysus arrives in Thebes in mortal disguise, avenging slander against his mother Semele by driving the women of Cadmus' house into maenadic frenzy, while the young king Pentheus refuses the new god and is lured to his destruction on the mountain. The play offers the fullest surviving dramatic treatment of Dionysiac epiphany, madness, and ritual, with choruses of Asian Bacchants and imagery of thyrsus, fawn-skin, and ivy that later poets repeatedly draw upon. Readers hunting intertexts will find in it a principal ancient source for Dionysus scenes, Bacchic possession, and the motif of divine retribution against sceptical rulers.
grc.euripides.cyclops: Euripides' Cyclops, the only complete satyr play to survive from Greek tragedy, recasts the Cyclops episode of Odyssey 9 as burlesque: Odysseus and his crew, blown off course to Aetna, find Silenus and his satyrs enslaved to the man-eating Polyphemus and eventually engineer the giant's blinding with wine and a stake. The opening speech of Silenus recounts Dionysus' wanderings and his punishment of the Tyrrhenian pirates before turning to the satyrs' servile life in the Cyclops' cave. Readers of intertexts will find a comic counterpoint to Homer's narrative with sustained verbal engagement with the epic, as well as a rare witness to satyr-drama conventions and to Dionysiac myth on the tragic stage.
grc.euripides.fragmenta: A collection of the surviving fragments of the Greek tragic poet Euripides, drawn from August Nauck's 1889 Teubner edition of the Tragicorum Graecorum Fragmenta. The material preserves what remains of tragedies that do not survive complete, ranging from isolated gnomic lines on women, wealth, nobility, and fortune to extended dialogue passages, some headed by play titles such as Panactes. Since much of this material reached the editor as quotations carried in later Greek authors, the collection offers a rich hunting ground for sententiae and for echoes of Euripidean diction and themes in subsequent literature.
grc.euripides.hecuba: Hecuba is a Greek tragedy by Euripides, of uncertain date, presented in Gilbert Murray's Oxford edition of the Euripidis Fabulae (1902) and running to 1,274 lines. The prologue is spoken by the ghost of Polydorus, youngest son of Priam and Hecuba, murdered for his gold by the Thracian guest-friend Polymestor after the fall of Troy. The play follows Hecuba through two linked catastrophes: the sacrifice of her daughter Polyxena at the tomb of Achilles, and her revenge upon Polymestor when her son's body washes ashore. Its concentrated treatment of captivity, lamentation, and the betrayal of xenia made it a touchstone for later Greek and Latin writers reworking the aftermath of the Trojan War.
grc.euripides.helen: Helen, a Greek tragedy by Euripides, is given here in Gilbert Murray's Oxford text of the Fabulae (1913) and runs to 1,714 lines. The play dramatizes the alternative tradition in which the real Helen never went to Troy: the prologue, spoken by Helen herself, relates how Hermes carried her to Egypt while Hera sent Paris a breathing phantom in her likeness, and the action follows her years of waiting under the protection of the Egyptian king until the shipwrecked Menelaus washes ashore and husband and wife contrive escape from Theoclymenus. Its sustained play on appearance and reality, and its wholesale reworking of the epic Helen story, make it a standing point of comparison for readers tracing the myth's variants across Greek poetry and drama.
grc.euripides.heracleidae: The Heracleidae is a Greek tragedy by Euripides, of uncertain date within the poet's career, dramatising the flight of Heracles' children from the persecution of Eurystheus and their reception as suppliants at Marathon in Attica. Opening with the prologue of the aged Iolaus, the play traces the Athenian decision under Demophon to defend the fugitives, the voluntary self-sacrifice of Macaria, and the capture of Eurystheus, whose dying oracle promises Athens lasting protection. In 1057 lines of iambic trimeter and lyric, it supplies rich material for readers of intertexts interested in supplication scenes, asylum and kinship obligation, the myth of the Heracleid return, and parallels with Euripides' other suppliant drama.
grc.euripides.hippolytus: Hippolytus is a Greek tragedy by Euripides, edited and translated by David Kovacs (Harvard University Press, forthcoming), running to 1,448 lines. The play opens with Aphrodite's prologue announcing her vengeance on Hippolytus, the chaste son of Theseus who honors Artemis and rejects marriage, and goes on to trace Phaedra's silent, consuming passion for her stepson and the catastrophe it brings at Troezen. With its framing opposition of Cypris and Artemis and its portrait of concealed eros, it became the canonical ancient treatment of the Phaedra–Hippolytus story and a standing point of comparison for later retellings and for the study of tragic intertextuality.
grc.euripides.iphigenia_tauris: Euripides' Iphigenia in Tauris is a Greek tragedy in 1478 lines, printed in Gilbert Murray's Oxford edition of the Euripidis Fabulae (1913). The prologue, spoken by Iphigenia herself, rehearses the sacrifice at Aulis and Artemis' substitution of a deer, by which the girl was carried off to the Taurians and installed as priestess of a cult that puts every Greek who lands on that shore to death. The action brings Orestes and Pylades to that shore, moves through the recognition of brother and sister, and ends with their escape from King Thoas bearing the image of Artemis. For readers of intertexts, the play offers a companion piece to the other Euripidean Iphigenia and Orestes dramas and a distinctive variant of the Aulis sacrifice and the matricide's aftermath, inviting comparison with parallel treatments in Greek epic and tragedy.
grc.euripides.orestes: Orestes, a Greek tragedy by Euripides, is presented here in Gilbert Murray's Oxford text of the Euripidis Fabulae (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1913) and runs to 1,705 lines. The play opens on the sixth day after Orestes, urged on by Apollo and aided by his sister Electra and his friend Pylades, has killed their mother Clytemnestra, and follows his collapse into madness, the Argive assembly's vote of death, the plot against Helen and the seizure of Hermione as a hostage, and the concluding settlement imposed by Apollo, who deifies Helen and ordains Orestes' marriage to Hermione and trial at Athens. Its prologue recapitulates the whole cursed genealogy of the house — Tantalus, Pelops, Atreus, Thyestes, Agamemnon — and the drama recasts the matricide legend treated in Aeschylus' Oresteia with pointedly revisionist emphases. The result is a fertile source of verbal and thematic parallels for readers tracing the Orestes myth, the rhetoric of guilt and madness, and the representation of divine justice across Greek literature.
grc.euripides.phoenissae: Phoenissae, a Greek tragedy by Euripides of uncertain date, dramatises the final ruin of the house of Cadmus: the curse of Oedipus, the rival claims of his sons Eteocles and Polynices to the rule of Thebes, and the deaths of Jocasta, the two brothers, and the young Menoeceus, prefaced by Jocasta's retrospective prologue on the city's history from Cadmus onward. Named for its chorus of Phoenician captive women, the play runs to 1,768 lines in Gilbert Murray's Oxford edition of 1913. Its teichoscopy of Antigone, the fraternal duel, and its laments became patterns repeatedly reworked by later poets, and the play stands beside Aeschylus' Seven against Thebes and Sophocles' Theban dramas as a central witness to the Theban legend.
grc.euripides.rhesus: Rhesus is a Greek tragedy attributed to Euripides, though its authorship has long been disputed and its date of composition is uncertain; it is printed in Gilbert Murray's Oxford edition of the Euripidis Fabulae (1913) and runs to 994 lines. Drawing on the Doloneia of Iliad Book 10, it dramatizes a single night of the Trojan War: Hector's rousing of his allies for a night assault on the Greek camp, the reconnaissance of Dolon, and the infiltration of the Trojan lines by Odysseus and Diomedes, who kill the newly arrived Thracian king Rhesus and drive off his horses. The play closes with the arrival and lament of the Muse over her son's body. For readers of intertexts it offers the only surviving Greek tragedy to stage a Homeric night raid, reworking Iliad 10 with substantial additions and departures from Homer.
grc.euripides.trojan_women: A Greek tragedy by Euripides, the Trojan Women stages the morning after the sack of Troy: Poseidon opens the play above the ruined city, and Hecuba, Cassandra, Andromache, and Helen learn their allotment to Greek masters while Polyxena lies sacrificed on Achilles' tomb and the boy Astyanax is brought in for burial. The drama unfolds as a chain of laments and formal speeches rather than a continuous plot, with the captive women's dirges over Priam, Hector, and the fallen city forming its structural spine. Its laments for Troy's women, its judgement of Helen, and its catalogue of Trojan suffering draw on the epic tradition of the city's fall and became a recurrent source of verbal and thematic echoes for later ancient drama and for post-classical retellings of the Trojan story.
grc.flavius_josephus.antiquitates_judaicae: A twenty-book Greek prose history by the Jewish author Flavius Josephus, transmitted in B. Niese's Berlin edition of 1892, which sets out the ancient history and constitution of the Jews from the creation of the world as recorded in the Hebrew scriptures, carrying the narrative onward until it joins his separate account of the war against Rome. Its preface, addressed to Greek readers and naming Epaphroditus as the patron whose encouragement secured the undertaking, dwells on the Septuagint translation made for Ptolemy II before turning to Moses as lawgiver and to the six days of creation. The work retells biblical narrative from Genesis forward in the manner of Greek historiography, supplying rationalising paraphrase, added causation, and ethnographic explanation throughout. Readers hunting parallels will find the opening books alone dense with reworked episodes—Adam and Eve, Eden and its rivers, the institution of the Sabbath—whose phrasing regularly diverges from and comments upon the scriptural account.
grc.flavius_josephus.josephi_vita: A Greek autobiographical apologia by Flavius Josephus, the Vita runs to 430 lines in B. Niese's Berlin edition of 1890 and defends the author's conduct against detractors, chief among them Justus of Tiberias, who had composed his own history of the same events. Josephus opens with an account of his priestly and Hasmonaean royal lineage, then recounts his youthful sampling of the Pharisaic, Sadducean, and Essenic ways of life, his sojourn with the desert ascetic Bannus, a shipwreck-marred voyage to Rome to win the release of imprisoned priests through the intercession of Poppaea, and his command in Galilee at the outbreak of the revolt against Rome. The narrative repeatedly cross-refers to Josephus's fuller books on the Jewish war, excusing omissions and promising more precise treatments elsewhere, which makes the work a natural meeting point for readers tracing overlapping war narratives and the conventions of Greek self-justifying autobiography.
grc.gaius_romanus.fragmenta: Greek fragments of Gaius (Caius) Romanus, an early ecclesiastical writer of Rome, transmitted through quotation in Eusebius's Ecclesiastical History and collected by Martin Joseph Routh in the second volume of his Reliquiae Sacrae (1846). The fragments preserve portions of the dialogue Gaius held at Rome under Bishop Zephyrinus with Proclus, a champion of the Phrygian heresy, together with further excerpts relayed by Eusebius on Cerinthus's earthly millennium, the fall and restoration of Natalius, and the heretics' bold corrections of the divine scriptures. In the dialogue Gaius points to the trophies of the apostles on the Vatican and on the road to Ostia, and counts only thirteen epistles of the apostle Paul, excluding that to the Hebrews. Readers of intertexts will find here early evidence for the shape of the Christian canon, for Roman commemorative topography, and for polemical phrasing that later ecclesiastical authors repeat.
grc.galen.de_atra_bile: De Atra Bile (On Black Bile) is a Greek medical treatise by Galen, printed in Kühn's Opera Omnia (Leipzig, 1823), which defends the study of the humors against Erasistratus and against Erasistratean, Asclepiadean, and Methodical physicians who dismissed humoral theory as useless to practice. Galen describes the visible characters of blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile, explains how black bile arises in the liver, is drawn off by the spleen, and produces conditions such as melancholy, cancer, anthrax, elephantiasis, hemorrhoids, and varicose veins, and sets out the diagnosis and purgative treatment of the melancholic humor. Readers of intertexts will find the treatise densely studded with quotation and discussion of earlier authorities—Hippocrates, Erasistratus, Diocles, Praxagoras, Philotimus, Pleistonicus, and Rufus of Ephesus—including verbatim excerpts on which Galen comments, so that it preserves both fragments of otherwise lost medical writers and an ancient physician's reading of Hippocratic passages.
grc.galen.de_dignoscendis_pulsibus: Galen's De Dignoscendis Pulsibus (On the Diagnosis of Pulses), printed in Kühn's Leipzig edition of 1824, constitutes the second part of the four-part theory of the pulse announced in its opening lines, the remaining parts covering differences of kind, causes, and what each pulse indicates. In Greek prose the second-century physician Galen defends the claim that systole as well as diastole is perceptible to a trained hand against the denial of the so-called Empiric physicians, and offers detailed instruction in palpation, the parts of each beat, and the recognition of rapid, slow, large, small, hard, faint and rhythmical pulses. The work repeatedly cites Herophilus, Erasistratus, Praxagoras, Archigenes and Agathinus, attacks the obscure definitions of full and empty pulses offered by Archigenes, and borrows the vocabulary of rhythm from music theory while quoting Heraclitus and alluding to Plato. For readers hunting parallels, it is a central witness to Galenic pulse terminology and to the web of citation linking Hellenistic medicine with philosophy and the technical arts.
grc.galen.de_dignotione_ex_insomniis: De Dignotione ex Insomniis is a short Greek treatise by Galen, preserved in Kühn's edition of his Opera Omnia (Leipzig, 1823), which sets out how dreams may be read as signs of the body's underlying condition. Visions of fire, smoke, rain, snow and related imagery are interpreted as indications of excess yellow bile, black bile, phlegm and other humours, with the further proviso that timing, recent food and the dreamer's daily habits and worries must also be weighed. The discussion distinguishes such somatic dreams from prophetic ones, illustrating the difficulty of telling them apart with cases like the wrestler who dreamt he stood in a pool of blood and the man whose leg turned to stone and was subsequently paralysed, and it explains how the soul, penetrating the body's depths in sleep, registers its internal state. Readers of intertexts will find here a compact witness to ancient medical oneiromancy, in which dream imagery serves humoral diagnosis rather than divination.
grc.galen.de_methodo_medendi: Galen's 'De Methodo Medendi' (On the Therapeutic Method), preserved in Kühn's nineteenth-century Leipzig edition of the Greek Opera Omnia, is a treatise on rational medical treatment addressed to a friend named Hiero, opening with Galen's justification for writing a work he had long delayed and an extended invective against Thessalus and the Methodic school of physicians. The surviving portion defines disease, symptom, and cause, distinguishes simples from compound conditions, and works through the treatment of wounds, ulcers, haemorrhage and their attendant affections such as inflammation, induration and ulceration, constantly demonstrating that cure must proceed from the causes of the deranged functioning rather than from experience alone or from Methodic 'commonalities'. Readers of intertexts will find the treatise dense with argumentative allusion: Galen repeatedly summons Plato, Aristotle, Theophrastus, the Stoics, Hippocrates, Erasistratus, Herophilus, Asclepiades, Hesiod and Homer as witnesses, cites his own earlier works (on elements, mixtures, natural faculties and the doctrines of Hippocrates and Plato), and models the dialectical method of division that he claims underlies sound therapeutics, making the work a central node for tracing the dialogue between medicine and philosophy in the imperial Greek period.
grc.galen.de_optima_doctrina: De Optima Doctrina is a short Greek philosophical polemic by Galen, printed in Kühn's Opera Omnia, aimed at the Academic teaching of Favorinus, whose advocacy of arguing on both sides of every question Galen finds inconsistent with the suspension of judgement (epochē). The treatise discusses the criterion of truth and the cataleptic impression, brings in Carneades, Chrysippus, Aristotle and Theophrastus, and refers to a lost Plutarchan dialogue in which Onesimus converses with Epictetus, while arguing that no teaching is possible unless sense perception and intellect are trusted as natural criteria. Readers hunting parallels will find it valuable as a source of quotations from and testimonia to Favorinus's lost books on the cataleptic phantasia and of Academic sceptical arguments known to Galen.
grc.galen.de_ossibus_ad_tirones: Galen's De ossibus ad tirones ('On Bones, for Beginners') is a compact Greek introduction to osteology, preserved in Kühn's Leipzig edition of the Opera omnia (1821). Addressed to novices in medicine, it first sets out the vocabulary of the subject—joints, symphyses, sutures, epiphyses, and the distinctions among kinds of articulation—and then surveys the skeleton bone by bone, from the skull, vertebrae, ribs, and sternum to the arms, hands, legs, and feet, with a digression on the teeth. Galen repeatedly corrects the counts and terminology of earlier anatomists and appeals to Hippocratic usage for names such as arthron. For readers hunting intertexts, the treatise offers a dense store of Greek anatomical terms and explicit commentary on the medical tradition from which later anatomical writing drew.
grc.galen.de_rebus_boni_malique_suci: A short dietetic treatise in Greek by Galen, the physician of the Roman imperial period, edited by Karl Gottlob Kühn in his Opera Omnia (Leipzig, 1823). Its argument is that health depends on generating good rather than bad humours (eukhymia and kakochymia), illustrated at the outset by successive famines among peoples subject to Rome, which bred sores, fevers, fluxes and mental disturbance, and by an autobiographical account of the regimen through which the author's father preserved him from seasonal illness. The main body classifies foods—bread and cereals, pulses, animal parts, nuts, orchard fruit, garden vegetables, fish, birds, wines and honey—according to the humour each produces, in explicit continuation of Hippocratic humoral teaching. For readers tracing parallels it offers dense material: named Italian and Asiatic wines, earlier medical authorities such as Praxagoras and Phylotimus, and repeated cross-references to Galen's own three books on the powers of foods.
grc.galen.de_semine: A Greek medical-philosophical treatise on semen, its function and generative power, printed in Kühn's edition of Galen's Opera Omnia (1822); the work surveys competing theories, contrasting the Hippocratic two-principle view of semen as both material and active cause with the Aristotelian doctrine that the male seed contributes only the principle of motion while the embryo takes substance from the menses, and adduces anatomical observation and experiment to argue that semen from both parents remains in the womb and shapes the foetus, before discussing the formation of the embryo, the vessels and membranes that nourish it, and the role of the testes and female genitalia. For readers of intertexts it is a densely allusive document, citing and polemicising against Aristotle's De generatione animalium, Hippocratic embryology, and the views of Empedocles, Herophilus, Athenaeus, Strato and Marinus, and it stands as a central witness to ancient debates on reproduction and physiological causation; the date of composition is not specified in the source record.
grc.galen.de_typis: A brief Greek medical treatise by the physician Galen, De Typis defines the typos of a disease as the ordered sequence of exacerbation and remission and surveys the periodic patterns of fevers. It distinguishes first and second, standing and moving, simple and compound types — quotidian, tertian, quartan, and semi-tertian fevers among them — and describes their symptoms, pulses, seasonal behaviour, and dangers, including differing ancient explanations of the semi-tertian's name, such as that of Agathinus. Quoting Hippocrates on the crisis of the tertian and appealing to what is handed down by him, the work offers a compact witness to Galen's engagement with the Hippocratic tradition. Readers of intertexts may value it as a source for the technical vocabulary of fever periodicity that recurs throughout ancient medical writing, edited in Kühn's Opera Omnia (Lipsiae, 1824).
grc.galen.de_venereis_ap_oribasium: A short Greek treatise on sexual intercourse, printed as 'De venereis apud Oribasium' in Kühn's edition of Galen's Opera Omnia (Leipzig, 1823) and preserved through excerpts made by the physician Oribasius. Attributed to Galen, the work rejects the Epicurean claim that sex serves no healthful purpose and instead sets out a regimen: the proper intervals and bodily states for intercourse, its warming and drying effects on the strong as against its harm to the weak, and corrective measures of preparatory exercise, cold bathing, and diet. Readers hunting intertexts will find Galenic humoral physiology applied to aphrodisia, and a passage whose transmission via Oribasius is central to the study of ancient medical regimen literature and of the excerpting tradition through which such fragments circulated.
grc.galen.quos_quibus_catharticis_medicament: A Greek medical treatise by Galen, edited in Kühn's Opera Omnia (Lipsiae, 1826) under the Latin title Quos quibus catharticis medicamentis et quando purgari oporteat — which patients are to be purged with which cathartic drugs, and when. Starting from the premise that purging healthy bodies is laborious and quickly exhausting, it sets out how to evacuate excess phlegmatic, bitter-bilious, melancholic, and serous humours in conditions such as gout, arthritis, apoplexy, epilepsy, melancholy, tertian fevers, and cancerous disorders, and how to prepare the body through rest, bland diet, and mild emetics before administering hellebore, colocynth, and related drugs, with attention to season, age, habit, the direction of evacuation, and the timing of doses in acute and chronic disease. Readers hunting parallels will find direct quotation of Hippocrates' Aphorisms, recurring humoural and pharmacological vocabulary, and first-person case histories of Galen's own patients that invite comparison with Hippocratic therapeutics and the rest of the Galenic corpus.
grc.galen.thrasybulus_sive_utrum_medicinae_s: A short Greek dialogue addressed to Thrasybulus, collected in Helmreich's Teubner Scripta Minora, takes up the question whether what is called hygiene belongs to medicine or to gymnastics and argues that the care of the body constitutes a single art, divided into a therapeutic branch for the sick and a preservative, hygienic branch whose subdivisions Galen sets out methodically. In the course of the argument the Pergamene physician attacks the trainers of athletes and the 'athletic' condition they produce as contrary to nature, while invoking Hippocrates and Plato on the ends and parts of the bodily arts. The discussion is intertextually rich: Galen quotes or paraphrases Hippocratic sayings on the athletic constitution, the Gorgias and Republic of Plato, Homeric verses on the worth of the physician, and a passage of Erasistratus's Hygienica, making the treatise a valuable witness for readers tracing the reception of those authors and the emergence of 'hygiene' as the name of a distinct art.
grc.galen.περὶ_τῶν_ἐν_ταῖς_τροφαῖς_δυνάμεων: A Greek medical treatise by Galen, On the Powers of Foods sets out the properties of foodstuffs and their effects on digestion and health, insisting that knowledge of a food's faculty rests on disciplined experience rather than on speculative causal argument. The opening chapters examine and correct earlier dietary writers, quoting Diocles and invoking Erasistratus and Mnesitheus, and the argument turns repeatedly to Hippocratic writings, above all the Epidemics and the book On Diet, whose attribution Galen weighs. Sustained discussion of digestibility, binding and purging foods, the humours, and the differing temperaments of individual bodies gives the work a dense web of verbal parallels with earlier Greek medicine. Readers of intertexts accordingly gain substantial quotation and adaptation of dietary writers otherwise preserved only in fragments.
grc.gorgias_of_leontini.ὑπέρ_παλαμήδους_ἀπολ: A short Greek forensic oration by Gorgias of Leontini, of uncertain date, presenting the mythical hero Palamedes' reply at Troy to the charge of treason brought against him by Odysseus, namely that he betrayed Greece to the barbarians. In a mere thirty-seven lines the speaker refutes the accusation by arguing that the alleged crime had no possible beginning, witnesses, means or rational motive, answers his accuser in kind, and closes with a defence of a blameless life and an account of Palamedes' inventions, from letters, numbers and written laws to weights, measures, military order and beacon signals. Composed for rhetorical display rather than an actual trial, the speech is a showpiece of antithetical Gorgianic prose and of the argument from impossibility. Readers of intertexts will find in it the classic rhetorical form of the wise man unjustly condemned, with echoes in the tragic Palamedes tradition, in Plato's defence of Socrates, and in later literary apologiai.
grc.gregory_of_nazianzus.christus_patiens: A Greek drama on the Passion of Christ, known as the Christus Patiens or Christos Paschon, attributed to Gregory of Nazianzus and of uncertain date. Its 2,655 lines present the betrayal by Judas, the lament of the Virgin, the Crucifixion and the burial through the mouths of the Theotokos, a chorus of virgins, an angel, Christ, John the Theologian, Joseph and Nicodemus. The prologue announces that the world-saving Passion will be declared 'after Euripides', and the play is a cento that refits verses of classical tragedy, chiefly Euripidean, to the Christian narrative. For readers of intertexts it is a central case of classical material transposed into Christian poetry, offering a compendium of tragic diction of suffering and lamentation reused for the Passion.
grc.heraclitus_of_ephesus.fragmenta: The surviving Greek fragments of Heraclitus of Ephesus, a Presocratic philosopher of uncertain date, are collected here in the arrangement of Hermann Diels' Die Fragmente der Vorsokratiker (Berlin, 1922), with Bywater's numbering noted alongside. The aphoristic fragments survive only as quotations embedded in later authors, among them Sextus Empiricus, Clement of Alexandria, Aristotle, Diogenes Laertius, Athenaeus and Columella, each citation given with its source. Their subjects include the logos that governs all things, the unity of opposites, fire as the cosmic principle, the ever-changing river, and the contrast between waking and sleeping souls. Since Heraclitus' phrasing and doctrines are repeatedly echoed, paraphrased and reworked across later Greek literature and philosophy, readers of intertexts will find here the primary wording against which such echoes can be measured.
grc.hero_of_alexandria.catoptrica: The Catoptrica is a Greek treatise on mirrors attributed to Hero of Alexandria and of uncertain date, printed here from the Teubner edition of Schmidt and Nix (1900). Its opening argument holds that since nature does nothing in vain, reflection must occur at equal angles, so that the visual ray passing from the eye to the mirror and thence to the object seen follows the shortest path; the claim is then established by a geometrical proof employing congruent triangles. The corpus preserves the work only as a brief opening passage running to two long lines. Readers of intertexts will find here a compact ancient formulation of the law of equal angles and of the shortest-path principle, phrasings that circulated in later optical writing.
grc.hero_of_alexandria.dioptra: The Dioptra is a Greek technical treatise by Hero of Alexandria, of uncertain date, on the construction and use of the dioptra, a sighting instrument for land surveying. After a preface praising the usefulness of dioptrics for aqueducts, fortifications, harbours, astronomy, geography and siege warfare, the work moves through numbered problems, from levelling ground for water channels and measuring inaccessible distances, river widths, heights and depths, to driving tunnels straight through mountains, laying out harbours and bridges on given curves, and measuring and dividing irregular tracts of land. Its demonstrations in the standard geometrical idiom, with lettered diagrams, cubit measurements and formulaic problem statements, make it a valuable witness for readers tracing the vocabulary of ancient engineering and the shared stock of Greek mathematical exposition.
grc.hero_of_alexandria.geodaesia_sp: A short Greek handbook on geodesy transmitted under the name of Hero of Alexandria and printed by Heiberg among the works attributed to Hero in the fifth volume of the Teubner edition, of uncertain date. It opens with a sequence of definitions of geometric fundamentals—point, line, plane, angle, circle, and rectilineal figures—closely following the opening of Euclid's Elements, then turns to the traditional account of geometry's origin in Egyptian land-surveying after the Nile's floods and to terminology for practical mensuration. Readers of intertexts will find its chief interest in its recycling of Euclidean definitional prose and in the surveying material it shares with the Geometrica of the Heroic corpus.
grc.hero_of_alexandria.pneumatica: Hero of Alexandria's Pneumatica, a Greek treatise on machines powered by air, water, and fire of uncertain date, opens with a sustained physical argument that air is a body and that a void exists only in dispersed particles or under compulsion, illustrated by experiments such as the suction sphere, the medical egg, and the cupping glass and supported by an appeal to Archimedes' work on floating bodies. The preface presents the treatise as a sequel to the author's four books on water clocks and as a collection and improvement of the discoveries of earlier philosophers and mechanicians. The bulk of the work then sets out, in recipe-like descriptions keyed to diagrams, a range of contrivances: bent and choked siphons, vessels that dispense hot or cold liquids at will, a mixing ladle, sympotic kraters that flow only when a companion vessel is filled, singing birds attended by a turning owl, and a trumpet sounded by the opening of temple doors. For readers of intertexts the treatise matters as a meeting point of natural philosophy, Archimedean hydrostatics, and practical mechanics, and as a formative source for later traditions of automata and mechanical marvels.
grc.hero_of_alexandria.stereometrica: Attributed to Hero of Alexandria and of uncertain date, the Stereometrica is a Greek handbook of solid mensuration offering rules and worked numerical examples for measuring spheres, cones, truncated cones, obelisk-shaped solids, cylinders, and columns. Its demonstrations repeatedly invoke named authorities, citing Archimedes on the sphere and cylinder (for instance that a circumscribing cylinder is half again the sphere, and that eleven cubes on the diameter equal twenty-one spheres) and Euclid on the cone as a third of its cylinder, alongside Euclidean-style definitions and occasional later editorial notes. A reader hunting intertexts will find here a practical, arithmetical reception of classical geometry, in which results from Archimedes and Euclid are recast as recipes for measurers and surveyors.
grc.herodianus.συμπόσιον: Συμπόσιον ('Symposium') is a very short compilation of etymological and lexicographical notes, of uncertain date and attributed to the grammarian Herodian, preserved as excerpts repeatedly introduced with the formula 'Herodian in the Symposium'. Its entries derive words for food, drink, and the symposium setting — such as βολβός, κάραβος, τάριχος, οἶνος, and ψωμοί — from supposed roots, and it quotes Homer and cites poets like Lycophron and Philoxenus in support. The piece offers readers of intertexts a witness to ancient etymological speculation and to the learned citation practices of the Greek grammatical corpus. It is edited by Augustus Lentz in Grammatici Graeci 3.1 (Leipzig: Teubner, 1867).
grc.herodotus.histories: The Histories of Herodotus of Halicarnassus, transmitted in nine books, announces at its outset the aim of preserving the great deeds of Greeks and barbarians from oblivion and of inquiring into the cause of their wars, opening with the rival Persian, Phoenician, and Greek accounts of the abductions of Io, Europa, Medea, and Helen. The narrative then moves through the Lydian story of Candaules, Gyges, and Croesus and onward to the rise of Persia and the conflict with the Greek world, interweaving ethnography, geography, genealogy, and embedded anecdotes. For readers hunting intertexts, the work is a central reservoir of mythic aetiologies, foreign logoi, and moralizing exempla whose phrasing and episodes recur throughout later Greek and Latin literature.
grc.hesiod.theogony: The Theogony, an ancient Greek epic poem in hexameters attributed to Hesiod and of uncertain date, opens with the poet's encounter with the Muses on Mount Helicon and his commission to sing of the race of the immortal gods. Across its 1042 lines it offers a cosmogony and succession myth, tracing the birth of the cosmos and the generations of the gods from Chaos through the reigns of Ouranos and Kronos to the establishment of Zeus's order, with catalogues of divine offspring and a prominent episode on Prometheus. For readers of intertexts it serves as a foundational repository of Greek myth repeatedly drawn upon and reworked by later Greek and Latin authors, and its proem on the Muses' power to tell truths like falsehoods is itself among the most alluded-to passages of Greek poetry.
grc.hippocrates.aphorismi: The Aphorismi transmitted under the name of Hippocrates, edited here from Émile Littré's Oeuvres complètes d'Hippocrate (Paris, 1844), form a compact collection of terse prose maxims on medicine. Opening with the celebrated 'Ὁ βίος βραχὺς, ἡ δὲ τέχνη μακρὴ' ('Life is short, the art long'), the work proceeds in numbered sections through pronouncements on diet, prognosis, sleep, fever, the seasons, the ages of man, and the treatment of acute and chronic disease. As one of the most widely quoted works of ancient prose, it supplied proverbs and points of reference to Greek, Latin, medieval, and Renaissance writers, and remains a frequent locus of intertextual echo. The date of composition, and the extent of Hippocrates' personal authorship as opposed to that of the Hippocratic corpus generally, are uncertain.
grc.hippocrates.de_aere_aquis_et_locis: De Aere Aquis et Locis (On Airs, Waters, and Places), transmitted under the name of Hippocrates in the Hippocratic Corpus and of uncertain date, is a treatise on environmental medicine addressed to the travelling physician. It opens with instructions for assessing an unfamiliar city's exposure to winds, waters, and the sun's course, then classifies waters by their effects on health and correlates seasonal changes with epidemic disease. Its latter part compares Asia and Europe, arguing that climate and terrain shape the bodies and characters of their inhabitants, with ethnographic excursuses on the Macrocephali, the people of Phasis, the Sauromatae, and the nomad Scythians. Its naturalistic explanations of conditions customarily deemed divine, together with an Asia–Europe contrast closely akin to Herodotean ethnography, make the treatise a key intertext for the study of ancient environmental determinism.
grc.hippocrates.de_aere_aquis_locis: De Aere Aquis Locis (On Airs, Waters, Places) is a treatise in Ionic Greek prose, of uncertain date, transmitted in the Hippocratic Corpus under the name of Hippocrates and edited from Émile Littré's Oeuvres complètes d'Hippocrate (Paris, Baillière, 1840). It instructs the physician arriving in an unfamiliar city to study the seasons, winds, waters, soil, and way of life of its inhabitants, and argues that such environmental conditions determine both the endemic diseases of a place and the physique and character of its peoples. The work moves from these methodological chapters, through an account of the year's weather as a basis for prognosis, to extended ethnographic discussions contrasting Asia with Europe and describing peoples such as the Macrocephali, the Phasians, and the nomad Scythians alongside their Sauromatian neighbours. Its doctrine of environmental determinism and its ethnographic episodes were widely reused and reworked by later ancient writers on medicine, geography, and ethnography, making the treatise a frequent source of textual parallels.
grc.hippocrates.de_capitis_vulneribus: De Capitis Vulneribus (On Wounds of the Head) is a Greek surgical treatise of the Hippocratic Corpus, transmitted under Hippocrates' name and of uncertain date. It opens with an account of the varying courses of the cranial sutures, likened to the shapes of the letters T, H and X, and of the differing thickness of the skull, then classifies the ways in which the bone may be wounded, sets out signs for diagnosis and prognosis, and prescribes treatment by incision, scraping and trepanation. Its precise anatomical vocabulary and systematic clinical reasoning made it a touchstone for later Greek and Latin medical writers on surgery, and readers tracing intertexts will find its phrases and doctrines recurrently echoed in the ancient medical tradition.
grc.hippocrates.de_diaeta_in_morbis_acutis: Attributed to Hippocrates and of uncertain date, the De Diaeta in Morbis Acutis ('On Regimen in Acute Diseases') is a short Greek medical treatise transmitted in the Hippocratic Corpus and printed in Émile Littré's complete edition. It opens with a polemic against the so-called Cnidian 'Sentences', denying that diseases can be reduced to a fixed catalogue of names, and then sets out the dietary management of acute and often fatal fevers such as pleurisy, peripneumonia, phrenitis, lethargus and causus, with detailed rules on barley gruel and its thin decoction, the choice of wines, honeyed, vinegar and plain drinks, bathing, and the harm caused by sudden changes of regimen. Its insistence on individualised, as painless as possible treatment and on the physician's judgement over inherited school doctrine made it a touchstone in later medical debate, and it offers rich parallels for discussions of dietetics, diagnosis and rivalry between medical sects.
grc.hippocrates.de_flatibus: A short Greek medical treatise from the Hippocratic Corpus, attributed to Hippocrates and of uncertain date, edited in Littré's Oeuvres complètes d'Hippocrate. It opens with a general reflection on the art of medicine and then advances a programmatic thesis: that air or pneuma, filling all things, is the single cause of disease, and that fever, dropsy, apoplexy, hemorrhages, and even the so-called sacred disease arise from its movements and mixtures within the body. Readers tracing intertexts will find in it an early and influential statement of pneumatic physiology and of the doctrine that opposites cure opposites, phrasing that echoes through later medical and philosophical accounts of breath, causation, and the unity of disease.
grc.hippocrates.de_fracturis: De Fracturis (On Fractures) is a Greek surgical treatise attributed to Hippocrates and of uncertain date, printed in Émile Littré's Œuvres complètes d'Hippocrate (Paris: Baillière, 1841). Composed in the technical Ionic prose of the Hippocratic Corpus, it prescribes methods for the reduction, bandaging, and aftercare of fractures of the forearm, upper arm, thigh, and shin, together with dislocations at the elbow, knee, and ankle, discussing dressings, splints, traction apparatus, diet, and the complications of faulty treatment such as suppuration and exfoliation of bone. Its craft analogies, anatomical observations, and polemic against showy practitioners make it a fertile source of parallels for readers tracing Greek medical vocabulary and ideas about technique, nature, and the body across ancient literature.
grc.hippocrates.de_prisca_medicina: De Prisca Medicina (Περὶ ἀρχαίης ἰητρικῆς, On Ancient Medicine), a prose treatise of the Hippocratic Corpus transmitted under Hippocrates' name and of uncertain date, argues that the art of medicine rests on long-accumulated empirical discovery rather than on the philosophical 'hypotheses' of hot, cold, wet, and dry. Against thinkers who found medicine on such postulates, a position the author associates with Empedocles and those who 'write about nature', the treatise traces the art's origin in the discovery of dietetic preparation suited to human nature, and surveys the mixtures and powers of humours, the effects of strong and weak food, the dangers of ill-timed repletion and emptying, and the influence of bodily shapes upon disease. For readers of intertexts it is a locus classicus of the engagement between early Greek medicine and Presocratic philosophy, and its vocabulary of κρᾶσις, humours, and δίαιτα echoes throughout later medical and philosophical prose.
grc.hippocrates.jusjurandum: Known as the Hippocratic Oath, a short Greek prose pledge transmitted in the Hippocratic Corpus and attributed to Hippocrates, of uncertain date, in which a medical apprentice swears by Apollo, Asclepius, Hygieia, Panakeia, and all gods to honour his teacher, to share the art only with worthy sworn pupils, and to heal for the benefit of the sick according to his ability and judgement. The oath binds the swearer to abstain from lethal drugs and abortive pessaries, to enter patients' houses only for their good and free of wilful harm and sexual misconduct, and to keep silence about what is seen or heard in treatment that ought not be disclosed. Readers of intertexts value it as the most famous ethical document of the corpus, widely echoed, alluded to, and debated in later Greek medical writing and in the enduring tradition of medical oaths.
grc.homer.hymns: The Homeric Hymns, a collection of thirty-three anonymous Greek hymns in dactylic hexameter transmitted under Homer's name, open with an invocation to Dionysus recounting conflicting traditions of his birth and proceed through praises of Demeter, Apollo, Hermes, Aphrodite, and many lesser deities. Of uncertain date and uneven length, the poems range from brief salutations of a few lines to extended mythological narratives of divine birth, disguise, and apotheosis. Composed in the same formulaic epic diction as the Iliad and Odyssey, they furnish abundant verbal and thematic parallels for readers tracing intertexts across Greek hexameter poetry.
grc.homer.iliad: The Iliad is an ancient Greek epic in dactylic hexameter, transmitted under the name of Homer and of uncertain date, presented here in T. W. Allen's Oxford edition of 1931. Its twenty-four books recount the wrath of Achilles during the Trojan War, from the quarrel with Agamemnon over Briseis through the deaths of Patroclus and Hector to Priam's ransom of his son's body. As the foundational poem of the Greek literary tradition it preserves the canonical tellings of many heroic myths and the formulaic diction later poets constantly reworked, making it an essential point of comparison for readers tracing echoes in epic, lyric, tragedy, and prose.
grc.homer.odyssey: The Odyssey is a Greek epic poem in dactylic hexameter, traditionally attributed to Homer and of uncertain date, edited here in Thomas W. Allen's Oxford text. Across twenty-four books it recounts Odysseus's homecoming from Troy, the wanderings he narrates in flashback among the Phaeacians, his return in disguise to Ithaca, and his revenge on the suitors of Penelope, framed by the maturing journey of his son Telemachus. Its motifs of nostos, wandering, disguise, hospitality, and recognition became models for Greek and Latin poets alike, and its phrasing and scenes recur throughout ancient literature, making it an essential point of comparison in the search for textual parallels.
grc.isaeus.speeches: The Greek collection of court speeches attributed to the orator Isaeus, presented here in the English translation by Edward Seymour Forster (1962), consists of forensic orations delivered before a jury. Nearly all of them contest inheritances: wills allegedly drawn up in anger and later revoked, the priority of nephews and other kin in claiming an estate, and the true intentions of the deceased. The opening speech, on the estate of Cleonymus, argues from witnesses and circumstantial evidence that a testament should be set aside in favor of nearer relatives who were closest to him in life. For readers tracing intertexts, the corpus supplies characteristic legal vocabulary and argumentative formulas concerning wills, kinship, and witnessing that recur throughout Greek prose.
grc.isocrates.speeches: Collection of speeches in Ancient Greek by the orator Isocrates, given here in the three-volume Harvard University Press edition prepared by George Norlin with an English translation (1980), running to roughly two thousand lines divided among twenty-one items. The opening speech is a protreptic address to the young Demonicus, urging him to inherit and imitate the virtue of his father Hipponicus and setting out maxims on piety, self-control, friendship, study, and the conduct of life. Composed in highly wrought periodic prose and dense with gnomic formulations, the speeches were widely echoed by later Greek and Roman writers and accordingly offer rich material for readers in search of verbal and thematic parallels.
grc.libanius.declamations_13-30: A Greek prose work by the rhetor Libanius, edited from the Teubner text of Richard Foerster (1913), comprising Declamations 13-30, a sequence of fictional speeches composed as school exercises in rhetorical imitation rather than for actual forensic delivery. The set opens with a long declamation spoken in the persona of a Corinthian addressing the Greeks on the outbreak of the Peloponnesian War, prosecuting Athens for the impious siege and starvation of Potidaea and dwelling at length on religious pollution, Hellenic solidarity, and the violence of Athenian imperialism. Such declamations deliberately recycle the situations, arguments, and phrasing of classical historiography and oratory, so the collection offers fertile ground for readers tracing verbal and thematic parallels with Thucydidean material and later rhetorical tradition. The work runs to 913 lines in a single book file.
grc.libanius.declamations_31-51: A collection of Greek prose declamations by Libanius, comprising speeches 31 to 51 as printed in Richard Foerster's Teubner edition of 1913, preserved in a single book file of roughly 1,259 lines. The speeches are rhetorical exercises in which imagined speakers plead invented cases before councils, courts, or assemblies, as in the opening oration where a man forced to surrender a hoard of five hundred drachmas under the city's treasury law begs the council to grant him hemlock. Stock school themes of wealth, misfortune, confiscation, and the law's letter versus its intent recur throughout, together with the exemplary figures, commonplaces, and phraseology that declamation shared with the earlier orators and poets. Readers hunting textual parallels will find the corpus a dense repository of formulaic argument and literary echo characteristic of ancient rhetorical education.
grc.libanius.orations_26-50: Orations 26–50 of Libanius, the fourth-century Greek sophist and teacher of rhetoric at Antioch, are presented here from Richard Foerster's Teubner edition of 1913 and comprise a set of Atticizing prose speeches addressed mainly to imperial governors and officials. The opening oration counsels a governor of Antioch, addressed as Icarion, to rule justly in contrast with his predecessor Proclus, defending the ordinary citizens of the city against a corrupt faction, and the surrounding speeches continue in the same vein of moral and political exhortation, touching on baths, theatres, taxation, prisoners, and the duties of magistrates. The collection exemplifies the deliberative and advisory oratory of late antique Greek paideia, saturated with the diction of classical Attic oratory and of Plato. A reader hunting textual parallels will find Libanius a prolific source, since his phrasing constantly reworks Demosthenic and Platonic models and in turn echoes through the rhetorical prose of later antiquity and Byzantium.
grc.lucian.alexander: Alexander (or Alexander the False Prophet) is a prose satire by Lucian of Samosata, cast as a letter of advice to his friend Celsus. It recounts the career of Alexander of Abonoteichus, a charlatan who founded an oracular cult of the snake god Glycon at Abonoteichus in Paphlagonia, exposing the incubated egg, the marionette serpent head, the sealed inquiries, and the doctored oracles by which he deceived the gullible, amassed a fortune, and pursued his vendetta against Christians and Epicureans. Readers of intertexts will find the work richly laced with parodic oracles in epic hexameters and allusions to Thucydides, Pythagoras, Plato, and the legendary serpentine birth of Alexander the Great.
grc.lucian.contemplantes: A short comic dialogue by Lucian of Samosata, of uncertain date, printed from Jacobitz's 1896 Teubner edition. Charon abandons his ferry to find out what human life is worth, and Hermes guides him to a lookout raised by piling Pelion on Ossa in imitation of Homer's Aloeidae, from which the pair survey cities and rulers, the threads the Fates spin for each person, tomb cults and funerary offerings, and the ruin of once-great cities such as Nineveh, Babylon, and Troy. Saturated with Homeric quotation and reworking historical episodes from the tradition of Herodotus, above all the exchange of Solon and Croesus on happiness, the dialogue's memento mori satire offers readers of intertexts a compact repertory of epic and historical allusion.
grc.lucian.dearum_iudicium: Dearum Iudicium, 'The Judgement of the Goddesses', is a short comic prose dialogue by Lucian of Samosata, of uncertain date. Hermes conducts Hera, Athena, and Aphrodite to Mount Ida, where the herdsman Paris is set to judge their beauty: the goddesses disrobe, exchange barbs, and press their bribes, until Aphrodite's promise of Helen wins from Paris the golden apple. For readers hunting textual parallels, the dialogue offers a pointed satirical reworking of the epic judgement of Paris, the myth that precipitates the Trojan War, parodying epic diction and deflating Olympian dignity while foreshadowing Helen's abduction. Its Ionic Greek and theatrical staging make it a compact witness to the afterlife of the Paris myth in Lucianic prose.
grc.lucian.dialogi_meretricii: A set of brief dialogues in Greek by Lucian of Samosata, of uncertain date, printed here from Karl Jacobitz's Teubner edition of the Opera. The scenes unfold among the hetaerae of Athens, their mothers, keepers, and lovers, and turn on jealous rivals, love-charms, mercenary affections, and schemes of marriage in a comic-satirical vein descended from New Comedy and the mime. For readers hunting intertexts, the dialogues weave dense echoes of comic and erotic tradition with lively colloquial Attic diction that yields parallels hard to find elsewhere.
grc.lucian.icaromenippus: A comic dialogue by Lucian of Samosata, the Icaromenippus presents Menippus the Cynic telling a friend how, despairing of the contradictory doctrines of the philosophers, he fitted himself with the wings of an eagle and a vulture and flew to the moon and thence to heaven. From the moon he surveys the littleness of human affairs, encounters the transformed Empedocles, and carries the Moon's grievance against natural philosophers to Zeus; the narrative moves through Zeus's assembly of the gods, an overhearing of the day's prayers and oaths, and a divine banquet, closing with the gods' resolve to destroy the philosophers and Menippus's return to announce the verdict in the Stoa Poecile. Lucian weaves quotation and parody of Homer, Attic tragedy, and comedy into a satire of Stoic, Epicurean, and Academic cosmology, and the dialogue's aerial perspective on human pretension and its dense web of classical allusion make it a rewarding stop for readers tracing Menippean satire and its echoes.
grc.lucian.patriae_encomium: A brief Greek prose encomium on the fatherland (Patriae Encomium), preserved under the name of Lucian of Samosata and printed in Jacobitz's third Teubner volume. The speaker argues that nothing is sweeter or more venerable than the patria, dearer even than a father and cherished by the gods for their own birthplaces, and that learning, wealth, fame, courage, and the longing of exiles and of the aged for burial in native soil all bear witness to it. The piece serves as a compact repertory of patriotic topoi from Greek rhetorical encomium, useful for tracing echoes and parallels in declamations, progymnasmata, and political oratory.
grc.lucian.podagra: A brief dramatic satire in Greek by Lucian of Samosata, the Podagra personifies gout as a monstrous daughter of Cocytus, born of the Fury Megaera and nursed with the milk of Alecto, whose torments are set above the mythological punishments of Tantalus, Ixion, and Sisyphus. The opening speech is a sustained tragic-style invocation and lament, as the afflicted speaker leans on his staff and calls up catalogues of springtime cult, from the rites of Cybele and Attis at Dindymon to the Corybantes and the Paean. For readers hunting parallels, the piece repurposes tragic diction, lyric catalogues, and ritual-hymn motifs for a comic anatomy of disease and its sufferers.
grc.lucian.rhetorum_praeceptor: Lucian of Samosata's Rhetorum Praeceptor is a satirical dialogue in which a self-confessed charlatan promises a young man instant success as an orator, prescribing shamelessness, swagger, pretentious Atticisms, and a stock repertoire of patriotic commonplaces in place of long laborious training. The speaker contrasts two allegorical roads to Rhetoric — a steep track following the traces of Demosthenes and Plato, and an easy flowered path of his own devising — mocks the imitation of the ancients enjoined by traditional teachers, and ends with a confession of his own disreputable career, from fortune-hunting marriage to fraudulent advocacy in the courts. Readers of intertexts will find dense parody of Hesiod's two roads, of Plato's winged chariot, and of the stock Persian-Wars material (Athos, the Hellespont, Xerxes, Leonidas), together with a pointed send-up of sophistic declamation and its diction.
grc.lucian.toxaris_vel_amicitia: A Greek dialogue by Lucian of Samosata, of uncertain date, carrying the alternative title On Friendship, in which Mnesippus the Greek and Toxaris the Scythian contend over which nation has produced the truer friends. The exchange opens with a debate on the Scythians' cult of Orestes and Pylades, then settles into an agreed contest in which each speaker recounts five stories of friendship, Mnesippus drawing on Greek figures such as Agathocles, Euthydicus, Eudamidas, Zenothemis and Demetrius of Sunium, Toxaris answering with Scythian tales sealed by blood-oath. Readers hunting intertexts will find the work interlaced with the Orestes–Pylades legend, with heroic Greek friendships such as that of Achilles and Patroclus, and with ethnographic lore about Scythian customs.
grc.lucian.verae_historiae: Lucian of Samosata's Verae Historiae (True Stories), a Greek prose satire printed here from Karl Jacobitz's 1896 Teubner edition, opens with a preface in which the narrator owns to writing plausible falsehoods about things he never saw or suffered, each marvel being aimed in mockery at some earlier poet, historian, or philosopher; Ctesias, Iambulus, and Homer's Odysseus are named outright. The narrative then recounts a fantastic voyage beyond the Pillars of Heracles, taking in a river of wine and vine-women on an Atlantic isle, a whirlwind flight to the Moon and its war against the inhabitants of the Sun, and life inside a vast whale, with a visit to Cloudcuckooland that explicitly recalls Aristophanes. Because the work parodies and even names its models, it serves as a rich meeting point for readers tracing the intertexts of travellers' tales, paradoxography, utopian fiction, and Homeric epic.
grc.lycurgus.against_leocrates: An Attic forensic oration in which the prosecutor Lycurgus brings an eisangelia against Leocrates, charging that he deserted Athens by sea immediately after the battle of Chaeronea, settled first in Rhodes and then for more than five years in Megara, exported his property and the cult objects of his ancestral hearth, and broadcast false news of the city's capture. The file transmits an ancient hypothesis, which analyses the stasis of the case, followed by the speech itself, proceeding through narrative, witness testimony, documents including a decree of Hypereides, and a challenge to torture the defendant's slaves, all framed by argument on the lawcourts as guardians of the laws, the temples, and the democracy. For readers tracing parallels, the speech offers dense Attic legal and civic diction, patriotic exempla on piety toward gods, parents, and fatherland, and set pieces on the education of the young through punishment and reward, themes that recur across Greek oratory.
grc.novum_testamentum.actus_apostolorum: The Actus Apostolorum, the Acts of the Apostles, is a book of the Greek New Testament, presented here in the SBL Greek New Testament edited by M. W. Holmes (2010). Composed in Imperial-era Koine prose by an author who does not name himself, and opening with an address to one Theophilus, it recounts the ascension of Jesus, the outpouring of the Holy Spirit at Pentecost, and the spread of the earliest Christian communities from Jerusalem outward, with the missionary career of Paul as its later centerpiece. Its blend of scriptural diction, formal speeches, and vivid travel narrative, including a famous shipwreck episode, made it a fertile source of phrases and scenes echoed throughout later Greek, Latin, and vernacular literature.
grc.novum_testamentum.ad_colossenses: The Epistle to the Colossians is a Christian letter in Greek prose of the Imperial era, attributed in its salutation to Paul the apostle, who writes with Timothy to the believers in Colossae; it appears here in the SBL Greek New Testament of Holmes (2010). Running to some ninety-five lines, it moves from thanksgiving and intercession to a hymnic celebration of Christ as the image of the invisible God, firstborn of creation and head of the church, before warning against seductive philosophy and the elemental powers of the world and giving ethical instruction for the community. Its dense and sometimes idiosyncratic Greek—plērōma, stoicheia tou kosmou, apolytrōsis—adapts the idiom of Hellenistic religion and philosophy, making the letter a productive site for readers tracing parallels among early Christian, Jewish, and Greco-Roman writing.
grc.novum_testamentum.ad_corinthios_i: The First Epistle to the Corinthians, a Greek Christian letter of the Imperial period that opens in the names of Paul, called to be an apostle, and Sosthenes and addresses the church of God at Corinth, presented here in the SBL Greek New Testament edited by M. W. Holmes (2010). The letter rebukes factionalism centred on Paul, Apollos, and Cephas, sets the wisdom of the crucified Christ against human rhetoric, and goes on to treat moral discipline, the Lord's Supper, spiritual gifts, resurrection, and the hymn to love. Its dense weave of Septuagintal quotation and allusion has made it a touchstone for tracing biblical and later Christian intertexts, and its Koine prose offers abundant parallels for readers of post-classical Greek.
grc.novum_testamentum.ad_corinthios_ii: Ad Corinthios II (2 Corinthians) is a Greek prose epistle of the Imperial era, presented in its opening verses as sent by Paul the Apostle, together with Timothy, to the church of God in Corinth and to the saints throughout Achaia. Combining thanksgiving, self-defense of Paul's travel plans and conduct, discipline of an offender, and sustained reflection on affliction and divine consolation, it ranks among the most personal and rhetorically charged of the canonical New Testament letters, and its later chapters press Paul's claims to apostolic authority against rival preachers while meditating on the veiled glory of the new covenant and the ministry of reconciliation. Because its Koine diction and scriptural idiom have saturated subsequent Greek Christian writing, the letter offers readers of intertexts a dense matrix of verbal and thematic echoes spanning the later literary tradition.
grc.novum_testamentum.ad_ephesios: The Epistle to the Ephesians is a Greek prose letter of the New Testament, attributed in its opening to the apostle Paul and addressed to 'the saints who are in Ephesus'; it is presented here in the SBL Greek New Testament edited by M. W. Holmes (2010). A product of the Imperial era, it opens with a great blessing over God's plan 'to sum up all things in Christ' and moves through teaching on salvation by grace, the reconciliation of Jews and Gentiles, and the church as the body of Christ, toward paraenesis on Christian conduct and spiritual warfare. Its elevated, liturgical diction and recurrent formulae — redemption, mystery, fullness, the heavenly places — echo throughout patristic and later Christian writing, making the letter a fertile source of verbal parallels for readers of intertexts.
grc.novum_testamentum.ad_hebraeos: Ad Hebraeos, the Epistle to the Hebrews, is a Greek prose epistle of the Imperial era handed down within the New Testament and printed here in the SBL Greek New Testament (2010). Its author names himself nowhere and the work lacks a conventional epistolary salutation, so it has come down without attribution. The epistle argues that the Son surpasses angels and Moses and acts as merciful high priest, building its case from a dense catena of Septuagintal quotations and allusions, psalms above all. For readers hunting textual parallels, it stands among the richest early Christian examples of Greek Jewish scripture reworked into sustained rhetorical prose.
grc.novum_testamentum.ad_philemonem: A brief Greek letter of the Imperial era, preserved in the New Testament and ascribed in its opening to Paul the apostle, who writes as a prisoner of Christ Jesus with Timothy as co-sender. Addressed to Philemon, Apphia, Archippus, and the assembly at their house, it appeals for the gracious reception of Onesimus, whom Paul calls his child begotten in bonds and no longer a slave but a beloved brother, promising to repay any wrong or debt owed to Philemon. At twenty-five lines it stands among the shortest documents of the New Testament, yet its dense vocabulary of bondage, partnership, brotherhood, and reconciliation has furnished later writers with a stock of phrases, making it a fertile point of departure for readers tracing intertextual echoes.
grc.novum_testamentum.ad_romanos: The Epistle to the Romans is a Greek prose letter of the Imperial era, part of the New Testament and printed here from the SBL Greek New Testament edited by M. W. Holmes (2010); its opening verses identify Paul, a called apostle, as the writer addressing the saints in Rome. Across 430 lines it builds a sustained argument on the gospel, the righteousness of God received through faith by Jew and Greek alike, divine judgment upon sin and unrighteousness, and the life of the Spirit, moving from salutation and thanksgiving into doctrinal argument, catalogues of vice, and ethical exhortation. For readers of intertexts the letter is a central hub: it cites and reworks the Jewish scriptures in Greek — as when it introduces 'the righteous shall live by faith' with an explicit formula of quotation — and its phrases and figures resound throughout later Christian Greek writing and the European literature shaped by it.
grc.novum_testamentum.ad_timotheum_i: The first of the two letters to Timothy in the Greek New Testament, a Koine prose epistle of the Imperial era that opens in the voice of Paul the apostle instructing his associate Timothy, who has been urged to remain in Ephesus; the work is edited in The Greek New Testament: SBL Edition (2010). Across its 113 lines it moves from warnings against heterodox teaching and endless genealogies, through thanksgiving for mercy shown to a persecutor turned apostle, to directions for prayer and for the conduct of men and women in the assembly and qualifications for bishops and deacons. Hymn-like christological sayings, 'faithful sayings' such as πιστὸς ὁ λόγος, and catalogues of vices give the letter a compositional texture that invites comparison with the other Pauline epistles and with Septuagintal diction. For readers of intertexts it functions as a hub, since its formulas and phrasing are echoed repeatedly in later Christian and Western literature and supply parallels across the biblical corpus.
grc.novum_testamentum.apocalypsis: The Apocalypsis (Revelation), the concluding book of the New Testament, is an early Christian apocalypse in Greek prose from the Imperial period, attributed within the work to a seer named John, who presents himself as receiving visions on Patmos and writing to seven churches in Asia. It opens with an epistolary frame and dictated letters to those seven congregations, then unfolds a series of throne visions, sealed scrolls, trumpets, plagues, and beasts, culminating in the fall of Babylon, the last judgment, and a new heaven and new earth. Its language is densely interwoven with echoes of the Septuagint, above all Daniel, Ezekiel, Isaiah, and Exodus, making it a central witness for readers tracing allusion and reworked scriptural imagery in early Christian and Second Temple literature.
grc.novum_testamentum.iacobi: The Epistle of James, a New Testament letter of uncertain date within the Imperial era, presents itself as written by James, 'a servant of God and of the Lord Jesus Christ', to 'the twelve tribes in the dispersion'. Its 108 verses of terse, wisdom-style Greek paraenesis treat endurance under trial, the instability of the double-minded, hearing versus doing the word, favoritism toward the rich, control of the tongue, the relation of faith and works, and the efficacy of prayer. For readers of intertexts the letter is a dense node of overlap, repeatedly echoing the Sermon on the Mount, drawing on Leviticus 19:18 and Septuagintal wisdom idiom, and invoking Abraham, Rahab, Job, and Elijah as exemplars.
grc.novum_testamentum.ioannes: The Gospel of John, a prose book of the Novum Testamentum written in Imperial-era Greek, opens with the Prologue hymning the Logos who was with God in the beginning, became flesh, and brought grace and truth in place of the law given through Moses. The narrative then turns to the testimony and baptism of John the Baptist, who hails Jesus as the Lamb of God and the chosen one of God, and to the calling of the first disciples at the Jordan. Quoting Isaiah ('a voice crying in the wilderness') and retelling the ministry in spare, repetitive diction, the work constantly weaves scriptural allusion into its Greek. Its distinctive vocabulary of Logos, light and darkness, witness, and the only-begotten Son recurs throughout later Greek Christian writing and invites comparison with earlier Jewish, Stoic, and Platonic usage of the same terms.
grc.novum_testamentum.ioannis_ii: The Second Letter of John (Ioannis II) is a thirteen-verse Greek composition of the New Testament, preserved in the SBL Greek New Testament edited by M. W. Holmes (2010), written in prose during the Imperial era by an author who names himself only 'the Elder,' leaving his identity otherwise unrecorded. Addressed to 'the elect lady and her children,' the letter urges continued walking in love and in the commandments 'from the beginning' while warning against deceivers who deny that Jesus Christ has come in the flesh, whom it labels the antichrist, and it instructs the community to withhold hospitality and even greeting from those who do not bring the doctrine of Christ. For readers of intertexts, its dense, distinctive Johannine vocabulary—truth, love, commandment, walking, antichrist, remaining in the teaching—overlaps closely with the First Letter of John and the Gospel of John, making it a compact locus for tracing the diffusion of Johannine language and motifs in early Christian writing.
grc.novum_testamentum.ioannis_iii: The Third Letter of John (Ioannis III), one of the three Johannine epistles of the New Testament, is a brief personal note in Koine prose whose sender identifies himself only as 'the Elder' (ὁ πρεσβύτερος). Addressed to a certain Gaius, it praises his hospitality to itinerant Christian missionaries, condemns the domineering conduct of Diotrephes, commends Demetrius, and closes with a promise of a visit 'mouth to mouth' and greetings among 'the friends'. Composed in Greek during the Imperial period, it is presented here from The Greek New Testament: SBL Edition (Holmes, 2010). For readers of intertexts, its Hellenistic epistolary formulae — the opening health wish, the reference to pen and ink, and the farewell greetings — align closely with conventions of contemporary Greek correspondence, while its vocabulary overlaps tellingly with the Fourth Gospel and the other Johannine letters.
grc.novum_testamentum.iudae: The Epistle of Jude, a Greek prose letter of the Imperial era in the New Testament, is attributed in its opening to Judas (Jude), servant of Jesus Christ and brother of James. Addressed to a community beloved in God the Father, it exhorts its readers to contend for the faith against intruders who pervert grace into licentiousness, marshalling a chain of exemplary figures: the unbelieving generation saved from Egypt, the angels who abandoned their station, Sodom and Gomorrah, Cain, Balaam, Korah, the archangel Michael disputing over the body of Moses, and the prophecy of Enoch, seventh from Adam. Though only twenty-five lines long, it is among the most allusion-saturated writings of the biblical corpus, echoing 2 Peter and drawing heavily on Jewish apocalyptic and pseudepigraphic tradition. Readers hunting textual parallels prize it for these dense borrowings from extra-biblical Jewish literature, among the clearest instances of non-canonical tradition embedded in the New Testament.
grc.novum_testamentum.marcus: The Gospel of Mark (Marcus), the second and shortest of the four canonical gospels of the New Testament, is a biblical narrative in Koine Greek prose of the Roman Imperial era, attributed to the name Mark. Opening with the preaching of John the Baptist, the citation of Isaiah, and the baptism of Jesus, it proceeds through a swift account of Jesus' Galilean ministry of teaching, healing and exorcism, told in a terse, paratactic style punctuated by the recurring adverb εὐθύς. Its 673 lines provide the narrative framework that Matthew and Luke follow and rework, making the work a central locus for synoptic parallels and for Septuagintal diction and scriptural quotation in early Christian Greek.
grc.novum_testamentum.matthaeus: The Gospel according to Matthew, transmitted in Greek within the Novum Testamentum, is a prose biblical narrative of the Roman imperial period and one of the four canonical gospels. It opens with Jesus' genealogy from Abraham through David, then narrates the virgin birth, the visit of the Magi, and the flight into Egypt, before proceeding through Jesus' teaching, miracles, passion, and resurrection across just over a thousand lines. A hallmark is the fulfillment formula, by which events of Jesus' life are repeatedly tied to words of the prophets, making the work a dense lattice of Old Testament citation in Koine prose. For readers tracing intertexts, Matthew is a central node: its phrasing, from 'the kingdom of heaven' to 'it is written', echoes through nearly all subsequent Christian Greek literature.
grc.novum_testamentum.petri_i: The First Epistle of Peter, a Christian letter in Koine Greek attributed to the apostle Peter and preserved in the New Testament, addresses the 'elect sojourners of the Diaspora' in Pontus, Galatia, Cappadocia, Asia, and Bithynia. Written in prose during the Imperial era and printed here in the SBL Greek New Testament, its 105 verses exhort believers to holiness, endurance under suffering, and submission to earthly authority, grounding their hope in Christ's resurrection and future revelation. The epistle draws densely on the Septuagint — the suffering servant of Isaiah, the cornerstone rejected by builders, the grass that withers — making it a central witness to early Christian appropriation of Jewish scripture and a rich source of phrases echoed by later Christian writers.
grc.oppian.halieutica: Oppian's Halieutica is a Greek didactic poem in five books of hexameter verse, addressed to an emperor styled Antoninus and promising an account of the sea's manifold tribes of fish. Its roughly 3,500 lines describe the kinds of fish and their haunts, their breeding, feeding, loves, and enmities, and the cunning devices, from hooks and nets to drugs, by which fishers take them, contrasting the perils of the angler adrift on open water with the safer sport of hunter and fowler. Composed in classicising epic diction, it preserves a wealth of ancient lore about marine life and fishing technique, and readers of intertexts will find in it a storehouse of catalogue formulas, similes, and phrasing that later Greek poets and prose writers echo.
grc.oppian_of_apamea.cynegetica: The Cynegetica, a Greek didactic poem on hunting in four books of hexameters, is the work of Oppian of Apamea. Its proem addresses an emperor Antoninus, born of Julia Domna and Septimius Severus, placing the poem in the Severan age. Framed as a dialogue between the poet and Artemis, it instructs the reader in the breeds and training of dogs and horses, the tactics of the chase, and the mating, birth, and rearing of wild beasts. For readers of intertexts it offers dense animal lore in Homeric diction with mythological digression, standing as the poetic counterpart to ancient didactic verse on fishing.
grc.pausanias.description_of_greece: Pausanias' Description of Greece is a Greek prose periegesis in ten books composed under the Roman empire, written by an author who places himself in the age of Hadrian and tours the regions of Greece region by region, beginning with Attica, the Piraeus and Athens. It records harbours, roads, tombs, sanctuaries, statues and paintings, pausing constantly for myths, king-lists, cult aetiologies and historical digressions ranging from Themistocles and the Persian wars to the Gallic attack on Delphi and the dynasties of the Ptolemies and Attalids. Homer, Hesiod, Pindar and Herodotus are cited or paraphrased among many authorities, and variant local traditions are reported throughout, making the work a central quarry for readers tracing allusions to Greek places, monuments and legends in other literature.
grc.philo_judaeus.de_mutatione_nominum: De Mutatione Nominum is a Greek allegorical treatise by the Hellenistic-Jewish exegete Philo Judaeus, expounding Genesis 17:1 and the divine appearances to Abraham.
