Translated by anonymous Jewish translators of the Hellenistic period, the book combines oracles of judgment and consolation against Judah, its kings, and the nations with prose accounts of the prophet's conflicts with priests, rulers, and rival seers. The Greek Jeremiah is considerably shorter and differently arranged than the Hebrew text familiar from later versions, so verbal parallels in Greek Jewish and Christian literature follow the Septuagint's distinctive Koine wording rather than that of the Hebrew. The text here derives from Henry Barclay Swete's Cambridge edition of 1905.
grc.septuaginta.joel: The Greek Joel, preserved in Swete's Cambridge Septuagint as the second book of the Twelve Prophets, renders into Hellenistic Greek a Hebrew prophecy attributed to Joel son of Bathuel and of uncertain date. In roughly seventy lines the book moves from a devastating locust plague, lamented in oracles and calls to fasting and weeping, to the promise that God's spirit will be poured out on all flesh and that the nations will be judged on the great day of the Lord. Its apocalyptic imagery — the trumpet alarm in Zion, a darkened sun and blood-red moon, the approach of an irresistible army — was widely echoed in later Jewish and Christian apocalyptic writing, most famously in the Pentecost speech of Acts, and the Septuagint wording supplies the Greek forms in which those echoes circulated.
grc.septuaginta.jonas: The Book of Jonah in its Greek Septuagint form, one of the Twelve Prophets in the volume edited by Henry Barclay Swete for Cambridge in 1905; the underlying Hebrew work is of uncertain authorship and date, while the Greek translation belongs to the Hellenistic period and circulated among Greek-speaking Jews. Its prose narrative follows the prophet's flight from a divine command to preach against Nineveh, the storm that overtakes his ship, his three days in the belly of a great fish, his psalm of thanksgiving from the fish's belly, the fasting and repentance of the Ninevites, and finally his angry dispute with God over mercy toward the enemy city. The book stands apart from the oracular material around it as continuous narrative, and its Greek wording diverges at points from the Hebrew it renders, which makes it useful for studying translation technique and variant textual traditions. Readers tracing intertexts will find here the source of the 'sign of Jonah' motif reused in early Christian literature, a sea-storm and lot-casting episode comparable to Greek epic and novel narratives, and a psalm that reworks language from other biblical songs.
grc.septuaginta.josue: The Book of Joshua (Josue) in its Greek version, part of the Septuagint rendering of the Hebrew Scriptures undertaken in the Hellenistic period by translators whose individual identities are unknown, printed here from Swete's Cambridge edition of 1901–1905. The narrative follows Joshua son of Nun from the death of Moses through the crossing of the Jordan, the spies and Rahab at Jericho, the fall of that city, the conquest of Canaan, and the apportionment of the land among the tribes, in plain biblical prose of 661 lines. Readers hunting intertexts will find in it a core reservoir of scriptural diction and motifs — the Jordan crossing, the scarlet cord, the fall of Jericho, the ἴσχυε καὶ ἀνδρίζου charge — that echo constantly through later Greek Jewish, patristic, and Christian writing, where the Greek form Ἰησοῦς for Joshua also underlies recurring typological play.
grc.septuaginta.judith: The Greek Judith of the Septuagint is a Hellenistic Jewish narrative in biblical prose, transmitted anonymously and printed here from Swete's edition of the Old Testament in Greek (Cambridge, 1896). The story opens with Nebuchadnezzar, figured as king of the Assyrians in Nineveh, defeating Arphaxad and despatching his general Holofernes to punish the western nations that refused submission; it proceeds through the siege of Bethulia to the deliverance accomplished by the widow Judith, who enters the enemy camp and kills Holofernes. For readers of intertexts the book offers distinctive Septuagintal Greek, dense scriptural allusion, and the Judith-Holofernes story that supplied a standing subject for later drama, poetry, and art.
grc.septuaginta.kritai: The Kritai is the Book of Judges in its Greek Septuagint form, a Hellenistic prose rendering of the Hebrew Bible presented here in Swete's Cambridge edition of 1901–1905. Continuing the story of Israel after the death of Joshua, the book recounts the tribes' wars with the Canaanites and their repeated cycles of apostasy, oppression, and deliverance by leaders such as Othniel, Deborah, Gideon, Jephthah, and Samson. Its Greek wording diverges at many points from the Hebrew, and the Septuagintal diction of Judges underlies countless echoes in later Greek, Latin, and Christian writing, making the work a productive hunting ground for intertextual parallels.
grc.septuaginta.machabaeorum_b: The Second Book of Maccabees (Machabaeorum B), transmitted in Greek within the Septuagint and printed here in Swete's Cambridge edition of 1901–1905, is a prose work of Hellenistic Jewish biblical literature, anonymous and of uncertain date. It opens with two festal letters from the Jews of Jerusalem to their brethren in Egypt, and proceeds to an account of the persecution under Antiochus, the Maccabean revolt, the martyrdom of the faithful, and the purification and rededication of the Temple, including the legend of the sacred fire preserved by Nehemiah. Its blend of Septuagintal idiom with the vocabulary of Greek historiography, together with its early treatments of martyrdom and resurrection, makes it a fertile source of parallels for readers tracing Jewish and Christian intertexts.
grc.septuaginta.machabaeorum_d: A treatise in Greek prose arguing that pious reason holds absolute sovereignty over the passions, preserved as the Fourth Book of Maccabees in appendices to editions of the Septuagint, here printed from Swete's Cambridge edition of 1901-1905. Anonymous and of uncertain date, it defines reason, passion, and the cardinal virtues before illustrating its thesis through the martyrdoms of Eleazar, the seven brothers, and their mother, who endured torture and death to purge their nation from tyranny. Despite its title it is not a historical narrative but a philosophical-rhetorical encomium that reworks the Maccabean martyrology, and its fusion of Stoic psychology and terminology with the Jewish law makes it a key witness for readers tracing Hellenistic philosophical vocabulary in biblical and para-biblical tradition.
grc.septuaginta.machabaeorum_i: The First Book of the Maccabees, transmitted in Greek within the Septuagint and printed here from Swete's Cambridge edition of 1905, is an anonymous Hellenistic prose work of biblical historiography. Opening with the conquests and death of Alexander the Great, it recounts the persecution of the Jews under Antiochus Epiphanes, the desecration of the temple, and the revolt led by Mattathias and his son Judas Maccabaeus. Its Septuagintal prose, imperial decrees, speeches, and narratives of martyrdom and armed resistance offer abundant parallels for readers tracing connections between biblical, Jewish, and classical historiographical traditions.
grc.septuaginta.nahum: Nahum in the Septuagint, the Greek version of the Hebrew scriptures produced in the Hellenistic period, stands here in Henry Barclay Swete's Cambridge edition of 1905. A short prophetic book of forty-eight lines, it opens as the vision of Nahum the Elkeshite and delivers oracles of divine zeal and vengeance against Nineveh, a lurid account of the city's sack and plunder, and a closing judgement upon its partner in iniquity, while Judah is bidden to keep its feasts in peace. Because the Greek rendering diverges at many points from the Hebrew and its phrasing was repeatedly echoed by later Jewish and Christian writers in Greek, the book offers fertile ground for readers tracing the migration of prophetic diction across texts.
grc.septuaginta.odae: The Odae, or Odes, form a collection of biblical canticles transmitted as an appendix in manuscripts of the Septuagint and printed as such in Swete's Cambridge edition of the Greek Old Testament (1905). The songs are prose canticles in Septuagintal Greek attributed to biblical figures, opening with the Song of Moses at the Red Sea ('Let us sing to the Lord, for gloriously has he been glorified') and continuing with the song of Deuteronomy 32 and related pieces; the constituent songs belong to the Hellenistic-era Greek Bible, though the compilation itself is of uncertain date. Because these canticles circulated liturgically and supplied a shared stock of phrasing for Greek-speaking readers, their language echoes throughout later hymnody, prayer, and poetry, making the collection a rich source of parallels for hunters of intertexts.
grc.septuaginta.proverbia: The Paroimiai is the Greek Proverbs of the Septuagint, the Hellenistic Jewish translation of the Hebrew scriptures, printed here from Swete's Cambridge edition of 1896. Its heading presents the work as the proverbs of Solomon son of David who reigned in Israel, and the book comprises paternal instruction, collections of moral maxims, and longer speeches of personified Wisdom, opening with the declaration that the fear of God is the beginning of wisdom. For readers of intertexts it offers a central repository of Greek biblical diction and wisdom themes, whose formulas—Wisdom crying aloud in the streets, the wayward son, the two paths—are echoed throughout later Jewish and Christian Greek writing.
grc.septuaginta.psalmi: The Psalms (Psalmi) appear here in the Hellenistic Greek rendering of the Septuagint, as printed in Henry Barclay Swete's Cambridge edition of 1896. The book gathers the psalms of praise, lament, penitence, and royal acclamation that carry Davidic superscriptions in their Greek titles, along with liturgical rubrics such as the διάψαλμα, and opens with the beatitude on the man who meditates on the law day and night. Since its Septuagintal wording frequently departs from the Hebrew and became the scriptural diction most readily quoted and echoed by later Greek prose and poetry, the Psalter is a primary hunting ground for verbal parallels.
grc.septuaginta.ruth: The Book of Ruth in the Septuagint is a Hellenistic Greek prose rendering of the Hebrew tale set in the days when the judges ruled, the work of anonymous translators of uncertain exact date. It recounts how Naomi, bereft of husband and sons in Moab, returns to Bethlehem with her devoted daughter-in-law Ruth, who gleans in the field of the kinsman Boaz and becomes his wife, grandmother of Obed and ancestress of David. The version appears in Henry Barclay Swete's Cambridge edition of the Old Testament in Greek and follows the Hebrew closely, serving as the form of Ruth current among Greek-speaking Jews and Christians. Readers of intertexts will find here the loyalty oath of Ruth, the gleaning and levirate-marriage motifs, and the characteristic translation diction of the Greek Bible that echoes through later Jewish and Christian writing.
grc.septuaginta.susanna_theodotionis: The Susanna printed here in the Greek version attributed to Theodotion, as edited by Henry Barclay Swete in the Cambridge Septuaginta, recounts how the virtuous Susanna, wife of Joakim in Babylon, is falsely accused of adultery by two elders and vindicated by the young Daniel's shrewd cross-examination of their testimony. The tale, composed in Hellenistic prose and transmitted among the Greek additions to Daniel, exists in more than one Greek form, and the Theodotionic rendering became the version most familiar in Christian tradition. Of uncertain date, it differs markedly in diction from the rival Old Greek text of the same story. Readers hunting intertexts will find in its sixty-four verses a locus for the motifs of false witness, judicial examination, and the vindication of the innocent, themes echoed in patristic exegesis, liturgy, and later retellings of the Susanna story.
grc.septuaginta.threni_seu_lamentationes: The Threni, or Lamentations, in the Septuagint is the Hellenistic Greek rendering of the biblical book of dirges over Jerusalem, set out in verses headed by the letters of the Hebrew alphabet and mourning the city left solitary like a widow, its ruined gates and sanctuary, and the exile of its people. The Greek translator is unnamed and the date of the version is unknown, though it belongs to the Hellenistic period; the wording follows Swete's Cambridge edition of 1905. As the canonical exemplar of civic and religious lament, it stands behind later Jewish and Christian laments over cities and catastrophes and supplies imagery and phrases repeatedly echoed in subsequent mourning poetry and liturgy.
grc.septuaginta.tobias: The Book of Tobit (Tobias) is preserved in Greek in the Septuagint and belongs to the Hellenistic Jewish biblical tradition, as printed in Swete's Cambridge Septuaginta of 1896. Composed in prose and cast as the first-person account of Tobit, a devout Israelite of the tribe of Naphtali deported to Nineveh, it interweaves his story of almsgiving, confiscation, and blindness with the journey of his son Tobias to Media, where under the angel Raphael's guidance he marries Sarah, drives off the demon Asmodeus, and returns with a fish-gall remedy that restores his father's sight. Its compact 243 lines combine folk-tale plotting, funerary piety, angelology, embedded prayers, and wisdom discourse in a providential family narrative. The book's phrasing and episodes recur throughout later Jewish and Christian writing, and its kinship with Greek adventure fiction makes it a frequent point of comparison for readers tracing intertexts.
grc.septuaginta.zacharias: The Zacharias printed in Swete's Cambridge Septuaginta (1905) is the Greek version of the prophetic book named for Zechariah son of Barachias, rendered anonymously into Greek in the Hellenistic period as part of the Jewish translation of Hebrew scripture. Its 211 lines carry the visions and oracles the book itself dates to the early years of Darius: night visions of horsemen among shaded mountains, four horns and four smiths, a measuring line stretched over Jerusalem, and the high priest Jesus (Joshua) cleansed before the angel of the Lord, alongside promises of Zion's rebuilding and the nations' resort to the Lord. Because its apocalyptic imagery of mounted riders, divine envoys, and restored Zion resounds through later Jewish and Christian writing, readers tracing intertexts will find the distinctive Greek phrasing of this version a recurring point of contact.
grc.sophocles.ajax: A Greek tragedy by Sophocles, transmitted here in Sir Richard Jebb's 1893 Cambridge edition, the Ajax follows the fall of the great hero after the award of Achilles' arms to Odysseus: his night assault on the Greek leaders becomes a slaughter of cattle, and his disgrace leads to suicide before the tents of the fleet. The opening exchange between Athena and Odysseus, who tracks the madman's trail to the hero's hut, introduces the play's governing themes of divinely sent delusion, shame, and the instability of human fortune, worked out through Tecmessa's supplication, Ajax's celebrated deception speech, and the dispute over his burial. For readers of intertexts it is a touchstone for the afterlife of the Ajax legend, the reworking of Homeric epic in Athenian drama, and a supply of sententiae that passed into proverbial use in Greek and Latin literature.
grc.sophocles.antigone: A Greek tragedy by Sophocles, printed in F. Storr's Loeb edition of 1912 and running to 1,256 lines of iambic dialogue interspersed with lyric choral song. The play opens with Antigone telling Ismene of Creon's recent edict that their brother Eteocles has been honourably buried while Polynices is to lie unburied on pain of death, and it goes on to dramatise her defiance of the decree and the clash between royal authority and the obligations owed to the dead. Because the Theban legend and the motif of forbidden burial were reworked throughout later Greek and Roman literature, the play serves as a key point of comparison for readers tracing intertexts in Euripides, Seneca, Statius, and subsequent receptions of the myth.
grc.sophocles.ichneutae: A satyr play attributed to Sophocles and of uncertain date, preserved on a papyrus from Oxyrhynchus (P. Oxy. 1174), edited by Arthur Hunt in 1912, and surviving in some 400 lines with extensive lacunae. The action treats the theft of Apollo's cattle by the infant Hermes: satyrs under Silenus, sent to hunt down the herd, proclaim a reward and follow the trail across the Greek mainland until it leads to the cave where Hermes contrives the lyre. Apart from Euripides' Cyclops it is the fullest surviving witness to satyric drama, and its version of the cattle-theft story invites comparison with the Homeric Hymn to Hermes for shared motifs, diction, and scenes of tracking, discovery, and the invention of music.
grc.sophocles.oedipus_at_colonus: The Oedipus at Colonus is a Greek tragedy by Sophocles, of uncertain date, dramatizing the final episode of the Oedipus legend: the blind hero, led by his daughter Antigone, reaches the sacred grove of the Eumenides at Colonus near Athens, where his long wanderings are to end. Its 1639 lines follow Oedipus through his reception by the Athenian king, his conflict with Creon and Polynices, and his enigmatic departure from life, while the choral songs include celebrated lyrics on Colonus itself and on the burdens of old age. For readers hunting intertexts, the play offers a late and distinctive shaping of the Theban saga, in dialogue with earlier treatments of the Oedipus story and rich in diction and motifs that later Greek and Roman writers could echo.
grc.sophocles.oedipus_tyrannus: A Greek tragedy by Sophocles, transmitted here in Sir Richard Jebb's annotated Cambridge edition of 1887. It opens with Thebes in the grip of pestilence, as suppliants gather at the altars and Oedipus, 'called glorious Oedipus by all', comes before the priest of Zeus; across its 1444 lines the king's inquiry into the murder of Laius turns upon his own parentage, ending in revelation and ruin. Its scenes of plague, investigation, and recognition have made it one of the most persistently echoed of Greek dramas and a rich source of parallels for later tragedy, poetry, and criticism.
grc.sophocles.philoctetes: Philoctetes, a Greek tragedy by Sophocles, is preserved here in the Loeb edition of 1913 with the English translation by F. Storr and runs to 1,369 lines. The action opens on the deserted shore of Lemnos, where Odysseus instructs the young Neoptolemus to win the confidence of Philoctetes, the hero marooned there with a festering wound, and so secure the bow of Heracles on which the fall of Troy depends. Much of the drama turns on Neoptolemus' conflict between expedient deceit and honest dealing, until Heracles himself appears to command a reconciliation. For readers tracing intertexts, the play is the canonical ancient staging of the Philoctetes legend, endlessly retold and contested by later dramatists and poets.
grc.sophocles.trachiniae: The Trachiniae is a Greek tragedy by Sophocles, preserved in some 1,226 lines of verse and presented here in Sir Richard Jebb's Cambridge edition of 1892. The prologue is spoken by Deianira, wife of Heracles, who recalls her wooing by the shape-shifting river-god Achelous, her rescue by Heracles in the contest for her hand, and the long anxiety of a marriage spent awaiting a husband perpetually absent on his labours. From this domestic opening the drama moves toward Heracles' homecoming to Trachis and the catastrophe wrought by the robe stained with Nessus' blood, a plot that centres the Heraclean myth unusually on the wife's perspective. Its pervasive allusion to the labours, loves, and mortal end of Heracles makes the play a natural point of comparison for intertexts across Greek epic, tragedy, and the mythographic tradition.
grc.soranus.de_signis_fracturarum: A short Greek surgical treatise attributed to Soranus, transmitted with his Gynaeciorum libri IV, De Fasciis and the Vita Hippocratis in Ilberg's Teubner edition of 1927. Its twenty-four sections give a systematic account of the signs of fractures, opening with a finely drawn taxonomy of cranial fractures (rhomge, enkope, kamarosis, engiesoma, empiesma and related forms) and then proceeding head to foot through nose, jaw, clavicle, scapula, spine, sternum, ribs, pelvis and the limbs, specifying for each site the deformity, palpable irregularity, grating sound and accompanying symptoms by which the injury is recognised. Its compact catalogue of fracture types and diagnostic vocabulary, much of it resting on ancient fracture lore shared with the Hippocratic surgical books, offers close verbal and doctrinal points of comparison for readers tracing parallels in ancient medical writing on fractures.
grc.soranus.gynaeciorum_libri_iv: The Gynaeciorum Libri IV is a four-book Greek treatise on women's medicine by the physician Soranus, preserved in the Teubner edition of Johannes Ilberg. It opens by dividing the art concerning women into an account of the midwife and of the conditions that come before her, and then offers a detailed portrait of the ideal midwife's intellect, character, and bodily aptitudes. Subsequent sections set out the anatomy of the uterus, vagina, and external genital organs before turning to menstruation — its onset, quantity, seasonal variation, and management — and to debates over lifelong virginity and the ages, signs, and times favorable to conception. Because Soranus repeatedly cites and rebuts earlier authorities such as Herophilus, Diocles, Mnesias, Themison, and Asclepiades, the work serves readers of intertexts as a dense hub of medical allusion and a valuable witness to the doctrines and vocabulary of earlier Greek medical writing.
grc.themistocles.epistulae: A collection of Greek letters attributed to Themistocles, the Athenian statesman of the Persian Wars, preserved in Rudolf Hercher's Epistolographi Graeci (1873). The letters, of uncertain date and pseudepigraphic, are composed in Themistocles' own voice and addressed to figures such as Pausanias, Aristides, Habronichus, Polynotus, and Admetus. They recount in epistolary form his ostracism, flight from Athens to Argos, Corcyra, and the Molossian court, his escape to the Persian king, and his warnings to Pausanias against Medism. Readers hunting intertexts will find a rhetorical, quasi-novelistic reworking of episodes canonical in the historiographical and biographical tradition concerning Themistocles and Pausanias.
grc.theocritus.epigrams: The Epigrams transmitted with the works of Theocritus form a compact collection of Greek verse, some 260 lines, preserved in the manuscripts and printed from Cholmeley's 1901 edition of the Idylls. Attributed to the Hellenistic bucolic poet, the pieces comprise dedications of rustic implements, epitaphs and verses honouring named poets, and love poetry, several of them of uncertain authorship. Readers hunting parallels will find compressed echoes of the Idylls' diction and of the wider Hellenistic epigram tradition, making the collection a rewarding site for intertextual comparison.
grc.theocritus.idylls: The Idylls of Theocritus, edited by R. J. Cholmeley (London, 1901), form the principal surviving collection of ancient Greek bucolic poetry, transmitted here in thirty poems written mainly in Doric hexameters. The collection opens with the goatherd's praise of Thyrsis and his song of the sorrows of Daphnis, and ranges across pastoral singing matches, descriptions of rustic cups and offerings, urban scenes, and mythological and epithalamic pieces. As the founding work of the pastoral genre, it supplied the stock situations and characters of bucolic verse — the amoebean song contest, the dying herdsman, Pan and the Nymphs — which later poets from Virgil onward reworked, making the collection a key source for tracing intertextual threads in the pastoral tradition.
grc.theophrastus.characters: The Characters, a Greek collection of brief ethical sketches attributed to Theophrastus and printed here in Hermann Diels' 1909 Oxford edition, takes up some three hundred lines defining distinct types of human disposition — the Ironical Man, the Flatterer, the Garrulous, the Boor and their fellows — each introduced by a general definition and illustrated with concrete behaviour. The opening preface, addressed to a certain Polycles by a speaker claiming ninety-nine years of observation, frames the sketches as memoranda by which the young may learn to choose the worthiest company. For readers hunting intertexts, the collection offers a compact catalogue of stock dispositions that answer to the flatterers, parasites and boors of comedy and satire, and it stands at the head of the European tradition of formal character-writing.
grc.tryphiodorus.the_taking_of_ilios: An epic poem of uncertain date, attributed to Tryphiodorus and printed with Colluthus and Oppian in A. W. Mair's 1928 Loeb edition. Its 691 hexameter lines recount the end of the ten years' war at Troy: the stratagem of the Wooden Horse, Laocoon's fate, the sack of the city, the deaths of Priam and Astyanax, the lot of the captive women, and the Greeks' departure for home. Taking up the story in the gap between the Iliad and the Odyssey, the poem reworks episodes and figures of the Trojan cycle — Achilles, Memnon, Rhesus, Penthesilea — in consciously Homeric diction, and accordingly offers dense material for verbal and thematic parallels across the epic tradition on the fall of Troy.
grc.zenobius_sophista.ἐπιτομὴ_ἐκ_τῶν_ταρραίο: An alphabetical collection of Greek proverbs transmitted under the name of Zenobius Sophista, epitomising the proverb compilations of Tarrhaeus and Didymus and printed by Leutsch and Schneidewin in the first volume of the Corpus paroemiographorum Graecorum (Göttingen, 1839). Each lemma receives a concise explanation of its meaning, often accompanied by an aetiological myth or historical anecdote, with citations of poets and scholars such as Eudoxus, Aristophanes, Cratinus, Callimachus, and Timaeus. The epitome, of uncertain date, preserves otherwise lost material from Greek comedy and early grammatical scholarship, and serves as a principal witness for proverbial phrasing and mythographic variants across ancient Greek literature.

it.dante.inferno: The first cantica of Dante's Commedia, thirty-four cantos in which the poet, lost in a dark wood in 1300, is led by Virgil down through the nine circles of Hell. Each circle punishes a class of sin by a penalty that mirrors it, and the damned tell their stories as the travellers descend to the frozen centre of the earth.
it.dante.purgatorio: The second cantica, thirty-three cantos on the mountain of Purgatory, where souls are cleansed of the seven capital vices on ascending terraces. Virgil guides Dante to the summit and the earthly paradise, where he departs and Beatrice takes his place.
it.dante.paradiso: The third cantica, thirty-three cantos ascending through the spheres of the heavens with Beatrice as guide, ending in the vision of God. Its subject matter is theology, light, and the limits of speech, and it repeatedly stages the poet's inability to report what he saw.

fro.chanson_de_roland: The oldest surviving French epic, about four thousand assonanced lines from the Oxford manuscript of the twelfth century. Roland, commanding Charlemagne's rearguard, is betrayed at Roncevaux and refuses to sound his horn for help until his men are lost, and the poem ends with Charlemagne's vengeance and the trial of the traitor Ganelon.

gmh.nibelungenlied: The Middle High German heroic epic of about 1200, in some 2,400 stanzas. Its first half tells of Siegfried's courtship of Kriemhild, his dragon-won invulnerability, and his murder by Hagen; its second half of Kriemhild's marriage to Etzel and the annihilation of the Burgundians at his court.

en.blake.songs_of_innocence: Songs of Innocence is a collection of short lyric poems by William Blake, some 393 lines in all, composed in simple ballad and hymn metres. The poems adopt the voices of children, nurses, shepherds and mothers, presenting childhood innocence through pastoral imagery of lambs, flocks and play, and the collection opens with an Introduction in which a piping poet is bidden by a laughing child to write down his happy songs. Recurrent figures of the Lamb and the watchful shepherd keep the diction close to Scriptural and hymnic language, while refrains and rhythms draw on nursery-rhyme and ballad traditions. The volume is habitually read beside its darker counterpart, Songs of Experience, whose poems answer several of these pieces motif for motif, making the pair a touchstone for studies of echoed and transformed phrasing.
en.bunyan.pilgrims_progress: Bunyan's Pilgrim's Progress is a prose allegory cast as a dream, in which the pilgrim Christian, laden with a burden of sin, flees the City of Destruction under the guidance of Evangelist and makes his way towards the Celestial City, meeting figures such as Obstinate and Pliable along the road. The narrative of some two thousand lines is steeped in scriptural diction and typology, and stands among the most widely read and imitated allegories in the English language. For readers of intertexts it offers a dense web of biblical allusion, emblematic personal names, and memorable places and images that later writers in English echo and rework persistently.
en.carroll.alice_in_wonderland: Alice in Wonderland is a Victorian prose fantasy by Lewis Carroll in which young Alice, chasing a waistcoat-pocketed White Rabbit, falls down a rabbit-hole into a subterranean world of shifting sizes, talking animals, and perverse logic. The narrative, running to 1630 lines divided across 12 book files, carries her from a pool of tears to a mad tea-party and on to the trial presided over by the Queen of Hearts. Its puns, literalised idioms, logical puzzles, and parodies of didactic and nursery verse have made the book a wellspring of phrases and motifs for later writers, and a natural point of comparison for readers tracing allusion and wordplay.
en.coleridge.rime_of_the_ancient_mariner: The Rime of the Ancient Mariner is a narrative poem in ballad measure by the Romantic poet Samuel Taylor Coleridge, running to 629 lines of archaic diction and insistent internal rhyme. It opens as an ancient mariner stops a wedding guest on his way to the feast and holds him with his glittering eye, compelling him to hear the tale of a sea voyage blighted by the killing of an albatross and beset by supernatural penalties of drought, a spectral crew, and long penance. For readers tracing intertexts it stands as a touchstone of Romantic supernatural verse, its images and phrases — the albatross about the neck, the ghostly ship, the mariner's glittering eye — passing into proverb and echoing throughout later poetry and prose.
en.cowper.task: Cowper's The Task is a long blank-verse poem of 5,184 lines arranged in six books, opening with a mock-heroic history of the sofa before turning, at a lady's command, to its humbler and broader theme. The proem recalls the author's earlier solemn songs of Truth, Hope, and Charity, undertaken with awe and a trembling hand, and marks a deliberate descent to quieter subjects. Across its books the poem moves from drawing-room, garden, and fireside to winter walks at evening, morning, and noon, mingling domestic description with moral, political, and devotional reflection. Its conversational blank verse, dense allusive texture, and exact observation of everyday life make it a rewarding source for readers tracing echoes and parallels in later English poetry.
en.edgar_allan_poe.the_raven: Edgar Allan Poe's 'The Raven' is a narrative poem of 108 lines in which a mourner grieving for the lost Lenore is visited at midnight by a stately raven whose unvarying answer drives him toward despair. Its insistent trochaic stanzas and recurring refrains ('nothing more', 'evermore', 'Nevermore'), together with its veneer of learned and classical allusion, have made it among the most quoted, imitated, and parodied poems in English. Readers hunting intertexts will find its refrain words and phrasings echoed throughout later poetry and prose, while its own allusive fabric—forgotten lore, classical antiquity, and promises of consolation—ties it to the elegiac tradition it at once inhabits and burlesques.
en.keats.eve_of_st_agnes: The Eve of St Agnes is a narrative poem in Spenserian stanzas by the English Romantic poet John Keats of the early nineteenth century, founded on the folk belief that a maiden who keeps the vigil of St Agnes with due rites may dream of her future husband. Set on a bitterly cold night in a feudal castle, the poem opens with the aged Beadsman at his devotions and passes from his chilly penance to the baronial revelry within, where the young lovers Madeline and Porphyro plot their flight from a feuding household. Its medieval setting, its deliberate echo of Spenserian form, and its dense sensuous imagery of heat and cold make it a natural point of comparison for readers tracing Keats's debts to Spenser, Shakespeare, and medieval romance.
en.keats.fancy: Fancy is a lyric of 94 lines by John Keats, written in quick rhymed couplets. It opens with the injunction 'Ever let the Fancy roam' and the claim that 'Pleasure never is at home', urging a listener seated at a winter fireside to release Fancy from the 'mind's cage-door' so that she may summon the lost beauties of spring, summer and autumn and mix their delights 'like three fit wines in a cup'. Its personified Fancy and Pleasure, its catalogue of seasonal imagery, and its fireside setting make it a compact Romantic statement on imagination as a power that redeems transience. For readers of intertexts, it offers rich ground for parallels with lyrics and odes on Fancy, the seasons, and the mind's escape from present circumstance.
en.keats.hyperion: An unfinished blank-verse epic by John Keats, Hyperion takes as its subject the overthrow of the Titans by the Olympian gods, opening on the deposed Saturn sunk in silent grief within a landscape that shares his fallen divinity. Its 885 lines unfold in heavily Miltonic blank verse thick with classical allusion, invoking figures such as Achilles, Ixion and the Memphian sphinx as it recasts Greek myth in Romantic terms of suffering, beauty and the passing of an older divine order. For readers hunting textual parallels, the poem offers a principal Romantic reworking of epic tradition, its phrasing repeatedly reshaping Milton and classical poetry, and its abrupt break-off marks it as one of the characteristic fragments of Romantic epic.
en.keats.isabella: Isabella is an early nineteenth-century narrative poem by the English Romantic poet John Keats, composed in ottava rima and running to 504 lines. It retells the Boccaccian story of Isabella and Lorenzo, whose secret love is cut short when Isabella's merchant brothers murder Lorenzo, after which the grieving Isabella exhumes his head and nurtures it in a pot of basil. The poem adapts the tale of Lisabetta and the basil pot from Boccaccio's Decameron, and its Romantic elaboration of that Italian source, together with its later afterlife in Victorian painting and poetry, makes it a productive site for tracing cross-period intertexts.
en.keats.lamia: A narrative poem by John Keats in rhymed couplets, Lamia opens with a mythological frame in which Hermes steals from Olympus to Crete in pursuit of a hidden nymph and is answered by a mournful voice rising from a 'wreathed tomb', the coiled body of a serpent who alone knows her retreat. The poem recounts how the serpent, restored to the form of the beautiful Lamia, wins the love of the young Lycius, until the cold gaze of the sage Apollonius destroys her illusory existence. Its reworking of the ancient lamia legend, blending classical myth, fairy-lore, and a sceptical probing of illusion against reason, makes it a natural hunting ground for readers tracing the serpent-woman and beautiful-deceiver motifs and Keats's richly allusive style through Romantic and later writing.
en.keats.lines_on_the_mermaid_tavern: A short lyric of twenty-six lines by Keats, addressed to the 'Souls of Poets dead and gone' and asking whether any Elysium can rival the Mermaid Tavern with its Canary wine, venison pies, and generous fellowship. The poem spins a fanciful tale in which the tavern's sign-board flies skyward and an astrologer beholds the poets 'pledging with contented smack / The Mermaid in the Zodiac', before closing with a refrain that repeats the opening question. Its playful evocation of the tavern celebrated in legend as a haunt of Elizabethan poets, together with its Robin Hood allusions, makes the piece a rewarding point of contact for readers tracing Keats's engagement with older English poetic traditions.
en.keats.ode_on_a_grecian_urn: A fifty-line ode by John Keats, addressed to a Grecian urn and to the figures carved upon it: piping musicians, a bold lover forever short of his kiss, boughs that never shed their leaves, and a mysterious priest leading a garlanded heifer to sacrifice. The poem sets the fixity and permanence of art against the transience of human passion, closing on the celebrated pronouncement that beauty is truth and truth beauty. Its phrasing, above all the final lines, has passed into common quotation, and the poem stands among the most persistently echoed lyrics in English, making it a recurrent point of reference for tracing allusion and intertext.
en.keats.ode_on_melancholy: Ode on Melancholy is a lyric of thirty lines by Keats, opening in a burst of prohibition against Lethe, wolf's-bane, nightshade, yew-berries, and other vehicles of oblivion and mournful contemplation. Against numbing escape, the poem urges that melancholy be savoured where it is most intense, dwelling with Beauty that must die and with Joy forever on the point of farewell, until Veil'd Melancholy is found enthroned in the very temple of Delight. Its dense cluster of classical allusions, together with its claim that the deepest perception of pleasure is inseparable from sadness, makes the ode a natural touchstone for readers tracing Keatsian sentiment and Greco-Roman echoes in later poetry.
en.keats.ode_to_a_nightingale: An eighty-line lyric ode by the Romantic poet Keats, in which the speaker, transported by a nightingale's song, weighs fantasies of escape through wine and through 'the viewless wings of Poesy' before confronting the weariness, mortality, and transience of beauty and love from which the bird's song offers no lasting release. The poem is densely allusive, invoking Lethe, the Dryad, Hippocrene, and Bacchus, and it closes by dissolving the boundary between vision and waking in its famous final question. For readers of intertexts it functions as a meeting point of the nightingale tradition inherited from classical and biblical song, and its phrases ('tender is the night', 'faery lands forlorn') have become touchstones echoed widely in later poetry and prose.
en.keats.robin_hood: Robin Hood is a lyric of sixty-two lines in rhyming couplets by John Keats, lamenting that the age of the Sherwood outlaws has passed away, with its bugle, bow, morris dancing, Little John, and Maid Marian now beyond recall. Its diction leans heavily on the medieval outlaw tradition, naming the 'song of Gamelyn' and echoing the ballad phrase 'grenè shawe' familiar from the Robin Hood gests. For readers tracing intertexts, the poem offers a Romantic reworking of late medieval ballad language and a compact witness to how the outlaw legend was carried into early nineteenth-century verse.
en.milton.comus: A masque by Milton, running to 1,053 lines of blank verse, it opens with the prologue of the Attendant Spirit, who descends from the court of Jove to watch over the children of a noble Peer as they pass through a perilous, enchanted wood. The drama centres on their encounter with Comus, the sorcerer of the title, and on the reward that virtue wins after 'this mortal change' for its true servants. Dense with classical mythology — Neptune's allotment of the sea-girt isles, ambrosial weeds, the golden key that opens the palace of eternity — and steeped in the diction of the English masque tradition, the work offers rich material for readers tracing Miltonic echoes and the interplay of classical and Christian themes.
en.milton.il_penseroso: A lyric of 176 lines in rhymed octosyllabic couplets by John Milton, 'Il Penseroso' opens by banishing 'vain deluding joyes' and hails 'divinest Melancholy' as a goddess of saintly visage, tracing her mythic descent from Vesta and Saturn. The poem unfolds the pleasures of the contemplative, studious and solitary life, its verse densely threaded with classical allusion — Morpheus, Memnon's sister, woody Ida and Jove among the figures of its opening movement. It forms the deliberate counterpart to Milton's companion piece 'L'Allegro', the two poems pairing Melancholy with Mirth in a matched structure much imitated by later poets. Readers hunting parallels will find in it a touchstone of the English tradition of praise-melancholy and a rich matrix of mythological echo and personification.
en.milton.l_allegro: L'Allegro is a lyric of 152 lines by John Milton, an exuberant invocation that banishes gloomy Melancholy and summons the goddess Mirth, Euphrosyne, in an opening passage dense with classical figures such as Cerberus, Styx, Venus, Bacchus, Zephyr, Aurora, and Hebe. In swift octosyllabic verse the poem sketches a day of dance, music, rural labour, and pastoral ease, closing with the speaker's resolve to live with Mirth. Conventionally paired with its companion piece on melancholy, Il Penseroso, it stands at the centre of the English mirth-and-melancholy tradition, and its layered classical and archaic echoes make it a productive point of comparison for readers tracing allusive parallels.
en.milton.lycidas: John Milton's Lycidas is a pastoral elegy of 193 lines in rhymed stanzas of roughly ten lines, lamenting Lycidas, a young shepherd-poet dead before his prime and imagined as lost at sea, floating 'unwept' upon his 'watry bear'. The speaker recalls the hillside pastures the two shared and calls upon the Muses, 'Sisters of the sacred well', to sweep the string, while the bucolic frame is peopled with satyrs, fauns, and the singer Damoetas. Working squarely within the classical pastoral tradition of the oaten flute and the monodic lament, the poem became a touchstone for elegiac writing in English, and its dense reworking of bucolic topoi makes it a rich hunting ground for intertextual parallels.
en.milton.paradise_lost: Paradise Lost is Milton's epic in blank verse, running to some 10,500 lines and divided into twelve books, which retells the biblical fall of humanity from the rebellion of Satan and his angels, through the war in heaven and the creation of the world, to the temptation and expulsion of Adam and Eve. Its opening invocation announces the design of justifying the ways of God to men, and the poem fuses Genesis with the conventions of classical epic — invocation, extended simile, and grand catalogue — while aiming at a scale 'unattempted yet in Prose or Rhime'. For readers of intertexts it is a central hub: it reworks Scripture, Homer, and Virgil, and its scenes, phrases, and characters echo throughout subsequent English poetry and prose.
en.milton.paradise_regained: Paradise Regained is a short epic in blank verse by Milton, arranged in four books and running to 2,070 lines, which retells the temptation of Christ in the wilderness as the act of obedience that reverses Adam's fall. Its opening invocation expressly frames the poem as a sequel to the 'happy Garden' of Paradise Lost, adapting Virgilian and Homeric epic conventions to deeds 'above heroic, though in secret done.' Much of the action consists of debate between Jesus and Satan rather than martial combat, drawing on the Gospel accounts of the temptation alongside classical epic machinery such as the adversary's aerial council. For readers of intertexts, the poem offers a dense network of biblical, classical, and self-referential allusion, inviting sustained comparison with Milton's earlier epic diction and argument.
en.milton.sonnets: A short collection of sonnets by John Milton, running to 128 lines and written in English and Italian. It opens with a nightingale sonnet that entwines bird lore, classical allusion and the twin claims of Love and the Muse, and then continues with Italian pieces in the Petrarchan manner, praising a beloved lady and playing on the poet's displacement from 'the fair Thames' to 'the fair Arno'. The bilingual imitation of Petrarchan diction and the dense classical and amorous allusions make the poems a productive source of parallels for readers tracing Milton's engagement with Italian and ancient verse traditions.
en.shakespeare.a_midsummer_night’s_dream: A Midsummer Night's Dream is a comedy by William Shakespeare, presented here in W. G. Clark's Globe Shakespeare edition. Opening in Athens with Theseus and Hippolyta awaiting their nuptials, the action interweaves the flight of Hermia and Lysander into the wood, the love-juice confusions among the four young Athenians, the quarrel of Oberon and Titania with the sprite Puck's mischief, and the tradesmen's rehearsal of Pyramus and Thisbe for performance before the duke. Its dense patterning of classical allusion, Ovidian metamorphosis, moonlight and dream makes the play a particularly fertile ground for readers tracing motifs and parallels. The work runs to 2,165 lines in the source record.
en.shakespeare.hamlet: An English tragedy by Shakespeare, Hamlet opens on the battlements of Elsinore, where sentinels and Horatio await the ghost whose revelation sets the prince's revenge in motion. Running to 4,058 lines in the Globe edition, the play weaves together revenge-drama conventions, feigned madness, a play-within-the-play, and the mortal reckoning that overtakes the Danish court. Its soliloquies — 'To be, or not to be' above all — and its controlling images of corruption, acting, and death have made it one of the most quoted works in English and a standing source of allusion for readers tracing the haunted watch, the reluctant avenger, and the world-as-stage trope.
en.shakespeare.richard_iii: Richard III is a history play by William Shakespeare, printed here in the Globe edition prepared by W. G. Clark, running to some 3,745 lines of blank verse and prose. It dramatizes the ruthless ascent of Richard, Duke of Gloucester, from the celebrated opening soliloquy, 'Now is the winter of our discontent,' through his plotting against his brothers and seizure of the English crown to his defeat and death at Bosworth. The villain's frank confession of his own deformity and ambition, his seduction of the audience as co-conspirator, and the play's mining of English chronicle material have made its speeches an unusually rich quarry of phrases and character types echoed throughout later literature.
en.shakespeare.sonnets: Shakespeare's Sonnets form a sequence of fourteen-line lyric poems, running to 2,464 lines in the corpus, addressed chiefly to a beloved young man and meditating on beauty, procreation, time, and mortality. The opening group urges the addressee to marry and beget an heir lest beauty perish with him, warning against the self-regarding waste of hoarding one's gifts. Composed in iambic pentameter on an alternating rhyme scheme closed by a couplet, the poems supplied later English verse with a stock of phrasings and figures - beauty's rose, the tender heir, the devouring assaults of Time - that are echoed and reworked constantly, making the sequence a prime hunting ground for parallel passages.
en.spenser.faerie_queene: The Faerie Queene, Edmund Spenser's allegorical epic romance of the Elizabethan age, runs to 37,630 lines and is divided here into six files, one for each of the poem's completed books. The opening stanzas introduce a gentle knight clad in mighty arms and bearing the bloody cross of his dying Lord, who rides beside a mourning lady leading a milk-white lamb on a quest assigned by Gloriana, queen of Faerie land, against a horrible dragon. Each book follows such a knight in Gloriana's service, turning chivalric adventure into a sustained moral, religious, and political allegory. Composed in a distinctive nine-line stanza and a deliberately archaic diction, and dense with echoes of classical epic, medieval romance, and scriptural typology, the poem rewards readers hunting parallels with earlier epic and romance traditions.
en.swift.gullivers_travels: Jonathan Swift's Gulliver's Travels is an early eighteenth-century prose satire cast as the factual account of the ship's surgeon Lemuel Gulliver, framed by a publisher's preface signed Richard Sympson and by Gulliver's letter to his cousin Sympson dated 1727. The work divides into four parts, matching the four files here, recounting voyages to Lilliput, Brobdingnag, Laputa, and the land of the rational Houyhnhnms and brutish Yahoos, and it parodies the conventions of travel writing while satirising politics, projectors and learned science, and human pride. Its invented peoples and coinages, from Lilliputian to Yahoo, quickly entered common usage, and echoes of Gulliver's voyages pervade later prose, verse, and polemic, making the work a recurrent source for writers hunting allusions and borrowings.
en.wordsworth.prelude: Wordsworth's The Prelude, preserved here in its fourteen-book form, is an autobiographical epic in blank verse running to 7,925 lines. It opens with the poet's escape from the city and his blessing on the breeze that greets him, and proceeds to chart the growth of his mind through childhood, education, travel, and communion with nature. Its blank verse is steeped in Milton, while its meditations on memory, imagination, and the natural world have been echoed and quarried by later poets, making the poem a rich source of verbal and thematic parallels.
en.world_english_bible.new_testament: The New Testament in the King James translation, preserved as twenty-six book files totaling 7,548 lines of early modern English prose. The work opens with Matthew's genealogy and nativity narrative and spans the four Gospels, Acts, the epistles, and Revelation, with marginal glosses and variant readings marked in braces. Its phrasing stands among the most heavily quarried sources in English literature, and verbal echoes of its chapters and verses recur throughout later poetry, fiction, sermons, and prose, making it a central touchstone for the study of biblical intertexts.
en.world_english_bible.pentateuch: The Pentateuch as presented here comprises the first five books of the Hebrew Bible—Genesis, Exodus, Leviticus, Numbers, and Deuteronomy—in the English rendering known as the King James Version, divided into five book files and running to some 5,850 lines. The narrative opens with the six days of creation and the garden of Eden, then proceeds through the generations of the patriarchs, the deliverance from Egypt, the covenant and law-giving at Sinai, and the wilderness journeyings, closing with the farewell discourses of Deuteronomy. For readers of intertexts, few sources repay attention more, since the diction and cadences of these books—'the Spirit of God moved upon the face of the waters' among them—have echoed through English-language literature in countless later works.
en.world_english_bible.revelation: The Book of Revelation, given here in the King James Version, is the final book of the New Testament, an apocalyptic prophecy framed as the visions received by John on the isle of Patmos and sent to seven churches in Asia. It opens with letters dictated to the churches of Ephesus, Smyrna, Pergamos, Thyatira, Sardis, Philadelphia, and Laodicea, and proceeds through visions of the heavenly throne, the opening of the seals, the beasts and Babylon, the last judgment, and the descent of the New Jerusalem. Its date of composition is uncertain, and the visionary names himself only as John. For readers tracing textual parallels, it is a persistent wellspring of imagery and phrasing — Alpha and Omega, the book with seven seals, the number of the beast — reused across later English and European writing.
